Punch: A hardened steel pin punch for driving out roll pins, starting holes, or breaching thin materials.

❓Why It's Needed

Extrication, rescue, and utility work require hand tools that hydraulic rescue tools can't do — precise work, small adjustments, and field repairs. This box covers scenarios from vehicle rescue to machinery entrapment to scene support.

⚠ VOLTAGE TESTER — CRITICAL AWARENESS
The document flags the voltage tester with multiple asterisks because it's easy to forget and catastrophic to need. Before touching any wire, panel, or component that could be energized — use the tester. Electricity on a fire or crash scene kills responders every year.
↑ Back to top
6

Compartment 6 — Water Rescue & Air Bottles

Officer's Side · Mustang Suit, Rope Throw, Carabiners, Air Bottles
Mustang Suit
AKA: Mustang suit, immersion suit, survival suit, dry suit (though a true dry suit is different), floatation suit.
+
📖What It Is

A marine-grade immersion suit (survival suit) that provides both thermal protection and buoyancy to a person in cold water. "Mustang" is a major manufacturer of marine immersion suits — the name has become genericized in many fire departments. These bright orange or red suits provide hypothermia protection for extended periods in cold water and keep the wearer afloat without effort.

🔧How to Use It
  1. Sit down if possible while donning — these suits are bulky.
  2. Step both feet into the legs and pull the suit up over your turnout gear or uniform.
  3. Slide both arms in and zip the front closure fully.
  4. Secure the hood, wrist closures, and any remaining fasteners.
  5. The built-in buoyancy will keep you face-up in water even if unconscious.
❓Why It's Needed

Cold water kills through hypothermia and incapacitation within minutes. A firefighter who enters or falls into cold water without thermal protection loses fine motor control within 3–5 minutes and can lose consciousness within 30 minutes. The Mustang suit extends survival time dramatically for rescuers operating in or near cold water.

🏷️Also Known As

Mustang suit, immersion suit, survival suit, dry suit (though a true dry suit is different), floatation suit.

⚠ CRITICAL SAFETY
The Mustang suit provides buoyancy but is not a substitute for training. If you are not trained in water rescue, do not enter the water — even suited up. Know the "Reach, Throw, Row, Go" priority order. Your suit keeps you alive if you go in accidentally; it doesn't make you a trained rescue swimmer.
Rope Throw Bag
AKA: Throw bag, rescue throw bag, rope bag, toss bag, Z-Rig bag (when configured for mechanical advantage).
+
📖What It Is

A bag pre-packed with a floating throw rope (typically 50–75 feet of ¼" polypropylene rope that floats). You throw the bag — not just the rope — to a victim in the water. The bag acts as a projectile and the rope pays out freely from the bag as it flies through the air.

🔧How to Use It
  1. Open the bag top and confirm the rope is loaded and the free end is in your hand.
  2. Stand upstream of the victim in moving water.
  3. Swing the bag underhand and release — aim to land the bag just past the victim so the rope crosses them.
  4. Shout "ROPE!" as you throw — victim should grab the rope, not the bag.
  5. Brace yourself and let the victim pendulum to shore on the rope.
  6. To repack: stuff the rope back in the bag loosely — do not coil it, or it will tangle on the next throw.
❓Why It's Needed

Fastest water rescue tool available for a shore-based rescuer. A throw bag can reach a victim 50–70 feet away in 2 seconds. Compare that to any other option and the value is obvious.

🏷️Also Known As

Throw bag, rescue throw bag, rope bag, toss bag, Z-Rig bag (when configured for mechanical advantage).

Water Helmet
AKA: Water rescue helmet, swift water helmet, rescue helmet.
+
📖What It Is

A water rescue helmet — designed with ventilation, a low profile, and secure fastening for water entry and current navigation. Unlike a structural firefighting helmet, a water rescue helmet won't trap water and drag you under, and is designed to stay on in current.

❓Why It's Needed

Head protection during water rescue operations. Swift water currents drive rescuers into rocks, debris, bridge supports, and other structures. A water rescue helmet is the appropriate PPE for this environment — your structural helmet is not.

🏷️Also Known As

Water rescue helmet, swift water helmet, rescue helmet.

Life Safety Ring + Strap with 3 Carabiners
AKA: Life ring, life safety ring, rescue ring, cinch ring; the carabiner strap: rescue webbing, haul strap, rescue anchor.
+
📋What They Are

Life Safety Ring: A rigid ring that fits around a victim's torso, keeping them at the surface and providing a grip point for rescuers.

Strap with 3 Carabiners: A rescue webbing strap with carabiner connectors for attaching the victim to a rescue system, or for building a simple mechanical advantage haul system or belayed water rescue.

📋Why They're Needed

Victim management in water rescue requires secure attachment. A panicked drowning victim will try to climb on top of a rescuer, potentially drowning both. The life ring keeps victim and rescuer at a managed distance. The carabiner strap connects victims to the rescue system for haul-out.

🏷️Also Known As

Life ring, life safety ring, rescue ring, cinch ring; the carabiner strap: rescue webbing, haul strap, rescue anchor.

×4 — Under Compartment 6 Air Bottles
AKA: Spare bottles, air cylinders, SCBA cylinders, spare air.
+
📋What They Are

Four additional SCBA cylinders stored under Compartment 6. These supplement the 3 bottles stored outside Compartment 2 for a total of 7 spare bottles on the apparatus. Same as the bottles at Comp 2 — check pressure, check valve open status, every day.

❓Why It's Needed

Sustained interior operations at a working fire, multiple victim rescues, and prolonged searches all consume air. Seven spare bottles give the crew the ability to sustain air-intensive operations without waiting for re-supply.

🏷️Also Known As

Spare bottles, air cylinders, SCBA cylinders, spare air.

↑ Back to top
7

Compartment 7 — Fire Extinguishers & Spill Control

Officer's Side · All four extinguisher types + EV fire blanket
💡 THE FOUR CLASSES OF FIRE — REVIEW
Class A = Ordinary combustibles (wood, paper, fabric). Class B = Flammable liquids/gases. Class C = Electrical equipment (energized). Class D = Combustible metals. Class K = Cooking oils/fats. Know which extinguisher matches which class.
Silver Bullet — Pressurized Water Extinguisher
AKA: Silver bullet, water can, pressurized water, 2½-gallon water can.
+
📖What It Is

A pressurized stainless steel cylinder (the "silver bullet" — named for its appearance) containing plain water under air pressure. Effective only on Class A fires (ordinary combustibles — wood, paper, fabric). No surfactant, no foam — just water.

🔧How to Use It

Pull the pin, aim the nozzle at the base of the fire, squeeze the handle, and sweep side-to-side. Capacity is approximately 2.5 gallons — enough for a small Class A fire. Not a substitute for a hose line.

❓Why It's Needed

Small smoldering fires (trash can, weed fire at the base of a building) can be hit with the silver bullet without deploying a full hose line. Fast, clean, no secondary contamination, no residue.

🏷️Also Known As

Silver bullet, water can, pressurized water, 2½-gallon water can.

⚠ CRITICAL SAFETY
Never use a water extinguisher on electrical fires (Class C) or flammable liquid fires (Class B). Water conducts electricity and will spread burning liquid fires. Know your agent and know your fire class.
ABC Dry Chemical Extinguisher
AKA: ABC extinguisher, dry chem, dry chemical, monoammonium phosphate, the purple K (different dry chem specifically for Class B).
+
📖What It Is

A pressurized cylinder containing monoammonium phosphate (dry chemical powder). The "ABC" rating means it's effective on Class A (combustibles), Class B (flammable liquids), and Class C (energized electrical) fires. It suppresses fire by interrupting the chemical chain reaction.

🔧How to Use It

PASS: Pull the pin, Aim at the base of the fire, Squeeze the handle, Sweep from side to side. Use in short bursts, starting from the near edge of the fire and sweeping through. Stay low, stay upwind.

❓Why It's Needed

Versatility. One extinguisher handles three classes. Ideal for vehicle fires, fuel-related fires, and any environment with multiple potential fire types. The most common extinguisher type you'll encounter.

🏷️Also Known As

ABC extinguisher, dry chem, dry chemical, monoammonium phosphate, the purple K (different dry chem specifically for Class B).

🔰 ROOKIE MISTAKE
Emptying the whole extinguisher in one shot and running out before the fire's knocked down. Use short controlled bursts. Dry chemical depletes fast and you can't reload on scene.
CO₂ Extinguisher
AKA: CO₂ extinguisher, carbon dioxide extinguisher, the CO₂.
+
📖What It Is

A high-pressure cylinder of liquid carbon dioxide that converts to gas when discharged, smothering the fire by displacing oxygen and cooling the fuel. Effective on Class B (flammable liquids) and Class C (electrical) fires. Leaves no residue — critical for protecting sensitive electrical equipment and electronics.

🔧How to Use It

PASS: Pull, Aim (hold the horn/nozzle — it will get extremely cold), Squeeze, Sweep. Keep distance — CO₂ discharges at -109°F and the horn can cause frostbite. Do not use in small enclosed spaces without ventilation — CO₂ depletes oxygen and can incapacitate rescuers.

❓Why It's Needed

Electrical panel fires, server rooms, electrical equipment fires. CO₂ leaves no residue and won't damage equipment the way dry chemical will. For any fire in or near sensitive electronics, CO₂ is the preferred agent.

🏷️Also Known As

CO₂ extinguisher, carbon dioxide extinguisher, the CO₂.

⚠ CRITICAL SAFETY — FROSTBITE RISK
The discharge horn on a CO₂ extinguisher reaches -109°F. Never grab the horn bare-handed. Wear gloves. The cold gas discharge also looks alarming — fire is still present even as you're applying CO₂. Don't stop before the fire is confirmed out.
Class K Extinguisher
AKA: Class K, wet chemical, kitchen extinguisher, Ansul R-102 (common commercial suppression system brand).
+
📖What It Is

A wet chemical extinguisher specifically designed for cooking oil and fat fires (Class K). Contains potassium acetate, potassium citrate, or potassium carbonate solutions that react with the cooking oil to form a soapy foam (saponification), effectively smothering the fire and preventing re-ignition.

🔧How to Use It

Apply gently and from a distance — do not spray directly onto burning oil at close range, which can cause splashing and spread the fire. Move the nozzle side-to-side in a sweeping motion across the oil surface. Allow the foam blanket to form and smother.

❓Why It's Needed

Commercial kitchen fires are common and extremely dangerous. A deep fryer or commercial range fire at full temperature (400°F+) will re-ignite if you don't permanently lower the temperature of the oil below its auto-ignition point. Class K agents are specifically formulated to achieve this where ABC dry chemical or CO₂ fail to prevent re-ignition.

🏷️Also Known As

Class K, wet chemical, kitchen extinguisher, Ansul R-102 (common commercial suppression system brand).

Oil Dry
AKA: Oil dry, kitty litter, absorbent granules, floor dry, Oil-Dri (brand name), absorbent, Speedy Dry.
+
📖What It Is

A clay-based granular absorbent — used to soak up small petroleum product spills (fuel, oil, hydraulic fluid) on roadways or incident scenes. Sold under various brand names including Oil-Dri and Speedy Dry; in the firehouse it's most commonly called "oil dry," though some old-timers still call it "kitty litter."

🔧How to Use It

Spread the granules over the spill, allow it to absorb the liquid (a few minutes), then sweep or shovel the saturated material into a bag or container for disposal. Temporary traction for slick roadway patches can also be created with dry application.

❓Why It's Needed

Vehicle accident scenes routinely produce fuel and fluid spills that create both fire risk and traffic hazard. Oil dry is the field-expedient solution for small spills without waiting for a hazmat team.

🏷️Also Known As

Oil dry, kitty litter, absorbent granules, floor dry, Oil-Dri (brand name), absorbent, Speedy Dry.

Fire Blanket — For Electric Vehicles
AKA: EV fire blanket, electric vehicle blanket, battery fire blanket, thermal containment blanket.
+
📖What It Is

A large, fire-resistant or fire-suppressing blanket specifically designed to be draped over a burning electric vehicle (EV). EV lithium-ion battery fires undergo "thermal runaway" — a self-sustaining chemical reaction that generates its own oxygen and cannot be extinguished with conventional water or dry chemical suppression. The blanket works by containing the heat and limiting oxygen to slow/halt the reaction, and by containing the fire to prevent spread to surrounding vehicles or structures.

🔧How to Use It
  1. Ensure no occupants remain in the vehicle (or perform extraction before blanketing).
  2. Unfold the blanket and approach from upwind.
  3. Drape the blanket completely over the burning EV, covering as much surface as possible.
  4. Continue to monitor — EV thermal runaway can reignite or break through containment.
  5. Large volumes of cooling water into the battery compartment remain the primary suppression method; the blanket is a containment/spread-control tool.
❓Why It's Needed

EV fires are an emerging and growing challenge for the fire service. Lithium-ion battery thermal runaway can require 3,000+ gallons of water to suppress, can take hours to extinguish, and can reignite hours or days later. The blanket is a practical, field-deployable tool to contain the hazard and prevent fire spread while managing the incident.

🏷️Also Known As

EV fire blanket, electric vehicle blanket, battery fire blanket, thermal containment blanket.

⚠ CRITICAL SAFETY — EV FIRES
Do not assume an EV fire is out just because flames are no longer visible. Thermal runaway can continue internally and reignite violently hours later. EV incidents require extended monitoring and documentation. Your turnout gear does NOT protect against the toxic gases (hydrogen fluoride, etc.) released in lithium-ion battery fires — stay upwind and in SCBA whenever working near burning EVs.
▶ WATCH IT IN ACTION

Above the Compartments — Ladders & Pike Poles

Officer's Side Exterior · Extension Ladder 24 ft, Roof Ladder 14 ft, Pike Poles 6 & 8 ft
24 ft Extension Ladder + Roof Ladder
AKA: Extension ladder, ext ladder, 24-footer; roof ladder, hook ladder, 14-footer.
+
📋What They Are

Extension Ladder (24 ft): A two-section aluminum extension ladder. At 24 feet of working length, it reaches second and some third-story windows — your primary egress/rescue ladder for residential structures.

Roof Ladder (14 ft): A 14-foot single-section ladder with hinged hooks at the top. The hooks are deployed at the ridge of a pitched roof so the ladder lays flat against the roof surface and stays put while a firefighter walks the rungs to work on the roof.

🔧How to Use Them
  1. Carry to the target, heel the butt of the ladder against the wall base.
  2. Set ladder angle at approximately 75 degrees (1 foot out for every 4 feet of height — the "1-in-4" rule).
  3. For rescue ladders: tip should extend 2–3 rungs above the window sill.
  4. For roof access: tip should extend 3–5 rungs above the roofline.
  5. Confirm the ladder is seated on solid ground — not on a soft surface, slope, or ice.
  6. Never stand on the top two rungs of any ladder.
📋Why They're Needed

Victim rescue from upper floors, secondary egress for trapped crews, roof access for ventilation, and any operation above the first floor where ground or apparatus access isn't available. Ground ladders save lives — know how to throw them fast and correctly.

🏷️Also Known As

Extension ladder, ext ladder, 24-footer; roof ladder, hook ladder, 14-footer.

⚠ CRITICAL SAFETY — LADDER PLACEMENT FOR RESCUE
When placing a ladder for victim rescue at a window, always place the tip of the ladder to the side of the window opening, not in front of it. A victim jumping before you reach the window will hit the ladder. Place the ladder with the tip beside the window frame — much safer for both of you.
▶ WATCH IT IN ACTION
YouTube: "fire service ground ladder throw and raise"
×2 — 6 ft & 8 ft (Above Compartments) Pike Poles
AKA: Pike pole, hook, ceiling hook, plaster hook, overhaul hook, pull hook, 6-footer, 8-footer.
+
📋What They Are

Long-handled tools with a sharpened steel point and hook at the top. Used for pulling, pushing, and probing materials at distance — specifically: pulling down burning ceiling materials, probing for fire in walls, moving burning debris, and clearing overhaul areas. The 6-foot and 8-foot lengths (plus the 4-6 ft closet pike in Comp 2) give you options for any ceiling height.

🔧How to Use Them

Use the point to punch into ceiling surfaces; use the hook to pull materials down and away. Work in a systematic pattern during overhaul — open the ceiling to reveal the full extent of fire travel above the ceiling plane. Keep your face mask on — opened ceiling cavities often contain superheated smoke and gas that release suddenly.

📋Why They're Needed

Overhaul and ventilation. You cannot see fire in a wall or ceiling until you open it. Pike poles let you do this efficiently from floor level without climbing or risk of contact with falling material.

🏷️Also Known As

Pike pole, hook, ceiling hook, plaster hook, overhaul hook, pull hook, 6-footer, 8-footer.

↑ Back to top
C

Inside the Cab

EMS Bags, Gas Meters, AED, Radios, Accountability, ERG
TOP SHELF
4-Gas CO Meter (O₂, CO, H₂S, Combustible Gas)
AKA: 4-gas meter, multi-gas meter, CGI (combustible gas indicator), MSA (brand name), RAE meter, atmospheric tester, gas monitor.
+
📖What It Is

A four-sensor electronic atmospheric monitor that simultaneously detects and measures: Oxygen (O₂) level, Carbon Monoxide (CO), Hydrogen Sulfide (H₂S), and combustible/flammable gas (typically measured as LEL — Lower Explosive Limit percentage). This is your primary atmospheric testing tool before and during entry into potentially hazardous atmospheres.

🔧How to Use It
  1. Turn on and allow to calibrate in fresh air — do not start in a contaminated atmosphere.
  2. Test the atmosphere BEFORE entry — poke the sampling probe through a keyhole, gap, or small opening first.
  3. Normal readings: O₂ 20.9%, CO 0 ppm, H₂S 0 ppm, LEL 0%.
  4. Alarm thresholds: CO >35 ppm (TWA), O₂ <19.5% or >23.5%, H₂S >10 ppm, LEL >10%.
  5. Never bypass or ignore alarms — the meter detects what your senses cannot.
❓Why It's Needed

CO is odorless and colorless. H₂S smells like rotten eggs at low levels but paralyzes your sense of smell at higher concentrations. Oxygen deficiency causes rapid incapacitation without warning. Combustible gas at 10% LEL is 10% of the way to an explosion. The meter detects all of these — your nose and eyes do not.

🏷️Also Known As

4-gas meter, multi-gas meter, CGI (combustible gas indicator), MSA (brand name), RAE meter, atmospheric tester, gas monitor.

⚠ CRITICAL SAFETY
Always bump-test your meter before every shift. A bump test (brief exposure to a known test gas concentration) confirms all four sensors are working. A meter that hasn't been bump-tested may show clean readings in a contaminated atmosphere and kill you. This is not optional.
Gas Trac (Methane Meter)
AKA: Gas Trac, gas tracker, methane meter, combustible gas indicator. NOT the HCN sensor — that is a separate device.
+
📖What It Is

The Gas Trac — a dedicated combustible gas detector optimized for natural gas (methane / CH₄) detection. Used for gas-leak investigations, suspected gas alarms, and confined-space air monitoring before entry.

🔧How to Use It

For gas investigations: sweep the meter through the space and watch the combustible gas percentage. Check low (some fuel gases are heavier than air) and high (methane is lighter — it accumulates near the ceiling). Bump-test before every shift.

❓Why It's Needed

Natural-gas leaks are a routine call type and a serious explosion risk. The Gas Trac quantifies the hazard — telling you not just that gas is present but at what percent of LEL — so you know whether to evacuate, shut utilities, or stand down.

🏷️Also Known As

Gas Trac, gas tracker, methane meter, combustible gas indicator. NOT the HCN sensor — that is a separate device.

HCN Sensor (Standalone)
AKA: HCN sensor, HCN meter, hydrogen cyanide detector, cyanide meter. Distinct from the Gas Trac.
+
📖What It Is

A dedicated standalone Hydrogen Cyanide (HCN) sensor — a separate device from the Gas Trac. HCN is produced in almost every structural fire from burning synthetics, foam, and plastics. It is one of the primary killers in smoke inhalation — more dangerous than CO in many fire scenarios.

🔧How to Use It

During and after a structure fire: sweep the sensor through the work area, monitor the HCN reading. Use it during overhaul to confirm SCBA is still required (it almost always is) and to inform any decisions about removing masks. Bump-test on the same schedule as the 4-gas and Gas Trac.

❓Why It's Needed

HCN is a fire-service silent killer. Modern building contents — foam furniture, synthetic carpets, plastics, composite materials — all off-gas hydrogen cyanide when they burn. The 4-gas meter does not have an HCN sensor; the Gas Trac on this rig is for methane only. The standalone HCN sensor fills that gap.

🏷️Also Known As

HCN sensor, HCN meter, hydrogen cyanide detector, cyanide meter. Distinct from the Gas Trac.

⚠ CRITICAL SAFETY — HCN AWARENESS
HCN has an IDLH (Immediately Dangerous to Life and Health) of just 50 ppm. Smoke from a typical house fire can contain 50–300 ppm of HCN. This is why you never, ever take your mask off inside a fire building or during active overhaul — even when flames are out, HCN and other toxins remain.
Hot Stick
AKA: Hot stick, voltage detector, tic tracer, non-contact voltage tester, sonar stick, electrical tester.
+
📖What It Is

A non-contact voltage detector on a long insulated pole — essentially a voltage sensor mounted on a fiberglass extension stick. When held near energized conductors or electrical components, it buzzes or lights up to indicate voltage presence without requiring physical contact.

🔧How to Use It

Extend the hot stick toward the suspected conductor or electrical component from a safe distance. If the meter activates (light, buzz, alarm), the object is energized — do not touch, do not get closer, notify your officer, and request utility company response.

❓Why It's Needed

Downed power lines, vehicle accidents involving utility poles, and fires near electrical infrastructure are extremely hazardous. The hot stick lets you test electrical status from a safe distance before committing personnel to the immediate hazard area.

🏷️Also Known As

Hot stick, voltage detector, tic tracer, non-contact voltage tester, sonar stick, electrical tester.

Blue Lockout / Tagout Bag
AKA: LOTO bag, lockout tagout kit, energy control bag.
+
📖What It Is

A bag containing lockout/tagout (LOTO) equipment — padlocks, hasps, locking devices, and warning tags used to physically lock out energy sources (electrical, hydraulic, pneumatic) during rescue operations at machinery or industrial incidents. Prevents a machine from being re-energized while someone is working on or near it.

❓Why It's Needed

Industrial and machinery entrapment rescues require positive control of energy sources. OSHA's LOTO standard (29 CFR 1910.147) exists because uncontrolled re-energization of machinery causes catastrophic injuries. When you're reaching into a machine to free a victim's hand, that machine must be positively locked off.

🏷️Also Known As

LOTO bag, lockout tagout kit, energy control bag.

MIDDLE SHELF — EMS BAGS
Red Jump Bag — "First In" EMS Bag
AKA: Jump bag, first-in bag, ALS bag, BLS bag, medic bag, go bag, the red bag.
+
📖What It Is

The primary emergency medical bag — the first bag taken to a patient. Contains the initial assessment and life-threat treatment supplies: airway adjuncts, oxygen masks, non-rebreather mask, blood pressure cuff, stethoscope, gloves, trauma dressings, tourniquets, pulse ox, and basic cardiac monitoring supplies. The exact contents vary by department protocol — know your bag's exact contents.

❓Why It's Needed

The first minutes of a medical emergency are the most critical. This bag is pre-packed, pre-organized, and designed for rapid deployment on any EMS call. You grab it and go — no sorting, no hunting.

🏷️Also Known As

Jump bag, first-in bag, ALS bag, BLS bag, medic bag, go bag, the red bag.

Green Airway Bag
AKA: Airway bag, green bag, intubation bag, respiratory bag, ventilation bag.
+
📖What It Is

A dedicated bag for airway management supplies — contains equipment for securing and maintaining a patient's airway. Typically includes: BVM (bag-valve-mask) resuscitator, oral and nasal airway adjuncts (OPA/NPA), suction bulb or device, end-tidal CO₂ monitoring supplies, supraglottic airway devices (King LT, iGel), intubation supplies if ALS-level, and oxygen delivery equipment.

❓Why It's Needed

Airway is the "A" in the ABCs of emergency medicine for a reason — it comes first. Without an open airway, nothing else matters. Having a dedicated bag means airway equipment is always organized, accessible, and complete.

🏷️Also Known As

Airway bag, green bag, intubation bag, respiratory bag, ventilation bag.

AED — Automated External Defibrillator
AKA: AED, defibrillator, defib, cardiac monitor (when a full 12-lead monitor is carried), the AED.
+
📖What It Is

A computerized device that analyzes a cardiac patient's heart rhythm, determines if a shockable rhythm (ventricular fibrillation or ventricular tachycardia) is present, and delivers a controlled electrical shock to attempt to restore a normal rhythm. The AED talks you through the process — it literally tells you what to do.

🔧How to Use It
  1. Power on the AED — it will begin verbal instructions immediately.
  2. Apply pads as shown in the diagram: one below the right collarbone, one on the left lateral chest wall below the armpit.
  3. Ensure all personnel are clear of the patient — shout "CLEAR!"
  4. Follow the AED's instructions for shock delivery or continued CPR.
  5. Resume high-quality CPR immediately after the shock — do not wait to check for a pulse.
❓Why It's Needed

Early defibrillation is one of the highest-impact interventions in cardiac arrest. For every minute of VF without defibrillation, survival decreases 7–10%. As the first arriving unit, your AED may arrive before ALS — it saves lives when used immediately.

🏷️Also Known As

AED, defibrillator, defib, cardiac monitor (when a full 12-lead monitor is carried), the AED.

⚠ CRITICAL SAFETY
Do not touch the patient during AED rhythm analysis or shock delivery. Ensure all personnel are visually confirmed clear before the shock. Post-shock, immediately resume CPR — do not interrupt compressions to check for a pulse until the AED or your officer instructs otherwise.
Small Orange Bag — Suction Device
AKA: Suction, suction device, portable suction, V-VAC, SSCOR, manual suction, the orange bag (suction).
+
📖What It Is

A portable suction device — manual (squeeze/bulb-type) or battery-powered — used to clear a patient's airway of blood, vomit, fluids, and secretions. Without suction, a compromised airway filled with fluid cannot be managed by BVM or any other airway device.

🔧How to Use It

Attach the appropriate suction tip (rigid Yankauer or flexible catheter), turn on or activate the device, and suction the visible airway using sweeping motions. Do not suction for more than 10 seconds at a time — you're also removing oxygen. Suction, then ventilate.

❓Why It's Needed

Vomiting during resuscitation is common — especially during CPR and BVM ventilation. Without suction, vomit enters the lungs and causes aspiration pneumonia and airway obstruction. Suction is non-negotiable for any unconscious or compromised patient.

🏷️Also Known As

Suction, suction device, portable suction, V-VAC, SSCOR, manual suction, the orange bag (suction).

Pet O₂ Mask
AKA: Pet O₂ mask, animal oxygen mask, pet resuscitator, Wallis mask (trade name).
+
📖What It Is

A set of oxygen masks sized for dogs, cats, and other small animals — typically a set of three sizes (small, medium, large) designed to fit over animal snouts and muzzles. Connected to standard oxygen supply equipment.

❓Why It's Needed

Animals — especially pets rescued from house fires — suffer smoke inhalation just like humans. Providing supplemental oxygen to a compromised animal buys time for veterinary care and often saves animals that would otherwise die from smoke inhalation. It's also a community relations and public trust tool — people care deeply about their pets.

🏷️Also Known As

Pet O₂ mask, animal oxygen mask, pet resuscitator, Wallis mask (trade name).

ALSO IN CAB — KEY ITEMS
ERG — Emergency Response Guidebook
AKA: ERG, Emergency Response Guidebook, DOT guidebook, hazmat guide, the orange book (for the orange-covered edition).
+
📖What It Is

The Emergency Response Guidebook (ERG), published by the US Department of Transportation, is a pocket reference for first responders at hazardous materials incidents. Organized by UN/NA chemical placard number or chemical name, it provides: initial isolation distances, protective action distances, recommended PPE level, fire response guidance, spill response guidance, and first aid information for hundreds of hazardous chemicals.

🔧How to Use It
  1. Read the placard on the vehicle or container — find the four-digit UN/NA number.
  2. Look up the number in the orange (or yellow/blue) section — find the Guide Number.
  3. Turn to that Guide page for response guidance.
  4. For certain highlighted materials, also check the Green Section for specific initial isolation and protective action distances.
❓Why It's Needed

On a hazmat incident, you're making life-safety decisions about isolation, evacuation, and approach with very little time and often no on-scene hazmat specialist. The ERG is your first-response reference. It could keep you from walking into a chlorine cloud, an explosive atmosphere, or a radioactive spill without knowing it.

🏷️Also Known As

ERG, Emergency Response Guidebook, DOT guidebook, hazmat guide, the orange book (for the orange-covered edition).

▶ WATCH IT IN ACTION
YouTube: "how to use the ERG Emergency Response Guidebook"
KnoxBox + Elevator Key
AKA: Knox key, rapid entry key, Knox system; elevator key: fire service key, elevator master key, recall key.
+
📋What They Are

KnoxBox Key: A master key to Knox-brand rapid entry key boxes mounted on commercial buildings. Building owners secure their keys inside these tamper-resistant boxes; the fire department holds the single master key on each apparatus. On a fire or alarm call, you use this key to open the Knox box and retrieve the building key — no forced entry required.

Elevator Key: A "fire service key" (often a triangular key or specific brand key) that allows firefighters to take manual control of elevator cars — stopping them at a specific floor, holding doors open, and using the elevator for personnel and equipment transport.

📋Why They're Needed

Knox boxes eliminate the need for forced entry at commercial structures on the vast majority of alarm responses. This saves thousands of dollars in damaged doors and saves time on every response. Elevator keys are critical for high-rise operations where elevators are the only practical vertical transport option.

🏷️Also Known As

Knox key, rapid entry key, Knox system; elevator key: fire service key, elevator master key, recall key.

⚠ CRITICAL SAFETY — ELEVATOR USE IN FIRES
Never use an elevator for evacuation in a fire. Use the elevator for firefighter equipment transport only, after positive confirmation that the floor the elevator services is not the fire floor. An elevator that opens on the fire floor can strand a crew in a smoke-filled shaft with no exit.
Accountability Velcro Name Board
AKA: Accountability board, passport system, PASSPORT, velcro board, NIMS accountability system.
+
📖What It Is

A velcro board or passport system used to track crew accountability at an incident. Each firefighter has a passport (a velcro card with their name and assignment). When entering the hazard zone, passports are left with the entry control officer. The board gives the IC and accountability officer a real-time picture of who is inside and who is outside.

🔧How to Use It

On arrival, remove your passport from your helmet or the apparatus board. Hand it to the entry control/accountability officer when entering the structure. Retrieve it when exiting. The board should always reflect who is currently inside the hazard zone.

❓Why It's Needed

If a MAYDAY is declared or a structural collapse occurs, the IC must know who is inside, what their assignment was, and where they were working. Accountability is how you recover a downed firefighter. Without it, you're searching blind in a building you can't safely enter.

🏷️Also Known As

Accountability board, passport system, PASSPORT, velcro board, NIMS accountability system.

⚠ CRITICAL SAFETY
Accountability is a culture, not just a tool. If your department uses a passport system, using it is non-negotiable on every entry. One firefighter who bypasses accountability on the day there's a MAYDAY is one firefighter who may not get found in time. Use the system. Every time.
↑ Back to top
T

Top of the Engine

Snow Shovel, Traffic Cones, Fire Paddle, Manifold, Dawn Soap

Top-of-Engine Equipment

  • Snow Shovel: For clearing snow from hydrant caps and access paths in winter. Always know where your hydrants are in snow — buried hydrants add precious minutes to water supply operations. Your district has them; know them.
  • 1" Garden Hose: Secondary utility hose stored on top for quick access. Same use as the one in the Engineer's compartment.
  • Traffic Cones: Scene perimeter and traffic management on road incidents. Place them immediately on arrival at any roadway incident — your rig protects you; cones extend that protection zone. Never underestimate traffic.
  • Fire Paddle: A flat paddle-style tool for patting out or smothering small ground fires — brush fires, grass fires, small flare-ups. Swatting/paddling beats a hose line for small spot fires in open terrain. Also called a Fire Swatter, flap, or beater.
  • Manifold for Fire Gun / Deck Gun: The supply manifold for the deck gun (master stream mounted on top of the apparatus). Multiple inlets allow multiple supply lines to feed the deck gun for maximum flow. This is your defensive exterior master stream — flows 500–1000+ GPM.
  • Dawn Soap and Brush in Bucket: For cleaning hose, equipment, and the apparatus itself. Also used as a foam additive for certain wetting applications on Class A materials (though Class A foam concentrate is preferred). The bucket and brush are the end-of-shift cleanup kit.
⚠ DECK GUN / MASTER STREAM SAFETY
When the deck gun is flowing, no one enters the building. Master streams are a defensive operation. The pressure and flow a master stream delivers will injure firefighters inside, cause structural compromise, and reduce steam-burn survivability. When the deck gun goes to work, interior crews come out. No exceptions.
↑ Back to top
≠

E62 vs. E61 — Key Differences

Know the differences — you may ride either rig
🚒 KNOW YOUR RIG
Both engines share most of their tool placement, but these differences matter on the fireground.

Differences at a Glance

  • Driver's Side Over Wheel — E62: Air bags stored here. E61: Pry axe (officer's tool) stored here instead.
  • Air Bag Location — E61: Stored in the compartment near the back on the driver's side (not over the wheel). E62: Over the wheel and in Comp 3.
  • Air Bag Controllers: Both engines have different controllers. Both systems inflate to 118 PSI maximum. Do not assume the controller is the same — verify which you're on before operating.
  • RIT Pack: E62 has it — top shelf of Comp 3. E61 does not — plan accordingly on RIT assignments.
  • Officer Side Rear — E61: Contains a crowbar, 2 shovels (spade and flat), and a Pig. E62: These items are not in that location.
  • Officer Side Middle — E61: Has ice cleats for boot bottoms. E62 does not.
  • Toolbox — E61: Contains a hacksaw. E62 toolbox does not.
🔰 ROOKIE MISTAKE — "SAME RIG" ASSUMPTION
Cross-trained firefighters who know E62 cold have been caught flat-footed reaching for air bags over the wheel on E61 and finding an officer's tool instead. Before every shift, confirm which engine you're riding and verify the differences. A 30-second orientation on the ramp is worth 30 seconds of confusion at an incident.
↑ Back to top

A final word from your instructor: A compartment check isn't a chore — it's your daily handshake with the rig. When you're crawling blind in a smoke-filled hallway at 3am, you won't be thinking about this guide. You'll be operating on muscle memory built during a thousand quiet moments of knowing exactly where everything lives. Build that muscle memory now, while you have time. Pick up every fitting. Say its name. Know what it does. Know why it's there. That's what makes a firefighter.

Stay low. Stay together. Stay safe.

📚 Utility 61 — Compartment Study Guide

Utility 61 is the department's multi-purpose support vehicle — water rescue capability, technical rescue tools, scene support, and hazmat initial response all in one platform. Know every bag, every bin, and every tool before you ride it.

📋 Click Here for more details and photos of Utility 61

📻

Front Dash — Communications

DuCom · Fireground radio · PA system
DuCom (Gray Microphone) +
AKA: DuCom, dispatch radio, main radio, county radio

What it is: A gray push-to-talk microphone connected to the DuPage County interoperable communications (DuCom) radio system. This is your primary channel for dispatch — assignments, updates, scene reports, resource requests.

Why you need it: Dispatch communication is your lifeline. Every assignment, address change, and resource request runs through DuCom. Losing contact with dispatch on a working incident is a safety problem.

How to use:
  1. Know which channel is assigned for your district before the call.
  2. Press and hold the PTT (push-to-talk) button.
  3. Wait 1 second after pressing before speaking — gives the repeater time to key up.
  4. Speak clearly: unit ID → message. Example: "Utility 61 to DuCom..."
  5. Release and wait for response.
  6. Never talk over another unit — listen first.
  • Wait 1 second before speaking. Keying and immediately talking clips the first word. "Utility 61" becomes "tility 61" — pause, then speak.
  • Gray = County/dispatch. Black left = Fireground. Black right = PA. Three mics, three channels — do not mix them up on scene.
Fireground Microphone (Black — Lower Left) +
AKA: Tac mic, tactical channel mic, fireground radio

What it is: The black push-to-talk microphone at the lower left of the dash, connected to the fireground (tactical) channel. Used for crew-to-crew communication at a working incident.

Why you need it: Fireground communication is separated from dispatch to avoid cluttering the county channel during operations. Command and crews talk on tac; dispatch stays on DuCom.

How to use:
  1. Confirm you're on the correct tac channel for the incident before transmitting.
  2. PTT, wait 1 second, speak: unit/location → message.
  3. Keep transmissions short and specific.
  4. Critical messages get three words first: Mayday, Emergency, or Emergency Traffic.
  • MAYDAY PROTOCOL: If a firefighter is lost, trapped, or injured — LOUD: "Mayday, Mayday, Mayday, [name], [company], [location], [situation]." Do not hesitate. Do not minimize. Key up and transmit.
PA System Microphone (Black — Upper Right) +
AKA: PA, public address, exterior speaker

What it is: The black microphone at the upper right connected to the external public address speaker. Broadcasts your voice to people outside the apparatus without opening a window.

Why you need it: Scene control at roadway incidents — directing bystanders, alerting pedestrians, instructing people to clear an area. Also useful for directing traffic or providing info to waiting family members.

  • PA beats rolling down a window and shouting. You control volume, you're audible over engine noise, and you keep both hands free.
↑ Back to top
🧤

Glove Compartment

Maps · Loading paper · Patient forms · Keys · Flares · Accountability
Maps — District Street Maps +
AKA: Street atlas, paper nav, district maps, A-to-Z

What it is: Paper street maps of Glen Ellyn and surrounding mutual-aid districts. Your GPS will fail — this won't.

Why you need it: When MDT or GPS goes down mid-run, you cannot lose time searching. The driver needs a backup nav option immediately.

  • Know where these are BEFORE you need them. In a real mayday you won't have time to dig.
  • Cross-reference the laminated district map on the MDT mount for quick orientation.
Truck Loading Instruction Paper +
AKA: Load chart, weight distribution sheet, apparatus loading guide

What it is: A reference sheet showing how the rig is loaded — weight distribution, item placement, and loading sequence.

Why you need it: Improper loading shifts the vehicle's center of gravity. It also creates liability if something shifts and injures crew. Know how this rig is supposed to be loaded.

  • If something gets moved, reference this before you make assumptions about where it goes back.
Patient Prepare Reports (Blank) +
AKA: PCR, patient care reports, run reports, medical forms, PRR

What it is: Pre-printed patient report forms for documenting medical calls when the MDT is unavailable.

Why you need it: Documentation is required by law. If the MDT crashes mid-call, you still need to document. These are your backup.

  • Date and time them accurately. Inaccurate EMS documentation is a legal problem, not just a paperwork problem.
Vehicle Name Laminate +
AKA: Rig ID tag, apparatus card, unit identifier

What it is: A laminated card identifying this vehicle as "Utility 61" — used for accountability and radio checks.

Why you need it: In a multi-agency incident, unit identification matters for command accountability and resource tracking.

  • Do not remove this from the vehicle. It stays in the glove box.
Spare Tire Lock Key (In Bag) +
AKA: Spare tire key, lug lock key, anti-theft key

What it is: A key that releases the locking lug nut securing the spare tire under the vehicle.

Why you need it: Without this key, you cannot access the spare tire. A flat tire on-scene with no spare is a crew-safety problem.

  • The bag it's in — know exactly where it is. This is not the time to discover you can't find it.
Road Flares (×2) +
AKA: Highway flares, fusees, emergency flares, road signals

What it is: Pyrotechnic warning devices that burn bright red/orange to alert oncoming traffic to a hazard zone.

Why you need it: Traffic is one of the leading killers of emergency responders on-scene. Flares establish a visible perimeter before cones and tape go up.

How to use:
  1. Strike the cap firmly against the igniter end — it lights like a match.
  2. Place upwind and uphill from any fuel or spill hazard.
  3. Never hold a lit flare near your face or over a fuel source.
  • Flares burn extremely hot. Do NOT throw them — walk them into position.
  • Check count on every rig check. Missing flares need to be restocked.
Passport Accountability Tags (Velcro) +
AKA: Passport, accountability tags, name tags, velcro tags, ICS accountability

What it is: Velcro-backed name tags used in the Passport accountability system to track personnel entering and exiting a hazard zone.

Why you need it: The Passport system is how command knows who is in a hot zone. Without your tag on the board, command doesn't know you're in there.

  • Your tag goes on the passport board when you enter. It comes off when you exit. No exceptions.
  • If your tag is missing from the board and you're not on scene, someone will be looking for you.
↑ Back to top
☢️

ERG Handbook

Emergency Response Guidebook — Yellow · Blue · Orange · Green pages
ERG — Overview +
AKA: Emergency Response Guidebook, orange book, DOT book, hazmat bible

What it is: The Emergency Response Guidebook (ERG) is published by PHMSA and is the first-responder reference for identifying hazardous materials and taking initial protective actions.

Why you need it: On a hazmat call, you have minutes to identify a chemical and establish a safe perimeter. The ERG gets you moving in the right direction while specialists are called.

  • The ERG is a guide for INITIAL response only — not a substitute for a hazmat team.
  • Know the three-step lookup: 4-digit ID number → orange section → isolation distances in green or orange tables.
ERG — Yellow Pages (ID Number Index) +
AKA: Yellow section, material ID index, four-digit lookup

What it is: An index sorted by the 4-digit UN/NA identification number found on placards, shipping papers, and containers.

Why you need it: When you arrive on scene and can read the placard number from a safe distance, yellow pages get you to the right guide number fast.

How to use:
  1. Find the 4-digit number on the placard.
  2. Look it up in the yellow pages.
  3. Note the guide number (e.g., Guide 128).
  4. Turn to that guide in the orange pages.
  • Do not approach to read the placard if you don't know what you're dealing with. Use binoculars first.
ERG — Blue Pages (Material Name Index) +
AKA: Blue section, chemical name index, alphabetical lookup

What it is: An alphabetical index of hazardous material names linking to their guide number.

Why you need it: If you have a shipping manifest or can identify the substance by name, the blue pages let you skip the placard lookup.

  • Blue pages are your backup when the placard number is obscured or you have verbal information about the material.
ERG — Orange Pages (Action Guides) +
AKA: Orange section, response guides, numbered guides

What it is: The core of the ERG — numbered guides (1–172+) each covering a category of hazardous materials with isolation distances, PPE requirements, fire response, and spill response.

Why you need it: Once you have a guide number from yellow or blue, the orange pages tell you: how far to isolate, what PPE is needed, and what not to do.

  • Read the highlighted FIRE and SPILL sections first — those are your immediate action priorities.
  • Potential hazards are listed from most to least severe. Read them all before you act.
ERG — Green Pages (Initial Isolation Distances) +
AKA: Green section, isolation tables, protective action distances, TIH table

What it is: Tables giving specific isolation and protective action distances for materials that are toxic-inhalation hazards (TIH) or water-reactive.

Why you need it: For the most dangerous materials — chlorine, ammonia, phosgene — the orange guide alone isn't enough. The green pages give precise downwind evacuation distances.

  • Small vs. Large spill distances matter enormously — don't confuse them.
  • Day vs. night conditions change protective action distances. Check both columns and use the larger distance if unsure.
ERG — UN vs. NA Numbers +
AKA: UN number, NA number, United Nations, North American, DOT placard number

What it is: UN numbers are international 4-digit codes for hazardous materials. NA numbers are North America-specific variants, often for materials not recognized internationally.

Why you need it: The ERG covers both. If you see a placard starting with "NA" it's still a valid lookup — same process.

  • Most placards show UN numbers. NA numbers appear primarily on domestic shipments of specific materials.
  • Either way, four digits, yellow pages, guide number, orange pages — same drill.

🚪

Door Pockets — Driver + Officer

Tape measure · Safety vests
Tape Measure +
AKA: Measuring tape, retractable tape, construction tape

What it is: A standard retractable measuring tape stored in the driver or officer door pocket.

Why you need it: Used at structural incidents, water rescue, and any scene requiring dimension measurement — room size, collapse zones, standpipe connections.

  • Return it to the door pocket every time. It's small and easy to lose on scene.
Roadway Safety Vest (×2 — One Per Door) +
AKA: Hi-vis vest, ANSI vest, traffic vest, road vest, reflective vest

What it is: High-visibility ANSI-rated safety vests — one in each door pocket. These go on before you step into a traffic environment.

Why you need it: Traffic is the #1 cause of on-scene firefighter fatalities. Hi-vis gear makes you visible to oncoming drivers and reduces strike risk.

  • Put it on BEFORE you exit the vehicle on any roadway call — not after.
  • Both vests should be on the rig after every call. If one got left on-scene, restock it immediately.

Front Bench

MDT · Map binders · Keys · Binders · Tape · Gloves · Manuals
MDT — Mobile Data Terminal +
AKA: MDT, onboard computer, CAD terminal, dispatch terminal, in-cab computer

What it is: The ruggedized in-cab computer running the CAD (Computer-Aided Dispatch) system. Shows run cards, maps, hydrant locations, and pre-plans.

Why you need it: The MDT is your primary source for incident address, cross streets, building pre-plans, prior incident history, and GPS navigation.

  • If the MDT goes dark mid-run, switch to paper maps immediately — don't waste time troubleshooting.
  • Never mount anything on or over the MDT screen. Obstructed displays cost lives.
Map Binders +
AKA: District maps, map book, plat book, street binders

What it is: Binders containing printed maps of the response district, hydrant locations, and mutual-aid coverage areas.

Why you need it: Backup navigation when the MDT fails. Also useful for command briefings when you need to physically show coverage areas.

  • Keep them organized and in the right binder. A mis-filed map is as useful as no map.
Maintenance QR Code +
AKA: Maintenance code, apparatus maintenance scan, repair QR

What it is: A QR code linking to the apparatus maintenance request or log system.

Why you need it: Any deficiency found during a rig check must be documented. The QR code gets you there fast without digging for paper forms.

  • If you find something broken on rig check, scan and report it BEFORE that rig goes back in service.
Insurance QR Code +
AKA: Insurance scan, apparatus insurance, vehicle insurance QR

What it is: A QR code linking to the apparatus insurance documentation.

Why you need it: Required if the vehicle is involved in an accident. Having fast access prevents delays with law enforcement or other parties.

  • Know where this is. You won't be calm when you need it, so find it now while you are.
Fuel Key +
AKA: Fuel card, gas key, fleet card, apparatus fuel key

What it is: A key or card used to access the department fuel station.

Why you need it: U61 takes diesel. Without the fuel key you cannot refuel the rig, which means it goes out of service. This is not optional.

  • Return the key to the bench after every fuel stop. It does not leave the vehicle.
Prairie Path Key +
AKA: Prairie path gate key, trail access key, bike path gate key

What it is: A key that opens gates along the Illinois Prairie Path and similar restricted-access trails in the district.

Why you need it: The Prairie Path runs through our response area. Medical emergencies on the path require off-road access. Without this key, you're on foot for a distance that can cost a patient their life.

  • This is a unique key — losing it means gates stay locked until a replacement is cut. Don't lose it.
Knox Box Key +
AKA: Knox key, master key, rapid entry key, Supra key

What it is: The Knox Box master key that opens Knox Boxes installed at commercial buildings, allowing rapid entry without forcing doors.

Why you need it: Breaking a door costs time and money. Knox Box access is faster, cleaner, and required by code in many commercial properties. This key must be on the rig at all times.

  • This key is strictly controlled. It NEVER leaves the vehicle except in the hands of an officer.
  • If you use it, log it. Knox key use is tracked and audited.
Key Tags +
AKA: Spare key tags, key labels, key identifiers

What it is: Blank or labeled tags used to identify keys on the key ring.

Why you need it: With multiple keys on the ring, unlabeled keys cause confusion and delay. Key tags keep the set organized.

  • If a tag falls off a key, replace it immediately. "I think this is the fuel key" is not good enough.
Gas Instructions +
AKA: Fueling instructions, fuel procedure card, diesel fill guide

What it is: A laminated card or sheet outlining the fueling procedure for U61.

Why you need it: U61 runs on diesel. Putting gasoline in a diesel engine destroys it. New crew members and probies need to verify before they pump.

  • DIESEL ONLY. Read the nozzle, read the label, confirm before you pump.
  • If you're ever unsure, stop and ask. A ruined engine is a far worse outcome than a delayed fuel stop.
Nitrile Gloves (Box) +
AKA: Exam gloves, medical gloves, purple gloves, BSI gloves

What it is: A box of nitrile examination gloves for medical call use.

Why you need it: Body Substance Isolation (BSI) is standard on every medical call. These go on before you touch a patient — every time, no exceptions.

  • Glove up BEFORE patient contact. If you're already in it, you're already exposed.
  • Check the box count on rig check. Running out of gloves mid-call is a BSI failure.
Do-Not-Cross Tape +
AKA: Scene tape, perimeter tape, barrier tape, black and yellow tape

What it is: Black-and-yellow "DO NOT CROSS" barrier tape used to establish a perimeter at fire or hazmat scenes.

Why you need it: Scene control starts with a perimeter. Tape keeps civilians, media, and bystanders out of the hot zone before cones and barriers are in place.

  • Use generously. A tight perimeter that keeps getting breached is worse than a wide one.
  • Secure the ends to something solid — tape that blows away in the wind does nothing.
Fire / Scene Tape +
AKA: Fire line tape, red fire tape, incident tape

What it is: Red or red-and-white "FIRE LINE — DO NOT CROSS" tape for post-fire and extended scene control.

Why you need it: After fire operations, fire tape establishes the investigation perimeter and keeps the public out while overhaul and investigation continue.

  • Different departments use different tape colors. Know which tape is which on this rig.
Owner's Manual +
AKA: Vehicle manual, apparatus manual, operator's manual

What it is: The OEM owner's manual for the U61 chassis.

Why you need it: Contains vehicle-specific information including warning indicators, fluid specs, tire pressures, and emergency shutdown procedures.

  • If a dash warning light comes on that you don't recognize, the answer is in this manual.
  • Don't try to Google it while driving. Know where the manual is so you can reference it safely.
↑ Back to top
🪑

Back Seat

Portables · AED · FIU · SMO · Med log · Clipboard · Box light · OB bag · Snow brush
Portable Radios (×4 total — 2 per side) +
AKA: Portables, handie-talkies, HTs, walkie-talkies, hand-helds

What it is: Four portable radios stowed in the back seat area — two on the driver side, two on the officer side. Pre-programmed with DuCom channels.

Why you need it: When crew splits up on scene, everyone needs radio communication. Portables are how you stay connected to command and to each other.

  • Grab a portable every time you dismount — even on "routine" calls.
  • Check battery level on rig check. A dead radio is no radio.
  • Know your channel assignment before you get out of the rig.
AED — Automated External Defibrillator +
AKA: AED, defibrillator, shock box, defib

What it is: A portable defibrillator that analyzes heart rhythm and delivers a shock to restore a normal rhythm in cardiac arrest.

Why you need it: Early defibrillation is the single most important intervention in ventricular fibrillation cardiac arrest. Every minute without it drops survival by 10%.

How to use:
  1. Power it on immediately on arrival at a cardiac arrest.
  2. Attach pads per diagram — upper right chest, lower left side.
  3. Clear the patient before analyzing and before shock.
  4. Follow AED prompts — it walks you through every step.
  • AED pads have an expiration date. Check it on rig check.
  • AED goes on the patient while CPR continues — do not stop compressions to set up unless you have to.
FIU Tub +
AKA: Fire Investigation Unit tub, FIU supplies, investigation bin

What it is: A tub containing Fire Investigation Unit supplies — used to support scene documentation and cause-and-origin investigation.

Why you need it: Utility 61 supports the FIU. When FIU responds, they need their supplies on-scene. Know what's in this tub so you can hand them exactly what they need.

  • Don't go through the FIU tub unless directed by FIU personnel or your officer.
  • Report to your officer if anything looks damaged, depleted, or out of place.
SMO Binder +
AKA: Standard Medical Operating binder, SMO reference, protocol binder

What it is: A binder containing Standard Medical Operating procedures and protocols for EMS calls.

Why you need it: When you have a protocol question mid-call and no time to look things up online, the SMO binder is your answer.

  • This is not casual reading material — it's an on-scene reference. Return it to the back seat after use.
Med Log Binder +
AKA: Medical log, EMS run log, call log binder

What it is: A binder for logging medical calls — run numbers, patient info, disposition.

Why you need it: Documentation is legally required and operationally essential. The med log binder is how U61's EMS activity gets tracked.

  • Fill it out on every medical call. Missing entries get noticed during audits.
Grey Clipboard +
AKA: Clipboard, scene clipboard, command clipboard

What it is: A standard hard-back clipboard, grey in color, used for scene paperwork and patient documentation.

Why you need it: You need a hard surface to write on at every call. The clipboard goes with you when you're managing scene documentation.

  • Keep blank paper stocked on it. A clipboard with no paper is dead weight.
Box Light +
AKA: Scene light, box lamp, portable scene lamp, work light

What it is: A portable battery-powered box light that provides broad illumination for working in low-light conditions.

Why you need it: Night calls, interior scenes, and dark environments require portable lighting. The box light hands-free illuminates a working area.

  • Check battery charge on rig check.
  • Point it at the work surface, not at your crew's faces.
Nitrile Gloves (Back Seat) +
AKA: Exam gloves, BSI gloves, medical gloves, rear seat gloves

What it is: A supply of nitrile gloves stored in the back seat for immediate access by rear-seat crew.

Why you need it: Rear-seat crew should be gloving up as the rig pulls up — these are here so they don't have to reach to the front bench.

  • Always check the count. Running out mid-call is not acceptable.
  • If the box gets wet, replace it — damp gloves tear when you're trying to glove up fast.
OB Bag +
AKA: Obstetrics bag, OB kit, delivery kit, childbirth bag

What it is: A kit containing supplies for emergency field delivery — gloves, clamps, blankets, bulb syringe, and related items.

Why you need it: Babies don't wait for the hospital. If a delivery is imminent in the field, this kit is how you support mom and protect the baby.

  • Know what's in it before you ever need it. Open it up and look during a downtime.
  • After any use, report to your officer immediately for restocking — this kit must be ready for the next call.
Snow Brush / Ice Scraper +
AKA: Snow brush, ice scraper, windshield brush

What it is: A brush and scraper combination for clearing snow and ice from the vehicle before response.

Why you need it: You cannot safely drive a vehicle you can't see out of. In winter months, this is a pre-response essential.

  • Clear ALL windows — not just the windshield. Check mirrors and lights too.
  • If you're slow clearing the windows, you're slowing down response time. Be efficient.
↑ Back to top
🚪

Back Left Door

Duct tape · Post-it notes
Duct Tape (×2 rolls) +
AKA: Duck tape, hundred-mile-an-hour tape, mil tape, gorilla tape

What it is: Two rolls of heavy-duty duct tape stored in the back left door pocket.

Why you need it: Duct tape is a universal field fix — sealing bags, securing equipment, temporary repairs on-scene, and patient packaging.

  • Two rolls because one always runs low. Check both on rig check.
  • If you pull a full roll, try to put it back with at least something left — communicate to your officer if it's low.
Post-It Notes +
AKA: Sticky notes, adhesive notes, note pads

What it is: Small adhesive notepad stored in the back left door.

Why you need it: Quick notes, labeling, leaving information on scene — Post-Its are surprisingly useful in the field.

  • Small thing. Know where it is.
↑ Back to top
🔧

Truck Bed — Tools

Halligan · Axe · Pike pole · Hot stick · Umbrellas · Shovel · Jumper cables · More
Halligan Bar +
AKA: Hooligan, Pro-bar, the bar, Halligan tool, irons

What it is: A forged steel forcible entry tool with a fork, adze, and pick. One of the most versatile tools on the rig.

Why you need it: Forcible entry, breaching, prying, ventilation — the Halligan does it all. Know how to use it before you need to.

  • Never use it as a step or seat — it's a precision tool, not a step stool.
  • The irons set (Halligan + flathead axe) are the standard forcible entry combination.
Flat Head Axe +
AKA: Flat axe, striking axe, fire axe, flathead

What it is: A single-bit axe with a flat poll (back face) used for striking the Halligan and for cutting.

Why you need it: The axe drives the Halligan during forcible entry — that's the irons technique. The cutting edge is for wood, not metal.

  • The poll drives the Halligan — use the flat back, not the blade edge.
  • Keep the blade covered when not in use. Exposed axe blades in a moving truck are a safety hazard.
Closet Pike Pole +
AKA: Short pike pole, closet hook, little pike, 4-foot hook

What it is: A shorter pike pole (approximately 4 feet) for working in confined spaces, closets, and interiors.

Why you need it: The full-size pike poles don't fit in tight spaces. The closet pike goes where the long ones can't — ceiling work in hallways, closets, and tight rooms.

  • Never push or stab with a pike pole toward a crew member on the other side of a ceiling.
AC Hot Stick +
AKA: Hot stick, voltage detector, non-contact voltage tester, live wire tool

What it is: An insulated extension tool used to safely probe or move energized electrical components from a safe distance.

Why you need it: Active electrical hazards can be invisible. The hot stick lets you test or move a suspected energized component without touching it.

How to use:
  1. Never assume a wire is dead.
  2. Use the hot stick to probe before touching any unknown wire.
  3. If it lights up or clicks — energized. Back out and call the utility company.
  • This is not a tool to improvise with. If you haven't been trained on it, do not use it without supervision.
Umbrellas (×3) +
AKA: Personal umbrella, crew umbrella, rain cover

What it is: Three full-size umbrellas stored in the truck bed for crew use in wet conditions.

Why you need it: Working a scene in the rain for an extended period is uncomfortable and can affect crew performance. Umbrellas protect paperwork, equipment, and crew during rehab.

  • Three umbrellas for a reason — check count on rig check.
Shovel +
AKA: Scoop shovel, flathead shovel, digging shovel

What it is: A full-size shovel stored in the truck bed for digging, debris movement, and utility work.

Why you need it: Used for trench operations, ground-level fire control, uncovering utilities, and debris management.

  • Check that the handle is solid. A broken handle mid-dig is a hand injury waiting to happen.
Jumper Cables +
AKA: Booster cables, jump cables, jump start cables

What it is: Heavy-duty jumper cables for jump-starting vehicles with dead batteries.

Why you need it: At MVAs, assists, and breakdowns, dead batteries are common. The jumper cables let U61 solve the problem directly.

How to use:
  1. Red to dead positive, red to good positive.
  2. Black to good negative, black to unpainted metal on the dead vehicle (not the battery terminal).
  3. Start the good vehicle, let it run 2 minutes, then attempt to start the dead vehicle.
  4. Remove in reverse order: black from unpainted metal, black from good negative, red from good positive, red from dead positive.
  • Never connect black to the dead battery's negative — arc risk and battery hydrogen gas explosion risk.
  • If the battery is cracked or leaking, do not jump it. Call a wrecker.
Measuring Wheel +
AKA: Distance wheel, rolling tape, surveyor's wheel, click wheel

What it is: A rolling measuring device that counts distance as it rolls — used for scene documentation and mapping.

Why you need it: At large incidents, water rescue, and investigations, measuring distances accurately matters for reporting and scene reconstruction.

  • Zero it before you start. A wheel with a number on it from the last call gives you garbage data.
PPE Masks (Box) +
AKA: N95 masks, surgical masks, respiratory protection, dust masks

What it is: A supply of disposable masks (N95 or surgical grade) for respiratory protection at medical, overhaul, and hazmat initial-response situations.

Why you need it: Overhaul creates carcinogenic smoke and dust. Medical calls may involve infectious patients. Masks are the minimum respiratory barrier for both.

  • N95 must be properly fitted — a loose N95 is a surgical mask.
  • Check count on rig check. A box that's down to three masks is a restocking problem.
SurpressAll Fire Suppressant +
AKA: SurpressAll, fire suppressant, foam alternative, Class A additive, wet stuff

What it is: A concentrated fire suppressant additive that increases water's effectiveness at penetrating and knocking down Class A fires.

Why you need it: SurpressAll allows a small amount of water to do what a large amount of plain water cannot — penetrate deep-seated fire in wood, debris, and dense material.

How to use:
  1. Mix per manufacturer ratio — usually a small amount per gallon.
  2. Apply through a nozzle with appropriate fog pattern.
  3. Let it work — this isn't a high-pressure flush, it's penetrating suppression.
  • Check the container seal on rig check — dried or crystallized suppresant is wasted product.
Hydrant Wrench +
AKA: Hydrant key, pentagon wrench, spanner, hydrant spanner

What it is: A pentagonal wrench used to open and close fire hydrant operating nuts.

Why you need it: Without a hydrant wrench, you cannot open a hydrant manually. If the apparatus wrench is in use, this is your backup.

  • Different hydrants have different operating directions — know your local hydrant type.
  • Don't overtighten when closing. You'll strip the nut and create a maintenance problem.
Blanket +
AKA: Emergency blanket, patient blanket, utility blanket, wool blanket

What it is: A utility blanket stored in the truck bed for patient comfort, hypothermia prevention, or equipment protection.

Why you need it: Hypothermia can complicate almost any patient presentation. A blanket buys time until ALS or hospital care.

  • After patient use, it goes for laundry — do not put a used patient blanket back in the truck bed unsealed.
ABC Fire Extinguisher +
AKA: Fire extinguisher, dry chem, multi-purpose extinguisher, handheld extinguisher

What it is: A portable ABC-rated dry chemical fire extinguisher for small fires — Class A (ordinary combustibles), B (liquids), and C (energized electrical).

Why you need it: Small fires caught early don't become big fires. The portable extinguisher handles incipient-stage fires before hose lines need to be deployed.

How to use:
  1. Pull the pin.
  2. Aim at the base of the fire.
  3. Squeeze the handle.
  4. Sweep side to side.
  • PASS — Pull, Aim, Squeeze, Sweep.
  • Check pressure gauge on rig check. Green zone = good. Red zone = out of service.
  • After any use, even partial, it needs inspection and likely recharge before going back in service.
↑ Back to top
🎒

Truck Bed — Medical Packs

Trauma pack · Airway pack · Water rescue bag · Cervical collars
Red Bag — Trauma Pack +
AKA: Trauma bag, red pack, first-in bag, trauma kit

What it is: A red-colored bag containing trauma supplies — bandaging, tourniquets, chest seals, hemostatic gauze, airways, and trauma assessment tools.

Why you need it: When you arrive at a traumatic injury — MVC, penetrating trauma, fall — the red trauma bag has everything you need for initial assessment and hemorrhage control.

  • Know what's in it. Don't open it for the first time on scene.
  • After every call, restock immediately. An incomplete trauma bag is a patient safety failure.
  • Tourniquets first for extremity bleeding. Don't mess around with pressure and bandaging on arterial bleeds.
Green Bag — Airway Pack +
AKA: Airway bag, green pack, BLS airway bag, ventilation bag

What it is: A green-colored bag containing airway management equipment — BVM (bag-valve-mask), oral and nasal airways, suction, oxygen, and related supplies.

Why you need it: Airway is always first. If the patient can't breathe, nothing else matters until you fix it. The green bag is dedicated to that job.

  • Know every item and how to use it before your first call.
  • BVM mask sizing matters — have the right size on before you need it.
  • Check O2 cylinder pressure on rig check. A low O2 bottle needs to be swapped.
Red Bag — Water Rescue +
AKA: Water rescue bag, throw bag, water ops bag, swift water bag

What it is: A red bag containing water rescue supplies — PFD (personal flotation device), throw bag, rope, and related water rescue equipment.

Why you need it: When U61 responds to water rescue incidents, this bag goes with you. The throw bag alone can be the difference between a rescue and a recovery.

How to use:
  1. Unpack and identify every item before any water rescue assignment.
  2. PFD goes on before you approach the water's edge.
  3. Throw bag: hold one end, throw the bag — not the rope.
  4. Shout to the victim to grab the bag and hold on.
  • Never enter the water without a PFD on. Ever.
  • A rescuer who becomes a victim doubles the problem and may cost two lives.
Blue Bag — Cervical Collars +
AKA: C-collar bag, blue bag, collar kit, cervical collar set

What it is: A blue bag containing multiple sizes of cervical collars for spinal immobilization.

Why you need it: Mechanism of injury alone can indicate spinal precautions. C-collars stabilize the cervical spine during movement and packaging.

How to use:
  1. Measure collar size: measure from the patient's chin to the top of the shoulder with fingers, then match to collar sizing guide.
  2. Apply with assistance — one person holds neutral alignment while the other places the collar.
  3. Check for a good fit — collar should not restrict breathing.
  • Wrong size collar creates movement rather than restricting it — size correctly.
  • Document C-collar application time and mechanism of injury for the hospital team.
↑ Back to top
📦

Truck Bed — Other Equipment

SCBA case · ABC extinguisher · Tailgate setup
MSA Airpack Case — SCBA, Air Bottle, Face Piece (Size M) +
AKA: MSA case, SCBA case, breathing apparatus case, self-contained breathing apparatus

What it is: A hard-sided case containing an MSA SCBA unit — including the pack harness, air cylinder, and a size-M face piece.

Why you need it: Utility 61 carries an SCBA for incidents requiring respiratory protection — hazmat initial response, confined space, or situations where the crew needs air.

  • The face piece is Size M. If you wear a different size and need SCBA, communicate that early.
  • Check cylinder pressure on rig check — a partial bottle needs to be swapped.
  • If this SCBA is deployed, notify your officer. It must be inspected and refilled before the next call.
ABC Dry Chemical Extinguisher (Bed) +
AKA: Second extinguisher, fire extinguisher, dry chem, backup extinguisher

What it is: A second portable ABC-rated dry chemical fire extinguisher stored in the truck bed — backup to the in-cab extinguisher.

Why you need it: One extinguisher can be depleted. Having a second means you still have options if the first is spent or unavailable.

  • Treat this like the primary — check pressure gauge on every rig check.
  • Two extinguishers, two separate checks. Don't assume one is good because the other is.
Tailgate Setup +
AKA: Tailgate gear, tailgate equipment, truck bed extension setup

What it is: Items and rigging associated with setting up the tailgate area for operations — staging, work surface, or equipment deployment.

Why you need it: Utility 61 functions as a support and utility platform. The tailgate setup allows the truck bed to serve as a staging and working area at extended incidents.

  • Know how to set it up and break it down efficiently.
  • Secure everything before moving the vehicle. Loose equipment in a moving truck is a hazard to everyone it passes.
