01
Section 1
Front Seat
1 item
📻 Radios
Portable / HT / Handie-Talkie
+
📋 What It Is

Battery-powered handheld transceivers that allow voice communication between crew members, command, dispatch, and mutual aid agencies. Programmed with your agency's tactical channels, mutual aid frequencies, and standard ICS channels. At least one radio per seat position is standard on a brush truck.

🔧 How to Use
  1. Power on and confirm full battery charge — this is part of your daily rig check, non-negotiable.
  2. Confirm you're on the correct assigned channel before leaving the station.
  3. To transmit: press and hold PTT, wait one full second before speaking to prevent clipping your first word.
  4. Speak clearly at a normal pace, directly into the mic. Release PTT when finished.
  5. Use ICS radio discipline — identify yourself, then your message: "Command from BT 62 — water supply established."
  6. Monitor your assigned channel. Never switch channels without notifying your officer.
💡 Why It Matters

Your radio is your lifeline. A firefighter who can't reach command is a firefighter in danger. On a brush truck working remote terrain, communication can be the difference between a manageable situation and a line-of-duty fatality.

⚡ Radio Discipline
Never key your radio while someone else is transmitting — this "steps on" their message and can block a critical communication. Always verify your channel before operating. And never go out of service without letting someone know.
02
Section 2
Glove Box
4 items
📗 ERG Book
Emergency Response Guidebook / Orange Book / DOT Guide
+
📋 What It Is

The Emergency Response Guidebook — published by the U.S. DOT — is a pocket-sized reference for identifying hazardous materials and determining initial safe response actions. Organized by UN/NA placard numbers, chemical names, and color-coded guide pages for isolation distances. A new edition is published every four years — verify your copy is current.

🔧 How to Use
  1. Identify the 4-digit UN/NA number on the vehicle's placard.
  2. Look it up in the yellow (numerical) or blue (alphabetical) index pages.
  3. Note the guide number (e.g., Guide 128) and turn to that orange-bordered page.
  4. Read Potential Hazards first — fire/explosion risk and health hazards.
  5. Follow the Public Safety section for initial isolation distances.
  6. For large spills or fires, use the green-bordered Table of Initial Isolation and Protective Action Distances.
  7. Relay findings to your officer and dispatch immediately.
💡 Why It Matters

Brush fires don't stay in the wildland. They reach propane tanks, agricultural chemical storage, and vehicles with hazmat placards. Before you get close to anything with a placard, you need to know what you're dealing with.

⚠️ Know Your Edition
An outdated ERG can give you wrong isolation distances. Check the edition year on the cover — if it's more than four years old, flag it for replacement.
🦟 Bug Spray
Insect Repellent / DEET
+
📋 What It Is

Personal protective spray — typically DEET-based — used to repel insects during wildland operations, extended scenes, and any deployment into wooded or brushy terrain.

🔧 How to Use
  1. Apply to exposed skin and clothing before deployment into brush or wooded areas.
  2. Avoid contact with eyes, mouth, and wounds.
  3. Reapply per product directions on extended operations.
💡 Why It Matters

Tick-borne illnesses and mosquito-transmitted diseases are real occupational hazards in wildland response. Lyme disease, West Nile, and others don't respect your turnout gear. Protect exposed skin.

🔑 Fuel Key
Fleet Fuel Key / Gas Card Key
+
📋 What It Is

A keyed or card-based access credential that allows the truck to be fueled at designated fleet fuel stations. Kept in the glove box for ready access during refueling.

🔧 How to Use
  1. Use at designated fleet fueling locations only.
  2. Follow proper fueling procedure: engine off, no ignition sources, operator present at pump at all times.
  3. Return the key to the glove box immediately after use.
  4. Report any fueling issues or errors to the officer immediately.
💡 Why It Matters

A brush truck that can't be fueled is a brush truck that can't respond. The key needs to be in the truck and in the glove box — not in someone's gear bag.

⚡ No Shortcuts During Fueling
Never leave the pump unattended while fueling. Diesel or gasoline spillage near an apparatus is a fire hazard. Engine off, no phones near the fill point, and you're watching the nozzle the entire time.
🗺️ Water Guides / Water Source Maps
Rural Water Supply Maps
+
📋 What It Is

Printed reference maps identifying pre-surveyed natural water sources in your response area — ponds, streams, swimming pools, cisterns, dry hydrants, and other potential drafting locations. May be laminated map sheets or a bound booklet.

🔧 How to Use
  1. When the tank is running low and no hydrant is available, pull the guide.
  2. Identify your current location and reference the nearest marked water source.
  3. Relay the location to your officer for routing decisions.
  4. Note any access limitations — weight-restricted bridges, narrow lanes, or locked gates that could block apparatus access.
💡 Why It Matters

In rural wildland operations, your onboard 250 gallons goes fast. Knowing where to get more water before you need it is the difference between staying in the fight and going out of service at the worst possible moment.

⚠️ Don't Rely on Memory
Water sources change — ponds dry up, access roads change, properties get fenced. The guides should be updated regularly. Never assume a pre-surveyed source is still accessible without verifying.
03
Section 3
Back Seat
4 items
🦺 PFD — Personal Flotation Device
Life Jacket / Life Vest
+
📋 What It Is

A Type III or Type V Coast Guard-approved life jacket — foam or inflatable — worn around the torso to maintain buoyancy in water. Keeps a person afloat even if incapacitated.

🔧 How to Use
  1. Pull the PFD over your head and secure all buckles and straps snugly.
  2. Fit check: it should not ride up over your chin when you pull upward on the front hem.
  3. For inflatable models: confirm the CO₂ cartridge is installed and the armed indicator is green before operating near water.
  4. Wear any time you are within arm's reach of an open water source during drafting or other water-hazard scenarios.
  5. Inspect before use: check for tears, missing buckles, and buoyancy integrity.
💡 Why It Matters

Drowning is a documented firefighter line-of-duty fatality category. If your crew is working near a pond, creek, or any open water — PFD goes on. No discussion needed.

⚡ "I'm Not Going in the Water"
The most dangerous words near any water hazard. The PFD goes on before the incident, not after you fall in. Put it on when the water source is identified, not when you're already leaning over it.
⚡ Hot Stick
Electrical Hot Stick / Safety Stick / Shotgun Stick
+
📋 What It Is

A fiberglass insulated pole — typically 4 to 6 feet — used to safely move or test energized electrical equipment without direct contact. Rated for specific voltage levels. Used in motor vehicle accidents and structural incidents involving downed power lines.

🔧 How to Use
  1. Before any use involving electrical hazards, confirm the hot stick's voltage rating matches or exceeds the hazard.
  2. Inspect for cracks, chips, or moisture contamination before use — any defect grounds it from service.
  3. Keep both hands behind the guard (the rubber collar) — never allow your grip to go past the guard toward the energized end.
  4. Use only when trained and authorized to do so. If in doubt, wait for the utility company.
💡 Why It Matters

Energized lines are invisible killers. A hot stick gives you standoff distance from an energized object — but only if it's rated, inspected, and used correctly. It is not a magic wand.

⚡ Step Potential
Downed lines energize the ground around them. Do not approach within 30 feet of a downed line. Even with a hot stick, you should not touch downed lines unless you are trained and conditions are confirmed safe. Establish a perimeter and call for the utility company.
⚠️ Storage Matters
Hot sticks stored in dirty, wet, or contaminated conditions lose their insulating properties. Keep it clean, dry, and in its protective sleeve.
🔦 Box Light / Big Flashlight
Hand Lantern / Scene Light / Area Light
+
📋 What It Is

A large-format, high-output battery-powered hand lantern designed for scene illumination rather than directional spotting. Provides broad area light for nighttime operations, vehicle extrications, and extended wildland deployments.

🔧 How to Use
  1. Power on and confirm charge status before deployment — check this during daily rig check.
  2. Use for broad area illumination of scenes, patient care areas, or equipment staging.
  3. Place on a stable, elevated surface (truck bumper, equipment box) to direct light where needed without hand-holding.
  4. When done, power off and return charged to the rig.
💡 Why It Matters

Nighttime brush operations are high-risk. You can't read terrain, identify hazards, or communicate hand signals in the dark. A scene light is scene safety.

⚠️ Battery Check
A dead light at a night scene is worse than no light at all — because you assumed you had it. Check charge on every shift.
🌊 Hose Bag with Garden Hose
Garden Hose / Soft Suction / Fill Hose
+
📋 What It Is

A length of standard garden hose — typically 50 feet — carried in a bag. Used for supplemental water fill from non-standard supply points: swimming pools, residential outdoor spigots, irrigation connections, or small ponds accessible by the hose alone.

🔧 How to Use
  1. Connect to a standard ¾-inch garden hose fitting at the source.
  2. Route to the tank fill inlet or pump suction connection.
  3. Ensure secure connection at both ends before opening the source valve.
  4. Monitor fill — do not overfill the tank.
💡 Why It Matters

Not every rural water source has a 2.5-inch port or a hard suction connection point. A garden hose bridges the gap — especially at residential properties with accessible outdoor spigots.

04
Section 4
Container — Back Seat
9 items
🌀 Small 1″ Hose
Forestry Line / Wildland Hose / Booster Hose
+
📋 What It Is

A section of 1-inch diameter single-jacket forestry hose — lighter and more flexible than structural attack hose. Standard NST threaded couplings. This is a backup section stored in the container, separate from the reel.

🔧 How to Use
  1. Connect to the pump's 1-inch discharge or an inline valve.
  2. Use for spot extinguishment, mop-up, or as an extension when the main hose reel line can't reach.
  3. Can be handed off to a second crew working a separate flank.
💡 Why It Matters

Fires don't cooperate with fixed hose lengths. A backup section means extra reach, a secondary line, or flexibility to hand off to another crew without giving up your primary line.

🔗 Strap
Utility Strap / Cargo Strap / Lashing Strap
+
📋 What It Is

A utility webbing strap — ratchet or cam-buckle style — used for securing loose equipment during transport, stabilizing objects at a scene, or improvised rigging.

🔧 How to Use
  1. Inspect buckle and webbing for cuts, fraying, or damaged components before use.
  2. Route webbing around or through the load, not just over it.
  3. For ratchet type: thread the webbing, take up slack by hand, then ratchet tight.
  4. Do not exceed the rated load capacity printed on the strap.
💡 Why It Matters

Unsecured equipment in a moving apparatus is a projectile. Straps keep gear in place and keep you safe.

🧼 Towel
Shop Rag / Utility Towel / Wipe-Down Towel
+
📋 What It Is

A utility cloth for equipment wipe-down, spill absorption, or field cleanup. Not a patient care item.

🔧 How to Use
  1. Use for wiping down wet or dirty equipment before storage.
  2. Absorb minor fluid spills on the truck or equipment.
  3. Clean up hands before handling sensitive equipment like radios or gauges.
💡 Why It Matters

Small detail, but a dirty rig is a poorly-maintained rig. Equipment that's cleaned after operations lasts longer and is easier to inspect.

🦺 Safety Vest
High-Visibility Vest / Reflective Vest / Hi-Viz
+
📋 What It Is

An ANSI-rated high-visibility vest worn over PPE or work clothes when operating in or near traffic — roadway incidents, vehicle assistance, and any scene with moving vehicle hazards.

🔧 How to Use
  1. Don the vest any time you are exposed to moving vehicle traffic.
  2. Wear over turnout gear or outerwear — visibility is the point, don't bury it under anything.
  3. Inspect for reflective strip integrity, especially after dark operations where degraded strips become more critical.
💡 Why It Matters

Being struck by a vehicle is a leading cause of firefighter line-of-duty deaths. Hi-viz doesn't guarantee safety — it improves it. Wear it before you need it, not after someone almost hits you.

⚡ "We'll Only Be a Minute"
That's when it happens. The vest goes on when you step out of the truck near traffic, every single time, regardless of how quick the stop is.
🗺️ Maps
Street Maps / Grid Maps / Area Maps
+
📋 What It Is

Paper street or grid maps of your primary and mutual aid response districts. Used when GPS fails, when you need to plan alternate routes, or when briefing crews on an operation.

🔧 How to Use
  1. Familiarize yourself with your primary response district map during study time, not at the scene.
  2. Identify major roads, water sources, and district boundaries before they matter.
  3. Keep maps dry and stored flat or folded — a map destroyed by moisture is worthless in the field.
💡 Why It Matters

GPS goes down, cell service fails, and tablets glitch. Paper maps don't. Know how to read your district without electronics.

🩹 Duct Tape
Duck Tape / 100 MPH Tape
+
📋 What It Is

Heavy-duty adhesive cloth tape. In the field, it's used for temporary equipment repair, securing loose covers, sealing, and improvised fixes.

🔧 How to Use
  1. Use for temporary field repair of torn tarps, hose wrapping, or securing loose equipment panels.
  2. Clean and dry the surface before applying for maximum adhesion.
  3. Keep a full roll — partial rolls that lose adhesion are useless.
💡 Why It Matters

The universal fix that buys time until a proper repair is made. On a wildland scene, it can keep marginal equipment operational through the incident.

🚧 Caution Tape
Barrier Tape / Scene Tape / Yellow Tape
+
📋 What It Is

Brightly colored (usually yellow) non-adhesive plastic tape used to establish scene perimeters, mark hazard areas, or delineate work zones.

🔧 How to Use
  1. Tie off to fixed objects — trees, bumpers, cones, signs — to create a perimeter line.
  2. Position high enough to be visible (at least chest height) but low enough to prevent ducking underneath without awareness.
  3. Brief crew on the perimeter before they work near it.
💡 Why It Matters

Scene control starts with clearly marked boundaries. If bystanders can wander in, someone gets hurt and it becomes your problem.

🗑️ Garbage Bags
Contractor Bags / Debris Bags / Black Bags
+
📋 What It Is

Heavy-duty plastic bags used for debris collection, equipment containment, and improvised waterproofing at extended operations.

🔧 How to Use
  1. Use for collecting debris, contaminated materials, or burned material during mop-up.
  2. Can be used as improvised waterproofing for equipment or patient covering in a pinch.
  3. Double-bag contaminated materials.
💡 Why It Matters

Mop-up generates debris. Scene cleanup and containment is part of the job, and having the right bags on the truck keeps operations professional.

📚 Public Education Materials
Pub Ed / Fire Prevention Stickers / Community Outreach Handouts
+
📋 What It Is

Fire prevention handouts, stickers, and community outreach materials kept on the truck for distribution during public contacts, school visits, or any public interaction during non-emergency operations.

🔧 How to Use
  1. Offer materials to community members during non-emergency public contacts and station visits.
  2. Keep materials organized and dry — don't hand out soggy or damaged materials.
  3. Know the basic message: smoke detectors save lives, call 911, stop-drop-roll.
💡 Why It Matters

Every public contact is a public education moment. You are a walking advertisement for fire prevention. A sticker that goes home with a kid might be the reason someone tests their smoke alarm.

05
Section 5
Rear — Water System
10 items
💧 250-Gallon Water Tank
Booster Tank / Onboard Water / Tank
+
📋 What It Is

A truck-mounted poly or fiberglass tank holding 250 gallons — the onboard supply that makes Brushtruck 62 a mobile attack unit. At 25–30 GPM through a 1-inch line, 250 gallons gives you roughly 8–10 minutes of continuous water.

🔧 How to Use
  1. Check and confirm full at the start of every shift.
  2. Fill via the tank fill inlet on the pump panel or rear access.
  3. Monitor your level during operations — communicate it to your officer at 50% and again at 25%.
💡 Why It Matters

You are not a fire engine. You do not have a hydrant. That 250 gallons is everything you brought to the fight — treat it like it's the last water on earth until you have a fill plan.

⚡ Never Surprise Your Officer
Call it out: "Officer, we're at half tank" at 125 gallons. "Quarter tank" at ~60 gallons. A dry truck with a crew in the field is a life-safety event. When the pump cavitates from running dry, impeller damage follows fast.
🚰 200' of 1″ Hose on Hose Reel
Reel Line / Booster Reel / Forestry Reel
+
📋 What It Is

A 200-foot section of 1-inch forestry hose wound on a motor-driven or hand-driven reel mounted to the truck's rear. This is your primary attack line on Brushtruck 62 — it deploys faster than hand-laid hose and retracts for quick relocation.

🔧 How to Use
  1. To deploy: pull the nozzle end and walk it out — do not reel-out under pressure unless designed for it.
  2. Charge the line by opening the reel discharge valve at the pump panel.
  3. Attack from the burned area (the black) when possible — never from ahead of the flame front.
  4. To retract: relieve pressure first, then reel in under tension to ensure even winding.
💡 Why It Matters

Speed matters in wildland attack. The reel lets you get water on a spot fire faster than hand-laying a shoulder load. Use it.

⚠️ Reel Winding
Uneven winding causes binding on the next deploy. When reeling in, keep tension on the hose to guide it evenly across the reel drum. A jammed reel in the field wastes precious time.
🔧 Handle for Hose Reel
Reel Handle / Manual Crank / Rewind Handle
+
📋 What It Is

The manual crank or engagement handle used to operate the hose reel when the motorized drive is unavailable or for fine control during rewinding.

🔧 How to Use
  1. Used when the electric reel motor is inoperative or when manual control is preferred for precise winding.
  2. Insert or engage per manufacturer design and crank steadily — maintaining tension on the hose as it winds.
  3. Store in the designated mounting bracket when not in use.
💡 Why It Matters

If the reel motor fails, this is how you get your hose back. Know where it is before you need it.

🖤 12' Hard Suction Hose (2 sections)
Hard Sleeve / Suction Hose / Hard Suction / Drafting Hose
+
📋 What It Is

Two 12-foot sections of rigid or semi-rigid suction hose — 2½-inch diameter — with female couplings. Used to draft water from natural sources (ponds, streams, swimming pools) when no hydrant is available. Total extension: 24 feet.

🔧 How to Use
  1. Connect sections together and attach a strainer to the water end before submerging.
  2. Connect the dry end to the pump's suction inlet.
  3. Position the strainer at least 2 feet below the water surface to prevent air entrainment.
  4. Prime the pump before opening the throttle — never run a dry centrifugal pump.
  5. After use: flush with clean water, inspect for cracks, and store in designated brackets.
💡 Why It Matters

In rural wildland operations, natural water sources are your lifeline after the tank runs out. Hard suction is what bridges the gap between your pump and that pond.

⚡ Air Leaks Kill Drafting Operations
Any loose coupling, crack, or uncapped inlet will break your prime. Check every connection before priming. A failed draft when you're out of tank water ends the operation.
🪣 Metal Filter / Strainer for Suction Hose
Suction Strainer / Foot Valve / Drafting Strainer
+
📋 What It Is

A metal mesh basket strainer that attaches to the end of the hard suction hose. Prevents debris — leaves, sticks, stones — from entering and damaging the pump during drafting operations.

🔧 How to Use
  1. Attach securely to the water-end coupling of the hard suction before submerging.
  2. Position at least 2 feet below the surface and away from the bottom — silt and debris collect there.
  3. After each use, clean the strainer thoroughly — clogged mesh will prevent adequate water flow.
💡 Why It Matters

A clogged strainer = no water. A missing strainer = debris in the pump = expensive pump damage. The strainer is cheap insurance.

🔺 Metal Wheel Chock
Wheel Chock / Chock Block / Tire Chock
+
📋 What It Is

A wedge-shaped metal block placed against a tire to prevent the vehicle from rolling when parked on sloped or uneven terrain — especially critical on rural hillsides and embankments.

🔧 How to Use
  1. Place against the downhill side of a tire any time the truck is parked on a slope.
  2. Wheel chocks are a supplement to — not a replacement for — setting the parking brake.
  3. Remove before moving the apparatus and return to its bracket immediately.
💡 Why It Matters

A brush truck can weigh 10,000+ pounds. On a slope, even a "good" parking brake can fail. The chock is the backup. Use it.

⚡ Slope + No Chock = Rolling Apparatus
An unchocked apparatus on a slope that begins to roll will not stop until it hits something — or someone. This is not theoretical. Chock your truck.
⛽ Plastic Gas Tank
Fuel Can / Jerry Can / Portable Fuel Container
+
📋 What It Is

A portable plastic fuel container — typically 1 to 5 gallons — carried to provide on-scene fuel for the portable water pump and any gasoline-powered equipment.

🔧 How to Use
  1. Use approved fuel containers only — no improvised bottles or non-vented containers.
  2. Fill from the fleet fuel station, not from the apparatus tank.
  3. Label clearly: "GAS" or "DIESEL" as appropriate for the equipment it fuels.
  4. Store in the designated external bracket — never inside the cab.
  5. Inspect for cracks, seal integrity, and vent cap function on each rig check.
💡 Why It Matters

The portable pump is useless without fuel. That gas can is what keeps it running on a remote fill site. Keep it full.

⚡ No Open Flames During Fueling
Gasoline vapor is invisible and heavier than air. No fueling near ignition sources. Engine off on all equipment before fueling. Do not smoke.
🔴 2½″ Hose — 50' Section
2½-Inch / "Two-and-a-Half" / Big Line
+
📋 What It Is

A 50-foot section of 2½-inch double-jacketed cotton-synthetic hose with standard NST couplings. Heavier flow capacity than the 1-inch reel line — used for high-volume supply or supplement when attack demands exceed the reel.

🔧 How to Use
  1. Shoulder-carry or accordion-pack for deployment.
  2. Connect to the 2½-inch pump discharge outlet.
  3. Use when you need higher volume than the 1-inch reel can deliver — tank refill assist, high-output structural support.
  4. After use, drain and reload properly — a wet, improperly packed line mildens and causes delays at the next incident.
💡 Why It Matters

The reel line handles most brush work. When you need more water — structural exposure, volume fill — the 2½-inch is what steps up.

⚠️ Flow Requires Nozzle Control
Opening a 2½-inch without a nozzle in place or with an inattentive operator is a safety hazard. The reaction force alone can knock a firefighter down. Two people on a big line if conditions allow.
🔵 1½″ Hose — 150' Roll (Cross Lay)
1½-Inch / "One-and-a-Half" / Cross Lay
+
📋 What It Is

A 150-foot section of 1½-inch attack hose, loaded in a cross lay on the rear of the apparatus for fast deployment. Provides more volume than the 1-inch reel with more maneuverability than the 2½-inch.

🔧 How to Use
  1. Pull from the cross-lay from the end designated for that side — don't pull against the load.
  2. Shoulder-carry or flake out behind the truck.
  3. Connect to the designated 1½-inch pump discharge.
  4. After use, drain completely and reload in the correct cross lay configuration.
💡 Why It Matters

Cross-lay hose is fast hose. It's positioned for quick pulls, and that speed matters on a spreading brush fire.

⚠️ Reload Matters
A poorly reloaded cross lay will hang up on the next pull. Take the time to load it right every time.
🌊 Fog Nozzle
Adjustable Fog Nozzle / Combination Nozzle
+
📋 What It Is

An adjustable nozzle providing spray patterns from a straight stream to a wide-angle fog. Used for fire attack, exposure protection, and crew protection.

🔧 How to Use
  1. Adjust to straight stream for long-range attack and penetration.
  2. Adjust to narrow fog for exposure protection and indirect attack.
  3. Wide fog creates a water curtain for crew protection — but reduces range significantly.
  4. Always inspect and confirm the shut-off is in the closed position before connecting to a charged line.
💡 Why It Matters

The nozzle is your primary tool at the end of the line. Know how it works before you're standing in front of a fire. The difference between a straight stream and a fog pattern is the difference between reaching a fire and drowning out 15 feet in front of you.

⚠️ Fog vs. Wind
A wide fog pattern in a strong wind disperses before it reaches the fire. Use a straight or narrow stream in windy conditions.
06
Section 6
Rear — Hand Tools
6 items
🪶 Brush Paddles — 3 Total
Fire Swatter / Flapper / Beater
+
📋 What It Is

Flat rubber or woven-fiber paddles on long wooden handles — used to beat out flames in light fuels. Three are carried to allow crew teamwork.

🔧 How to Use
  1. Approach from the side — never from downwind or directly ahead of the flame front.
  2. Strike with a firm, flat-angle downward slap, dragging the paddle slightly toward you — this smothers the fire by cutting oxygen.
  3. Work in short strokes, moving parallel to the fire edge, not perpendicular into it.
  4. Rest the paddle periodically — rubber paddles melt with continuous flame contact.
  5. Two firefighters working in tandem (leap-frog smothering) suppress a fire line faster than one working alone.
💡 Why It Matters

Simple tool, effective technique. In light brush and grass fuels, a paddle can put out fire faster than a hose line and without the water supply concern.

⚡ Wind and Fire Behavior
Never position yourself ahead of or downwind of the flame front. Fire spreads fastest with the wind. Always work from the black (burned area) or from the flanks. Maintain your escape route.
🪝 Pike Poles — 2 Total
Pike / Hook / Ceiling Hook
+
📋 What It Is

Long-handled metal hooks used to pull apart burning or smoldering material, expose hot spots, move debris, and overhaul structure or wildland fires.

🔧 How to Use
  1. Use to rake burning debris away from structures or fuel sources.
  2. Pull burning material apart to expose hot spots for water application.
  3. Keep a firm two-handed grip — pike poles generate leverage forces that can pull you off balance.
  4. Work from outside the collapse zone when overhaul involves structural material.
💡 Why It Matters

Overhaul is where fires reignite. The pike pole lets you get into the debris without putting your hands in it. Use it.

🗽 New York Pole
NY Roof Hook / Rubbish Hook / Multi-Purpose Hook
+
📋 What It Is

A longer, heavier version of the pike pole with a modified hook head designed for pulling ceilings, opening walls, and moving large debris. Named for its origin in FDNY operations.

🔧 How to Use
  1. Use for high-reach pulling operations — ceilings, upper-floor windows, elevated debris.
  2. The weight and length provide leverage advantage over standard pike poles for dense material.
  3. Work in pairs on extended reaches — one person on the tool, one spotting for stability.
💡 Why It Matters

Bigger tool, bigger reach. When a standard pike pole isn't getting the leverage you need, the NY pole steps up.

✂️ Bolt Cutters
Wire Cutters / Gate Cutters
+
📋 What It Is

Heavy-duty compound leverage cutters for cutting through locks, chains, wire fencing, and light metal. Used for access at locked gates, fenced properties, and entanglements.

🔧 How to Use
  1. Position the jaws over the target — for locks, cut the shackle, not the body.
  2. Apply steady, even force — don't jerk or twist.
  3. Stand clear of the cut piece — severed chain or wire can snap back.
  4. After use: inspect jaws for nicks or alignment issues. Blunt jaws won't cut.
💡 Why It Matters

Rural brush fires reach private property behind locked gates. Waiting for a key costs time you don't have. Bolt cutters give you access when access is critical.

⚠️ Know When to Cut
Cutting a padlock is a property action. Your officer authorizes it. Don't freelance gate access without authorization unless there is an immediate life-safety emergency.
🪝 Halligan Bar
Haligan / Hooligan / Pry Bar / Kelly Tool / The Bar
+
📋 What It Is

A multi-purpose forged steel forcible entry tool with a fork/adz end and a pick end. The single most versatile tool in the fire service for prying, twisting, striking, and breaching.

🔧 How to Use
  1. Fork end: insert between door and frame to pry outward — pair with a flathead axe for the "irons" technique.
  2. Adz end: use for prying, chocking, or as a striking surface.
  3. Pick end: insert into gaps, keyways, or panels for leverage.
  4. Grip well back from the working end — keep hands clear of the work zone.
💡 Why It Matters

This is a fundamental tool of the fire service. Whether it's on a brush truck or a heavy rescue, knowing the Halligan is non-negotiable.

💡 Learn the Irons
The Halligan and a flathead axe, used together, are called the irons. The axe is the driver; the Halligan is the lever. Together they open most residential doors in seconds. Practice the technique.
🫙 Plastic Funnel
Fuel Funnel / Filling Funnel
+
📋 What It Is

A plastic pour funnel used to direct fuel or fluids into small-opening tanks or containers without spillage.

🔧 How to Use
  1. Used when filling the portable pump with gas from the fuel can — the pump fill neck is small.
  2. Rinse after fuel use to prevent residue buildup.
  3. Store in the designated spot — a missing funnel means fuel spills during filling.
💡 Why It Matters

Small detail. But spilling fuel when filling a pump on a wildland fire scene is a very bad look — and a genuine hazard. The funnel prevents that.

07
Section 7
Water Pump
1 item
⚙️ Portable Water Pump — 2½″ Inlet / 1½″ Outlet
Gas Pump / Honda Pump / Drafting Pump / Portable Pump
+
📋 What It Is

A small, gasoline-powered centrifugal pump — self-contained with its own engine, 2½-inch suction intake, and 1½-inch discharge outlet. Designed to draft water from natural sources when the truck's onboard pump is not optimally positioned, or to supplement supply at remote locations.

🔧 How to Use
  1. Position the pump as close to water level as practical — centrifugal pumps have a lift limit (typically 10–25 feet).
  2. Connect hard suction hose with metal strainer to the 2½-inch inlet.
  3. Connect attack or supply hose to the 1½-inch outlet.
  4. Check fuel and oil level per manufacturer markings.
  5. Cold start: choke on → pull starter cord firmly → advance choke as engine warms → set operating throttle.
  6. Prime the pump if required — confirm water at discharge before advancing throttle fully.
  7. Shutdown: reduce throttle → choke to off/run → shut off fuel valve → allow to cool before moving.
💡 Why It Matters

When the truck can't get close enough to the water, the portable pump goes where the truck can't. It turns any pond, stream, or pool into a water supply.

⚡ Inlet and Outlet Are Not Interchangeable
The 2½-inch is the inlet (suction). The 1½-inch is the outlet (discharge). Connecting to the wrong port gives you zero water. Also: never run the pump dry — impeller damage occurs rapidly without water. If prime is lost, shut down and re-prime before restarting.
08
Section 8
Hydrant Bag
9 items
🚰 Gate Valve
Hydrant Gate / Auxiliary Valve / HAV
+
📋 What It Is

A large-diameter valve installed between a hydrant outlet and your supply line, giving you local on/off flow control without shutting down the entire hydrant.

🔧 How to Use
  1. Connect the gate valve directly to the hydrant outlet before opening the hydrant.
  2. Open the hydrant fully — hydrants are designed for full open or full closed; never throttle at the stem.
  3. Control flow using the gate valve's handwheel.
  4. When done: close gate valve first, then close hydrant, then bleed the line.
💡 Why It Matters

Without a gate valve, your only flow control is the hydrant itself — repeatedly opening and closing damages the seat. The gate valve maintains full hydrant pressure while you independently manage flow.

🌊 1″ Garden Hose
Small Supply / Fill Hose / Garden Line
+
📋 What It Is

A standard 1-inch garden hose section stored in the hydrant bag for supplemental fill operations or low-flow applications where a large-diameter hose is impractical.

🔧 How to Use
  1. Connect to a garden hose fitting at the source, or to a reducer from a hydrant port.
  2. Route to tank fill inlet for slow-fill operations.
  3. Not suitable for fire attack — flow rate is insufficient.
💡 Why It Matters

When the only water source is a residential spigot or a small outdoor connection, the garden hose bridges the gap for refilling. It's slow, but it's water.

🔧 Hydrant Wrench
Spanner / Hydrant Tool / Pentagonal Wrench
+
📋 What It Is

A pentagonal-socket wrench used to open and close fire hydrants. Fits the pentagonal operating nut on top of the hydrant.

🔧 How to Use
  1. Place the socket over the pentagonal nut on top of the hydrant.
  2. Turn counter-clockwise to open, clockwise to close.
  3. Open hydrants slowly to prevent water hammer.
  4. Always open fully when hydrant is in use — partial opening causes seat damage.
💡 Why It Matters

You cannot operate a fire hydrant without the right wrench. This is non-negotiable equipment. Know where it is.

⚠️ Wrong Tool Damages Hydrant
Using an adjustable wrench or pipe wrench on a pentagonal nut rounds the corners. That hydrant may be inoperable for the next incident. Carry and use the right tool.
🔧 Small Spanner Wrench
Small Spanner / 1¾″ Spanner / Gas Shutoff Tool
+
📋 What It Is

A small hose-coupling spanner wrench fitting 1¾-inch couplings. Also used as a gas meter shutoff tool at residential structures.

🔧 How to Use
  1. Use to tighten or break 1¾-inch hose couplings when hand-tightening is insufficient.
  2. For gas shutoff: fit the square boss of the spanner over the gas meter valve stem and turn 90 degrees to shut off.
  3. Store in the hydrant bag in the designated location.
💡 Why It Matters

Two tools in one. The spanner handles hose connections and doubles as a gas shutoff at a structure fire scene — a common first action at working residential fires.

🔧 Large Spanner Wrench
Large Spanner / 5″ Spanner / LDH Spanner
+
📋 What It Is

A large hose-coupling spanner wrench fitting 5-inch large-diameter hose (LDH) Storz or threaded couplings. Required for tightening and breaking LDH connections by hand.

🔧 How to Use
  1. Use to tighten 5-inch LDH couplings at hydrant connections or relay supply points.
  2. Strike with a mallet if needed to break a stuck coupling — do not use a hammer directly on the coupling body.
💡 Why It Matters

5-inch LDH is heavy and its couplings are large. You need the right-sized tool to work it safely and efficiently.

🖤 Black Electrical Tape
Electrical Tape / E-Tape
+
📋 What It Is

General-purpose vinyl insulating tape. Used for temporary electrical insulation, labeling, and minor equipment sealing in the field.

🔧 How to Use
  1. Use for temporary electrical insulation of exposed wire ends or damaged insulation.
  2. Wrap hose coupling threads to protect them during storage.
  3. A few wraps around a coupling that won't stay tight can buy you an incident.
💡 Why It Matters

Small, lightweight, surprisingly useful. The tape goes on something that's failing and keeps it functional through the incident.

🔌 Steamer-to-Storz Connector
Storz Adaptor / Steamer Adaptor / Hydrant Adaptor
+
📋 What It Is

A brass or aluminum adaptor that converts a hydrant's 4½-inch steamer port (threaded) to a 5-inch Storz coupling. Allows connection of large-diameter hose directly to the hydrant's high-volume port.

🔧 How to Use
  1. Connect the threaded end to the steamer port of the hydrant (wrench-tight).
  2. Connect your 5-inch Storz LDH to the Storz end.
  3. Inspect threads and Storz lugs before each use — damage prevents a seal.
💡 Why It Matters

The steamer port is the highest-volume port on a hydrant. The Storz adaptor unlocks that capacity for large-diameter supply. Without this adaptor, you're limited to the smaller 2½-inch ports.

🔌 2½″ Storz Adaptors — Male and Female
Storz Male / Storz Female / 2½″ Storz / Hose Adaptor
+
📋 What It Is

A pair of Storz-pattern adaptors for 2½-inch hose — one male, one female — allowing connection of standard threaded hose to Storz-equipped apparatus or hydrant ports.

🔧 How to Use
  1. Use to interface threaded 2½-inch hose with Storz-equipped apparatus.
  2. Storz connections are quarter-turn — align, push, and twist to lock.
  3. Inspect lugs and gaskets before each use.
💡 Why It Matters

Storz is the standardized coupling used on large-diameter hose and many modern apparatus. Having both male and female adaptors means you can connect to either style of setup you encounter.

🔧 Pipe Wrench
Stillson Wrench / Plumber's Wrench
+
📋 What It Is

An adjustable wrench with serrated jaws designed to grip and turn round-stock objects — pipes, nipples, fittings — that cannot be gripped by a standard box wrench.

🔧 How to Use
  1. Adjust jaw to fit the object before applying force — the jaw self-tightens under load in one direction.
  2. Use for stubborn hydrant connections, pipe fittings, or any rounded hardware that resists other tools.
  3. Do not use on hex-head bolts or nuts — the serrated jaw will damage them.
💡 Why It Matters

In the field, you meet connections that were installed by a plumber, not a firefighter. The pipe wrench handles what a spanner cannot.

📚 How to Use This Guide

Every piece of equipment on Engine 61 has a job. Your job is to know where it lives, what it does, and how to put it to work before someone tells you to. Use this guide before every compartment check until you can walk the rig blindfolded.

Click any card title to expand the full study entry. Use the search bar to find any tool instantly. Gold callouts = safety-critical. Green callouts = rookie tips. Blue callouts = pro knowledge.

⚡

E61 vs. E62 — Know the Differences

READ THIS FIRST — before you ever ride E61
⚠️
Critical — Don't Mix These Up If you've been training on E62, pay close attention here. Several compartments are in different spots, and the airbag system is different. Grabbing the wrong tool in the wrong spot costs lives.
Driver's Side Over-Wheel Compartment
AKA: Wheel well compartment
+
📋E61 Has

Pry Axe (Officer's Tool) — E61 stores the pry axe / officer's tool here, over the driver's-side wheel.

📋E62 Has

Air Bags — E62 stores its airbags in this same over-wheel location. E61 does NOT.

📍Where are E61's Air Bags?

E61 stores its air bags in Compartment 3, bottom shelf — near the back on the driver's side. Don't go hunting for them over the wheel on this rig.

Air Bag Controllers — E61 vs. E62
AKA: Air bag control box, inflation controller
+
🔧What to Know

E61 and E62 use different air bag controller models. The controller stays with its bags — do not swap them between rigs. That said, both systems inflate to 118 PSI maximum safe operating pressure.

⚠️
Never Exceed 118 PSI Overpressure can cause a bag to rupture or blow out from under a load. Always monitor the controller gauge and stop inflation when the load is stabilized, not when the gauge maxes out.
RIT Pack — E62 Only
AKA: Rapid Intervention Team pack, PASS pack
+
📋Know the Difference

E62 carries a RIT pack on the top shelf of the rear compartment (Comp 3, Driver's Side Rear). E61 does not have a RIT pack. If you're riding E61 and get assigned a RIT role, coordinate with command regarding which rig is supplying that equipment.

⚠️
Correction (8/16/2026) — E62 Carries ONE RIT Pack, Not Two A brief source doc update on 8/15/2026 had added a second location — a RIT pack staged on the top shelf of E62's Engineer's Compartment (Comp 1). That's been corrected: E62 carries a single RIT pack, and it's in Comp 3 (Driver's Side Rear), as stated above. If you're riding E61 and get pulled onto a RIT assignment off E62, that's the only spot to check — don't waste time on the Engineer's Compartment.

Flagged from source doc, undetailed
+

The source compartment doc added a bare line item reading only "Cabin Compartment" under the E61-specific differences list, with no further detail on what changed or what it refers to. Rather than invent an explanation, this guide is flagging it as-is. If you know what this refers to, get it added to the doc properly — a one-word note like this helps nobody at 2 AM.

Hose Line Equipment
Trash Line — 100 ft, 1¾" Preconnected
AKA: Minuteman line, trash pack, bump line
+
📖What it is

A preconnected, 100-foot 1¾" attack line stored in the front cab area. It's the fastest line to pull for small, quick-knockdown fires.

❓Why it's needed

Speed matters. For dumpster fires, small vehicle fires, or any quick knock-down scenario, the trash line gets water flowing without pulling the full crosslay.

🔧How to use
  1. Confirm pump is charged and line is bled.
  2. Grab the preconnected coupling — it's ready to go.
  3. Advance the line toward the fire, keeping slack manageable.
  4. Open nozzle smoothly — avoid the water hammer of a sudden burst.
Watch: 1¾" Hose Advancement
1¾" Crosslay — 200 ft, Fog Nozzle (×2)
AKA: Minute-man load, crosslay, pre-connect
+
📖What it is

Two 200-foot 1¾" attack lines stored in the side/middle hose bed, loaded as crosslays so they can be pulled from either side of the truck. Each comes with a fog nozzle.

❓Why it's needed

The bread-and-butter residential attack line. 1¾" flows about 150–180 GPM — enough to knock down most structure fires with good mobility.

🔧How to use
  1. Grab the nozzle end from whichever side you're working.
  2. Pull the hose straight off the bed — the crosslay feeds off itself.
  3. Advance with your partner while maintaining a working loop.
  4. Fog nozzle: straight stream for penetration, wide fog for knockdown and exposure protection.
✅
Rookie TipDon't pull the entire load at once — take what you need to reach the door, then have your partner feed the line. Dragging excess hose through a structure wastes energy and creates trip hazards.
Watch: Crosslay Deployment
2½" Crosslay — 200 ft, Smooth Bore Nozzle
AKA: Big line, two-and-a-half, deuce-and-a-half
+
📖What it is

A 200-foot 2½" attack line with a smooth bore nozzle. Heavy-caliber attack — flows 250+ GPM at working pressure.

❓Why it's needed

When a 1¾" line isn't going to cut it — commercial structures, large volume fires, or when you need reach and penetration that fog can't provide. Also used for exterior master-stream support.

🔧How to use
  1. This line requires at least 2 firefighters to advance safely.
  2. Smooth bore: no pattern adjustment — aim matters. Point at the base of the fire.
  3. Coordinate closely with the pump operator — this line demands significantly more pressure.
⚠️
Nozzle ReactionA 2½" line at full flow will knock you off your feet if you're not set. Get your stance right — feet staggered, nozzle person braced, backup person directly behind pushing forward. Never open this line solo.
Watch: 2½" Line Advancement
5" Supply Hose — 30 ft (Front) + 1,000 ft (Rear Middle)
AKA: Large diameter hose, LDH, five-inch, supply line
+
📖What it is

Large diameter supply hose used to move water from the hydrant to the engine's intake. The 30-ft section up front connects quickly via Storz fitting; the 1,000-ft rear load handles long relays.

❓Why it's needed

5" flows up to 1,500+ GPM — far more than 2½" supply line. It's the artery of your water supply. Without a proper lay, you run the tank dry.

🔧How to use
  1. Front 30-ft: used for short connections, nurse tanker hookups, or finishing a lay.
  2. Rear 1,000-ft: laid from the hydrant (forward lay) or from the scene (reverse lay) as commanded.
  3. Always couple Storz fittings with the locking lug fully seated — a half-connected Storz under pressure will blow off.
⚠️
Storz Coupling — Seat It FullyStorz couplings are quarter-turn. If you hear a pop or see the coupling spinning freely under pressure, the coupling has failed. Always verify the locking lug is engaged before the engineer charges the line.
Watch: LDH Hose Lay
Highrise Pack 150' of 1 3/4"
AKA: Standpipe pack, hi-rise kit
+
📖What it is

A prepackaged kit for standpipe operations in high-rise buildings. Contains a short length of 1¾", plus connectors to attach to a building's standpipe system.

🔧Contents
  • Small length of 1¾" hose
  • 90-degree connector (bend around corners/floor outlets)
  • T connector with pressure gauge (monitor standpipe pressure)
  • Wye connector (split one outlet into two lines)
  • Vise grips (to open stiff or painted-over standpipe valves)
❓Why it's needed

In high-rises, the engine can't stretch hose up 20 floors. The building's standpipe system delivers water to each floor — you connect at the floor below the fire and advance up. The pressure gauge ensures you're not getting too much or too little pressure from the standpipe.

💡
Pro TipStandpipe pressures can be wildly variable — too high, and the nozzle reaction will throw your team; too low, and you have no reach. The T with pressure gauge lets you know what you're working with before you open the nozzle. Target ~100 PSI residual at the nozzle.
Watch: Standpipe Operations
Storz to Steamer Adapter + Hydrant Wrench
AKA: Storz adapter, steamer cap, hydrant key
+
📖What it is

Storz adapter: Converts the Storz end of 5" LDH to connect to a hydrant's 4½" steamer port (NST thread).
Hydrant wrench: Operates the hydrant's operating nut to open/close the water supply.

❓Why it's needed

Storz and NST (National Standard Thread) are two different coupling systems. The adapter bridges them. The hydrant wrench gives you mechanical advantage to open a stiff or frozen hydrant.

✅
Rookie TipOpen a hydrant slowly. A sudden surge creates water hammer that can damage the hydrant, blow hose couplings, and knock you down. Open fully — most hydrants are fully open when the stem stops turning (usually 12–15 turns). Never leave a hydrant partially open.
Blitz Fire — 300 ft, 3" Preconnected
AKA: Blitzfire, portable master stream, ground monitor
+
📖What it is

A preconnected 3" line feeding a portable ground-level master stream device (the BlitzFire monitor). It can flow 500+ GPM hands-free once set up.

❓Why it's needed

Defensive or transitional attacks on larger fires where attack lines can't safely advance. Also useful for protecting exposures. The device is self-supporting — set it, aim it, and get out.

🔧How to use
  1. Pull the 3" line and connect to the BlitzFire monitor.
  2. Position the monitor at a safe standoff distance from the structure.
  3. Aim the nozzle at your target (base of fire or exposure).
  4. Signal the engineer to charge the line.
  5. Fine-tune aim from the side — never stand directly behind a flowing master stream.
⚠️
Master Stream = Defensive OperationOperating a master stream inside an occupied or potentially occupied structure is almost always prohibited. The kinetic force of the water stream at this flow rate is powerful enough to injure firefighters inside. Confirm defensive posture before flowing.
Watch: BlitzFire Deployment
🔩

Compartment 1 — Engineer's Compartment

Driver's side · 3 shelves · Hose fittings, spanners, hydrant bag
Top Shelf
Black Tool Box
AKA: Engineer's box, maintenance kit
+
📖What it is

A portable tool box kept on the top shelf of Comp. 1, containing maintenance and utility items for the rig and equipment.

🔧Contents
  • Grease
  • 2 screwdrivers
  • Needle nose pliers
  • Carb Cleaner
  • Food-grade silicone
  • Heat gun & attachments
  • Lube stick
  • 2 Storz connectors (1 is a reducer, 30° angle)
  • Nozzle — fits deck gun and BlitzFire
  • Small utility flags (pink, 12" on wire)
❓Why it's needed

The engineer maintains the rig. This box has the tools to perform field maintenance — lubricating couplings, cleaning carbs on power equipment, and sealing threads. The food-grade silicone is used on pump packing and fittings that contact drinking water supply lines.

💡
Pro Tip — Lube StickThe lube stick is for coupling threads and gaskets. Dry-threading a coupling under fire conditions can seize it permanently. A quick swipe before connecting keeps everything moving. Check that gaskets are present and in good shape every time you lube a coupling.
Airpack (SCBA)
AKA: Air pack, bottle, self-contained breathing apparatus, SCBA
+
📖What it is

A self-contained breathing apparatus — a cylinder of compressed air worn on the back with a regulator and face mask. Provides breathable air in IDLH (immediately dangerous to life or health) environments.

❓Why it's needed

Smoke, carbon monoxide, hydrogen cyanide, and dozens of toxic gases are in every structure fire. Your lungs don't get a second chance. No air pack = no entry into a fire building. Period.

🔧Donning — Abbreviated Steps
  1. Check cylinder pressure (should be ≥90% — know your rig's minimum).
  2. Don harness — secure shoulder straps, chest strap, and waist belt.
  3. Connect regulator to face piece.
  4. Don face piece and ensure full seal (no beard — EVER under SCBA).
  5. Open cylinder valve — listen for PASS alarm test.
  6. Take 2-3 test breaths to confirm airflow.
  7. Activate PASS device in "armed" mode before entry.
⚠️
Low Air Alarm — Don't Ignore ItWhen your low-air alarm sounds, you have roughly one-third of your air remaining. That's your signal to begin exiting immediately — not finish the task, not wait for your partner. Call "mayday" if you become disoriented. The alarm is not a suggestion.
Watch: SCBA Donning Watch: Low Air Procedures
Middle Shelf — Couplings & Nozzles
Double-Ended Spanners (×2) — Storz & Hose
AKA: Spanner wrench, coupling wrench
+
📖What it is

A flat, bar-shaped wrench with different-sized hooks/jaws on each end for tightening or loosening hose couplings. Double-ended means two different sizes on one tool.

❓Why it's needed

Hose couplings tighten with water pressure. You cannot disconnect them by hand after a line has been flowed. A spanner gives you the leverage to break the coupling loose without destroying the gasket or threads.

✅
Rookie TipAlways bleed the line before trying to uncouple it. A charged hose under even residual pressure will resist uncoupling — and when it finally pops free, water and the fitting will fly. Bleed first, then spanner.
Wye Ball Valves — 2½" to 1½" (×2)
AKA: Gated wye, wye valve, wye connector
+
📖What it is

A Y-shaped fitting with one 2½" inlet and two 1½" gated outlets. Each outlet has a ball valve that can be independently opened or closed.

❓Why it's needed

Splits one supply line into two attack lines. Useful when you need two lines from one outlet — or when you're working off a standpipe port and want to feed two lines from one connection.

🔧How to use
  1. Connect the 2½" inlet to your supply (engine outlet or standpipe).
  2. Connect your 1½" attack lines to each outlet.
  3. Open the inlets independently as each team is ready.
  4. Ball valves allow one line to be shut while the other remains charged — critical in standpipe ops.
Fog Nozzles (×2)
AKA: Combination nozzle, adjustable nozzle, fog tip
+
📖What it is

An adjustable attack nozzle that delivers water in patterns ranging from a straight stream to a wide 30° or 60° fog pattern by rotating the bale or bail ring.

❓Why it's needed

Versatility. Straight stream for reach and penetration; narrow fog for compartment knockdown; wide fog for heat absorption and crew protection in doorway operations.

🔧Pattern Selection
  • Straight stream: maximum reach, minimal water loss — interior attack
  • Narrow fog (15–30°): good knockdown, cooling overhead
  • Wide fog (60°+): crew protection at door, exposure protection
⚠️
Don't Fog in a Smoke-Filled HallwayA wide fog pattern in a confined space will steam the environment — scalding anyone inside, including your crew. Use straight stream inside structures unless you know the space is clear.
Watch: Fog vs. Smooth Bore
Reducer Fittings — Multiple Sizes
AKA: Reducer, adapter, increaser
+
📖What's here
  • 2 small reducers (unspecified size)
  • 1 reducer — 1¾" to 1"
  • 1 steamer to Storz
  • 4 reducers — 2½" female to 1¾" male
  • 1 cap for 1¾"
❓Why they're needed

No two water systems use the same coupling size. Reducers and adapters let you connect mismatched hose diameters, interface with building systems, or cap unused ports. The 1¾" cap seals an unused outlet to prevent pressure loss.

💡Pro Tip

Know your reducers by heart. On a fireground you don't have time to trial-and-error. Male fittings have external threads; female fittings have internal threads. A 2½"F to 1¾"M reducer connects a larger female outlet to a smaller male hose end.

Male-to-Male & Female-to-Female Connectors
AKA: M2M, F2F, double male, double female, sexless adapters
+
📖What's here
  • 6× 2½" connectors: 2 F2F, 2 M2M, 2 CFD
  • 6× 1¾" connectors: 2 F2F, 2 M2M, 2 CFD
❓Why they're needed

Sometimes two hose ends or fittings are the same sex and won't connect. A double-male or double-female connector solves this instantly. CFD connectors are Chicago FD-standard couplings for mutual aid interoperability.

💡
Mutual Aid NoteCFD couplings ensure E61 can connect to Chicago Fire Department apparatus and vice versa. If you're on a mutual aid assignment in Chicago, your CFD connectors are your best friends. Know which pouch they're in before you go.
Bottom Shelf — Hydrant Bag
Hydrant Bag
AKA: Hydrant kit, hydrant pack
+
📖What it is

A dedicated bag containing everything needed to make a hydrant connection. Kept together so the hydrant person grabs one bag and has everything.

🔧Contents
  • 2 hydrant wrenches
  • 2 steamer-to-Storz adapters
  • 2 small spanners with gas valve notch
  • 2 wedges
  • 1¾" gate valve
  • Storz to 1¾" female
  • 3 double-ended spanners
  • Rubber mallet
  • Pipe wrench
  • Rope (for moving hose)
❓Why the rubber mallet?

Frozen hydrant caps, damaged Storz lugs, and stubborn operating nuts all happen in the field. The mallet lets you tap things into place without damaging threads. Don't hammer a coupling without it.

✅
Hydrant Person's RuleGrab the bag, lay the line, make the connect, signal the engineer, and get out of the roadway. Every second at the hydrant is a second the engine is running on tank water. Move with purpose.
25 ft of 5" LDH Supply Hose
AKA: Five-inch, large-diameter hose, supply hose, LDH
+
📖What it is

A 25-foot section of 5-inch large-diameter hose (LDH) stored on the bottom shelf of the Engineer's Compartment. Used to supplement or extend supply connections when positioning doesn't allow direct hydrant-to-engine connection.

❓Why it's needed

This short section bridges gaps in supply layouts — when the hydrant is close but not close enough for the primary supply section, this 25 feet makes up the difference without pulling a full hose load. It also provides a second short section for multi-source supply operations.

⚠️
CRITICAL SAFETY — LDH Under PressureNever stand over or step on charged 5" hose. A failed Storz connection at operating pressure is catastrophic. Always verify Storz couplings are fully seated and locked before charging. Never improvise with a partially-seated coupling.
🪓

Compartment 2 — Hand Tools & Forcible Entry

Driver's side · Irons, pike pole, bolt cutters, K-tool
Halligan Bar (Halligan)
AKA: The Hooligan, bar, Pro-bar, Halligan tool
+
📖What it is

A ~30" forged steel bar with a curved claw/fork on one end and a flat adze + pick on the other. The most versatile forcible entry tool in the fire service.

❓Why it's needed

Opens doors, windows, padlocks, walls, and floors. Vents roofs. Pulls ceilings. The Halligan does it all. It's the single most important tool for firefighter survival and rescue access.

🔧Basic Door Forcing ("The Irons")
  1. Pair with a flat-head axe to make "the irons."
  2. Place the adze (fork end) into the door gap near the lock.
  3. Drive it in with the flat-head axe.
  4. Rotate the bar to gap the door frame.
  5. Push the fork behind the bolt and lever the door open.
⚠️
Try Before You PryAlways try the door handle before forcing. More doors are unlocked than you'd think. Forcing an unlocked door wastes time and causes unnecessary damage. Maintain crew accountability while you work — don't force entry until you're ready to advance.
Watch: Halligan Door Forcing
Flat Head Axe
AKA: Pick head axe (pick end version), fire axe, striking tool
+
📖What it is

A fire service axe with a flat striking face on one side and a cutting blade on the other. Used to drive the Halligan and as a standalone cutting/breaching tool.

❓Why it's needed

Together with the Halligan, "the irons" is the #1 forcible entry combination in the fire service. The flat face drives the Halligan precisely; the blade cuts wood, breaches walls, and ventilates.

✅
Rookie Tip — Keep Your Set TogetherThe Halligan and flat-head axe should travel together as a set ("the irons"). On scene, if you have the Halligan, your partner should have the axe. Never separate them — if you need one, you need both.
Maul (Sledgehammer)
AKA: Sledge, striking tool, mall
+
📖What it is

A tool with a wedge shape on one side and a sledge hammer on the other.

❓Why it's needed

When a flat-head axe doesn't have enough mass for heavy steel doors or commercial locks, the maul provides far more striking force. Common in commercial forcible entry.

💡
Pro TipOn heavy commercial doors, pair the maul with the Halligan instead of the axe. Two-person technique: one holds the Halligan in position, the other drives it with the maul. Communication is everything — "set?" "ready" before swinging.
Closet Pike Pole
AKA: Short pike, closet hook, rubbish hook
+
📖What it is

A short (4–6 ft) version of the standard pike pole with a metal hook/pick at the end. Designed for confined spaces where a full-length pole won't maneuver.

❓Why it's needed

Pulling ceilings, opening walls, checking for fire extension in attics, and overhauling in tight spaces where the full-length hook would be unwieldy.

Bolt Cutters — Medium & Large
AKA: Bolt cutters, chain cutters, dikes (for small)
+
📖What's here

Medium: Has a hook attachment for cutting barbed wire. Large: Standard heavy-duty bolt cutters for padlocks, chains, fencing.

❓Why they're needed

Gates, fences, padlocked doors, and chain-link fencing stand between you and access to victims or a fire. Bolt cutters defeat them without power tools or prying.

🔧How to use
  1. Open the handles fully for maximum jaw spread.
  2. Position jaws on the hardened shackle of a padlock — NOT on the lock body.
  3. Apply force in a smooth, controlled squeeze — don't jerk.
  4. For barbed wire: use the medium cutter with hook to capture and cut individual wires while keeping wire tension away from your face.
⚠️
Barbed Wire HazardCut barbed wire under tension snaps back with serious injury potential. Always cut with face protection on, cut one wire at a time, and release tension before reaching past the cut point. Use the medium cutter's hook to manage wire position.
Captain's Tool / Pry Axe (Officer's Tool)
AKA: Officers tool, Pry-axe, Pak-Tool, Pro-tool
+
📖What it is

A multi-purpose hand tool combining a prying edge, striking face, and sometimes a hook or pike — all in a compact form an officer can carry alongside a radio. E61 stores this on the inside swinging door of Comp. 2 AND over the driver's-side wheel.

❓Why it's needed

Officers need a tool they can carry without dropping a radio. The officer's tool gives them enough capability to probe conditions, force a door, or pry debris without needing a full set of irons.

K-Tool (in Leather Case)
AKA: K-tool, lock puller, key tool
+
📖What it is

A metal tool shaped like a "K" that extracts lock cylinders from commercial door locks, allowing a key to be inserted in the exposed mechanism to open the door without damaging the door itself.

❓Why it's needed

On commercial properties, forcing a door destroys expensive hardware and leaves the building unsecured. The K-tool provides less-damaging entry — hook it over the lock cylinder, drive it in with the Halligan, then use a key or pick to turn the mechanism.

🔧How to use
  1. Slide the K-tool over the lock cylinder face.
  2. Drive the tool down with a striking tool (usually the flat-head axe) to bite into the cylinder.
  3. Use the Halligan as a lever to pull the cylinder out of the door.
  4. Insert a key or use a set screw tool to operate the exposed lock mechanism.
Watch: K-Tool Technique
Manhole Cover Remover
AKA: Manhole tool, pick hook, cover lifter
+
📖What it is

A heavy-duty hooked or pinned tool that engages the recessed hole or slot in a manhole cover, allowing it to be safely lifted and moved without fingers getting pinched.

❓Why it's needed

Manhole covers can weigh 100–300 lbs. Gas leaks, electrical fires, or rescue situations underground require access. Never try to pry a manhole cover with a Halligan — use the right tool.

⚠️
Before Opening a ManholeA confined space with a potential gas or electrical emergency can have explosive or IDLH concentrations at the rim. Use your gas meter (4-gas or HCN meter from the cab) BEFORE opening. NEVER lean over an open manhole.
Air Tanks — Outside of Comp. 2 (×3)
AKA: SCBA cylinders, air bottles, spare cylinders
+
📖What it is

Spare SCBA air cylinders stored on the exterior face of Compartment 2. These are ready for cylinder swap when a primary cylinder runs low on extended operations.

❓Why it's needed

A standard SCBA cylinder gives roughly 30–45 minutes of air at moderate exertion. Extended fires, technical rescues, or large structure searches exceed this. Spare cylinders extend air supply for crew rotations.

✅
Check During Every Rig CheckVerify all 3 spare cylinders are full (≥90% rated pressure) every shift check. A spare cylinder found empty when someone needs it has zero value.
💨

Compartment 3 — Rescue, Ventilation & Air Bags

Driver's side · Air bags · Fan · Cellar nozzle · Work lights
Cellar Nozzle on a Cellar Pipe
AKA: Bresnan distributor, cellar pipe, distributor nozzle
+
📖What it is

A rotating distributor nozzle attached to a rigid or semi-rigid pipe. When inserted through a small hole in a floor or ceiling, the nozzle spins and distributes water in a 360° pattern into the space below or above.

❓Why it's needed

Cellar fires and sub-floor fires are extremely dangerous to attack directly. The cellar pipe lets you put water into that space from above through a small opening, without sending a crew into a deadly below-grade environment.

🔧How to use
  1. Identify the fire location below the floor.
  2. Cut or locate a small access hole in the floor (6–8" is typically enough).
  3. Connect the cellar pipe to a charged 2½" or 3" attack line.
  4. Lower the rotating nozzle through the hole.
  5. Open the line — the nozzle spins and distributes water throughout the space.
💡
Rarely Used, But Critical When NeededKnow where this tool is and how it works before you need it. Cellar fires are disproportionately deadly. You don't want to be learning this tool's location while standing on a burning floor.
Watch: Cellar Pipe Operation
Portable Work Lights (×2)
AKA: Scene lights, work lights, portable lights, Akron lights
+
📖What it is

Battery-powered portable LED lights for illuminating incident scenes, interior search areas, and work zones. These appear to be Akron brand units.

❓Why it's needed

Smoke, night operations, and power outages mean zero visibility. Work lights illuminate scenes for victim search, overhaul, and crew safety. They also signal the scene perimeter to incoming vehicles.

✅
Always Verify Charge on Rig CheckPortable lights that aren't charged are useless. Check the battery indicator every shift. If a light is dead when you need it at 3 AM, that's a preventable problem that starts with you during the morning check.
Ventilation Fan
AKA: PPV fan, positive pressure fan, smoke ejector, blower
+
📖What it is

A high-volume fan used to push fresh air into a structure (PPV — positive pressure ventilation) to clear smoke and improve visibility and air quality for firefighters and victims.

❓Why it's needed

Smoke is the #1 killer in structure fires — it kills more victims than flames. Rapid ventilation removes smoke, improves survivability for trapped occupants, and improves firefighter visibility.

🔧How to use (PPV)
  1. Position the fan 6–8 feet from the entry door opening.
  2. Fan cone should cover the entire door opening — no gaps.
  3. Open a single exit point (window or door) on the opposite side of the structure.
  4. Start the fan — air enters, smoke exits the designated opening.
  5. Control the exit opening to direct flow through fire areas.
⚠️
Always Plug It In After UseThe document specifically notes: "Make sure it's plugged in." This fan is likely corded or rechargeable. A dead or uncharged fan is useless on scene. After every use — check it in, plug it in.
⚠️
PPV Can Accelerate FireNever start a PPV fan unless the fire is controlled or suppressed. Pushing fresh air into an active fire feeds it oxygen and can cause flashover or rapid fire spread. Always coordinate PPV with attack crew — "PPV on my mark."
Watch: PPV Ventilation
Air Bags — 3 Bags + Yellow Control Box
AKA: Pneumatic lifting bags, rescue air bags, high-pressure bags
+
📖What it is

Flat, flexible bags made of reinforced rubber/neoprene that inflate with compressed air to lift extremely heavy loads — vehicles, collapsed structural elements, machinery. The yellow control box regulates inflation from the air supply.

❓Why it's needed

Vehicle accidents, building collapses, and industrial entrapment create situations where a victim is pinned under hundreds or thousands of pounds. Air bags can lift a loaded school bus. They work where hydraulic spreaders can't reach.

🔧How to use
  1. Assess the load — identify the lift point and anticipated travel distance.
  2. Place cribbing before inflating — never trust the bag alone to hold a load.
  3. Insert the bag in the smallest gap possible (bags work best at low profiles).
  4. Connect the supply hose from an air cylinder to the control box, then bag to controller.
  5. Inflate slowly — watch cribbing, watch load movement.
  6. Maximum inflation: 118 PSI. Stop at load cleared, not max pressure.
  7. Crib as you go — one inch up, one inch of wood in.
⚠️
Never Stack More Than Two BagsStacking more than two bags creates instability. Use the largest bag on the bottom. If you need more height, build cribbing boxes instead. A collapsed stack under a load is catastrophic.
⚠️
Crib As You Go — Always"One inch up, one inch of wood in." Cribbing catches the load if the bag fails or is punctured. An uncribbed load can fall back on the victim and the crew. This is non-negotiable technique.
Watch: Air Bag Rescue Operations
Cribbing
AKA: Box crib, step chocks, crib blocks, wood cribbing
+
📖What it is

Short sections of hardwood (usually 4"×4" or 6"×6") used to stabilize and support loads — primarily vehicles and structural elements during rescue operations.

❓Why it's needed

Vehicles and structures can shift, collapse, or move unexpectedly during rescue. Cribbing locks the load in place, protecting both the victim and the rescue crew from sudden movement.

💡
Build Box CribsCross-layer wood in alternating directions to build stable box structures. A properly built box crib can support tons of weight. Practice building them before the call — it's a fundamental skill that directly determines whether people live or die.
Small Step Ladder
AKA: Step stool, A-frame ladder, folding ladder
+
📖What it is

A compact, self-supporting A-frame step ladder for short elevation gains — accessing elevated equipment, vehicle rooflines, or performing above-head work.

❓Why it's needed

Not every access challenge requires a ground ladder. The step ladder is faster to deploy and provides a stable work platform for things like breaking skylights, accessing elevated machinery, or working on vehicle roofs.

Transformer Nozzles
AKA: Piercing nozzle, through-the-lock nozzle, small opening applicator
+
📖What it is

Specialty nozzles designed to deliver water spray through very small openings — a keyhole, vent hole, or small drilled entry — into a burning void, wall, or enclosed space without requiring a full opening.

❓Why it's needed

Some fires in voids, walls, or enclosed machinery can't be reached through normal attack lines without major destructive opening. Transformer nozzles deliver water precisely into the fire area through a minimal opening.

🚗

Rear Middle — Extrication Equipment

Hurst tools · Hydraulic ram · Reciprocating saw · Batteries
Hurst Rescue Cutter
AKA: Jaws of Life (cutter), hydraulic cutter, extrication cutter
+
📖What it is

A battery-powered hydraulic cutting tool with hardened steel blades capable of cutting through vehicle A, B, C posts, door hinges, and roof metal. Part of the "jaws of life" system.

❓Why it's needed

Modern vehicles have high-strength steel (UHSS/AHSS) and airbag systems that make manual extrication impossible. The Hurst cutter severs structural steel in seconds to create relief cuts and free entrapped patients.

🔧Key Techniques
  1. Power the tool with a charged Hurst battery (6 available — top shelf).
  2. Position blades perpendicular to the cut location — not at an angle.
  3. Cut away from the patient — always direct cut debris away from the victim.
  4. A/B/C post cuts: cut low, then high on each post to remove the roof.
  5. Keep the cutting blades 6+ inches from airbag cylinders and SRS components.
⚠️
Hybrid/EV Vehicles — Disconnect Power FirstElectric and hybrid vehicles carry high-voltage battery packs (300–800V). Cutting into certain areas without first disconnecting the 12V auxiliary battery or using the emergency cut-off can electrocute the crew. Always identify vehicle type before starting extrication and consult the ERG.
Watch: Hurst Cutter Technique
Hurst Rescue Spreader
AKA: Jaws of Life (spreader), hydraulic spreader, spreaders
+
📖What it is

A battery-powered hydraulic spreading tool with two arms that open and close to pry apart vehicle components. Also has a chained grab function for pulling.

❓Why it's needed

Opens crumpled doors, displaces dashboards, and spreads door frames to create space around a pinned victim. Often the first tool deployed at an extrication.

🔧Basic Operations
  1. Insert tips into a gap (door crease, frame edge).
  2. Activate spread — tips push apart, opening the gap.
  3. Reposition deeper as the gap opens.
  4. For door removal: spread the hinge area, then cut hinges, then spread the latch.
  5. For dashboard displacement: use in combination with the Hydraulic Ram.
✅
Always Protect the PatientBefore using any power tool near a victim, cover them with a salvage cover or backboard to protect from glass, metal shards, and debris. Have a dedicated crew member maintaining patient contact throughout extrication.
Watch: Spreader Extrication
Hydraulic Ram
AKA: Ram, extension ram, pushing ram, porto-power
+
📖What it is

A hydraulic cylinder that extends under pressure to push components apart — primarily used for dash displacement and steering column relief.

❓Why it's needed

In frontal crashes, the dashboard and firewall can intrude onto a victim's lower body. The ram pushes the dash forward and up, creating space for the patient. The Quick Kick ram support (silver with teeth) anchors the ram against seat frames or floor structures.

💡
Quick Kick SupportThe Quick Kick (silver, toothed support) is the ram's base anchor. Without it, the ram slides and you lose purchase. Always set the Quick Kick first — it locks against the seat rail or vehicle floor structure to give the ram something to push against.
Watch: Dashboard Displacement
Reciprocating Saw
AKA: Recip saw, Sawzall, demo saw, hack saw (power)
+
📖What it is

A battery-powered reciprocating saw for cutting through vehicle components, seat belt anchors, convertible top mechanisms, plastics, and thin structural elements that the hydraulic tools can't address.

❓Why it's needed

Some extrication problems require precision cuts in tight spaces. The recip saw excels at cutting seat belt anchor bolts, plastic interior panels, and soft-top vehicle materials where hydraulic tools are too large or damaging.

⚠️
Blade Selection MattersA metal-cutting blade must be used for metal — a wood blade will bind and fail. Check blade type before use. When cutting near the patient, use controlled short strokes and shield with your off-hand when possible.
Window Punch
AKA: Glass punch, spring punch, Resqme tool
+
📖What it is

A spring-loaded punch tool that shatters tempered glass (side and rear windows) with a single strike to the corner of the glass, causing it to crumble into small, relatively harmless pieces.

❓Why it's needed

Fastest method for accessing a vehicle through a side window. Works in seconds — no setup required. Used before the hydraulic tools to give immediate access to the patient for assessment.

⚠️
Works on Tempered Glass OnlyLaminated glass (front windshields and some rear windows on newer vehicles) will NOT break with a window punch — it's designed to flex. Use the recip saw or cutter on laminated glass. Always identify glass type before striking.
Hurst Batteries (×6) + Battery-to-AC Connector
AKA: Tool batteries, Hurst power cells, portable power
+
📖What it is

Six high-capacity batteries powering the cordless Hurst extrication system (cutter, spreader, ram). The battery-to-AC connector (noted with asterisks in the document — meaning it's critical) allows AC power tools to run off the battery system when needed.

❓Why it's needed

The battery-powered Hurst system gives you complete mobility — no hydraulic hose management. Six batteries ensure extended operations without power interruption. The asterisks in the document signal this connector as especially important to know.

⚠️
Check Battery Charge Every ShiftAll 6 batteries should be fully charged and rotating in the charging system. A dead battery during extrication means restarting with a fresh battery — precious seconds lost. The battery-to-AC connector should also be inventoried — its asterisks indicate it was specifically flagged as important.
Double-Ended Spanners (×2)
AKA: Spanner wrench — see C1-03 for full entry
+
📋Note

Additional set of double-ended spanners stored in the rear middle compartment — same tool as Comp. 1. Having spanners in multiple locations ensures they're always accessible regardless of which side of the rig you're working. See C1-03 for full usage details.

🪝

Rear — Left Side & Backboards

New York hooks · Attic ladder · Backboards
New York Hooks — 6 ft & 8 ft
AKA: NY hook, drywall hook, plaster hook, long-handled hook
+
📖What it is

A long pole with a narrow, hardened hook at the end — specifically designed for pulling drywall and plaster ceilings and walls during overhaul and search operations. The narrow hook reaches into wall cavities easily.

❓Why it's needed

Overhaul — pulling burned ceilings and walls to expose hidden fire — is how you prevent rekindles. The NY hook's narrow profile gets between studs and lath better than a pike pole, making it more effective in modern construction.

💡
6 ft vs. 8 ftUse the shorter 6-ft hook in tighter spaces (hallways, small rooms). The 8-ft gives you standoff distance from burning material. Always pull ceilings from a doorway or corner — not under them. What goes up comes down on your head.
Attic Ladder — 10 ft
AKA: Folding ladder, attic ladder, interior ladder
+
📖What it is

A compact, lightweight folding ladder (10 feet) used primarily for attic access through ceiling hatches or pull-down openings.

❓Why it's needed

Attic fires require access above the ceiling line. The attic ladder fits through standard 22"×30" attic openings and provides stable access for firefighters and hose lines.

⚠️
Test Before You Trust ItBefore sending a firefighter up an attic ladder at a working fire, ensure the attic floor structure is intact. Sound the floor with your tool before committing weight. Attic fires weaken truss construction rapidly.
Backboards (×2)
AKA: Long backboard, spine board, LSB
+
📖What it is

Full-length rigid plastic or composite boards used to immobilize trauma patients with suspected spinal injuries during rescue and transport.

❓Why it's needed

Motor vehicle accidents, falls, and structural collapses create spinal injury risk. Moving a patient with an unstable spinal fracture without immobilization can cause permanent paralysis or death.

✅
Protect First, Move SecondThe board isn't just for transport — it's a tool to control the patient during extrication. Slide it into position before lifting, maintain inline stabilization throughout, and never rush spinal packaging under pressure.
🔐

Compartment 5 — Officer Side Forcible Entry & Search

Axes · Search rope · RASP · PFDs · Tool box
Pick Head Axe / Fire Axe
AKA: Pickhead axe, fire axe, pick axe
+
📖What it is

An axe with a cutting blade on one side and a pointed pick on the other. The pick is used to pierce roofing materials, pry up floorboards, and get purchase on surfaces the blade can't grab.

❓Why it's needed

Roof ventilation, floor breaching, and opening utility boxes. The pick end gets into tight spots where the Halligan adze would be unwieldy.

RASP — 200 ft Search Rope
AKA: Search line, safety rope, tag line, RASP rope
+
📖What it is

A 200-foot search rope with marker beads every 100 feet and butterfly knot stoppers. Used to guide search teams through large, zero-visibility structures and to navigate back to the exit.

❓Why it's needed

In a large structure fire with zero visibility, disorientation kills firefighters. The RASP rope provides a physical lifeline — follow it one way to go deeper, follow it back to exit. The beads and knots tell you how far you've traveled without seeing anything.

🔧How to use
  1. Anchor the rope at the door or entry point.
  2. One firefighter manages the rope bag; the team advances.
  3. Feel the bead markers — 1 bead at 100 ft, 2 beads at 200 ft (know your rig's system).
  4. Butterfly knots are stoppers — don't slide past them without accounting for them.
  5. To exit: reverse direction, follow the rope hand-over-hand to the anchor point.
⚠️
Never Separate from the RopeIf you lose contact with the RASP rope in zero visibility, you are lost. In a hostile environment, you have minutes. Maintain contact at ALL times. If your partner loses the rope, stop — don't advance until they regain contact.
Watch: Search Rope Techniques
Pig Drain Cover
AKA: Drain cover, spill containment mat, drain plug, storm drain cover
+
📖What it is
