A flexible, impermeable cover designed to seal over storm drains to prevent contaminated water from hazmat incidents, spills, or firefighting runoff from entering the storm sewer system. This is NOT the same as the Pig Tool / Pig / Pig Axe — that is a separate striking tool (a pig axe with a pick on one side and a flat head on the other). Three separate items, three different jobs.

❓Why it's needed

Fireground runoff contains hydrocarbons, fire suppressants, and chemical contamination. Environmental regulations require containment when possible. Covering storm drains prevents pollutant discharge — it's both legal compliance and environmental protection.

💡
Pig Tool vs. Pig vs. Pig Drain CoverThe "Pig Tool" (also called "the Pig" or "Pig Axe") is a striking tool — pick on one side, flat head on the other. The "Pig Drain Cover" is this storm-drain mat. Don't confuse them on a radio call.
Utility Rope Bags ×2 — 150 ft each
AKA: Utility line, general-purpose rope, throw rope
+
📖What it is

A general-purpose 100-foot rope (length to be confirmed) for non-life-safety applications — moving hose, securing equipment, pulling items, or improvised rigging.

❓Why it's needed

Utility rope is the duct tape of the fireground. Securing ladders, moving debris, creating makeshift lines — a good length of utility rope solves problems across every kind of emergency.

⚠️
NOT a Life-Safety RopeUtility rope is not rated for life-safety applications. Never use it to support the weight of a person during rescue or rappel operations. Life-safety rescue requires NFPA 1983-rated rope. Know the difference.
Red Bag — 4 PFDs & 1 Throw Preserver
AKA: Life jackets, personal flotation devices, throw bag, ring buoy
+
📖What it is

PFDs: US Coast Guard-approved life jackets providing buoyancy for water rescue operations. Throw preserver: A ring buoy or weighted throw bag tossed to a victim to provide flotation without entering the water.

❓Why it's needed

Water rescue calls — vehicle in water, flood rescue, ice rescue. You need flotation before entering any water environment. The throw preserver allows victim contact without crew entering the water — always the preferred first step.

⚠️
Don Before You Go Near WaterA PFD does no good on the truck. Put it on before approaching any water hazard — even shallow water. Fast-moving water above ankle depth has enough force to knock you down. Donning a PFD takes 15 seconds; drowning takes less.
W-Tool
AKA: Battery ram, hydraulic spreading tool, door jam spreader
+
📖What it is

A hydraulic hand tool for spreading door jambs and frames, particularly on residential doors. Can also be used as a compact battery-powered ram to drive breaching operations.

❓Why it's needed

When a Halligan won't give you enough gap on a reinforced door, the W-tool provides hydraulic spreading force to overcome deadbolts and security doors.

Tool Box — General Hand Tools
AKA: Maintenance tool box, utility kit
+
🔧Contents (full list)
  • Screwdrivers (various sizes)
  • Socket wrench + sockets
  • Hacksaw
  • Box cutter
  • Zip ties
  • Tape measure
  • Pipe wrench
  • Hammer
  • Teflon tape
  • Adjustable crescent wrench
  • Small crowbar
  • Wire cutters
  • Window glazing tool
  • Razor scraper
  • Small sledgehammer
  • Voltage tester ⚡⚡⚡
  • Allen key wrench set
  • Pliers
  • Punch
  • 3 metric box wrenches (18mm + 2 others)
⚠️Voltage Tester — Critical Item

The asterisks (***) in the document flag the voltage tester as especially important. Used to verify whether electrical systems are energized before cutting, breaching, or working near them. Always test before you touch anything electrical.

⚠️
Voltage Tester — Don't Skip This StepThe voltage tester is in this box for a reason. At vehicle accidents, utility emergencies, and building fires, electrical hazards are present. Touch a live wire without testing first and you become a patient. Test. Every. Time.
🌊

Compartment 6 — Middle Officer / Water Rescue

Mustang suit · PFD · Ice rescue · Rope bag · Air bottles
Mustang Suit
AKA: Dry suit, immersion suit, survival suit, survival drysuit
+
📖What it is

A Mustang brand dry/immersion suit that provides thermal protection and buoyancy for firefighters performing water rescue operations. Keeps the wearer dry and insulated from cold water.

❓Why it's needed

Cold water incapacitation happens fast — in 50°F water, you can lose swimming ability in under 3 minutes and lose consciousness in 30. The Mustang suit provides the thermal protection needed for an effective rescue.

⚠️
Wear with a PFD AlwaysThe Mustang suit provides buoyancy but it is not a substitute for a PFD. Always wear the PFD over the suit. In moving water, the combination provides critical redundancy if you go under.
Ice Spikes & Ice Cleats
AKA: Ice awls, ice picks, ice claws, crampons (cleats)
+
📖What it is

Ice spikes: Hand-held picks worn around the neck — if you fall through ice, you jam them into the ice surface to pull yourself out. Ice cleats: Traction devices that strap to boots for walking on ice without falling.

❓Why it's needed

Ice rescue — a victim (or rescuer) falls through frozen surface ice. The spikes are the only reliable way to self-rescue from an ice breakthrough. The cleats let you approach the hole without becoming a victim yourself.

⚠️
Never Go Onto Ice AloneIce rescue requires a complete system: cleats on your boots, spikes around your neck, PFD on your chest, a safety rope secured to shore, and a tender holding the line. You don't approach open ice without all of these in place. Period.
Watch: Ice Rescue Techniques
Rope Throw Bag
AKA: Throw bag, rescue throw rope, toss bag
+
📖What it is

A bag filled with floating rescue rope, designed to be thrown to a victim in the water. The rope feeds out of the bag as it travels, deploying 50–75 feet of line in a single throw.

❓Why it's needed

Throw before you go — it's the fastest and safest first intervention in water rescue. Reach, throw, wade, row, go — in that order. The throw bag can reach a victim in seconds without endangering a rescuer.

🔧How to throw
  1. Open the bag top. Hold the free end of the rope — do NOT let go of it.
  2. Identify your target. Aim past them — the rope lands across them.
  3. Underhand throw for accuracy; overhead for distance.
  4. Tell the victim: "CATCH!"
  5. Once they grab the rope, brace yourself and let them swing to shore.
  6. If miss: re-stuff the bag quickly, or hand over hand to retrieve and rethrow.
Watch: Throw Bag Technique
Life Safety Ring
AKA: Ring buoy, life ring, life preserver ring, throw ring
+
📖What it is

A buoyant ring thrown to a victim to place around their body, providing flotation while they are pulled to safety.

❓Why it's needed

For conscious victims who can actively grab something — the ring is larger and more visible than a throw bag rope, making it easier to grab in a panic. Also used when a victim is exhausted and can't hold a rope.

Strap with 3 Carabiners
AKA: Rescue strap, webbing with biners, rescue system
+
📖What it is

A flat webbing strap with three carabiners for quickly constructing a simple rescue haul or anchor system, or securing a victim during a rescue.

❓Why it's needed

Creates quick anchor points, secures victims to stretchers, or provides a simple redirect in a water rescue haul system. Carabiners allow fast attachment without knots under stress.

Water Helmet
AKA: Swift water helmet, rescue helmet, water rescue helmet
+
📖What it is

A specialized helmet designed for water rescue — lighter than a structural helmet, with drainage holes, and a positive buoyancy design that won't drag you under if it fills with water.

❓Why it's needed

Head protection in water rescue environments. Water can push you into submerged debris, bridge structures, or rocks. Your structural fire helmet is not appropriate for water rescue — it's heavy, doesn't drain, and can actually trap you.

Air Bottles — Under Compartment (×4, 2 per side)
AKA: SCBA spare cylinders — see C2-09 for full entry
+
📍Location Note

Four additional SCBA air cylinders stored under the middle officer compartment — 2 on each side. Combined with the 3 spare cylinders outside Comp. 2, Engine 61 carries 7 spare SCBA cylinders total. Check all of them every shift.

🧯

Compartment 7 — Extinguishers & Special Hazards

Silver bullet · ABC · CO2 · K-class · Fire blanket · Oil dry
Silver Bullet — Pressurized Water Extinguisher
AKA: Water can, pressurized water, stored-pressure water extinguisher
+
📖What it is

A silver stainless steel pressurized water extinguisher — approximately 2.5 gallons of water under stored pressure. Effective on Class A fires (wood, paper, cloth, plastic).

❓Why it's needed

Small incipient Class A fires — trash fires, small outdoor fires, smoldering materials — are handled with the water can without pulling a full hose line. Also used for cooling hot spots during overhaul.

⚠️
NEVER on Electrical or Cooking OilWater on energized electrical equipment causes electrocution risk. Water on hot cooking oil causes a violent steam explosion (Class K fires). Use the correct extinguisher for the correct fire class — always.
ABC Dry Chemical Extinguisher
AKA: Dry chem, multi-purpose extinguisher, monoammonium phosphate
+
📖What it is

A dry chemical extinguisher effective on Class A (ordinary combustibles), Class B (flammable liquids), and Class C (electrical) fires. Contains monoammonium phosphate powder under nitrogen pressure.

❓Why it's needed

The most versatile portable extinguisher — handles most common fire types. Critically useful for flammable liquid spill fires and vehicle fires before lines are deployed.

🔧PASS Technique
  • Pull the pin
  • Aim at the base of the fire
  • Squeeze the handle
  • Sweep side to side at the base of the flames
💡
Residue IssueABC dry chem leaves a highly corrosive residue that destroys electronics and engine components. Don't use it inside a vehicle or on electrical equipment unless you have no other option. It will cause significant secondary damage.
CO₂ Extinguisher
AKA: Carbon dioxide extinguisher, CO2 can
+
📖What it is

A carbon dioxide extinguisher (Class B and C). Discharges a cloud of CO₂ gas that displaces oxygen and cools the fire — leaves no residue.

❓Why it's needed

Ideal for electrical fires and sensitive equipment (server rooms, vehicle interiors, laboratory equipment) where residue from dry chemical would cause massive secondary damage.

⚠️
Short Range + Oxygen DisplacementCO₂ is effective only at close range (3–5 feet). In confined or enclosed spaces, the CO₂ cloud can displace enough oxygen to incapacitate the user. Don't use CO₂ in a small enclosed space without ventilation — and never hold the horn directly with bare hands (it reaches -110°F and causes frostbite).
Class K Extinguisher
AKA: K-class, wet chemical, kitchen extinguisher
+
📖What it is

A wet chemical extinguisher designed specifically for high-temperature cooking oil and fat fires (Class K). Discharges a fine mist of alkaline solution that saponifies (turns to soap) cooking oil, preventing re-ignition.

❓Why it's needed

Restaurant kitchen fires. Cooking oil superheats far above the autoignition point. Water causes a violent explosion (steam + oil mist = fireball). The K-class extinguisher is the only safe option for these fires.

⚠️
Cooking Oil Fire = Class K ONLYNever use water or ABC dry chem on a burning fryer or deep fat. The violent steam explosion from water can project burning oil 20+ feet. Know your fire class. In a restaurant kitchen: turn off the heat, cover the pan if possible, use the K-class extinguisher.
Watch: Class K Fire Demonstration
Fire Blanket — Electric Vehicle
AKA: EV fire blanket, battery fire suppression blanket, EV suppression blanket
+
📖What it is

A large-format fire-suppression blanket designed to be draped over an electric vehicle undergoing battery thermal runaway. It contains and suppresses the fire while reducing heat release and toxic gas dispersion.

❓Why it's needed

EV battery fires (thermal runaway) are extraordinarily difficult to extinguish with conventional hose lines — they can require tens of thousands of gallons of water applied directly into the battery pack. The EV blanket offers a viable containment strategy while protecting exposures and the public.

⚠️
EV Fires Are Not Standard Car FiresA lithium-ion battery in thermal runaway generates its own oxygen — you cannot smother it. The blanket suppresses, it does not extinguish. Plan for extended operations, toxic gas exposure, and potential re-ignition hours after apparent suppression. SCBA is mandatory throughout.
Watch: EV Fire Tactics
Oil Dry
AKA: Kitty litter, absorbent, oil absorbent, clay absorbent, floor dry, Speedy Dry
+
📖What it is

Granular clay absorbent material used to soak up fuel, oil, and other liquid spills on roadways and at incident scenes.

❓Why it's needed

Vehicle accidents routinely spill fuel, oil, and transmission fluid. These create slip hazards and fire risks. Spreading absorbent neutralizes the hazard, allows the roadway to be reopened, and complies with spill containment requirements.

🪜

Above Compartments — Ladders & Pike Poles

Ground ladder 24 ft · Extension ladder 14 ft · 2 pike poles
Ground Ladder — 24 ft
AKA: Extension ladder, 24-foot ladder, ground ladder
+
📖What it is

A 24-foot aluminum two-section extension ladder. Reaches second and third floor windows for rescue and firefighter egress. Extended to working length by the halyard (rope) system.

❓Why it's needed

Rescue from upper floors. Firefighter access and egress routes. Ventilation access to upper-floor windows. Your ladder is your second way out when interior conditions deteriorate.

🔧Placement
  1. Base of ladder: 1 foot out for every 4 feet of height (75° working angle).
  2. Tip should extend 3 rungs above the roofline or windowsill.
  3. Butt the feet — engage the spur into the ground or have a spotter foot the ladder.
  4. Heel the ladder against the building before climbing.
⚠️
Throw Early — Don't WaitThrow your ladders on arrival, before you need them for rescue. A ladder thrown after a Mayday is often too late. As part of your initial size-up, identify ladder placement opportunities for every floor with potential occupants.
Watch: Ground Ladder Operations
Roof Ladder — 14 ft
AKA: Extension ladder (short), 14-foot roof ladder
+
📖What it is

A shorter 14-foot extension ladder for first-floor window access, low roof access, or bridging gaps. Also effective as a utility ladder in tight areas.

❓Why it's needed

The 24-footer is overkill for a first-floor window rescue. The 14-footer is faster to throw, easier to carry alone, and gets the job done in most residential first-floor scenarios.

Pike Poles — 6 ft & 8 ft (Above Compartments)
AKA: Pike pole, plaster hook, overhaul hook, ceiling hook
+
📖What it is

Long poles with a sharp hook and pointed tip for pulling ceiling and wall materials during overhaul and fire attack. The 6-ft and 8-ft lengths offer different reach options.

❓Why it's needed

Fire hides in walls, ceilings, and void spaces. Overhaul means pulling everything that could conceal a smoldering ember. A pike pole lets you do this with standoff distance from debris and potential falling materials.

✅
Pull Toward You, Not Over YouAlways pull ceiling material toward you and to the side — never directly overhead. A ceiling full of wet plaster and debris is extremely heavy and will injure you if it lands on you. Work from a doorway when possible.
🚨

Inside Cab

Medical gear · Gas monitors · Radios · ERG · Vests
Red Jump Bag — "First In"
AKA: First-in bag, jump bag, trauma bag, med bag
+
📖What it is

The primary EMS/first aid response bag grabbed on arrival at any medical or trauma emergency. Contains initial assessment and stabilization equipment.

❓Why it's needed

Most fire department responses are medical. The first-in bag gets you to the patient with the tools to assess and begin treatment within seconds of arriving on scene.

Green Airway Bag
AKA: Airway kit, airway bag, airway management bag
+
📖What it is

A dedicated bag containing airway management equipment — BVM (bag-valve mask), suction, oral/nasal airways, and oxygen delivery devices.

❓Why it's needed

Airway management is the most critical skill in emergency medicine. A secured airway is the first priority on any unconscious or respiratory-distressed patient. This bag ensures you have everything to manage it.

AED — Automated External Defibrillator (ZOLL)
AKA: AED, defib, defibrillator, shock box
+
📖What it is

A ZOLL automated external defibrillator that analyzes cardiac rhythm and delivers an electrical shock to restore normal rhythm in ventricular fibrillation (VF) or pulseless ventricular tachycardia (VT).

❓Why it's needed

Cardiac arrest survival drops ~10% for every minute without defibrillation. Early defibrillation is the most effective treatment for shockable cardiac rhythms. This is the difference between life and death.

🔧Operation
  1. Power on — follow audio/visual prompts.
  2. Attach pads: upper right chest + lower left side (or as labeled).
  3. Ensure no one is touching the patient: "I'm clear, you're clear, everyone clear!"
  4. AED analyzes rhythm automatically.
  5. If shock advised: press shock button when prompted.
  6. Immediately resume CPR after shock.
⚠️
Clear Before ShockingEnsure EVERYONE — including you — is clear of the patient before pressing the shock button. Contact with the patient during shock delivery will transfer current to the bystander. "I'm clear, you're clear, everybody's clear" — then shock.
Watch: AED Operation
4-Gas Monitor (CO, O₂, H₂S, Combustible)
AKA: Multi-gas monitor, 4-gas meter, Gas Track Monitor
+
📖What it is

An electronic gas detector that simultaneously monitors four gases: carbon monoxide (CO), oxygen (O₂), hydrogen sulfide (H₂S), and combustible gas (%LEL). Alarms at specific threshold levels.

❓Why it's needed

CO, H₂S, and combustible gases are invisible and odorless at deadly concentrations. O₂ deficiency can incapacitate instantly. The 4-gas meter is your ears and eyes for hazards you cannot sense yourself.

🔧Alarm thresholds (typical)
  • CO: alarm at 35 ppm (TWA) / 200 ppm (ceiling)
  • O₂: alarm below 19.5% (deficient) or above 23.5% (enriched)
  • H₂S: alarm at 10 ppm
  • Combustible (%LEL): alarm at 10% LEL — evacuate at 25% LEL
⚠️
Always Bump-Test Before UseA gas monitor that isn't bump-tested may give false readings. A bump test exposes the sensors to known gas concentrations to verify alarm response. Don't enter any potentially hazardous environment trusting a gas monitor that hasn't been verified that shift.
Watch: Gas Monitor Training
HCN Sensor (Standalone)
AKA: Hydrogen cyanide monitor, cyanide detector — distinct from the Gas Trac
+
📖What it is

A dedicated standalone meter for detecting hydrogen cyanide (HCN) — a separate device from the Gas Trac. HCN is a byproduct of burning synthetic materials, plastics, and nitrogen-containing materials.

❓Why it's needed

HCN is 35x more toxic than CO by concentration. Modern structure fires produce significant HCN from burning synthetics. It's a major factor in firefighter and victim fatalities. It's odorless at lethal concentrations and not detected by a standard 4-gas meter.

⚠️
HCN Is UnderappreciatedThe fire service is increasingly recognizing HCN as a major killer. Your SCBA protects you — but when victims are in a smoke environment, HCN cyanide toxicity can make CPR-alone resuscitation fail. Know that this hazard exists and report any exposure concerns to EMS for antidote consideration.
Hot Stick
AKA: Voltage detector, non-contact voltage tester, electrical probe
+
📖What it is

A non-contact voltage detection tool that senses the presence of AC electrical voltage without touching a wire or conductor — it beeps or lights up when within range of a live conductor.

❓Why it's needed

Downed power lines, damaged electrical panels, and flooded structures all present electrocution risks. The hot stick tells you whether something is energized before you touch it.

⚠️
Hot Stick Says Dead ≠ SafeA non-contact tester not alarming is not a guarantee of safety — batteries may be dead, or the tester may be out of range. If in doubt, treat all conductors as energized. Contact your utility company before working around any suspected downed lines.
ERG — Emergency Response Guidebook
AKA: ERG, orange book, DOT guidebook, hazmat guide
+
📖What it is

The Department of Transportation Emergency Response Guidebook — a quick-reference manual for identifying hazardous materials, determining initial isolation distances, and selecting appropriate protective actions for hazmat incidents.

❓Why it's needed

At hazmat incidents, you need to know what you're dealing with before you approach. The ERG identifies materials by UN/NA placard number, name, or container type, and gives immediate response guidance.

🔧How to use
  1. Identify the material — by 4-digit ID number (yellow section), name (blue section), or placard (orange section).
  2. Look up the Guide number for that material.
  3. Turn to the Guide page (orange guides in center) for initial action guidance.
  4. If the material is highlighted in green, it requires protective action distances — use the green table pages for isolation distances.
✅
Know It Before You Need ItPractice finding materials in the ERG during downtime. When you're on a hazmat call with vehicles on fire, you don't have time to learn the book. The first 3 minutes of a hazmat call, you're reading the ERG — not running toward the incident.
Knoxbox Key
AKA: Knox box, rapid entry key, master key, RES-Q key
+
📖What it is

A secured key that opens Knox Box rapid-entry systems mounted on commercial buildings. Knox Boxes hold building master keys, allowing fire departments access without forced entry.

❓Why it's needed

After-hours commercial alarms and working fires in locked buildings — forcing entry takes time and causes damage. The Knox key opens the box in seconds, and the building key inside opens the building without destructive force.

⚠️
Handle With Care — This Key Is EverythingThe Knox key opens hundreds of buildings in your response district. It must stay with the rig at all times and return to its secured location after every use. Loss of a Knox key is a major security incident requiring re-keying of the entire Knox system.
Elevator Key
AKA: Firefighter elevator key, Phase II key
+
📖What it is

A specialized key that activates Firefighter Phase I and Phase II elevator operations in buildings with elevator systems. Used to recall elevators to the lobby or to manually control them for firefighter access.

❓Why it's needed

In high-rise firefighting, carrying gear up 20+ flights of stairs is exhausting and time-consuming. The elevator key allows firefighters to use elevators safely — controlling which floor they stop on and preventing civilian use during the emergency.

⚠️
NEVER Take an Elevator to the Fire FloorElevators are taken to two floors below the reported fire floor — then stairs are used. Elevator shafts can fill with smoke, and an elevator that opens on the fire floor traps you. Two floors below, always.
Accountability Velcro Name Board
AKA: Passport system, ID board, personnel accountability report (PAR) board
+
📖What it is

A velcro board where firefighter name tags ("passports") are attached on arrival at a scene. Tracks who is operating, with what crew, in what area.

❓Why it's needed

Personnel accountability is how Incident Command knows who is inside a building. If a Mayday is declared, the accountability board identifies missing personnel and their last known assignment.

⚠️
Accountability Saves LivesThe accountability system only works if EVERYONE participates. Never go into a structure without your tag on the board. When you exit, take your tag with you. A Mayday search starts with the accountability board — make sure it's accurate.
Pet O₂ Mask
AKA: Animal oxygen mask, pet oxygen, veterinary O2 mask
+
📖What it is

A set of soft, cone-shaped oxygen masks sized for dogs, cats, and other small animals. Allows delivery of supplemental oxygen to animals rescued from structure fires.

❓Why it's needed

Pets are important family members, and animal rescues generate significant public goodwill. Animals rescued from smoke-filled structures frequently have CO poisoning and benefit greatly from early O₂ therapy. These masks make that possible.

Blue Lock-Out/Tag-Out Bag
AKA: LOTO bag, lockout kit, energy isolation bag
+
📖What it is

A bag containing lockout/tagout equipment — padlocks, hasps, and tags used to secure energy sources (electrical, pneumatic, hydraulic) in the "off" position during rescue and technical operations at industrial or commercial emergencies.

❓Why it's needed

Industrial rescue, machinery entrapments, and utility emergencies require energy isolation before firefighters can safely work in the hazard zone. LOTO prevents unexpected re-energization that could injure or kill the crew and victim.

💡
Note on ContentsThe document notes "Contains?" — meaning contents should be verified and inventoried. Make sure you do this during shift check and document what's actually inside this bag.
Cab — Middle Shelf (Medical Bags cont.)
Dark Blue Collar Bag
AKA: C-spine bag, trauma collar bag, cervical collar kit
+
📖What it is

A bag dedicated to cervical spine immobilization equipment — most commonly a set of cervical collars in multiple sizes (pediatric through large adult) for patients with potential spinal injury.

❓Why it's needed

Cervical collars are applied to every trauma patient with a mechanism of injury suggesting spinal involvement — vehicle accidents, falls, diving incidents. Getting the right collar size on quickly is a critical early intervention. A dedicated bag means you're not hunting through the jump bag while your partner holds manual stabilization.

🔧Sizing a Collar
  1. Maintain manual inline stabilization throughout.
  2. Measure from the patient's shoulder to the bottom of the chin — match to collar size chart.
  3. Apply collar without moving the head/neck.
  4. Confirm it's snug but not restricting breathing.
  5. Manual stabilization is maintained even after the collar is placed.
⚠️
A Collar Does Not Replace Manual StabilizationA cervical collar alone does not fully immobilize the spine. Manual inline stabilization must be maintained until the patient is fully secured to a long backboard or stretcher. The collar is a supplement, not a substitute.
Small Orange Bag — Suction Unit
AKA: Suction bag, portable suction, aspirator
+
📖What it is

A portable battery-powered or manual suction device with a collection canister, suction tubing, and rigid (Yankauer) and flexible catheters. Used to clear a patient's airway of blood, vomit, secretions, and fluid.

❓Why it's needed

A blocked airway kills fast. Unconscious and trauma patients frequently vomit, bleed, or produce secretions that obstruct the airway. You cannot ventilate through an obstructed airway — suction clears the path for oxygen delivery.

🔧How to use
  1. Power on the unit — confirm adequate suction strength.
  2. Select the appropriate catheter: Yankauer (rigid) for the mouth; flexible for nasopharynx.
  3. Insert catheter to the visible obstruction — do not advance blindly.
  4. Apply suction while withdrawing in a slow circular motion.
  5. Suction for no more than 10 seconds at a time — pause to oxygenate in between.
⚠️
10 Seconds Max — Then OxygenateSuctioning removes oxygen along with the obstruction. Limit suction to 10-second intervals and provide ventilation between passes. An hypoxic patient from over-suctioning is an avoidable complication.
Watch: Suction Technique
Cab — Third Shelf (Gas Meters, Scene Control & Documentation)
CO₂ Meter
AKA: Carbon dioxide detector, capnometer, CO2 sensor
+
📖What it is

A standalone carbon dioxide (CO₂) gas detector for measuring CO₂ concentrations in a space. Distinct from the CO (carbon monoxide) reading on the 4-gas meter — CO₂ is the product of normal combustion and respiration, and reaches dangerous levels in confined spaces and after certain fires.

❓Why it's needed

CO₂ at elevated concentrations (above 2–3%) causes headache and impairment; above 10% it can cause unconsciousness in minutes. In structure fires, below-grade spaces, and industrial incidents, CO₂ buildup can be life-threatening and is not detected by a standard 4-gas meter (which measures CO, not CO₂).

💡CO vs CO₂ — Know the Difference

CO (carbon monoxide) — colorless, odorless, product of incomplete combustion. Measured in ppm. Binds hemoglobin. Deadly at low concentrations. Detected by the 4-gas meter.

CO₂ (carbon dioxide) — colorless, odorless, product of complete combustion and respiration. Measured in % or ppm. Displaces oxygen and causes respiratory distress at high concentrations. Requires this separate CO₂ meter.

💡
Use Both Meters on CO CallsMany "CO alarm" calls involve multiple combustion byproducts. Bring both the 4-gas meter AND the CO₂ meter into confined spaces — they measure different hazards. A good reading on one doesn't mean the other is clear.
Fire Wipes & Contractor Bags
AKA: Decon wipes, Windex wipes, contaminant wipes
+
📖What it is

Fire Wipes: Large-format disposable wipes specifically formulated to remove soot, carbon black, PAHs (polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons), and other fireground carcinogens from skin and equipment. Contractor Bags: Heavy-duty plastic bags for bagging contaminated gear and equipment after a working fire.

❓Why it's needed

Post-fire decontamination is one of the most important and underused cancer-prevention measures in the fire service. Fireground carcinogens absorb through the skin within minutes of exposure. Wipes remove contaminants immediately. Contractor bags isolate contaminated gear from clean cab air during transport back to the station.

⚠️
Wipe Down Before You Get Back In the CabThe biggest source of carcinogen exposure is re-entry into the cab wearing contaminated gear. Wipe exposed skin (neck, face, hands) before getting back in. Bag the hood. This 60-second habit is one of the most impactful cancer-prevention actions you can take every single call.
Watch: Post-Fire Decon
After Fire Survey Clipboard & Patient Clipboards
AKA: Fire investigation form, PCR clipboard, documentation board
+
📖What it is

After Fire Survey clipboard: A standardized form and board for documenting fire origin, cause, and damage observations after a structure fire — critical input for the fire investigation process. Patient Clipboards: Hard backing boards for completing EMS patient care reports (PCRs) in the field.

❓Why it's needed

Documentation is a legal and professional obligation. The after-fire survey establishes the baseline record for fire investigation, insurance, and arson prosecution. PCRs are the legal medical record of care — inaccurate or missing PCRs create liability and harm continuity of care.

💡
If It Isn't Written, It Didn't HappenIn emergency services, documentation is everything. Get in the habit of accurate, timely documentation on every call. Your memory fades; a well-written PCR or fire survey doesn't. This protects you, your crew, and your department.
Fire Tape & Caution Tape
AKA: Scene tape, barrier tape, hazard tape, Do-Not-Cross tape
+
📖What it is

Fire tape: Red and white or red barrier tape specific to fire department use — establishes the fire line perimeter. Caution tape: Yellow barrier tape for general hazard perimeter marking.

❓Why it's needed

Scene perimeter control protects the public from hazards and preserves fire scene evidence. Civilians entering an uncontrolled fire scene create rescue liabilities and contaminate investigation evidence. Tape goes up fast and stays up until the scene is cleared.

🔧Best Practice

Establish the largest perimeter you can manage initially — it's easier to tighten a perimeter than expand one after bystanders have entered. Use anchor points (trees, vehicles, street signs) to keep tape taut and at chest height so it's visible and not a trip hazard.

Red Biohazard Bags
AKA: Red bags, biohazard waste bags, infectious waste bags
+
📖What it is

OSHA-regulated red polyethylene bags bearing the universal biohazard symbol, used for disposal of medical waste — bloody gloves, bandages, suction catheters, and any materials that have contacted blood or body fluids.

❓Why it's needed

Blood-borne pathogen (BBP) exposure is a serious occupational hazard. Regulatory compliance (OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1030) requires segregated disposal of infectious waste. Red bags keep contaminated materials contained and prevent bloodborne pathogen exposure to everyone downstream.

⚠️
Gloves On, AlwaysBefore touching any patient or patient care equipment, gloves are on. No exceptions. After care, gloves go in the red bag. Wash hands at the first opportunity. BBP exposure — Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, HIV — is preventable with consistent PPE use.
Camera
AKA: Digital camera, documentation camera, scene camera
+
📖What it is

A dedicated digital camera (Canon, based on the photo in the document) for photographing fire scenes, evidence, patient injuries (with appropriate consent), and damage documentation.

❓Why it's needed

Photos document fire origin and cause evidence, support fire investigation and arson prosecution, establish liability records, and create training documentation. A good photo taken immediately on scene is worth ten written descriptions taken from memory later.

💡
Shoot Wide, Then TightWhen documenting a fire scene, start with wide establishing shots showing the whole scene, then progressively zoom in on specific areas of interest (point of origin, char patterns, evidence). Always photograph before disturbing anything — you can't un-move evidence.
FIU Investigation Box
AKA: Fire investigation unit box, evidence kit, FIU kit
+
📖What it is

A dedicated container for fire investigation supplies — evidence bags, markers, labels, collection tools, and chain-of-custody documentation — used by or in support of the Fire Investigation Unit (FIU).

❓Why it's needed

Proper evidence collection and chain-of-custody documentation is critical for arson prosecution. Improperly handled evidence can be inadmissible in court. The FIU box ensures the right tools are available immediately after fire suppression when the scene is fresh.

💡
Protect the Scene Before FIU ArrivesUntil investigators arrive, your job is to protect the origin area from unnecessary disturbance. Minimize overhaul in the suspected origin area. Document what you observe. Don't let bystanders or non-essential personnel near the origin — every footstep destroys potential evidence.
PR Box — Stickers & Public Relations Materials
AKA: Community relations kit, fire prevention materials, PR kit
+
📖What it is

A box containing public relations materials — typically firefighter-themed stickers for children, fire prevention literature, and department contact cards — distributed during community interactions and non-emergency contacts.

❓Why it's needed

Community trust and public education are foundational to fire department mission. Every interaction with the public is an opportunity to build the relationship, reinforce fire safety, and make a child's day. A badge sticker takes two seconds and creates a memory that lasts a lifetime.

2 Extra SCBA Masks
AKA: Spare face piece, SCBA facepiece, air mask
+
📖What it is

Two spare SCBA face pieces stored in the cab. Sizes are noted as TBD in the source document — this should be verified and documented on your rig check.

❓Why it's needed

Face pieces can be damaged (cracked lens, torn mask seal, broken valve) and must be replaced before use. Spare masks ensure operations aren't interrupted by equipment failure. Also used when a crew member's personal face piece is unavailable.

⚠️
Verify Sizes on Every Shift CheckThe source document notes "Sizes?" — this is an open question. Know what sizes are in those spare masks. A size medium on a large-headed firefighter won't seal, which means no IDLH entry. Confirm fit before you need it.
Binoculars
AKA: Field glasses, binos, optics
+
📖What it is

A standard pair of field binoculars for visual reconnaissance from a safe standoff distance.

❓Why it's needed

Size-up begins on the way to the scene and continues on arrival. Binoculars allow the officer to assess smoke conditions, fire volume, rescue situations, and hazmat placards from a safe distance — before the apparatus is committed to a position. At wildland-interface fires, they're essential for tracking fire behavior across terrain.

💡
Hazmat Placard ReadingAt suspected hazmat incidents, use the binoculars to read the 4-digit UN/NA number on placards from a safe distance BEFORE approaching. Identify the material in the ERG first — then decide your approach. Don't drive up to read the placard.
Cab — Bottom Shelf
Flood Light
AKA: Scene flood light, portable flood, work light, portable scene light
+
📖What it is

A high-output portable flood light for broad area illumination of incident scenes — larger and brighter than the portable work lights in Comp. 3. Used to illuminate large outdoor areas, intersection accidents, or extended operations.

❓Why it's needed

Night and low-visibility operations require scene lighting for crew safety, patient assessment, documentation, and traffic control. A well-lit scene is a safer scene — for your crew and for passing motorists who can clearly see the operation.

✅
Position to Illuminate, Not BlindDon't point flood lights toward traffic — you'll blind approaching drivers. Angle them to illuminate the work area while keeping outward glare controlled. Also consider positioning them so your crew doesn't cast shadows over the work area.
Hot Feet
AKA: Chemical foot warmers, foot heat packs, disposable foot warmers
+
📖What it is

Single-use air-activated chemical foot warmer packets that slip inside boots or shoes and generate heat for several hours.

❓Why it's needed

Extended outdoor operations in cold weather — long car accidents, structure fires in winter, technical rescues — expose crew to cold ground conduction through boots. Cold, numb feet reduce dexterity, increase fatigue, and raise hypothermia risk. Hot Feet keep your crew functional on long cold calls.

💡
Crew Welfare = Crew PerformanceKeeping your crew warm on extended winter incidents isn't soft — it's operational. Cold firefighters make mistakes, move slowly, and tire faster. The officer who thinks about crew welfare produces better outcomes.
Blankets
AKA: Emergency blankets, rescue blankets, patient blankets
+
📖What it is

Emergency thermal blankets — either disposable mylar-type space blankets or reusable wool/synthetic rescue blankets — for patient warming and scene use.

❓Why it's needed

Hypothermia is a serious complication in trauma patients, cardiac arrest patients, and victims of exposure. Keeping a patient warm preserves their physiology while you work. Blankets also protect patients from debris during extrication and provide modesty coverage.

💡
Warm the Ground, Not Just the TopA patient lying on cold concrete loses heat from below faster than above. If possible, place a blanket under the patient as well as over them. Cold ground conduction is a major source of heat loss that's easy to prevent.
Also in Cab — Under Seats & General Cab Storage
Vests (Under Seats)
AKA: High-visibility vest, safety vest, hi-viz vest, ANSI vest
+
📖What it is

ANSI/ISEA-rated high-visibility reflective safety vests stored under the cab seats for rapid access. Typically bright yellow-green or orange with retroreflective striping.

❓Why it's needed

NFPA 1500 and MUTCD (Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices) require firefighters working in or near traffic to wear high-visibility apparel. Being struck by a vehicle is one of the leading causes of line-of-duty death for firefighters.

⚠️
Put It On — Every TimeStructural turnout gear is not high-visibility in traffic. A yellow-green vest over your gear makes you dramatically more visible to drivers. Highway incidents, vehicle accidents, and any call in a roadway — vest goes on. This rule saves lives and it takes five seconds.
4 Portable Radios
AKA: HT (handie-talkie), portable, brick, radio, walkie-talkie
+
📖What it is

Four portable two-way radios in the cab — one for each crew member. These are the primary communication tools on the fireground, connecting individual firefighters to their crew, their company, and Incident Command.

❓Why it's needed

Communication is the backbone of coordinated fireground operations. A firefighter without a working radio is isolated. Radios transmit Maydays, coordinate ventilation and attack, relay conditions to command, and call for additional resources.

🔧Radio Discipline Basics
  • Listen before you transmit — don't step on active traffic.
  • Press PTT (push to talk) — pause one second — then speak clearly and slowly.
  • Identify yourself: "Engine 61 to Command" — then your message.
  • Keep transmissions short and clear. Use standardized terminology.
  • A Mayday transmission interrupts all other traffic: "Mayday, Mayday, Mayday — [your name] — [location] — [nature of emergency]."
⚠️
Check Battery Charge Every ShiftA dead radio inside a burning building is a death sentence. Verify all 4 radios are fully charged during the morning rig check. Test each one. A radio that doesn't key up in the station parking lot won't key up when you need a Mayday.
Watch: Radio Communication Training
Water (Crew Hydration Supply)
AKA: Bottled water, hydration supply, crew water
+
📖What it is

Water kept in the cab for crew hydration before, during, and after emergency operations.

❓Why it's needed

Firefighting is among the most physically demanding activities a human can perform. Heat stress and dehydration degrade cognitive function, physical performance, and cardiac function. Dehydration begins impairing performance before you feel thirsty — stay ahead of it.

💡
Hydrate Before, During, and AfterYou're losing water through sweat inside your gear from the moment you don it. Start hydrating before the call if possible. After a working structure fire, drink before you feel thirsty — you're already behind. Heat-related illness is preventable with consistent hydration habits.
☀️

Top of Engine

Snow shovel · Traffic cones · Fire paddle · Dawn soap
Fire Paddle
AKA: Fire swatter, flap, grass fire swatter, brush fire swatter, fire flapper
+
📖What it is

A long-handled tool with a flat rubber or leather flap used to beat out grass, brush, and small ground fires by smothering the flames directly.

❓Why it's needed

Fast, effective, water-free extinguishment for small grass and brush fires. Where running a hose line would be impractical or too slow, the swatter snuffs flames directly.

Manifold for Fire Gun
AKA: Hose manifold, deck gun manifold, water cannon manifold
+
📖What it is

A multi-outlet manifold that connects to the deck gun (mounted on top of the engine) and distributes water supply from multiple hose inputs for high-volume master stream operations.

❓Why it's needed

The deck gun requires significant water supply. The manifold allows multiple supply lines to combine and feed the master stream, ensuring volume and pressure are maintained during extended operations.

Dawn Soap & Brush in Bucket
AKA: Surfactant, wetting agent, Class A foam supplement
+
📖What it is

Dish soap and a brush stored in a bucket on top of the engine. Used as an impromptu surfactant/wetting agent or for washing down contaminated equipment after hazmat or fire operations.

❓Why it's needed

Decontamination of tools and equipment after fires reduces carcinogen exposure. Surfactant in water reduces surface tension, helping water penetrate deep-seated fires and porous materials more effectively.

💡
Decon MattersFirefighter cancer rates are significantly elevated due to carcinogen exposure. Wiping down gear, tools, and your skin after every working fire is one of the simplest things you can do to protect your long-term health. The bucket and brush on top of the rig make it easy — use them.
Traffic Cones
AKA: Road cones, pylons, safety cones
+
📖What it is

High-visibility orange traffic cones for scene management — blocking traffic, defining work zones, and protecting firefighters from vehicle traffic.

❓Why it's needed

Struck-by incidents from passing vehicles kill firefighters. Cones placed quickly on arrival help define the scene perimeter. Work with law enforcement to establish full scene control, but don't wait for them to place your first cone.

❓Why it's needed

Struck-by incidents from passing vehicles kill firefighters. Cones placed quickly on arrival help define the scene perimeter. Work with law enforcement to establish full scene control, but don't wait for them to place your first cone.

Snow Shovel
AKA: Push shovel, scoop shovel, snow pusher
+
📖What it is

A full-size snow shovel stored on top of the apparatus for clearing access routes, hydrant ports, and working areas during winter operations.

❓Why it's needed

A buried hydrant cap or a snow-packed path to the front door costs critical minutes on a working fire in winter. Clearing hydrant ports and entry paths is one of the first jobs on a winter fire scene — and it starts with having a shovel.

💡
Connect to the Hydrant FlagsThose small pink utility flags in the Comp. 1 tool box are for marking buried hydrants before the first snowfall. Work with your district before winter to flag hydrants so they're findable in 18 inches of snow — the shovel and the flags work as a team. Proactive hydrant marking is some of the highest-value pre-incident work you can do.
1-Inch Garden Hose
AKA: Garden hose, wash-down line, utility hose
+
📖What it is

A standard 1-inch diameter garden hose stored on top of the apparatus for low-pressure utility water tasks — washing down equipment, flushing contaminants, wetting smoldering debris during overhaul, and post-incident decontamination rinse.

❓Why it's needed

Not every water task needs a charged attack line. The garden hose delivers gentle controlled flow perfect for tool wash-down, gear decontamination, and small-volume cooling during salvage. Using a preconnected attack line for these tasks wastes time, water, and causes unnecessary property damage from flow rate.

✅
Decon Station in 30 SecondsGarden hose + Dawn soap + brush bucket = a complete field decon station. After any working fire, take 60 seconds to rinse tools, gloves, and boots before stowing them. Contaminated tools re-contaminate your gloves every time you handle them. Break the cycle.
🗺️

📝 Final Notes — Keep This Guide Current

A few entries in the source document still carry open questions — the SCBA mask sizes in the cab top shelf, utility rope exact length, LOTO bag contents, and some tool box metric wrench sizes. Every time you do a rig check and confirm one of these, report it to your company officer to get the document updated.

The source document itself says it best: "There will always be changes to where things go — so check first." This guide gives you the foundation. The actual rig gives you the truth. Walk it. Every. Shift.

Remember the three habits that separate good probies from great ones: check the rig, know where everything is, and put it back exactly where you found it.
