100 ft Trash Line — Preconnected
AKA: Minute-man line, bump line, quick attack
+
📖What it is

A preconnected 1¾" attack line for fast, small-fire knockdowns — pulled from the front of the apparatus.

❓Why it's needed

Speed. Small fires, dumpster calls, car fires — get water flowing before pulling a full crosslay.

⚠️
Bleed Before You AdvanceConfirm the line is bled and flowing before advancing. A water-logged hose that isn't moving flows nowhere and creates dangerous back-pressure.
Watch: 1¾" Attack Line Basics
1¾" Crosslays — 200 ft ×2, Both Preconnected
AKA: Crosslay, minute-man, pre-connect
+
📖What it is

Two 200-foot 1¾" lines loaded as crosslays — accessible from either side of the apparatus. Both are preconnected and ready to pull.

❓Why it's needed

Your primary residential attack line. Flows ~150–180 GPM with good mobility for most structure fires.

✅
Pull Straight Off the BedDon't yank the whole load — pull what you need to reach the door, then have your partner feed the line. Dragging excess hose through a building wastes energy and creates trip hazards.
Watch: Crosslay Deployment
🔩

Engineer's Compartment

Left top · Right top · Middle · Bottom
Left Top Shelf
Towels
AKA: Shop towels, rags, decon towels, clean-up rags
+
📖What it is

Heavy-duty shop towels or cotton rags stored on the left top shelf of the engineer's compartment. Used for wiping down equipment, cleaning spills, drying couplings, and general field maintenance.

❓Why it's needed

A dry coupling threads and seats better than a wet one. Towels dry out hydrant connections, wipe grease and grime off fittings, and clean up minor fluid spills at accident scenes. They also serve as impromptu padding to protect equipment during transport.

🔧How to use

Keep them accessible for quick coupling dry-off before connecting hose, wiping down the pump panel gauges for clear readings, and post-incident equipment wipe-down. Restock when the supply runs low — it's easy to forget until you need one.

✅
Decon First StepA towel dry-off of exposed skin (neck, hands, face) is a fast first-pass decon while you're still at the scene before reaching for the Fire Wipes in the cab. It removes surface soot before it absorbs further into skin.
30-Degree Storz Adapter
AKA: Angled Storz, elbow Storz, offset Storz
+
📖What it is

A Storz-to-Storz coupling with a 30-degree offset angle. Allows LDH connections where a straight coupling would be too bulky or misaligned.

❓Why it's needed

Tight hydrant connections, close-quarters lay hookups, and apparatus intake connections where a straight Storz would create a kink or stress point.

💡
Unique to E60The 30-degree Storz is specifically listed on E60. On a tight intake connection next to the pump panel, this fitting can be the difference between a sealed connection and a kinking hose.
Pickup Tubes for Foam/Gel
AKA: Eductor tubes, foam pickup tubes, siphon tubes
+
📖What it is

Clear or colored tubes that insert into the Chief Eductor and draw foam concentrate or gel from a container via venturi effect. The flowing water stream creates suction that pulls concentrate into the water stream.

❓Why it's needed

The eductor system can't work without pickup tubes — they're the delivery straw that draws foam concentrate from buckets or carboys into the water stream to create finished foam.

⚠️
Match Tube to ConcentrateDifferent foam concentrates require different induction rates (1%, 3%, 6%). Confirm the eductor percentage setting matches the concentrate you're using. A mismatch creates either ineffective foam or wastes concentrate.
Reducers — Multiple Sizes
AKA: Adapters, incrementers, swaged fittings
+
📖What's Here

Multiple hose reducers and adapters for connecting mismatched coupling sizes. Standard fire service reducers (2½"F→1¾"M, 1¾"→1", steamer→Storz, etc.). These bridge the gaps between different hose diameters and thread types across the apparatus and at hydrant connections.

🔧How to use

Select the reducer that bridges your two coupling sizes. Female end receives the male thread; male end inserts into the female coupling. Hand-tighten first, then snug with a spanner wrench. For Storz: quarter-turn lock. Check gasket condition before every connection — a missing gasket under pressure means a failed coupling. Carry a handful of spare gaskets in the hydrant bag.

💡
Know Your ThreadsNST (National Standard Thread) is the US standard. Storz is quarter-turn coupling. CFD uses a Chicago-specific thread pattern. Know which end connects to what before you need it under pressure.
Duct Tape
AKA: Duck tape, gaffer tape, utility tape
+
📖What it is

Heavy-duty cloth-backed adhesive tape. Used for field-expedient repairs, securing loose items, labeling, and emergency patching on non-pressurized surfaces.

❓Why it's needed

Duct tape is the universal field repair tool. Sealing cuts in tarp, securing wiring, temporarily patching equipment, marking hazard zones — it solves dozens of small problems at every incident.

Right Top Shelf
SCBA — Self-Contained Breathing Apparatus
AKA: Air pack, bottle, airpack, SCBA
+
📖What it is

A self-contained breathing apparatus providing compressed air supply for entry into IDLH (immediately dangerous to life or health) environments. Includes cylinder, regulator, harness, and face piece. Every IDLH environment requires SCBA — structure fires, gas leaks, confined spaces, hazmat incidents.

⚠️
Low Air Alarm = Exit NowWhen the low-air alarm activates you have roughly one-third of your supply left. Begin exiting immediately — not when the task is done. If disoriented, declare Mayday. The alarm is not a suggestion.
Watch: SCBA Donning Procedures
Extra Air Bottle
AKA: Spare cylinder, spare SCBA cylinder, backup bottle
+
📖What it is

A spare SCBA air cylinder stored on the top right shelf for cylinder swap during extended operations.

❓Why it's needed

A standard 45-minute cylinder depletes faster under high exertion. Extended rescues, large searches, or technical operations can exhaust a cylinder before the job is done. This spare keeps the engineer's crew in the game.

✅
Check Every ShiftVerify the spare cylinder is ≥90% full on every rig check. A half-empty spare is only half a solution.
Middle Shelf
Foam Nozzle — 125 GPM (Orange)
AKA: Foam tip, foam applicator, Class A nozzle
+
📖What it is

An orange nozzle specifically calibrated for foam/gel application — 125 GPM flow rate. The orange colour codes it as the foam nozzle so it's never confused with standard attack nozzles.

❓Why it's needed

Foam application requires a specific nozzle that properly aerates the foam solution to produce finished foam. Using a standard fog nozzle doesn't produce proper finished foam — you need this dedicated applicator for effective foam operations.

🔧How to use

Connect downstream of the eductor. Aim at the base of a fuel fire or apply to exposures for Class A suppression. The 125 GPM rate is calibrated to produce finished foam at the correct expansion ratio with E60's eductor setting.

Chief Eductor (Foam Eductor)
AKA: Foam eductor, in-line eductor, proportioner
+
📖What it is

An in-line venturi device that mixes foam concentrate (via pickup tubes) into the water stream at a precise ratio to create foam solution. The Chief brand is a high-quality in-line eductor.

❓Why it's needed

Class A foam dramatically increases water's penetrating ability and heat absorption for structure fires. Class B foam suppresses flammable liquid fires by creating a vapor-sealing blanket. The eductor is the mixing engine that makes foam operations possible.

🔧How to use

  1. Insert pickup tube into foam concentrate container.
  2. Connect eductor inline between pump discharge and attack line.
  3. Set eductor percentage to match concentrate (1%, 3%, or 6%).
  4. Maintain minimum 200 GPM flow through eductor — below this, venturi effect fails.
  5. Keep pickup tube submerged — if it sucks air, you're flowing water, not foam.

⚠️
Minimum Flow Rate is CriticalThe venturi in an eductor requires a minimum flow velocity to create suction. Below ~200 GPM, the eductor stops drawing concentrate and you're flowing plain water while thinking you're applying foam. Always maintain adequate pump pressure.
Watch: Foam Eductor Operation
Gated Wye — 2½" to (2) 1½"
AKA: Gated wye, wye valve, wye connector
+
📖What it is

A Y-shaped fitting with one 2½" inlet and two 1½" gated outlets. Each outlet has an independent ball valve.

❓Why it's needed

Splits one supply line into two independently controlled attack lines. Critical for standpipe operations — connect to one standpipe outlet, feed two attack lines off one port.

Fog Nozzles ×2
AKA: Combination nozzle, adjustable nozzle
+
📖What it is

Adjustable-pattern nozzles delivering water from straight stream to 60° wide fog by rotating the bale.

❓Why it's needed

Versatility: straight stream for reach and penetration; narrow fog for compartment knockdown; wide fog for crew protection and exposure protection.

⚠️
Don't Fog a Smoke-Filled HallwayWide fog pattern in a confined space steams the environment — scalding everyone inside. Use straight stream for interior attack unless you know the space is clear.
Rope to Move Charged 5" Hose
AKA: Hose rope, load rope, moving rope
+
📖What it is

A length of rope used to drag or reposition charged 5" large diameter hose. A full charged 5" line is extremely heavy and cannot be repositioned by hand alone.

❓Why it's needed

A charged 5" line can weigh several pounds per foot. Repositioning it without a mechanical advantage (rope looped through couplings and pulled) is impossible for one or two people.

Adaptors — M2M, F2F, CFD, 2½"→1¾"
AKA: Double male, double female, sexless adapters, CFD couplings
+
📖What's Here

M2M (double male) — connects two female ends. F2F (double female) — connects two male ends. CFD — Chicago Fire Department thread pattern for mutual aid interoperability. 2½"→1¾" — reduces large line to attack hose size. Know which pouch they live in before a mutual aid assignment.

Bottom Shelf
Eye Protection
AKA: Safety glasses, goggles, eye-pro, PPE
+
📖What it is

Safety glasses or goggles for eye protection during overhaul, extrication, salvage operations, and any activity generating debris.

❓Why it's needed

Flying debris from overhaul, glass shards from vehicle extrication, and chemical splashes are ongoing hazards. Eye injuries can be instantly career-ending.

Hydrant Bag
AKA: Hydrant kit, hydrant pack
+
🔧Contents
  • Hydrant wrenches
  • Steamer-to-Storz adapters
  • Spanners with gas valve notch
  • Wedges
  • Gate valve
  • Rubber mallet
  • Pipe wrench
  • Rope to move hose
✅
Grab the Whole BagThe hydrant person grabs one bag and has everything. Don't cherry-pick items. Bring the whole bag — what you leave behind is what you'll need.
Gate Valve
AKA: Hydrant gate, auxiliary valve, inline valve, hydrant assist valve (HAV)
+
📖What it is

A large in-line valve for 2½" or larger hose that can be opened or closed to control flow independently of the pump panel. This is a gate valve — not a ball valve. Internally it uses a sliding gate to seal the waterway, opened and closed with a handwheel through several full turns.

❓Why it's needed

Allows flow control at the point of connection — attach to a hydrant outlet or standpipe connection and control flow without signaling the engineer. Critical for standpipe operations.

🔧How to use

Thread the gate valve onto the hydrant outlet or standpipe port before connecting your attack line. Leave it fully closed when connecting. Once lines are charged and crews are ready, crack the gate valve open slowly with the handwheel to pressurize the line. To replace a nozzle or bleed the line, close the gate valve (multiple turns) rather than signaling the engineer to drop pressure on the entire pump.

25 ft of 5" Hose
AKA: Short LDH section, finish section
+
📖What it is

A short 30-foot section of 5" large diameter hose stored in the bottom of the engineer's compartment for finishing a lay or nurse tanker hookup.

❓Why it's needed

When the main LDH supply lay is too long or too short by a short distance, this finish section bridges the gap. Also used for tanker/tender hook-ups.

Smooth Bore Nozzles
AKA: Solid stream nozzle, smooth bore tip, stacked tips
+
📖What it is

Fixed-orifice nozzles that deliver a solid, unbroken stream of water. Available in multiple bore sizes for different flow rates (e.g., 1⅛", 1¼", 1½").

❓Why it's needed

Maximum reach, maximum penetration, and maximum impact on the fire. Smooth bore nozzles outperform fog nozzles in high-heat, deep-seat fires where reach matters more than pattern.

💡
Smooth Bore vs. FogFog nozzles are versatile. Smooth bore nozzles go farther, hit harder, and don't steam-up the environment. For commercial fires, car fires, and any situation needing reach, smooth bore is often the better choice.
🪓

Middle Compartment — Driver's Side

Hand tools · Nozzles · Entry tools · Deck gun
Air & Scene
3 Air Tanks
AKA: SCBA spare cylinders, spare bottles, air supply
+
📖What it is

Three spare SCBA air cylinders stored for crew cylinder swap during extended operations.

❓Why it's needed

Cylinder swaps keep crews operating without interrupting the work. Three spares cover a full crew rotation.

🔧How to swap a cylinder

  1. Exit the hazard area before swapping — never swap in an IDLH environment.
  2. Shut down the cylinder valve on the depleted bottle.
  3. Breathe down remaining air and disconnect the regulator.
  4. Open the cylinder yoke — release the depleted bottle.
  5. Insert the fresh cylinder, seat it fully, and close the yoke.
  6. Open the valve slowly — confirm pressure reads full on the regulator gauge.
  7. Re-don face piece and verify airflow before re-entering.

✅
Check All 3 Every ShiftAll three must be ≥90% full. A partially filled spare is a liability. Check pressure, condition, and valve operation every morning.
Quartz Light (Side-Mounted)
AKA: Scene light, quartz flood, mounted work light
+
📖What it is

⭐ Don't Forget This One. A high-output quartz work light mounted on the side of the engine. The source document specifically flags: "Don't forget the big quartz light on the side of engine." It's easy to overlook a mounted item during a rig check — it has no compartment door to remind you. Provides broad scene illumination for nighttime operations and extended incidents.

⚠️
Easily Overlooked on Rig CheckBecause it's mounted externally rather than in a compartment, this light is the most frequently missed item during compartment checks. Walk the entire exterior of the rig on every check — not just the doors.
Deck Gun Equipment
Deck Gun Ground Mount
AKA: Ground monitor mount, blitz gun base, portable monitor base
+
📖What it is

A heavy-duty base that allows E60's deck gun to be dismounted from the top of the apparatus and used as a freestanding ground-level monitor.

❓Why it's needed

Flexibility in master stream positioning. Instead of being locked into the deck gun's fixed position on top of the rig, the ground mount lets you set the monitor at the optimal angle and standoff — around a corner, in a doorway, or at a different elevation.

🔧How to use

  1. Remove the deck gun from its rooftop mount (requires two people — it's heavy).
  2. Secure the gun into the ground mount base.
  3. Position in optimal location.
  4. Connect 3" or 2½" supply line.
  5. Charge and aim. The mount provides stability against nozzle reaction.

Deck Gun Nozzle
AKA: Master stream tip, deck gun tip, smooth bore monitor tip
+
📖What it is

The nozzle tip for E60's deck gun (mounted master stream). May be smooth bore or fog pattern depending on configuration.

❓Why it's needed

The deck gun nozzle is separate so it can be swapped — different bore sizes or pattern types depending on the operation. Always confirm the nozzle is properly secured before flowing.

⚠️
Secure Before FlowingA nozzle tip that isn't properly seated on the monitor will blow off under master stream pressure. Confirm it's locked before signaling the engineer to charge the line.
Entry Tools
Halligan Bar
AKA: Hooligan, Pro-bar, Halligan tool, the bar
+
📖What it is

The iconic forcible entry tool — a forged steel bar with adze/fork on one end and pick on the other. Used with the flat-head axe as "the irons" to force doors, open walls, and vent.

❓Why it's needed

The single most important forcible entry tool in the fire service. Opens residential and commercial doors, pulls ceilings, breaches walls, and provides leverage in dozens of situations.

⚠️
Try Before You PryAlways try the door handle first. More doors are unlocked than you think. Forcing an unlocked door wastes time and causes unnecessary damage.
Watch: Halligan Door Forcing
Halligan with Gas Turn Off
AKA: Gas-shutoff Halligan, utility Halligan, gas-key Halligan
+
📖What it is

A Halligan bar fitted with an integrated gas turn-off feature — a notch or attachment sized to the standard residential gas-meter shutoff square so a single tool can both force entry AND turn off the gas at the meter.

❓Why it's needed

At a structure fire or gas-leak call, controlling the gas supply at the meter is one of the first utility tasks. Carrying a separate gas key adds weight and another item to lose. The gas-turnoff feature on the Halligan keeps the function with a tool you'll already have in hand.

💡
E60-Specific ToolThe Halligan with gas turn off is specifically called out on E60. Know where it is so you can distinguish it from the standard Halligan. At any structure fire or gas-leak call, this is the tool that goes with the firefighter assigned to utility control.
⚠️
Shutting Gas Is a Utility Company Job at Confirmed Gas LeaksDon't shut a gas meter unless your department's SOG authorizes it and you're sure of the action. Turning a gas meter off incorrectly or at the wrong valve can cause an explosion or leave the building without heat during dangerous conditions.
Pickhead Axe / Fire Axe (×2 — Standard + Red)
AKA: Pick head axe, fire axe, pick axe
+
📖What it is

Axes with a cutting blade on one side and a pointed pick on the other. E60 carries a standard pickhead axe and a distinct RED pickhead axe (color-coded for identification).

❓Why it's needed

Roof ventilation, floor breaching, wall opening, and striking the Halligan. The red axe may be color-coded for a specific crew role or assignment — know your company's protocol.

Flat Head Axe
AKA: Striking axe, flat axe, fire axe
+
📖What it is

An axe with a flat striking face and cutting blade. Pairs with the Halligan as "the irons" — the flat face drives the Halligan precisely into door gaps.

❓Why it's needed

Half of the most critical forcible entry combination in the fire service. Keep it with the Halligan.

✅
Keep the Irons TogetherHalligan + flat axe = the irons. If you have one, your partner should have the other. They travel as a set.
Sledgehammer / Maul
AKA: Sledge, striking tool, mall
+
📖What it is

A heavy sledgehammer for high-force striking on commercial doors, padlocks, and masonry.

❓Why it's needed

When the flat-head axe doesn't have enough mass. Commercial steel doors and high-security locks require the maul's additional striking force.

Officer's Tool / Pry Axe
AKA: Captain's tool, officer's tool, pak-tool, pro-tool
+
📖What it is

A compact multi-purpose prying and striking tool sized for a company officer to carry alongside a radio — combines prying edge, striking face, and hook/pike.

❓Why it's needed

Officers need a tool they can carry without dropping the radio. Gives enough capability to probe conditions, force a door, or pry debris without a full set of irons.

K-Tool
AKA: Lock puller, K-tool, key tool, cylinder puller
+
📖What it is

A metal tool shaped like the letter "K" that extracts lock cylinders from commercial doors — allowing a key tool to operate the exposed mechanism without full door destruction.

❓Why it's needed

Less-damaging entry on commercial properties. Preserves the door and frame and leaves the building securable after the incident.

🔧How to use

  1. Slide K-tool over the lock cylinder face.
  2. Drive down with axe to bite into cylinder.
  3. Use Halligan to lever cylinder out.
  4. Insert key tool to operate mechanism.

Watch: K-Tool Forcible Entry
Nozzles
Cellar Nozzle
AKA: Bresnan distributor, cellar pipe, spinning nozzle
+
📖What it is

A rotating distributor nozzle on a cellar pipe that, when inserted through a small floor hole, spins and distributes water in 360° into the below-grade space.

❓Why it's needed

Below-grade fires are extremely dangerous to attack directly. The cellar pipe puts water into cellar fires from above through a small opening — without sending a crew into a deadly sub-grade environment.

🔧How to use

  1. Identify fire location below floor.
  2. Cut or locate a small access hole (6–8" minimum).
  3. Connect to a charged 2½" line.
  4. Lower rotating nozzle through hole.
  5. Open line — nozzle spins and distributes water throughout space.

Watch: Cellar Nozzle Operation
Piercing Nozzle
AKA: Transformer nozzle, penetrating nozzle, through-the-lock nozzle
+
📖What it is

A specialty nozzle designed to deliver water spray through very small openings — keyholes, drilled holes, or vent openings — into enclosed burning voids without requiring a large opening.

❓Why it's needed

Wall and void-space fires that can't be reached through normal attack lines. Insert through a small drilled or existing opening and deliver water directly to the fire pocket.

Fan Hanger
AKA: Window mount, fan bracket, PPV bracket
+
📖What it is

A bracket or frame device that suspends a PPV ventilation fan in a doorway or window opening — holding it in position without someone having to hold it manually.

❓Why it's needed

Hands-free fan operation frees up a firefighter who would otherwise be standing at the door holding the fan. The hanger positions the fan to cover the full door opening for optimal PPV air movement.

🔧How to use

Secure the fan hanger in the door or window frame, mount the fan, adjust to cover the opening fully with the cone of airflow, then start the fan. The hanger should be sized to match the fan and opening.

💡
Unique to E60The fan hanger is specifically called out on E60. Knowing this tool exists and where to find it can significantly speed up PPV setup on working structure fires.
Fire Tape
AKA: Barrier tape, scene tape, fire line tape
+
📖What it is

Red/white barrier tape for establishing fire scene perimeters.

❓Why it's needed

Controls access to the fire scene, protects the public from hazards, and preserves evidence for investigation.

⚡

Rear Compartment — Driver's Side

10KW Generator · Power tools · Lighting · Ventilation fan
10KW Generator
AKA: Generator, gen set, portable power, 10 kilowatt generator
+
📖What it is

A 10-kilowatt gasoline or diesel portable generator providing 110V and/or 220V electrical power for lighting, power tools, and emergency equipment at incident scenes.

❓Why it's needed

Large-scale scene lighting, power tools for extended extrication, running saws and fans, and providing electrical power to emergency operations where utility power is unavailable or has been shut down.

🔧How to use

  1. Position in ventilated area — exhaust fumes are deadly in enclosed spaces.
  2. Ensure fuel level is adequate (check each shift).
  3. Connect grounded extension cords and lights before starting.
  4. Start per manufacturer procedure (typically choke, pull-start or electric start).
  5. Allow to warm up before applying full load.
  6. Never exceed rated capacity — 10KW = ~83 amps at 120V.

⚠️
CO Poisoning Risk is RealA generator running inside or near a structure creates deadly carbon monoxide concentrations within minutes. ALWAYS operate outdoors, away from doors and windows. Your 4-gas monitor should alarm — treat it seriously.
💡
Unique to E60 — Know Your Power Budget10KW at 120V = roughly 83 amps total. A typical scene light draws 5–8 amps; the Sawzall pulls 12–15 amps; battery chargers pull 5 amps each. Add it up before you plug in — running the generator beyond rated capacity will trip the breaker and cut power to everything simultaneously. Prioritize lighting first, then tools.
Watch: Generator Safety and Operation
200 ft Roll of Electrical Cord
AKA: Extension cord, power cord, electrical reel
+
📖What it is

A 200-foot heavy-duty electrical extension cord on a reel, used to run power from the generator to scene lighting and tools.

❓Why it's needed

200 feet of reach from the generator position means you can power lights and tools deep into a structure or around the perimeter of a large incident without repositioning the generator.

⚠️
Never Coil Under LoadA coiled extension cord under electrical load creates an inductor that generates heat, which can melt insulation and start fires. Always fully uncoil the cord before applying load.
B Post Cover
AKA: B-pillar cover, door post protector, extrication pad
+
📖What it is

A protective pad or cover placed over a vehicle's B-pillar (the structural post between the front and rear doors) during extrication — protecting the victim from sharp cut edges.

❓Why it's needed

When you cut the B-post for roof removal or door displacement, the metal edge becomes razor-sharp. The B-post cover shields the patient and crew from lacerations during and after the cut.

✅
Always Cover Before You CutApply B-post cover BEFORE making any cuts near the pillar. A sharp edge at head level during extrication is an avoidable hazard.
Plug-In Lights (Scene Lights)
AKA: Scene lights, portable lights, plug-in work lights
+
📖What it is

Portable scene lights powered by the generator via the electrical cord. Illuminate work areas, incident perimeters, and victim access points.

❓Why it's needed

Nighttime operations, smoke-obscured scenes, and overcast weather all reduce visibility to dangerous levels. Adequate scene lighting reduces trip hazards, improves patient assessment, and makes the scene visible to approaching vehicles.

Reciprocating Saw (Sawzall)
AKA: Recip saw, Sawzall, demo saw, hack saw (power)
+
📖What it is

A battery or corded reciprocating saw for cutting through vehicle components, seat belts, plastics, and tight-space structural elements that hydraulic tools can't address.

❓Why it's needed

Seat belt anchor bolts, interior trim, soft-top vehicle materials, and narrow-clearance cuts where hydraulic tools are too large or destructive.

⚠️
Blade Selection MattersMetal-cutting blade for metal — a wood blade binds and fails. Confirm blade type before use. Use controlled short strokes near patients.
Ventilation Fan
AKA: PPV fan, positive pressure ventilation fan, blower
+
📖What it is

A high-volume fan for positive pressure ventilation — pushes fresh air into a structure to clear smoke and improve conditions for firefighters and victims.

❓Why it's needed

Smoke is the leading killer in structure fires. Rapid ventilation clears smoke, improves survivability for trapped occupants, and gives attack crews better visibility.

⚠️
PPV Can Feed a FireNever start a PPV fan unless the fire is controlled or suppressed. Pushing fresh air into an active fire feeds oxygen and can cause flashover. Always coordinate with the attack crew before starting.
Plug Adaptors (110V Compatible)
AKA: Electrical adapters, power adapters, outlet adapters
+
📖What it is

Electrical outlet adaptors allowing the generator's power to interface with standard 110V household devices, tools, and equipment.

❓Why it's needed

Standard tools, battery chargers, and medical equipment are designed for household current. Adaptors ensure the generator's power output is usable across all standard equipment without modification.

Cribbing
AKA: Crib blocks, box crib, shoring blocks, step chocks
+
📖What it is

Short blocks used to build stable, stacking supports under lifted or displaced loads during rescue operations. Cribbing goes hand-in-hand with air bags and hydraulic tools — as you lift, you crib. The load is always supported by cribbing, never by equipment alone.

❓Why it's needed

Air bags can fail. Hydraulic jacks can leak down. A vehicle can shift. Cribbing is the passive, fail-safe support that protects the victim and the rescuers regardless of equipment failure. "An inch up, an inch of crib in" — never an exception.

Small Step Ladder
AKA: Step ladder, A-frame ladder, folding step stool
+
📖What it is

A compact self-supporting folding ladder for short elevation access — reaching elevated controls, working above head height, or accessing vehicle rooflines.

❓Why it's needed

Not every access problem requires a ground ladder. The step ladder deploys in seconds and provides a stable platform for precision elevated work.

🌊

First Compartment — Officer's Side

Water rescue · Foam · Supply hose · Coping tool
Top Shelf
Akron Coping Tool (Hose Hoist)
AKA: Hose hoist, coping tool, standpipe hose tool
+
📖What it is

A hose management tool (Akron brand) designed to redirect, support, or hoist hose in high-rise and standpipe operations. Typically hooks over railings or balconies to haul hose up elevator shafts or stairwells without dragging it over sharp edges.

❓Why it's needed

In high-rise operations, advancing hose up multiple floors is physically exhausting and damaging to hose if dragged over concrete corners. The coping tool provides a redirecting friction point so a small crew can hoist significant hose lengths without equipment damage.

🔧How to use

Hook the tool over the railing or structural edge at the desired floor. Thread the hose through or around the coping tool's redirecting surface. Have crews haul hose upward — the tool bears the friction load instead of the hose coupling against the staircase edge.

💡
Unique to E60The Akron coping tool is specifically listed on E60 — not on all engines. High-rise buildings in your response area make this tool important. Know where it lives so it's in your hand before you're staring up a 20-flight stairwell.
Utility Rope — 100 ft
AKA: Utility line, general-purpose rope, work rope
+
📖What it is

A general-purpose 100-foot rope for non-life-safety utility applications — hoisting tools, securing equipment, moving hose, and improvised rigging.

❓Why it's needed

Utility rope is the duct tape of the fireground — it solves dozens of small problems. Moving debris, securing ladders, rigging loads.

⚠️
NOT a Life-Safety RopeUtility rope is NOT rated for supporting human weight. Never use for rappelling or rescue suspension. Life-safety operations require NFPA 1983-rated rope.
Spare Battery
AKA: Spare battery pack, backup power cell
+
📖What it is

A spare rechargeable battery pack for tools or electronics on E60.

❓Why it's needed

Tool batteries deplete during extended operations. A spare keeps critical tools running when the primary battery is exhausted.

✅
Verify Charge Every ShiftA spare battery at 10% charge is no spare at all. Check charge status on every rig check.
Middle Shelf — Water Rescue
Synching Rescue Collar
AKA: Synching collar, rescue collar, water rescue collar, victim recovery collar
+
📖What it is

A specialized water-rescue collar designed to slip around a victim and be cinched (synched) tight, securing them so a rescuer or rope team can haul them to safety without the victim slipping out.

❓Why it's needed

A panicked or unconscious water-rescue victim is hard to grip. The synching collar gives the rescuer a hands-free, secure attachment point — once cinched, the victim is locked in for the haul to shore.

🔧How to deploy
  1. Approach the victim from behind if possible.
  2. Loop the collar over their head and chest.
  3. Pull the cinch line to tighten — snug but not crushing.
  4. Maintain hold of the line as the team hauls the victim toward the bank or boat.
⚠️
Confirm It's Cinched Before You PullAn unsecured collar slides off when tension is applied. Confirm the cinch is tight before signaling the haul team — losing a victim mid-haul puts you in the water for round two.
Mustang Suit
AKA: Immersion suit, dry suit, survival suit, cold water suit
+
📖What it is

A thermal dry/immersion suit providing thermal protection and buoyancy for water rescue operations in cold water environments.

❓Why it's needed

Cold water incapacitation happens fast — in 50°F water, swimming ability is lost in under 3 minutes. The Mustang suit provides the thermal protection needed to survive and complete a rescue.

⚠️
Wear with a PFDThe Mustang suit provides some buoyancy but is not a substitute for a PFD. Always wear a PFD over the suit.
Water Helmet
AKA: Swift water helmet, rescue helmet, water rescue helmet
+
📖What it is

A lightweight rescue helmet designed for water operations — has drainage holes, positive buoyancy, and won't trap you underwater if it fills with water (unlike a structural fire helmet).

❓Why it's needed

Head protection in water rescue. Fast water pushes you into submerged obstacles. Your structural helmet is too heavy and would actually endanger you in water.

Water Rescue Rope
AKA: Throw rope, water rescue line, safety rope
+
📖What it is

A dedicated rope for water rescue — either a throw bag (rope packed for quick throwing) or a floating rescue line.

❓Why it's needed

Reach extends rescue capability without putting crew in the water. Throw the rope to the victim — they grab it, you pull. Throw before you go.

Watch: Throw Bag Water Rescue
Bottom Shelf
Manual Pump Can (Silver Bullet)
AKA: Manual pump can, pressurized water extinguisher, water can, silver bullet
+
📖What it is

A manual pump-pressurized stainless steel water extinguisher (~2.5 gallons) for Class A fires — small incipient fires, trash fires, and cooling hot spots during overhaul. The user pumps the handle to build pressure inside the can — there is no factory-charged propellant cartridge.

❓Why it's needed

Fast, no-hose-line-needed knockdown of small Class A fires. Also used for cooling smoldering materials during overhaul without the destructive force of a full attack line.

⚠️
Never on Electrical or Cooking OilWater on energized electrical = electrocution. Water on hot cooking oil = violent steam explosion. Know your fire class before you pull the trigger.
Gel Foam
AKA: Compressed Air Foam (CAF), fire gel, Class A foam
+
📖What it is

Fire-suppression gel or Class A foam that, when applied to a surface, dramatically reduces its flammability and helps extinguish or prevent ignition. More clingy than plain water — adheres to vertical surfaces.

❓Why it's needed

For wildland-urban interface fires, exposure protection, and Class A fire suppression. Gel foam covers surfaces and provides sustained water retention — plain water runs off immediately, but gel stays where you put it.

🔧Application

Use with the orange foam nozzle and the Chief Eductor for proper mixing. Can also be applied manually from a container. Apply to exposures ahead of the fire front or to burning material for suppression.

💡
Protect Exposures ProactivelyApply gel to structures or vegetation that are threatened but not yet burning. Pre-treating with gel can prevent ignition even when the fire reaches the treated area — one of the most valuable tools in interface operations.
Oil Dry (Kitty Litter)
AKA: Absorbent, clay absorbent, oil absorbent, oil dry
+
📖What it is

Granular clay absorbent for soaking up spilled fuel, oil, and other liquids at motor vehicle accidents and spill incidents.

❓Why it's needed

Fuel spills create fire and slip hazards. Environmental regulations require containment. Absorbent neutralizes the hazard, allows road reopening, and prevents storm drain contamination.

Life Vests (×multiple)
AKA: PFDs, personal flotation devices, life jackets
+
📖What it is

US Coast Guard-approved life jackets providing buoyancy for water rescue operations — additional vests beyond the horse collar, for multiple crew members.

❓Why it's needed

Water rescue may require multiple crew members near or in water. Every crew member operating near water must have a PFD on — not just the primary rescue swimmer.

50 ft of 5" Hose (Second Section)
AKA: LDH finish section, short supply section
+
📖What it is

A second 50-foot section of 5" large diameter hose stored on the officer side for additional supply flexibility.

❓Why it's needed

Having a second 50-foot section allows longer short lays, nurse tanker connections on the officer side, and backup supply if the engineer's side section is already committed.

🔐

Middle Compartment — Officer's Side

Hand tools · Forcible entry
Small Bolt Cutter
AKA: Mini bolt cutter, small cutter, chain cutter
+
📖What it is

A compact bolt cutter for padlocks, chains, small hasps, and cable locks where the large bolt cutter is too bulky.

❓Why it's needed

Many access situations involve standard commercial padlocks that don't require the full-size cutter. A smaller tool in a tighter space gets the job done faster.

Pig Tool
AKA: The Pig, Pig Axe, combination pick/flat-head striking tool
+
📖What it is

A combination striking and forcible-entry tool — a flat head on one side and a pick on the other. This is NOT a Pig Drain Cover. The Pig Drain Cover is a separate item — a flexible mat that seals storm drains to contain runoff. The Pig Tool / "the Pig" / Pig Axe is a hand tool. Same name, completely different jobs.

❓Why it's needed

Versatility — flat head for striking and driving, pick for puncturing and pulling. A compact tool that handles overhaul, light forcible entry, and breach work without carrying multiple separate tools.

⚠️
Three Items, Three Different Jobs"Pig Tool" / "PIG" / "Pig Axe" = the striking tool. "Pig Drain Cover" = the storm-drain mat. Don't conflate them on the radio — confusion costs time when somebody yells for "the pig."
Sledgehammer / Maul
AKA: Sledge, striking tool
+
📖What it is

Heavy sledgehammer for maximum striking force on reinforced commercial doors, masonry, and heavy-gauge locks.

❓Why it's needed

When the flat-head axe or maul in the driver's side compartment is in use, this provides a second striking tool — critical when multiple crews are simultaneously forcing entry.

Pick Head / Fire Axe
AKA: Pickhead axe, fire axe, roofing axe
+
📖What it is

An axe with blade and pointed pick — roof ventilation, floor breaching, and wall opening.

❓Why it's needed

Roof operations and floor/wall breaching. The pick end gets purchase in roofing materials and floor decking that the blade can't start without a hole.

Halligan Bar (Officer Side)
AKA: Hooligan, Pro-bar, bar, Halligan tool
+
📖What it is

A second Halligan bar stored on the officer side. See MDD-05 for full entry.

❓Why it's needed

Having a Halligan accessible from both sides of the apparatus means the crew member arriving on the officer side has immediate access to the primary forcible entry tool without crossing to the driver's side.

Flat Head Axe (Officer Side)
AKA: Flat axe, striking axe, fire axe
+
📖What it is

Second flat head axe on the officer side — see MDD-08 for full entry.

❓Why it's needed

Accessible from the officer side. Pairs with the officer-side Halligan to give the officer crew their own set of irons.

🧯

Rear Compartment — Officer's Side

Extinguishers · High Rise · Salvage · Decon
Extinguishers
Silver Bullet — Pressurized Water
AKA: Water can, silver bullet, stored-pressure water
+
📖What it is

Pressurized water extinguisher — 2.5 gallons, Class A fires only.

❓Why it's needed

Quick knockdown of small Class A fires without pulling a hose line. Also used in overhaul for cooling hot spots.

⚠️
Class A OnlyNever use on electrical (electrocution) or cooking oil (steam explosion).
ABC Dry Chemical Extinguisher
AKA: Dry chem, multi-purpose extinguisher, monoammonium phosphate
+
📖What it is

Multi-purpose dry chemical extinguisher — Class A, B, and C fires. Monoammonium phosphate powder under nitrogen pressure.

❓Why it's needed

The most versatile portable extinguisher — handles fuel spills, electrical, and ordinary combustible fires.

💡
Residue WarningABC dry chem leaves corrosive powder that destroys electronics and engine components. Use CO₂ for sensitive electronics when possible.
CO₂ Extinguisher
AKA: Carbon dioxide extinguisher, CO2 can
+
📖What it is

Carbon dioxide extinguisher for Class B and C fires — no residue, clean agent.

❓Why it's needed

Electrical fires and sensitive equipment where dry chemical residue would cause secondary damage.

⚠️
CO₂ DisplacementIn confined spaces, CO₂ displaces oxygen. Keep exposures brief. Never hold the horn bare-handed — it reaches -110°F and causes frostbite.
High Rise Operations
High Rise Pack
AKA: Standpipe pack, hi-rise pack
+
📖What it is

A prepackaged kit for standpipe operations — contains short length of 1¾" hose with fittings for connecting to building standpipe systems.

❓Why it's needed

High-rise firefighting requires connecting to building standpipe systems at the floor below the fire. The pack provides everything needed — hose, pressure gauge, wye, connectors — in one grab.

📋Contents typically include

Short 1¾" attack length, 90-degree connector, T-connector with pressure gauge, wye, vise grips for stiff standpipe valves. Pressure gauge is critical — standpipe pressures vary wildly and can be too high or too low to work with.

⚠️
Two Floors Below — AlwaysNever take the elevator to the fire floor. Take to two floors below, then stairs. An elevator opening on the fire floor traps you in smoke and heat.
High Rise Bag
AKA: Hi-rise bag, standpipe bag, high-rise equipment bag
+
📖What it is

A separate bag from the High Rise Pack — E60 carries both. The High Rise Bag contains additional hose lengths, extra fittings, or supplemental equipment for extended standpipe operations beyond what the pack provides.

❓Why it's needed

Extended high-rise operations — multiple floors, long standpipe stretches, or complex connection scenarios — require more equipment than a single pack provides. The bag gives you the overflow capacity.

💡
E60 Has Both — Know the DifferenceE60 specifically carries a High Rise Pack AND a High Rise Bag as separate items. Know what's in each so you can grab the right one. The pack is your immediate first-in kit; the bag provides extended-ops support.
Salvage & Decontamination
Tarps
AKA: Salvage covers, tarps, poly sheeting
+
📖What it is

Heavy-duty waterproof tarps for salvage operations — protecting contents from water damage during firefighting operations.

❓Why it's needed

Salvage operations can save more property value than fire suppression alone. Furniture, electronics, and personal items destroyed by water after the fire is extinguished represent a preventable loss. Tarps reduce secondary damage.

Blanket
AKA: Rescue blanket, patient blanket, thermal blanket
+
📖What it is

Emergency thermal blanket for patient warming and debris protection during extrication and rescue.

❓Why it's needed

Hypothermia is a serious complication in trauma patients. Covering a patient also protects them from debris and provides modesty. Warm the ground AND the top.

Tool Box
AKA: Maintenance tool box, utility kit, hand tools
+
🔧Contents

A general tool box containing maintenance and utility items — screwdrivers, wrenches, pliers, sockets, voltage tester, tape measure, and field-repair tools. Used for rig maintenance, equipment repair, and utility tasks at incidents. Verify contents during every shift check.

⚠️
Voltage Tester — Never Skip ItA voltage tester in this box is a safety item, not a convenience. Test before you touch any electrical component on a call.
2 Shovels — Scoop & Spade
AKA: Shovels, spades, mop-up shovels
+
📖What it is

Two shovels stored in the officer rear compartment — a flat-blade scoop and a pointed spade for different tasks.

❓Why it's needed

Scoop shovel: moving sand, dirt, debris, and absorbent. Spade shovel: digging, breaking ground, and moving compacted material. Overhaul, wildland mop-up, and hazmat cleanup all require shovels.

Decontamination Buckets and Soap
AKA: Decon buckets, decon kit, post-fire decon
+
📖What it is

Buckets and soap specifically designated for post-incident decontamination — rinsing contaminated tools, gear, and equipment after fires and hazmat exposures.

❓Why it's needed

Firefighter cancer rates are significantly elevated due to carcinogen exposure. PAHs, benzene, formaldehyde, and dozens of toxic compounds are present on gear after every structural fire. Decon reduces this exposure dramatically.

🔧Decon Protocol

  1. Scene: Wipe face, neck, and hands with Fire Wipes (cab) before getting back in the apparatus.
  2. At the rig: Fill decon bucket with water + soap. Scrub tools, gloves, and boots before stowing.
  3. At the station: Bag contaminated gear for washing — don't carry it through the station.
  4. Personal: Shower before eating, drinking, or touching your face. Change clothes.
  5. Never: Wear contaminated gear home, sit in your personal vehicle in gear, or eat/drink on scene.

⚠️
Decon Is Not OptionalCarcinogen exposure after structural fires is a medical certainty. Decontamination immediately after every working fire is one of the most impactful health habits a firefighter can develop. Use the buckets.
🚗

Rear of Engine

Ladders · Hurst Combi · Ram · Backboards · Hose
Ladders — Middle Rear Compartment & Top
Hose Card — Clipboard
AKA: Hose Card, load record, hose inventory, hose test record
+
📖What it is

A physical clipboard mounted in the cab (or rear compartment area) tracking every individual hose section on E60 by its unique ID number, length, location on the rig, and annual service test status. Sections marked with "T" have been tested in the current year. The record is a legal compliance document and a tool for accurate accountability during rig checks.

❓Why it's needed

NFPA 1962 requires fire hose to be service-tested annually. The Hose Card is E60's evidence of compliance — it shows which sections have been tested and which are due. If a section is swapped out or replaced (damaged, failed test), the record must be updated immediately. During a rig check, comparing the clipboard to the actual hose loads confirms that every section is accounted for and in its correct position.

🗂️E60 Hose Section Layout
LocationKey SectionsTotalsNotes
Left Hose BedD-64 (50'), D-183 (100'), D-244–D-264 (up to 400')400 ftMain left bay supply
2½" Skid LoadC-775 (50'), C-181 (100'), C-171 (150')150 ft skidSmooth bore nozzle attached
Front CrosslayB-145 (50') through B-50 (200')200 ftPreconnected attack
Rear CrosslayB-235–B-232 (50'–200')200 ftPreconnected attack

Middle Hose BedG-132 (100') through G-199 (1,000')1,000 ft5" LDH supply
💡
T = Tested This YearSections marked "T" on the clipboard have passed their annual service test. Any section without a "T" is either due for testing or has failed. During your rig check, you don't need to memorize every ID — but you should know where the clipboard is and be able to verify that the hose loads match the record. If something doesn't add up, flag it to your company officer before going available.
⚠️
Update the Record When Hose ChangesIf any hose section is swapped, removed for repair, or replaced after a failure, the Hose Card must be updated that shift. Operating with an out-of-date record means you can't confirm testing compliance — and it can mean a different section is in a position than expected, which matters during a midnight supply lay.
📋 View E60 Hose Record Photo
10 ft Folding Ladder
AKA: Attic ladder, folding ladder, interior ladder
+
📖What it is

A compact folding ladder for attic access through ceiling hatches and tight-space elevation requirements.

❓Why it's needed

Attic fires require above-ceiling access. The 10-footer fits through standard 22"×30" attic hatches.

24 ft Extension Ladder
AKA: Ground ladder, two-section ladder, 24-footer
+
📖What it is

A two-section 24-foot aluminum extension ladder — primary rescue/access ladder for second and third floor windows.

❓Why it's needed

Rescue from upper floors. Firefighter access and egress routes. The 1-to-4 rule: 1 foot out for every 4 feet of height for proper working angle.

⚠️
Throw Early — Don't WaitLadders belong up on arrival, before you need them for rescue. A ladder thrown after a Mayday is too late.
14 ft Roof Ladder
AKA: Roof ladder, short extension, single section ladder
+
📖What it is

A 14-foot single-section ladder with roof hooks for securing it to a ridge — allows working on steep-pitch roofs without sliding.

❓Why it's needed

Roof ventilation on pitched roofs requires a stable footing. The roof hooks grab the ridge and the ladder becomes a walkway/workspace on sloped surfaces.

6 ft Pike Poles ×2 (Top of Ladder Compartment)
AKA: Pike poles, ceiling hooks, plaster hooks
+
📖What it is

Two 6-foot pike poles stored on top of the ladder compartment. Used for pulling ceilings, opening walls, and overhaul.

❓Why it's needed

Overhaul requires pulling burned ceiling and wall materials to expose hidden fire. Pull toward you and to the side — never directly overhead.

✅
Pull from the DoorwayWork ceiling pulls from a doorway or protected corner when possible. Material falling from above is heavy and unpredictable.
2 Backboards
AKA: Long backboard, spine board, LSB
+
📖What it is

Full-length rigid spinal immobilization boards for trauma patients with suspected spinal injuries during rescue and transport.

❓Why it's needed

Unstable spinal fractures + movement = paralysis or death. Two boards allow simultaneous patient management for multi-victim incidents.

Extrication Equipment
Hurst Combi Tool — Cuts AND Spreads
AKA: Combi tool, combination cutter-spreader, jaws of life (combo), Hurst combo
+
📖What it is

This is what makes E60's extrication setup unique. The Hurst Combi Tool is a single hydraulic tool with blades that both cut (like a cutter) AND spread (like a spreader). One tool does the job of two.

❓Why it's needed / Why it's different

Most engines carry a separate Hurst cutter AND Hurst spreader (like E61). E60 has the Combi tool instead — a single device that switches between cutting and spreading modes. This is faster to set up (one tool vs. two) and lighter, but means there's only one extrication tool working at a time.

🔧How to use

  1. Connect to power source (hydraulic or battery).
  2. For spreading: open blades and insert into gap, activate spread.
  3. For cutting: position blades perpendicular to cut target, activate close.
  4. Never use blades at an angle — perpendicular contact is required for clean cuts.
  5. Keep blade tips away from SRS/airbag components (min. 6 inches).

⚠️
One Tool = One Function at a TimeWith a separate cutter and spreader (like E61), two crew members can work simultaneously. With the Combi tool, only one operation happens at a time. Plan your sequence before you start: spread the door, then cut the hinges — not both at once.
⚠️
Know This Before a CallIf you've been training on E61's cutter+spreader setup, consciously reset before riding E60. There is no separate spreader. There is no separate cutter. There is ONE Combi tool. Adjust your mental sequence accordingly.
Watch: Hurst Combi Tool Extrication
Ram Jam + Braces for Ram Tool
AKA: Ram support, ram jam, spreader support
+
📖What it is

The Ram Jam is a support device that braces the Hurst ram during dashboard displacement and other pushing operations. The braces are additional support pieces that anchor the ram against the vehicle floor or seat structure.

❓Why it's needed

A hydraulic ram under load needs something to push against. Without the Ram Jam and braces, the ram slides off the seat rail or floor structure instead of transmitting force to the dashboard. The support system is what makes the ram effective.

🔧Setup

  1. Insert the ram into the target gap (dashboard to floor).
  2. Position the Ram Jam base against the floor/seat rail anchor point.
  3. Add braces as needed for stability.
  4. Activate the ram — it pushes the dash forward while the Ram Jam holds the base.

💡
Unique E60 TerminologyE60 calls this the "Ram Jam" — E61 uses a "Quick Kick ram support." Same concept, different brand/name. If you're on mutual aid or at training and someone calls for the Quick Kick equivalent, this is E60's version.
Pry Tool + Pry Bar
AKA: Pry bar, pinch bar, wonder bar, crow bar
+
📖What it is

Two prying tools for levering, separating components, and creating gaps. The pry tool is typically shorter with a flat wedge end; the pry bar is a longer round bar with curved hook ends.

❓Why it's needed

Different prying tasks need different leverage lengths and geometries. The shorter tool works in tight spaces; the longer bar provides more leverage for heavy components.

2 Shovels — Scoop & Pointed (Rear)
AKA: Mop-up shovels, scoop shovel, spade
+
📖What it is

Second set of shovels stored at the rear of the engine — scoop and pointed styles.

❓Why it's needed

Having shovels accessible from both the officer side and the rear means crews on either side have immediate access during overhaul, mop-up, and cleanup operations.

Rear Hose Bays

Cab Compartment

AED · Gas monitors · TIC · OB kit · Medic bag · Comms
Medical & Patient Care
💡
Hose Card — Clipboard in Cab E60 carries a Hose Card clipboard tracking every individual hose section by ID number. Each section (e.g., D-64, B-129, G-199) has a length and a "T" marking if it was tested that year. During rig check, verify the clipboard matches the actual hose loads. If a section was replaced, the record must be updated. The record is your paper trail for hose testing compliance. See the E60 Photos & Details doc for the current clipboard photo.
AED — Automated External Defibrillator
AKA: AED, defib, defibrillator, shock box
+
📖What it is

An automated external defibrillator that analyzes cardiac rhythm and delivers electrical shock to restore normal rhythm in VF/VT cardiac arrest.

❓Why it's needed

Cardiac arrest survival drops ~10% for every minute without defibrillation. Early defibrillation is the most effective treatment for shockable cardiac rhythms.

⚠️
Clear Before ShockingEveryone clear — including you — before pressing the shock button. Announce: "I'm clear, you're clear, everybody's clear." Then shock.
Watch: AED Operation Training
Medic Bag
AKA: Medical kit, first-in bag, trauma bag, EMS bag
+
📖What it is

The primary EMS response bag for medical and trauma emergencies — contains assessment tools, bandaging, airway management, and initial stabilization equipment.

❓Why it's needed

Most fire department responses are medical. The medic bag gets you to the patient with the tools to assess and begin treatment within seconds of scene arrival.

OB Kit — Obstetrics Kit
AKA: Birth kit, delivery kit, OB bag
+
📖What it is

A kit containing sterile supplies for emergency childbirth — gloves, drapes, cord clamps, bulb syringe, cord cutter, and infant blanket.

❓Why it's needed

Emergency childbirth (imminent delivery that can't wait for ALS or hospital) is a genuine field scenario. The OB kit provides the minimal sterile equipment needed to assist a delivery safely.

🔧Key steps

  1. Ensure warm environment and lay mother on her back.
  2. Don OB gloves — this is a sterile procedure.
  3. Support the baby's head as it crowns — do NOT pull.
  4. After delivery: clamp cord in two places, cut between clamps.
  5. Clear baby's airway with bulb syringe, dry and stimulate.
  6. Wrap infant and keep warm. Transport both mother and infant.

💡
Unique to E60The OB kit is specifically listed in E60's cab but not called out on all engines. Know it's there and review the steps before you need them — emergency deliveries don't announce themselves with much lead time.
2 Face Pieces — Large & Medium
AKA: SCBA face piece, air mask, spare mask
+
📖What it is

Two spare SCBA face pieces (size Large and size Medium) stored in the cab for crew members whose masks have failed or who need replacement face pieces.

❓Why it's needed

A cracked lens, torn seal, or malfunctioning valve makes a face piece unusable. Spare pieces in known sizes (L and M) mean an equipment failure doesn't pull a firefighter from operations.

✅
Know Which Size Fits YouIf you wear a size Large or Medium, confirm these are the right sizes during your rig check. A face piece that doesn't fit won't seal — and a face piece that doesn't seal means no IDLH entry.
Extra Gloves
AKA: Work gloves, extrication gloves, latex gloves, structural gloves
+
📖What it is

Additional gloves stored in the cab — may include both structural firefighting gloves and medical/extrication gloves.

❓Why it's needed

Gloves are the most frequently torn, lost, or contaminated piece of PPE. Having extras in the cab means a torn glove at a medical call doesn't leave you without hand protection.

Gas Detection & Hazmat
4-Gas Monitor
AKA: Multi-gas monitor, 4-gas meter, Gas Track Monitor
+
🔧What it detects
GasAlarm AtIDLH
CO (carbon monoxide)35 ppm1,200 ppm
O₂ (oxygen)<19.5% or >23.5%<16%
H₂S (hydrogen sulfide)10 ppm50 ppm
Combustible gas (%LEL)10% LELVaries
⚠️
Bump-Test Before Every ShiftA gas monitor with failed sensors reads safe when it isn't. Bump-test (brief exposure to known gas) to confirm sensor response. Never trust an untested meter.
Gas Trac (Methane / HCN Meter)
AKA: Gas tracker, methane meter, HCN meter, cyanide detector
+
📖What it is

The Gas Trac unit monitors methane (natural gas) and hydrogen cyanide (HCN). The HCN sensor is typically integrated into the Gas Trac unit.

❓Why it's needed

HCN (hydrogen cyanide) is generated by burning synthetics and plastics — it's 35× more toxic than CO by concentration and is a major factor in fire victim fatalities. Methane detection is essential for gas leak emergencies.

⚠️
HCN Is UnderestimatedHCN toxicity is a leading cause of fire victim deaths that CPR alone can't reverse. When HCN is suspected, report exposure to EMS for potential antidote consideration.
TIC — Thermal Imaging Camera
AKA: TIC, thermal camera, FLIR, heat camera
+
📖What it is

A handheld infrared camera that detects temperature differences — displaying heat signatures in real-time. Shows hot spots through smoke, finds victims in low visibility, and identifies hidden fire in walls and ceilings.

❓Why it's needed

Zero-visibility interior operations. The TIC reads heat, not light — it sees through smoke. Finding a victim in a smoke-filled room, identifying fire extension in a wall, or checking for hot spots during overhaul all happen faster and safer with a TIC.

🔧How to use

  1. Power on — allow brief warm-up.
  2. Hold so the display faces you, lens forward toward the environment.
  3. White/bright = hot. Black/dark = cold (on standard palette — some units reverse this).
  4. Scan walls and ceilings for hot spots during overhaul.
  5. Sweep at floor level when searching for victims (victims are warm; smoke obscures light but not heat).

✅
TIC Is a Tool, Not a GuaranteeA TIC can show you heat signatures through smoke, but it can't tell you structural integrity, air quality, or the source of heat. A hot wall could be fire extension or a steam pipe. Use TIC data in context — it supplements but doesn't replace your other senses and training.
Watch: Thermal Imaging Camera Firefighter Use
Hot Stick
AKA: Non-contact voltage tester, electrical probe, voltage detector
+
📖What it is

A non-contact voltage detection tool — beeps or lights up when within range of energized AC conductors without requiring physical contact.

❓Why it's needed

Downed power lines, damaged panels, and flooded structures present electrocution risks. Test before you touch.

⚠️
No Reading ≠ SafeA non-alarming Hot Stick isn't a guarantee of safety — batteries may be dead or you may be out of range. Treat all conductors as energized unless confirmed dead by the utility.
Communication, Access & Scene Control
Knox Box Key
AKA: Knox key, rapid entry key, master key
+
📖What it is

A secured key that opens Knox Box rapid-entry systems on commercial buildings — providing immediate access to building master keys without forced entry.

❓Why it's needed

After-hours commercial calls. The Knox key opens the box in seconds and avoids destructive forced entry on locked buildings.

⚠️
Handle With Care — This Key Opens EverythingThe Knox key opens hundreds of buildings in your district. It must stay secured with the rig at all times. Loss requires re-keying the entire Knox system in your coverage area.
Battery Chargers
AKA: Battery charger, charging station
+
📖What it is

Charging units for tool batteries, portable radio batteries, and device batteries stored in the cab.

❓Why it's needed

Dead batteries mean non-functional tools and radios. The chargers ensure all batteries are ready at the start of every shift and can be recharged between calls.

Caution Tape
AKA: Scene tape, barrier tape, yellow tape
+
📖What it is

Yellow caution/barrier tape for establishing scene perimeters and warning the public away from hazards.

❓Why it's needed

Uncontrolled scene access endangers the public and destroys investigation evidence. Tape goes up early and stays up until the scene is cleared.

Fire Wipes
AKA: Decon wipes, post-fire wipes, carcinogen wipes
+
📖What they are & why they matter

Large-format disposable wipes formulated to remove fireground carcinogens (PAHs, benzene, soot) from skin and equipment. Wipe exposed skin (neck, face, hands) before getting back in the cab after every fire. The cab is a clean zone — don't contaminate it with post-fire carcinogens on your skin and gear.

⚠️
60 Seconds, Every FireThe most impactful cancer-prevention habit you can build. Wipe before you ride. Bag your contaminated hood. Shower at the station before eating.
Vests
AKA: High-visibility vests, ANSI vests, hi-viz
+
📖What it is

ANSI/ISEA-rated high-visibility reflective vests for working in or near traffic.

❓Why it's needed

Being struck by a vehicle is a leading cause of firefighter LODDs. Structural turnout gear is not high-visibility. Vest goes on at every traffic-adjacent call — every time, no exceptions.

Water Bottles
AKA: Crew hydration, water supply
+
📖What it is

Water stored in the cab for crew hydration before, during, and after emergency operations.

❓Why it's needed

Firefighting is among the most physically demanding activities possible. Dehydration impairs performance before you feel thirsty. Drink proactively — especially after working in gear.

✅
