Water Supply Fittings · Adapters · High-Rise · Hydrant Bag · K-12 Blades
Gated Wye
AKA: Wye, gated wye, water thief (different — see below), "the wye"
+
📖What it is & what it does

A Y-shaped fitting that splits one larger supply line into two smaller discharge lines, each with its own gate (shutoff valve). Common configuration: one 2½" inlet → two 1½" or 1¾" outlets. Used for stretching attack lines off a larger supply line, supplying multiple crews from one supply, or feeding two 1¾ lines from a single 2½ stretched up a stairwell.

🧩Parts
  • Inlet (single, larger): Female swivel, receives the supply line.
  • Two outlets (smaller): Male threads, feed the attack lines.
  • Two ball valves / gate handles: Open/close each outlet independently — that's what "gated" means.
  • Body: Cast aluminum or brass.
🏷️Alternate names

"Wye," "gated wye." Note: a "Water Thief" is a different tool — it has one larger outlet that passes through PLUS gated smaller outlets, used for adding lines without breaking the supply.

🚿
Rookie Mistake — Opening Both Gates With Only One Line AttachedIf you open a gate on an outlet that has no hose attached, you've just charged a free-flowing 2½" hole and water blasts everywhere — usually right into the lap of whoever's standing there. Verify hose is connected and the receiving crew is ready BEFORE you open the gate. Open slow.
Storz Connectors
AKA: Storz, quarter-turn couplings, "the Storz"
+
📖What it is & what it does

Sexless quarter-turn couplings — both halves are identical, no male/female distinction. Line up the lugs, push them together, twist a quarter turn, locked. Used everywhere on LDH (Large Diameter Hose), hydrant connections, and fast-deploy fittings. Faster than threaded couplings and won't cross-thread on you.

🧩Parts
  • Coupling body: Aluminum (most common) or brass.
  • Two lugs (cams): The hooked tabs that engage the matching slots.
  • Rubber gasket / O-ring: Seats between the two faces — pre-shift, check the gasket. No gasket = leak under pressure.
  • Locking clip (Kochek lock or similar): Prevents accidental quarter-turn release.
🏷️Alternate names

"Storz" (universal), "quarter-turn couplings," "cam-and-groove couplings" (technically a different design but related family).

🪢
Rookie Mistake — Forgetting the GasketA Storz coupling without its rubber gasket will not seal. Under pressure it sprays a high-pressure jet of water sideways. The gasket lives in the female face; if it's missing, cracked, or dirty, you replace or clean it BEFORE you charge the line. Carry spare gaskets on rig check.
Female / Female Adapters
AKA: Double female, F/F, "the double female"
+
📖What it is & what it does

An adapter with female threads on both ends. Used to join two male-ended hoses together when you've crossed your couplings, or to mate two male-threaded discharges. Looks pointless until you need one — and then you really, really need one.

🧩Parts
  • Body: Short brass or aluminum sleeve.
  • Two female swivels: Each end mates to a male thread.
  • Two rubber gaskets: Inside each female end.
🏷️Alternate names

"Double female," "F-to-F," "F/F."

🔧
Rookie Mistake — Cross-ThreadingNST and NH are NOT the same thread pattern as IPT or NPT. Forcing a female swivel onto wrong threads ruins both. Hand-tight first. If it doesn't spin on smoothly, stop. Wrong fitting. Find the right adapter.
Male-to-Male Adapter
AKA: Double male, M/M, "the double male"
+
📖What it is & what it does

An adapter with male threads on both ends. Used to join two female-ended hoses together — same logic as the double female, opposite gender. Lives in the kit because the day you need one is the day your couplings won't connect any other way.

🧩Parts
  • Body: Short brass or aluminum sleeve.
  • Two male threaded ends.
🏷️Alternate names

"Double male," "M-to-M," "M/M."

🧠
Carry Both, Use EitherDouble-male and double-female adapters belong in the same kit and the same compartment. If you're reaching for one, there's a 50/50 chance you actually need the other. Pull both, identify which fits.
Storz Reducer
AKA: Reducer, step-down, "the Storz reducer"
+
📖What it is & what it does

An adapter that steps a larger Storz coupling DOWN to a smaller threaded coupling — typically a 5" Storz on one side, 2½" NH male thread on the other. Lets you take a 5" LDH supply and feed it into a 2½" intake or discharge. Critical when you're working from a 5"-supplied scene but the closest connection is sized for a smaller line.

🧩Parts
  • Storz half: Standard Storz coupling, larger size.
  • Threaded half: Smaller-diameter NH thread (typically male).
  • Gasket on the Storz side.
🏷️Alternate names

"Reducer," "Storz-to-NH reducer," "step-down adapter."

💧
Rookie Mistake — Reducing Then Maxing FlowJust because the adapter physically fits doesn't mean the smaller hose downstream can handle the supply pressure. Reducing from 5" to 2½" creates a chokepoint. Verify your pump pressure and your downstream line's rating. A 2½" line behind a reducer is still rated for 2½" pressure, not 5".
Intake Cap with Chain
AKA: Intake cap, suction cap, blind cap, "the cap"
+
📖What it is & what it does

The threaded or Storz cap that closes off the pump's large intake when it's not in use. The chain keeps the cap tethered to the pump so it doesn't disappear when somebody pulls it off in a hurry. Without a cap, debris, dirt, and bugs get into the intake and end up in the pump.

🧩Parts
  • Cap body: Storz or threaded to match the intake.
  • Pull lugs / handle: Two lugs for a spanner wrench to break it loose if it's seized.
  • Tether chain: Bolted to the cap, anchored to the pump body.
  • Gasket: Same as any coupling — seal it.
🏷️Alternate names

"Intake cap," "suction cap," "blind cap," "stinger cap" (older), "the cap."

⛓️
Rookie Mistake — Cap Bouncing Around LooseIf the cap is off and dangling on its chain while the rig moves, it bangs against the pump panel and damages the threads. Removed cap = secured in the compartment, OR seated back on the intake hand-tight. Don't leave it swinging.
Angled Connectors
AKA: 30° elbow, 45° elbow, angled adapter, "the elbow"
+
📖What it is & what it does

Bent/angled couplings that redirect hose flow without forcing the hose itself to bend sharply. Used at hydrants where the supply line geometry would otherwise kink the hose, or at intakes that face an awkward direction. A smooth-flow angled fitting keeps friction loss reasonable; a kinked hose adds dramatic friction loss and can rupture under pump pressure.

🧩Parts
  • Angled metal body (typically 30° or 45°).
  • Storz or threaded ends.
  • Gasket.
🏷️Alternate names

"Angled adapter," "elbow," "30° connector," "45° connector," "deflector."

📐
Rookie Mistake — Forgetting It ExistsProbies pull on a kinked hose for ten minutes trying to make it lay flat when one elbow fitting would have solved the problem in thirty seconds. Look at the geometry. If the hose is fighting the connection, ASK if there's an angled adapter — there usually is.
High-Rise Pack — 150 ft 1¾" + Gated Wye, Shoulder-Carry
AKA: High-rise pack, hi-rise bundle, "the high-rise"
+
📖What it is & what it does

A pre-built bundle of 150 feet of 1¾" hose with a gated wye, packed in a shoulder-strap carry bag so a crew can sling it on, climb a stairwell, and drop into a high-rise standpipe connection. The gated wye lets you split off attack lines after you reach the fire floor. Standpipe operations in a high-rise are exhausting and slow; the pack is built so one firefighter can carry it up many flights without dropping pieces.

🧩Parts
  • 150 ft of 1¾" hose: Packed in a folded/snake load for fast deployment.
  • Gated wye: Splits 2½ into two 1¾.
  • Shoulder-carry bag: Padded strap, top opening, designed for one-shoulder carry up stairs.
  • Nozzle (often packed separately or attached).
🏷️Alternate names

"High-rise pack," "high-rise bundle," "hi-rise," "standpipe pack," "Cleveland load" (the loading pattern, sometimes).

🏢
Rookie Mistake — Standpipe Outlet Pressure FailureHigh-rise standpipes do NOT always deliver good pressure. Some are dead, some are partially closed, some are reduced-flow design. Probies who hook up to a standpipe and assume "water is water" can find themselves at the door with a flaccid, useless line. Have a backup plan — pumping the standpipe from outside if needed, and know the building's standpipe class.
🦴
Carry With the Right Shoulder for the StairsRight-hand stairs vs left-hand stairs determines which shoulder the pack rides on — you don't want the bundle smacking the wall on every flight. Plan the carry before you start climbing.
High-Rise Bag — 2½" Section, Pressuremeter T, Elbow, Vise Grips
AKA: Standpipe kit, hi-rise tool bag, "the standpipe bag"
+
📖What it is & what it does

A second bag dedicated to standpipe operations — but instead of hose, it carries the tools you need to connect to a standpipe outlet, measure pressure, and improvise around broken equipment. The Pressuremeter T is the centerpiece. You connect it inline, you see exactly what pressure the standpipe is actually delivering.

🧩Parts
  • Short section of 2½" hose: For the standpipe-to-wye stretch.
  • Pressuremeter T (in-line gauge T-fitting): A T-shaped fitting with a pressure gauge — installs inline so you can read real pressure mid-stretch.
  • Elbow connector: For redirecting flow at the outlet.
  • Vise grips: Standpipes have stuck handles, broken caps, mangled threads. Vise grips solve roughly half of those problems.
  • Bag itself: Carry-strap or backpack-style.
🏷️Alternate names

"Standpipe bag," "hi-rise tool bag," "standpipe kit," "the T-bag" (informal — refers to the Pressuremeter T).

📊
Rookie Mistake — Skipping the Pressure ReadIf you connect to a standpipe and DON'T install the pressuremeter T, you don't actually know what you're working with. The gauge tells you whether you've got 75 psi (marginal) or 150 psi (good) at the outlet. Without that data, you're guessing. Slow down, install the T, read the number, then stretch.
2× Fog Nozzles
AKA: Fog nozzles, combination nozzles, automatic nozzles, "the fogs"
+
📖What it is & what it does

Spare/swappable fog nozzles. A fog nozzle has adjustable flow (gallons per minute) and adjustable pattern from straight stream to wide fog. Versatile — handles interior attack, exterior cooling, exposure protection, and hydraulic ventilation. Replaces a damaged nozzle, gets put on a stretched line that wasn't preconnected, fits a high-rise wye.

🧩Parts
  • Inlet coupling (female swivel): Connects to the hose.
  • Shutoff valve / ball valve: Lever handle on top, opens and closes the flow.
  • Flow selector ring (some models): Sets GPM (95 / 125 / 150 / 185 / 200).
  • Pattern adjustment: Twist the front bumper — straight stream → narrow fog → wide fog.
  • Front bumper: The rubber-coated outer ring at the tip.
🏷️Alternate names

"Fog nozzle," "combination nozzle," "automatic nozzle" (specific type), "TFT" (brand), "Akron" (brand), "the fog."

🌀
Rookie Mistake — Wide Fog Inside the StructureWide-fog pattern inside a burning structure entrains hot products of combustion and can push fire onto crews behind you (the "smoke explosion" phenomenon). Interior attack = straight stream or narrow fog, generally. Wide fog is for exterior cooling or hydraulic ventilation. Know your tactic before you twist the bumper.
🚿
Open and Close SLOWLYSnapping the bail open creates water hammer that can rupture hose or damage the nozzle. Open the bail in a smooth, deliberate motion. Same on close.
Hydrant Bag — Wrench · Spanners · Mallet · Gate Valve · Storz · LDH Rope
AKA: Hydrant kit, hydrant bag, "the hydrant tools"
+
📖What it is & what it does

A self-contained bag holding every tool needed to make a connection to a fire hydrant. The hydrant person grabs this and steps off the rig before the apparatus pulls forward to lay supply. Built so one firefighter can deploy the bag, find the hydrant, open it, and connect — alone if necessary.

🧩Parts (inside the bag)
  • Hydrant wrench: The pentagonal-socket wrench for the operating nut on top of the hydrant.
  • Spanners: Wrenches to break loose threaded caps and tighten connections.
  • Rubber mallet: For tapping a stuck cap free, or seating a Storz home.
  • In-line gate valve: Installs on a hydrant outlet so the hydrant person can shut down ONE supply line without closing the whole hydrant.
  • Storz connectors: Adapt the hydrant's NST/NH threads to Storz LDH.
  • LDH rope: Used to tie off the LDH supply to the hydrant or secure the hose during deployment.
  • The bag itself: Wear-resistant, designed to throw onto pavement at the curb.
🏷️Alternate names

"Hydrant bag," "hydrant kit," "FDC bag" (when used for FDC connections), "stretch bag."

🚒
Rookie Mistake — Hydrant Person Forgets the BagProbie jumps off, runs to the hydrant, and realizes the bag is still on the rig that's now pulling away. Now there's no wrench, no Storz adapter, and no water. The hydrant bag goes WITH the hydrant person the moment the rig starts the lay. Drill this until it's muscle memory.
🔓
Open the Hydrant SLOWLY and ALL THE WAYHydrants that are partially open create cavitation and damage the valve. Half-open is worse than fully closed. Crack it slow to flush debris, then OPEN ALL THE WAY. Listen for the water column to flow. Then connect.
K-12 Blades
AKA: K-12 blades, rescue saw blades, abrasive discs, "the spare blades"
+
📖What it is & what it does

Spare cutting discs for the K-12 (rotary cut-off) saw. Different blades for different materials. Stored separately from the saw so when one wears out, gets glazed over, or shatters, the operator can swap in a fresh blade without taking the saw out of service.

🧩Parts & types
  • Abrasive composite blade (for steel/iron): Black, wears down with use. Designed for ferrous metal.
  • Masonry/diamond blade (for concrete/brick): Diamond-segmented edge. Do NOT use on metal.
  • Maximum RPM marking: Stamped on the blade. Respect it.
  • Arbor hole / mounting hub: Standardized to fit the K-12.
🏷️Alternate names

"K-12 blades," "rescue blades," "abrasive discs," "cutoff discs," "carbide" (specific type), "diamond blade" (specific type).

💀
Rookie Mistake — Wrong Blade for the MaterialPutting a masonry diamond blade on metal will shatter at 5,000 RPM and send shrapnel into your femoral. Putting an abrasive on concrete glazes it useless in seconds. CHECK THE BLADE BEFORE EVERY CUT. The blade is labeled — read it. If you don't know, ASK before pulling the trigger.
🪚

Driver's Side Rear Middle Compartment

Sawzall · Grinder · Chainsaw · K-12 · Fuel · Chain Lube · Tool Kit · Spanners · Hydrant Wrench · O-Rings
DeWalt Sawzall
AKA: Sawzall, recip saw, reciprocating saw, "the Sawzall"
+
📖What it is & what it does

A handheld reciprocating saw — push/pull blade action. DeWalt is the brand on this rig, the whole tool family is called "Sawzall" after the Milwaukee original. Cuts almost anything with the right blade: wood, metal, drywall, copper pipe, vehicle pillars. Most versatile cutting tool in the compartment. Used heavily in extrication, overhaul, and forcible entry on bolted/screwed assemblies.

🧩Parts
  • Blade: Wood blades have coarse, large teeth. Metal blades have many fine teeth. Bi-metal blades cut nail-embedded wood.
  • Blade clamp / quick-release: Twist to open, drop the blade in, twist to lock.
  • Shoe (front foot): Press against the workpiece to reduce blade chatter.
  • Variable speed trigger.
  • Battery (DeWalt platform): Verify charge on rig check.
🏷️Alternate names

"Sawzall" (Milwaukee brand-as-generic), "recip saw," "reciprocating saw," "tiger saw" (older term), "hognose."

⚙️
Rookie Mistake — Wrong Blade, Wasted CutWood blade on metal stalls in two seconds. Metal blade on wood walks off the line. Choose deliberately. Spare blades live with the saw — don't return one in the wrong slot.
🧱
Hidden Wires & PipesRecip saws happily cut through electrical wires, gas lines, brake lines, hydraulic lines, and people. Know what's on the other side of the wall, the door, or the seat before you plunge.
Angle Grinder
AKA: Grinder, side grinder, 4½ grinder, "the grinder"
+
📖What it is & what it does

A handheld grinder running a small (4½") abrasive or cutting wheel. Used for precision metal cutting where the K-12 is too big or too aggressive — cutting a stuck bolt, slicing rebar, cutting a lock shackle, grinding burrs off cut metal. More controlled than the K-12 in tight spaces.

🧩Parts
  • Cutting/grinding disc: Match disc to job — thin = cutting, thick = grinding.
  • Wheel guard: Positioned to deflect sparks AWAY. Never remove it.
  • Side handle: Two-hand operation, always.
  • Spindle lock button: Press to change discs — NEVER while running.
  • Trigger / paddle switch.
🏷️Alternate names

"Grinder," "angle grinder," "4½ grinder," "side grinder," "disc grinder."

💥
Rookie Mistake — Removing the GuardGrinder wheels shatter at 11,000 RPM. Probie removes the guard "for clearance," wheel disintegrates, shrapnel goes into the femoral. The guard never comes off. Period. If you can't fit with the guard, switch to a smaller wheel or a different tool.
Chainsaw with Roof Guide
AKA: Vent saw, roof saw, ventilation saw, "the chainsaw"
+
📖What it is & what it does

A gas-powered chainsaw fitted with a ROOF GUIDE accessory — a depth-gauge attachment that prevents the saw from cutting too deep into a roof. Used for vertical ventilation cuts on wood-decked roofs. The roof guide rides on the roof surface and limits how far the chain plunges, so you cut through the deck but NOT the joists/rafters below.

🧩Parts
  • Bar & carbide chain: Carbide-tipped chain shrugs off roofing nails and shingles that would dull standard chain in seconds.
  • Roof guide attachment: Mounted on the bar; rides on the roof surface to limit cut depth.
  • Sprocket, oiler, bar oil reservoir.
  • Two-stroke engine + fuel mix tank.
  • Chain brake.
  • Front/rear handles, kickback guard.
🏷️Alternate names

"Roof saw," "vent saw," "Stihl" (brand-as-generic), "ventilation saw," "depth-stop saw."

🪵
Rookie Mistake — Cutting the JoistThe roof guide is THERE so you cut the decking but NOT the structural member. Without the guide (or with it set wrong), you cut through a rafter and weaken the very surface you're standing on. People have fallen through their own vent holes. Verify the guide is installed and set correctly BEFORE you climb.
↪️
Plan Your Retreat PathCut so your escape route is always UPHILL of the cut and OPPOSITE side from where the hole opens. Don't cut around yourself onto a peninsula of decking that breaks free.
K-12 Rotary Saw
AKA: K-12, K-saw, rescue saw, cut-off saw, "the K-12"
+
📖What it is & what it does

The gas-powered rotary cut-off saw. Spinning 12–14" abrasive or diamond disc at violent RPM. Cuts steel, masonry, concrete, rebar, metal-decked roofs. The workhorse for forcible entry on commercial roll-up doors, cutting locks/bars, and ventilation cuts in metal decks. The K-12 makes a LOT of noise, throws a LOT of sparks, and demands respect.

🧩Parts
  • Blade (abrasive composite OR diamond): Match to the material. Spares stored in DSFM compartment.
  • Blade guard (rotating): Set to deflect debris AWAY from operator and patient.
  • Two-stroke engine: Requires premixed fuel.
  • Pull start, throttle, choke.
  • Two-hand grip + belly guard.
🏷️Alternate names

"K-12" (model name, used generically), "K-saw," "cut-off saw," "rescue saw," "partner saw," "Stihl" (different brand, same job), "quickie saw."

🔥
Rookie Mistake — Cutting Without a Charged Line Standing ByThe K-12 throws sparks 20 feet. Cutting near fuel, in a fuel-soaked structure, or in any atmosphere that COULD ignite, demands a charged hose line and a spotter watching the spark path. Always. If a fire flashes from your sparks, the hose line is the only thing between the crew and a really bad day.
⛽
Two-Stroke Fuel OnlyPlain pump gas without oil = seized engine. Fuel cans are labeled. Don't guess.
Saw Consumables & Accessories — Fuel, Chain Lube, Tool Kit, Spanners, Hydrant Wrench, O-Rings
AKA: Saw supplies, consumables, "the saw room tools"
+
📖What it is & what it does

All the supporting items stored in the saw compartment that keep the saws running and the hose connections tight. Without fuel and chain lube, the K-12 and chainsaw are dead weight. Six items total: Fuel for K-12 and Chainsaw — premixed two-stroke fuel (gasoline + two-stroke oil at the correct ratio); Chain Lube — bar and chain oil that keeps the chainsaw bar and chain from seizing; Tool Kit for Chainsaw — bar wrench, scrench, spare spark plug, and adjustment tools specific to the chainsaw; Small Spanners — hose wrenches for 1¾" and 2½" couplings; Hydrant Wrench — pentagonal-socket wrench for the hydrant stem nut; O-Rings for hose swivel — replacement gaskets for hose coupling swivels.

🧩Parts
  • Two-stroke fuel can (premixed): Labeled, sealed. K-12 and chainsaw both run two-stroke — plain gasoline seizes the engine. The mix ratio matters (typically 50:1). Do NOT use straight gas.
  • Chain lube / bar oil: Separate from the fuel. Drip-feeds the bar during cutting. Without it the chain overheats and stretches or snaps.
  • Chainsaw tool kit (scrench): Combined screwdriver/wrench tool for bar adjustment, plus bar wrench and spare spark plug.
  • Small spanners (2): Double-ended hose wrenches, 1¾" NH one side, 2½" NH the other.
  • Hydrant wrench: Pentagonal socket for the hydrant operating nut.
  • O-ring set: Rubber swivel gaskets for hose couplings — must be pliable, not cracked.
🏷️Alternate names

Fuel: "two-stroke mix," "premix," "saw gas." Chain lube: "bar oil," "chain oil." Tool kit: "scrench kit," "chainsaw tools." Spanners: "hose spanners," "spanner wrenches." Hydrant wrench: "pentagon wrench," "hydrant key." O-rings: "swivel gaskets," "coupling gaskets."

⛽
Rookie Mistake — Wrong Fuel in the SawBoth the K-12 and the chainsaw are two-stroke engines. They require premixed fuel — gasoline plus two-stroke oil at a specific ratio (check the saw's manual, typically 50:1). Straight gasoline with no oil will seize the engine within minutes of running. The fuel can in this compartment is labeled — read it before you pour. If you're ever unsure, ASK before you start the saw.
🔗
Rookie Mistake — Skipping Chain Lube CheckThe chainsaw's bar oil reservoir is separate from the fuel tank. A dry bar will overheat the chain, stretch it, and potentially snap it mid-cut — on a roof, in a car, in a structure. Check the bar oil level pre-shift and top off after extended use. It runs down faster than you think.
💧
Rookie Mistake — Ignoring a Leaking SwivelA leaking O-ring under pump pressure drops GPM and sprays water on the crew. It's a 30-second fix if you have the spare gasket. Note it, report it, swap it at the next safe opportunity.
🫁

Driver's Side Rear Compartment — Air & RIT

3 SCBAs · RIT Pack · RASP Rope Line
3× SCBAs
AKA: Airpacks, SCBA, bottles, "the packs"
+
📖What it is & what it does

Three complete Self-Contained Breathing Apparatus sets — cylinder, harness, regulator, facepiece, the works. Tower 62 is a multi-role rig; in addition to the SCBAs each crew member wears, these spare/standby sets are available for the platform operator, an additional firefighter staging on the deck, or a quick swap during long-duration operations. See the dedicated SCBA Equipment Study Guide for full anatomy and operation.

🧩Parts (summary — see SCBA guide for detail)
  • Cylinder (4500 psi composite).
  • Harness & carrier assembly.
  • Second-stage regulator.
  • Facepiece.
  • HUD, ICM, power module.
  • PASS alarm.
🏷️Alternate names

"Airpack," "SCBA," "bottle" (specifically the cylinder), "the pack," "MSA G1" (Glen Ellyn's platform).

📊
Rookie Mistake — Spare Pack at Half-PressureA spare SCBA on a rig that's been sitting for a week loses pressure to a slow leak nobody noticed. The firefighter who grabs it during a working fire has 30 minutes of air on the gauge but 12 minutes of breathing time. Check ALL bottle pressures at rig check. Anything below 90% of service pressure (~4050 psi) gets flagged and either refilled or swapped.
RIT Pack
AKA: RIT pack, RIT bag, FAST pack, downed firefighter pack, "the RIT"
+
📖What it is & what it does

The Rapid Intervention Team air pack — a dedicated, ready-to-deploy SCBA assembly carried specifically for rescuing a downed firefighter. When a Mayday comes over the radio, this is what we grab. Includes a full cylinder, transfill hose to supply or refill a trapped firefighter's pack, a spare mask, and a drag harness.

🧩Parts
  • SCBA cylinder — full pressure.
  • Regulator / first stage.
  • Transfill hose (UAC — Universal Air Coupling): Connects to a downed firefighter's SCBA.
  • Spare facepiece.
  • Carry handle & drag harness.
  • Distinctively colored bag so it's never confused with a regular SCBA.
🏷️Alternate names

"RIT pack," "RIT bag," "FAST pack" (Firefighter Assist & Search Team), "rescue bottle," "downed firefighter pack," "Mayday pack."

🆘
Rookie Mistake — Touching the RIT Pack for Routine WorkThe RIT pack is NOT a backup SCBA. NOT for refilling your own bottle. NOT for the second crew. It is locked, loaded, and untouched UNTIL a firefighter goes down. If the RIT pack gets borrowed for routine use and then a Mayday comes in, somebody dies because of it. Walk past it. Use the regular SCBAs.
RASP Rope Line
AKA: RASP rope, bailout rope, escape line, "the bailout"
+
📖What it is & what it does

A Rapid Ascent / Self-Rescue / Personal escape rope line. Designed for firefighter self-rescue when interior conditions deteriorate and exit through the door isn't an option — go out the window, anchor the rope, and rappel/descend to the ground. Glen Ellyn carries the RASP system; other departments may use different brand systems with the same function. Used in extremis when the building is killing you.

🧩Parts (typical RASP / bailout kit)
  • Bailout rope (typically 30–50 ft of fire-rated escape rope): Heat-resistant aramid (Technora/Kevlar) or specialized escape rope.
  • Anchor hook (escape anchor, e.g. Crosby hook): Bites onto window sill, door frame, or structural element.
  • Descent control / brake device: Friction device that controls descent rate.
  • Carrying bag / pouch: Worn on the firefighter, accessible by feel.
  • Connection point on bunker gear / harness.
🏷️Alternate names

"Bailout system," "personal escape rope," "self-rescue rope," "RASP" (specific brand/product), "FF escape rope," "the bailout."

🪟
Rookie Mistake — Treating Bailout as TheoreticalThe bailout rope is a "last 30 seconds of your life" tool. Firefighters who have NEVER trained with it, never practiced anchor placement, never gone out a window in PPE on the line — that's the firefighter who freezes when the moment comes. Train with this tool. Don't touch it in real life if you haven't trained on it.
📐
Anchor Selection MattersA window sill that looks solid may be made of soft pine or rotten wood. Confirm the anchor will take 2× your weight as a minimum. Sill, door frame, A/C bracket, structural beam — different anchors, different reliability.
🔌

Driver's Side Rear Compartment — Power & Climbing

30A Generator · 200 ft Cable · Cords · Plug Adapters · Fan · Road Salt · Tower Climbing Harness
30 Amp Generator
AKA: Generator, genny, portable power, "the genny"
+
📖What it is & what it does

A portable gas-powered 30-amp generator. Provides 120/240V AC power on scene — runs scene lights, the wet vac, smoke ejectors, electric tools, the submersible pump, anything that needs an outlet. Tower 62 has multiple power sources but the portable generator is the one you can carry away from the rig to wherever the work is happening.

🧩Parts
  • Engine (typically Honda or Briggs): Pull-start or electric-start small engine.
  • Fuel tank: Gasoline, check level pre-shift.
  • Oil reservoir: Check level pre-shift — low oil shuts it down.
  • Outlets: Twist-lock 30A and standard duplex 120V.
  • Circuit breakers: Reset if a load trips them.
  • Ground lug: Attaches a ground rod if SOP requires.
  • Frame & carry handles.
🏷️Alternate names

"Generator," "genny," "portable genny," "Honda" (brand-as-generic), "the genny."

☠️
Rookie Mistake — Generator Running in an Enclosed SpaceGas generators produce CO. A generator running inside a basement, garage, or enclosed structure kills the people inside in minutes. Always run the generator OUTSIDE, in the open, downwind of the work area. If you're using it during a structure fire, position so its exhaust isn't going INTO the building.
⛽
Refuel ColdHot engine + gasoline = fire. Shut the generator down, let it cool a minute, then refuel. Spilling gas on a hot exhaust manifold ignites.
200 ft Electrical Cable
AKA: Power cord, extension cable, "the long cord"
+
📖What it is & what it does

A 200-foot heavy-gauge electrical cable for getting power from the generator (or the rig's inverter) to remote work areas. 200 feet is a long stretch — that's the cable you reach for when the scene is across a yard, into a basement, or down a hallway away from the truck.

🧩Parts
  • Heavy-gauge conductor (10 or 12 AWG): Thicker than household extension cords.
  • Outer jacket: Abrasion- and weather-resistant.
  • Twist-lock connector at one end: 30A locking plug.
  • Standard duplex (or pigtail) at the other end (sometimes).
  • Reel or cable box: For deployment/retrieval without tangles.
🏷️Alternate names

"Extension cord," "power cord," "feeder cable," "shore cord," "200-footer."

⚡
Rookie Mistake — Damaged Cable in WaterA cable with a cut or worn jacket lying in standing water at a flooded-basement call is a death trap. Inspect cable BEFORE deployment. Any nicks, melted spots, or exposed conductor — OUT OF SERVICE. Trips on a frayed cable have ended firefighters' lives.
🪢
Don't Coil Hot CableA coiled cable carrying high amperage builds heat. Lay the cable in long sweeping loops, not tight coils, especially when running near maximum amperage. And NEVER coil it while energized.
Extension Cords
AKA: Drop cords, jumper cords, "the extension cords"
+
📖What it is & what it does

Shorter heavy-duty extension cords (typically 25, 50, or 100 ft) used to chain power from the long 200-ft feeder out to individual tools and lights. Multiple cords let you split power to multiple work areas.

🧩Parts
  • Heavy-gauge cord (typically 12 AWG).
  • Three-prong grounded plug + socket.
  • Strain relief at the connectors.
🏷️Alternate names

"Drop cord," "jumper cord," "extension cord," "12-gauge cord."

⚡
Rookie Mistake — Daisy-Chaining Too FarVoltage drops over distance. Chaining 200 ft of feeder + 100 ft of extension + 50 ft of extension = serious voltage drop at the tool. Underpowered tools run hot and fail. Keep total run lengths reasonable, and use heavier-gauge cords for longer runs.
Plug Adapters
AKA: Adapters, pigtails, twist-lock adapters, "the adapters"
+
📖What it is & what it does

Adapter pigtails that convert between plug types — twist-lock 30A to standard 120V duplex, NEMA L5-30 to standard 5-15, and so on. Lets tools designed for one plug standard work with generators or outlets designed for another.

🧩Parts
  • Source plug: Twist-lock or other industrial-style.
  • Target socket: Standard household three-prong.
  • Short cord between them (pigtail).
🏷️Alternate names

"Pigtail adapter," "twist-lock adapter," "plug adapter," "L5-30 adapter."

🔌
Rookie Mistake — Adapter Mismatch = Wrong VoltageAn adapter that physically fits doesn't mean the voltage matches. Plugging a 120V tool into a 240V outlet via adapter ruins the tool and creates a fire hazard. Verify voltage before connecting.
Fan
AKA: Smoke ejector, ventilation fan, PPV (depending on type), "the fan"
+
📖What it is & what it does

An electric ventilation fan. Depending on the model on this rig, it functions as either a Positive Pressure Ventilation (PPV) fan — pushing fresh air INTO a structure to drive smoke OUT through a planned exhaust opening — or as a smoke ejector pulling air OUT. Used during overhaul and during coordinated attack ventilation.

🧩Parts
  • Frame / housing: Steel cage with protective mesh.
  • Fan blade.
  • Electric motor + power cord.
  • Mounting feet or hangers (window hangers if smoke ejector).
  • Tilt adjustment: Aim the airflow.
🏷️Alternate names

"PPV fan," "ventilation fan," "smoke ejector" (different — see below), "blower."

🌬️
Rookie Mistake — Uncoordinated VentilationPushing or pulling air into a structure without knowing where the fire is and where the exhaust opening is can drive flames into uninvolved areas, push fire ONTO the attack crew, or feed a hidden smoldering fire and cause a flashover. Ventilation is COORDINATED — the attack crew agrees on timing, the IC approves, the exhaust opening is opened FIRST. Don't fire up the fan and start blowing.
Road Salt
AKA: Salt, ice melt, traction salt, "the salt"
+
📖What it is & what it does

Bagged road salt for winter operations. Spread on icy patches at scenes to give crews traction and prevent slip-and-falls. Also melts thin ice over time. Lives on the rig year-round in Midwest fleets because winter weather doesn't ask permission.

🏷️Alternate names

"Ice melt," "rock salt," "traction salt," "calcium chloride."

❄️
Rookie Mistake — Salting LateFirst five minutes on a winter MVA scene: salt the working area BEFORE crews start moving heavy gear. Slip-and-fall injuries on the fireground are a leading cause of lost work time.
Safety Harness for Tower Climbing
AKA: Tower harness, climbing harness, ladder harness, fall-arrest harness, "the harness"
+
📖What it is & what it does

A full-body fall-arrest safety harness used when working ON the aerial — climbing the bedladder, working at heights on the ladder rungs, or doing rescues that require leaving the bucket. The harness clips into a tether that connects to a structural anchor. If a firefighter falls, the harness catches them before they hit the ground.

🧩Parts
  • Shoulder straps + sub-pelvic strap: Full body, NOT just a waist belt.
  • D-rings (dorsal and chest): Anchor attachment points.
  • Adjustable straps + buckles: Fit the harness snugly over bunker gear.
  • Lanyard / tether (typically separate): Connects harness to anchor.
  • Carabiner / connector (locking): Anchor-side connection.
🏷️Alternate names

"Tower harness," "climbing harness," "fall-arrest harness," "ladder belt" (older, different design — waist only, NOT acceptable for fall arrest).

🪜
Rookie Mistake — Climbing the Stick Without ItTower 62's ladder goes way up. People DO fall off aerial ladders, especially at the tip and on icy rungs. The harness is mandatory when leaving the bucket, leaving the bed, or climbing the ladder. "I'm only going up to the third rung" — that's how dead firefighters start sentences.
🧷
Inspect Before EVERY UseWebbing wears, stitching unravels, hardware corrodes. Look at every strap and buckle BEFORE you wear it. Any visible damage or "I don't know what that is" — out of service, swap to a different harness.
🪜

Rear Engine Compartment

Big-bore Hose · Ladders · Pike Poles · NY Hooks · Folding Ladders · Ceiling Poles
3" Hose
AKA: Three-inch, supply line, "the 3-inch"
+
📖What it is & what it does

3-inch diameter hose — bigger than attack hose, smaller than LDH supply. Used as a supply line for longer stretches where 2½ would have too much friction loss, or as a feeder line to a portable monitor / deck gun. Tower 62 carries lengths for water supply versatility.

🧩Parts
  • 3" double-jacket hose.
  • NH-thread couplings (typically 2½ NH on 3" hose).
  • Carrying loops where loaded.
🏷️Alternate names

"3-inch," "three-inch," "supply line," "intermediate hose."

💧
Rookie Mistake — Confusing 3" with 2½"The couplings look similar; the hose diameter is the giveaway. Mixing them up at a complicated water-supply layout creates friction loss calculations that the engineer didn't plan for. Read the size stenciled on the hose body.
5" Hose
AKA: Five-inch, LDH, supply hose, "the big line"
+
📖What it is & what it does

5-inch Large Diameter Hose (LDH). The primary water-supply hose from hydrant to pumper, or pumper to pumper in a relay. Moves a LOT of water with much less friction loss than smaller hose. Tower 62 carries several lengths to extend supply when needed. See the 25-ft jumper section (DSF-01) for coupling details.

🧩Parts
  • 5" hose body.
  • Storz couplings, both ends.
  • Locking clips.
  • Carrying straps for off-loading bundles.
🏷️Alternate names

"Five-inch," "LDH," "Large Diameter Hose," "supply hose," "soft suction" (outdated).

⚖️
Rookie Mistake — Underestimating Charged 5" Weight5" hose holds ~1.7 GALLONS per running foot — about 14 lb per foot when charged. A 100-ft length holds 170 gallons and weighs 1,400 lb. You don't move charged 5". Plan the layout, charge ONCE in the right position. Moving charged LDH causes injuries.
2× 35 ft, 2-Section Extension Ladders
AKA: 35-foot extension, 2-section extension, "the 35"
+
📖What it is & what it does

Two extension ladders, 35 feet each at full extension, 2-section construction (a base/bed section + a fly section). Used to access second and third stories of residential and commercial buildings, place on the side of a structure for window access or ventilation work, or use as a personnel ladder during operations. 35 ft is the standard reach for residential second-story access.

🧩Parts
  • Beds (base) section: The wider, lower section. Sits on the ground.
  • Fly section: The narrower, upper section that extends up.
  • Rungs: Cross-pieces between the rails.
  • Halyard: The rope (or chain) used to raise the fly section.
  • Pulley: Rope feeds through pulley at top of bed section.
  • Pawl / dog locks: Spring-loaded hooks that engage rungs and LOCK the fly in extended position. CRITICAL.
  • Butt / spurs (feet): Metal feet at the bottom — bite into ground.
  • Tip: The top of the fly section.
  • Rails / beams: The two long vertical structural members.
🏷️Alternate names

"Extension ladder," "two-section," "35," "the 35-footer," "two-fly" (less accurate — this is single-fly two-section).

🦴
Rookie Mistake — Pawls (Dogs) Not EngagedYou extend the ladder, the pawls drop into the rungs with a click. If you climb without verifying BOTH pawls are seated on rungs, the fly section comes back down on you. Probies have fallen off ladders and broken backs because they trusted the halyard tension instead of the dogs. After every extension, look up — both pawls visible, both seated. Then climb.
📐
75° Climbing AngleThe classic rule: foot of the ladder out from the wall by ¼ of the ladder's working length. Too steep = tip-over backwards. Too shallow = ladder slides out at the foot. Practice the angle until you can set it without thinking.
28 ft, 2-Section Extension Ladder
AKA: 28-foot extension, residential extension, "the 28"
+
📖What it is & what it does

A 28-foot 2-section extension ladder. Shorter than the 35, deploys faster, reaches second-story windows on most residential structures. The go-to ladder for shorter-reach jobs where the 35 is overkill. Same construction and parts as the 35-foot ladder.

🏷️Alternate names

"28-footer," "the 28," "two-section 28," "residential extension." Same parts as REAR-03 above.

⚖️
Rookie Mistake — Grabbing the Wrong LengthProbies grab the heavier 35 when the 28 would do — wears the crew out, takes longer to deploy. Look at the building. Match the ladder to the job. The lieutenant calling for "a ladder" may have a specific one in mind — ASK.
2× 20 ft Roof Ladders
AKA: Roof ladder, hook ladder, "the 20-foot roof"
+
📖What it is & what it does

A straight (single-section) 20-foot ladder with retractable HOOKS at the tip. Used during vertical ventilation: lean the ladder against the eave, climb up, flip the hooks open at the top, and the hooks GRAB the ridge of the roof. The ladder now anchors itself to the roof, the firefighter walks UP the ladder onto the roof surface, and the ladder doesn't slide off while they're working.

🧩Parts
  • Two rails + rungs: Same as any ladder.
  • Retractable hooks at the tip: Spring-loaded or manually-flipped. Folded flat when stored; flipped open when in use.
  • Butt spurs (bottom feet).
🏷️Alternate names

"Roof ladder," "hook ladder," "ventilation ladder," "the 20-footer."

🪝
Rookie Mistake — Climbing Before Hooks Are SetYou bring the ladder up, but you don't flip the hooks open and verify they're SEATED over the ridge before you commit weight to it. The ladder slides down the slope, takes you with it, you go off the edge of the roof. The hooks must be visible, locked over the ridge, and tested before you climb beyond the eave.
16 ft Roof Ladder
AKA: 16-foot roof, short roof ladder, "the 16"
+
📖What it is & what it does

A shorter roof ladder, 16 feet, for steeper or smaller roofs where the 20-footer is too long. Same hook-and-anchor concept. Used on smaller residential roofs or when the 20s are in use elsewhere.

🏷️Alternate names

"16-footer," "the 16," "short roof," "short hook ladder." Same parts as REAR-05.

📏
Match Ladder to Roof PitchShort ladder on a long slope = you're working from the bottom edge with no reach to the ridge. Pick the ladder that puts the hooks AT the ridge with the firefighter able to work above the eave.
12 ft Pike Pole
AKA: 12-foot hook, long pike, NY hook (specific design), "the 12"
+
📖What it is & what it does

The longest pike pole on this rig. Twelve feet of reach. Used for pulling ceilings in higher commercial spaces, reaching attic spaces, breaching upper-floor windows from below, and checking for fire extension high overhead. Big leverage, big reach, big risk of contacting overhead electrical service drops.

🧩Parts
  • Hook head: Pike point + curved hook + sometimes a flat scraping blade.
  • Ferrule: Metal sleeve between head and handle.
  • Long fiberglass handle (12 ft): Non-conductive (if fiberglass) — important.
  • Butt cap / D-grip.
🏷️Alternate names

"12-foot pike," "long hook," "ceiling hook," "the 12," "NY hook" (specific design pattern).

⚡
Rookie Mistake — Power Line ContactTwelve-foot poles reach service drops, telephone lines, and overhead electrical. Even fiberglass conducts when wet. Look UP before any long-pole swing. Probies have been electrocuted by a single careless raising motion.
10 ft Pike Pole
AKA: 10-foot hook, "the 10"
+
📖What it is & what it does

Ten-foot pike pole. Slightly shorter than the 12 — useful in residential ceilings where 12 is overkill but 8 doesn't quite reach. Same anatomy as the 12. Pull ceilings, check for extension, breach drywall.

🏷️Alternate names

"10-foot pike," "the 10." Same parts as the 12-foot.

⚡
Look UP First — Same RuleAny long pole near overhead electrical: look UP. Always.
2× 8 ft Pike Poles
AKA: 8-foot hook, standard pike, "the 8"
+
📖What it is & what it does

Eight-foot pike poles — the most common length for residential overhaul work. Easy to maneuver in standard-height rooms, reaches average ceilings, doesn't get in the way like the longer poles. Two on the rig so two firefighters can pull ceilings simultaneously.

🏷️Alternate names

"Eight-foot pike," "standard pike," "the 8." Same parts as longer poles.

🩹
Pull Diagonally, Not Straight DownHook into ceiling, then sweep AWAY from your body and head. Material falls. Stand to the side of where it'll land.
2× 6 ft Pike Poles
AKA: 6-foot hook, short pike, "the 6"
+
📖What it is & what it does

Six-foot pike poles for tight spaces — hallways, smaller rooms, closets, where the 8-foot is too long. Two of them for paired ceiling-pull work in cramped quarters.

🏷️Alternate names

"Six-foot pike," "short pike," "the 6."

📏
Pick the Length That FitsWrong-length pike in a small room means swinging into walls and crew. Match the pike to the space. Two firefighters with 6-foot poles work tight quarters far better than one with a 12.
10 ft + 12 ft Folding Ladders (one of each)
AKA: Attic ladder, folding ladder, scuttle ladder, "the folding ladders"
+
📖What it is & what it does

One 10-foot and one 12-foot folding ladders — compact, hinged ladders that collapse flat for storage. Used to access attic scuttle holes, drop into basements, and any place where a rigid extension ladder won't fit. The 12-footer gives extra reach in taller interior spaces. Both are light enough for a single firefighter to deploy.

🧩Parts
  • Folded sections: Hinged segments that fold flat.
  • Locking hinges: Snap into the rigid position. Verify locked before climbing.
  • Rungs and rails.
🏷️Alternate names

"Attic ladder," "scuttle ladder," "folding ladder," "compact ladder," "the folding 10" (10-ft), "the folding 12" (12-ft).

🪺
Rookie Mistake — Climbing Without Verifying Hinges LockedThe folding hinge has a positive lock. If you climb without confirming the lock engaged, the ladder folds under you. Push down on each hinge after deployment — it should not move. Then climb.
5× New York Hooks
AKA: NY hook, San Francisco hook, plaster hook, "the NY"
+
📖What it is & what it does

The NY hook is a specific pike-pole head design with a curved, blade-edged hook + a piercing pike. Designed in New York for breaching the heavy plaster-and-lath ceilings common in older NY tenement construction. The blade slices through plaster, the pike anchors into the wood lath, and a sharp pull brings the whole assembly down. Five on the rig means a full crew can pull ceilings simultaneously.

🧩Parts
  • Curved blade hook: Sharper than a standard pike-pole hook — designed to CUT.
  • Pike point.
  • Handle (varies, often fiberglass).
🏷️Alternate names

"NY hook," "New York hook," "plaster hook," "San Francisco hook" (similar design), "Boston rake" (related).

✂️
Rookie Mistake — Treating It Like a Standard PikeThe NY hook is SHARPER than a standard pike. The blade can slice gear, gloves, and skin if mishandled. Store with the head protected and never carry it with the blade pointing toward yourself or a crewmate.
2× Ceiling Poles
AKA: Ceiling hook, drywall hook, pole hook, "the ceiling poles"
+
📖What it is & what it does

Two additional pole-style hooks specifically configured for ceiling work — drywall pull, fire-extension checks, gentle prying. Different head design from the NY hooks (less aggressive blade, more pulling-curve). Two firefighters can pair on ceilings without taking the NYs out of service.

🏷️Alternate names

"Drywall hook," "ceiling hook," "ceiling pole."

🧱
Modern vs. Old ConstructionModern drywall = light material, comes down easy. Old plaster-and-lath = takes the NY hook and significant force. Match the tool to the ceiling type. Don't burn out on a drywall ceiling using the NY hook when a ceiling pole would work twice as fast.
🔌

Officer's Side Rear Compartment

Road Sand · Fan · 30A Generator · 200 ft Cord · Cords · Adapters
Road Sand
AKA: Sand, traction sand, absorbent sand, "the sand"
+
📖What it is & what it does

Bagged sand for traction and small-spill absorption. Differs from salt — sand doesn't melt ice but provides immediate grip on slick surfaces and absorbs small fluid spills. Used at MVAs in winter, on slick decking, and as a backup absorbent when oil-dry runs short.

🏷️Alternate names

"Traction sand," "road sand," "absorbent sand."

❄️
Sand vs. SaltSand = immediate traction, no melting. Salt = slower-acting, melts ice. Both have a job; don't substitute one for the other. Sand on a frozen-over scene gives you walking surface FAST.
Fan (Officer's Side)
AKA: Second fan, backup ventilation fan, "the OS fan"
+
📖What it is & what it does

A second electric ventilation fan. Same construction and use as the driver's side fan (DSRG-05). Two fans on the rig means two compartment fans can be deployed — one PPV at the entry, one ejector pulling smoke from a far window — and you have redundancy if one fails. See DSRG-05 for full parts breakdown.

🏷️Alternate names

"Fan," "PPV fan," "ventilation fan," "smoke ejector" (depending on type), "blower."

🔄
Two-Fan Coordinated VentilationTwo fans aimed at the same opening = airflow conflict. Two fans set up as INTAKE + EXHAUST = coordinated airflow. Plan the airflow pattern BEFORE starting either fan.
30 Amp Generator (Officer's Side)
AKA: Second genny, backup generator, "the OS genny"
+
📖What it is & what it does

A second portable 30-amp generator. Same as DSRG-01 — gives Tower 62 two independent portable power sources so two work zones can have power simultaneously, and if one generator fails, the other keeps the scene running. See DSRG-01 for full parts breakdown.

🏷️Alternate names

"Genny," "second generator," "backup power."

☠️
Same Rule — Outside OnlyBoth generators are gas-powered. CO production is a deadly hazard in any enclosed space. NEVER run a generator inside, in a basement, in a garage, or with exhaust pointed at the working crew.
200 ft Power Cord
AKA: Long cord, 200-footer, feeder cable, "the OS long cord"
+
📖What it is & what it does

A second 200-foot heavy-gauge power cord. Same as DSRG-02. With two long cords and two generators, the truck can power TWO independent work zones 200 feet apart from the rig — very useful at sprawling commercial scenes or large structure fires.

🏷️Alternate names

"Power cord," "200-footer," "feeder cable."

🪢
Reel It In Properly200-ft cords tangle if dumped back in the compartment. Coil onto a reel, or do figure-8 coils into the cable box. Twisted-tangle cords are useless when speed matters next time.
Extension Cords (Officer's Side)
AKA: Drop cords, jumpers, "the extension cords"
+
📖What it is & what it does

Second set of shorter heavy-duty extension cords. Same as DSRG-03. Chains power from the long 200-ft feeder out to individual lights and tools.

🏷️Alternate names

"Drop cord," "jumper," "extension cord."

⚡
Voltage Drop ReminderLong chains of extension cord drop voltage at the tool. Use heavier gauge for longer runs.
Plug Adapters (Officer's Side)
AKA: Adapters, pigtails, "the OS adapters"
+
📖What it is & what it does

Backup set of plug-style adapter pigtails. Same as DSRG-04. Convert between twist-lock 30A and standard 120V duplex.

🏷️Alternate names

"Pigtail," "adapter," "L5-30 adapter."

🔌
Verify Voltage Match Before Plugging InAdapter that physically fits ≠ correct voltage.
🌀

Officer's Side Rear Middle Compartment

DeWalt Powered Fan · 3 Bags Utility Rope
DeWalt Powered Fan
AKA: DeWalt fan, battery fan, cordless fan, "the DeWalt"
+
📖What it is & what it does

A battery-powered DeWalt fan. Differs from the larger gas/electric ventilation fans — this is smaller, portable, and runs off the cordless tool battery platform. Used for small-area ventilation, personal cooling at rehab, drying out gear, or moving air in a confined space where dragging a generator and cord is impractical.

🧩Parts
  • Fan housing & blade.
  • DeWalt 20V battery slot: Shares batteries with the cordless tool platform.
  • Speed switch (typically multi-speed).
  • Tilt/rotate base.
  • USB power output (some models): Charge a phone or radio off the fan battery.
🏷️Alternate names

"DeWalt fan," "battery fan," "cordless fan," "jobsite fan."

🔋
Rookie Mistake — Borrowing the Tool BatteriesIf the DeWalt fan is using the only fully-charged battery on the rig, you've taken cordless power away from the cordless tools. Plan battery rotation — fan runs on one pack, swap-in spares stay charged for tools.
3× Bags Utility Rope
AKA: Utility rope, rope bags, "the utility ropes"
+
📖What it is & what it does

Three bags of utility rope. NOT life-safety rated — utility rope is for hauling tools up to a working position, tying off equipment, lashing, securing, dragging hose lines, and any general-purpose rope use that doesn't involve supporting a human body. Pre-bagged means deploy-fast: pull out, throw the bag, rope feeds out clean.

🧩Parts
  • Rope: Synthetic (typically polypropylene or nylon), various diameters.
  • Bag: Stuff sack with drawstring closure.
  • Working end secured at the top of the bag so it doesn't disappear into the coil.
🏷️Alternate names

"Utility line," "utility rope," "tag line," "haul line," "the ropes."

🆘
Rookie Mistake — Using Utility Rope for Life SafetyUtility rope is NOT rated for human body weight in rescue operations. Using it to lower a victim, lower a firefighter, or for any rope rescue = catastrophic failure waiting to happen. Life-safety rope (kernmantle, NFPA-rated) is a different product. Know which is which BEFORE the moment of crisis.
🪓

Officer's Side Middle Compartment — The Irons

Axes · Halligans · Sledges · Shovels · K-tool · Bolt Cutters
2× Flat Head Axes
AKA: Flat axe, FH axe, marrying axe, "the flat-head"
+
📖What it is & what it does

Two fire-service axes with one cutting bit and one flat striking face. The cutting edge chops; the flat poll drives a Halligan. Marries with the Halligan to form "the irons" — the most basic forcible-entry set in the American fire service. Two on the rig means a full crew can pair multiple sets.

🧩Parts
  • Cutting bit / edge: SHARP. Keep it sharp.
  • Flat poll / striking face: Hardened steel.
  • Head / cheek.
  • Handle: Fiberglass or hickory.
  • Grip end / swell.
🏷️Alternate names

"Flat-head axe," "FH axe," "marrying axe," "irons axe," "fireman's axe."

🪓
Rookie Mistake — Dull Axe DeflectsDull edge glances off the target and into your leg. Sharp edges bite where you swing. Sharpen between calls. A dull axe is a dangerous axe.
2× Halligans
AKA: Halligan bar, hooligan tool, the bar, "the Halligan"
+
📖What it is & what it does

Two Halligan bars — the most iconic forcible-entry tool in the American fire service. One-piece forged bar with an adze (chisel), a pointed pick, and a forked claw at the ends. Forces doors, windows, locks, padlocks, gas valves, manholes, just about anything that doesn't want to open. Marries with the flat-head axe to make "the irons." Two on this rig means two crews can each have a complete set.

🧩Parts
  • Adze end: Wide curved blade for prying doors at the lock side.
  • Pick: Sharp point 90° to the adze — drives into locks and tight spots.
  • Fork / claw: Two-pronged forked end opposite — pulls hardware, pries at hinges.
  • Shaft / throat / shoulder: The bar between the heads — your lever and grip surface.
🏷️Alternate names

"Halligan bar," "the bar," "hooligan tool," "Pro-Bar."

🚪
Rookie Mistake — Forcing the Wrong WayMost American residential doors swing INWARD. You drive the adze between door and jamb on the lock side and force AGAINST the swing. Forcing outward on an inward-opening door wastes time and bends metal without opening anything. Know which way the door swings BEFORE you commit. Hinges visible = outward swing. No hinges = inward.
2× Pick Axes
AKA: Pickhead axe, PH axe, fire axe, truckie's axe
+
📖What it is & what it does

Axes with a cutting bit on one side and a sharp PICK on the other. The pick punctures and pulls; great for hooking sheet metal, prying roof decking, overhauling, and pulling ceilings. Cutting bit chops like a flat-head. Two on the rig.

🧩Parts
  • Cutting bit.
  • Pick point.
  • Head / cheek.
  • Handle.
🏷️Alternate names

"Pickhead axe," "PH axe," "pick axe," "truckies' axe," "fire axe."

🎯
Rookie Mistake — Pick End UnsheathedThe pick is sharp. Probies clipping it to their gear with the pick exposed have stabbed themselves and crewmates. Sheath it. Store it pick-down. Mind the pick every time you set it down.
⛔
NEVER Strike a Halligan with the PickThe pick is brittle. Strike a Halligan with the FLAT-HEAD only. A snapped pick becomes a projectile.
2× Sledgehammers
AKA: Sledge, mule, persuader, "the sledge"
+
📖What it is & what it does

Heavy two-handed striking hammers. 8 or 10 lb typical. Drive Halligans into stubborn doors, break masonry, pulverize locks. Slower swing than an axe but vastly more striking energy. Two on the rig so two sets of irons can work in parallel.

🧩Parts
  • Head: Heavy steel block, two flat striking faces.
  • Handle: Long fiberglass or wood haft.
  • Grip: Textured at the swinging end.
🏷️Alternate names

"Sledge," "mule," "persuader," "the big hammer."

🦵
Rookie Mistake — Striker PositioningWhen two firefighters work the irons together, the Halligan operator's head is right next to the striker's swing. Miss-strikes happen. Striker stands offset; Halligan operator's face turned AWAY. Helmets and visors DOWN.
2× Shovels
AKA: Spades, scoops, "the shovels"
+
📖What it is & what it does

Standard shovels for scooping saturated absorbent, moving debris, clearing snow at scene access, digging out stuck wheels, and any task where you need to move material by hand. Two on the rig — square-point and round-point typical.

🏷️Alternate names

"Spade" (pointed), "scoop" (flat), "snow shovel."

⚡
Sparks on Hazmat AbsorbentSteel shovels strike asphalt and rock = sparks. Sparks + fuel-soaked absorbent = ignition. Use the non-sparking shovel in the spill kit if you're shoveling flammable absorbent.
K Tool
AKA: K-tool, lock-pulling tool, "the K"
+
📖What it is & what it does

A small forged-steel tool designed specifically to pull the cylindrical lock mechanism out of a residential door. The K-tool's teeth bite into the lock face; you set the Halligan's adze into the K-tool's slot; the Halligan provides leverage; the lock cylinder pulls out cleanly. Faster and quieter than smashing the door — and it leaves the door reasonably intact for the homeowner afterward.

🧩Parts
  • K-shaped body: Hardened steel.
  • Lock-biting teeth: Grip the lock face when forced in.
  • Slot: Accepts the Halligan adze.
  • Often carried with a related "A-tool" or "R-tool" for difficult locks.
🏷️Alternate names

"K-tool," "lock-pulling tool," "K-puller," "the K."

🔑
Rookie Mistake — Using the K-Tool on a Deadbolt ThrowThe K-tool pulls the lock CYLINDER. It doesn't help if the deadbolt is thrown into the strike plate. Read the lock — if the bolt is extended, the K-tool pull doesn't open the door, you still need to defeat the bolt mechanism. Train on the actual technique before relying on it in real-time.
Bolt Cutters
AKA: Bolt cutters, padlock cutters, "the cutters"
+
📖What it is & what it does

Standard heavy-duty bolt cutters. Long compound-leverage handles, hardened steel jaws. Cuts padlocks, chains, fencing, rebar (up to a point), and bolted connections. Faster than a saw for soft steel padlock shackles and chain. Doesn't throw sparks.

🧩Parts
  • Hardened cutting jaws: Look for chipping or rolling — that's the failure mode.
  • Pivot pin.
  • Compound leverage linkage: Multiplies hand force.
  • Long handles with grips.
  • Adjustment bolt (some models): Sets jaw alignment.
🏷️Alternate names

"Bolt cutters," "padlock cutters," "chain cutters," "the cutters."

🔗
Rookie Mistake — Cutting Hardened ShacklesBolt cutters work on softer steel padlock shackles. Hardened-steel padlocks (American Lock 700 series, similar) will damage the jaws before they cut. If the shackle is case-hardened, switch to a saw with the right blade. Don't ruin the cutters trying to brute-force a hardened lock.
⚒️

Officer's Side Front Middle Compartment — Heavy Tools

Closet Pikes · Fire Maul · Pig Axe · Pry Bars · Large Bolt Cutters · Scene Light
2× Closet Pikes (D-Handle)
AKA: Closet hook, drywall hook, D-handle pike, "the closet pikes"
+
📖What it is & what it does

Short-handled pike poles built for tight quarters — closets, bathrooms, hallways. D-HANDLE grip on the butt end (the D-shaped loop) gives you a positive grip when pulling DOWN on the hook. Used to pull ceilings and check for fire extension where a 6 or 8-footer can't swing.

🧩Parts
  • Pike + hook head.
  • Short handle (typically 2–4 ft).
  • D-handle: The looped grip at the butt end.
  • Ferrule.
🏷️Alternate names

"Closet hook," "drywall hook," "D-handle pike," "short hook," "Boston rake" (similar design).

⛓️
Rookie Mistake — Pulling Straight Down on Your SpinePull diagonally, rotate hips, not back. D-handle is short — your face is close to whatever falls. Stand to the side of the pull.
Fire Maul (Sledge with Wedge)
AKA: Maul, wedge maul, splitting maul, "the maul"
+
📖What it is & what it does

A heavy hammer with a sledge face on ONE side and a wedge (axe-like blade) on the other. The sledge drives a Halligan or breaches walls; the wedge end splits wood and pries. More versatile than a plain sledge for forcible entry — the wedge bites into door edges and helps pry them open.

🧩Parts
  • Sledge face (one side of head).
  • Wedge / splitting blade (other side).
  • Head / cheek.
  • Handle.
🏷️Alternate names

"Fire maul," "maul," "splitting maul," "wedge maul," "Pulaski" (related fire-service tool, slightly different)."

⚒️
Rookie Mistake — Wrong End ForwardTwo-faced tools demand attention. Striking with the wedge when you wanted the sledge can chip the wedge or glance off. Know which face you're swinging EVERY time.
Pig Axe (Flat-Head with Pick)
AKA: Pig, pig tool, pick-axe combo, "the pig"
+
📖What it is & what it does

A specialty axe with a flat-head striking face on one side and a pick on the other. Combines functions of a flat-head axe (driving Halligans, breaching) with a pick axe (puncturing, prying, ripping sheet metal). Less common than the standard FH or PH axes; this design has its devotees in older urban fire service. Useful when you only want to carry ONE tool but need both functions.

🧩Parts
  • Flat-head striking face.
  • Pick point on opposite side.
  • Head / cheek.
  • Handle.
🏷️Alternate names

"Pig," "pig axe," "pick-and-poll axe," "pick-flat combo."

🐷
Rookie Mistake — Don't Strike the Pick End on a HalliganThe pick is brittle. Only the flat face strikes the Halligan. Same rule as the pick-head axe.
Pry Bar
AKA: Crowbar, wrecking bar, "the pry bar"
+
📖What it is & what it does

A standard pry bar — typically 18–24 inches of forged steel with a flat chisel end and a hooked nail-pulling claw at the other. Used for prying open doors, popping windows, removing trim, lifting heavy objects a small distance. Smaller than a Halligan but easier to get into tight spaces.

🧩Parts
  • Chisel / pry end: Slightly bent, for getting purchase under edges.
  • Claw end: V-notched for pulling nails.
  • Shaft: Hex or round forged steel.
🏷️Alternate names

"Crowbar," "wrecking bar," "claw bar," "pry bar."

🩺
Rookie Mistake — Wrong Tool for the JobPry bar is GREAT for trim, small panels, light forcible entry. NOT a Halligan substitute on a heavy commercial door. Match the tool to the size of the job.
Long Pry Bar
AKA: Long crowbar, demolition bar, "the long pry"
+
📖What it is & what it does

An extended pry bar (typically 36–60 inches). More leverage than the standard pry bar — handles bigger jobs: removing heavy nailed-on boards, prying open jammed truck cabs, levering large objects. Long handles = more force at the working end, but less control in tight spaces.

🏷️Alternate names

"Long crowbar," "demolition bar," "wrecker," "the long pry."

💪
Rookie Mistake — Overloading the BarLong bars give massive mechanical advantage. Use too much force on something that won't move and the bar bends, the fulcrum slips, or the bar snaps. Steady pressure, not panic-yanking. If it doesn't move, change the angle or switch tools.
Large Bolt Cutters
AKA: Big bolt cutters, heavy cutters, 48-inch cutters, "the big cutters"
+
📖What it is & what it does

Larger bolt cutters than the standard pair in the Irons compartment. 36 or 48 inches of handle length. The extra leverage cuts heavier chain, larger padlock shackles, and thicker rebar. Two-handed operation; sometimes a two-person operation on the heaviest stock.

🏷️Alternate names

"Big bolt cutters," "heavy bolt cutters," "48-inch cutters," "the big ones."

🩸
Rookie Mistake — Standing Where the Cut Piece Will FlyA chain link cut under tension releases stored energy. The cut end can swing or fly. Stand offset, anticipate where the cut piece will go, and keep your face turned away.
Large Light (Scene Lighting)
AKA: Scene light, work light, flood light, "the big light"
+
📖What it is & what it does

A large portable scene-lighting fixture — typically a multi-head telescoping work light or a high-output LED floodlight. Set it up to illuminate the work area at night incidents, overhaul scenes, extrications, or any scene where the rig-mounted lights don't reach. Runs off generator/inverter power.

🧩Parts
  • Light head(s): Multiple LED or halogen heads for area coverage.
  • Telescoping stand or tripod base.
  • Power cord with grounded plug.
  • Switches per head.
  • Aiming joints.
🏷️Alternate names

"Scene light," "work light," "flood light," "Akron" (related portable scene light), "tower light" (different — refers to the rig-mounted boom)."

⚡
Rookie Mistake — Tripping Crew on the CordLight cords across a working scene cause falls. Route cords against walls, tape them down across walking paths, or run them over the work area instead of through it.
🧹

Officer's Side Front 2 Middle Compartment — Salvage

Tarps · Wet Vac · Portable Lights · Tool Box · Submersible Pump
Tarps
AKA: Salvage covers, salvage tarps, "the tarps"
+
📖What it is & what it does

Heavy waterproof covers used to protect victim property from water damage during suppression and overhaul. Throw tarps over furniture, electronics, family photos BEFORE water hits them. Also used as ground covers for tool layout, patient packaging, and extrication staging. Note: the source document writes "Traps" — this is the salvage covers.

🧩Parts
  • Tarp body: Vinyl or coated canvas, waterproof.
  • Grommets at corners and edges.
  • Hemmed reinforced edges.
  • Folded for fast deployment.
🏷️Alternate names

"Salvage covers," "salvage tarps," "covers," "ground cover." (The document's "Traps" is a typo for "Tarps.")

💧
Rookie Mistake — Deploying Too LateBest time to throw salvage covers is BEFORE the engine company opens the line. Train yourself to anticipate water — second you see flame, eyes start looking for what to cover.
Wet Vac
AKA: Shop vac, wet/dry vac, water vac, "the wet vac"
+
📖What it is & what it does

A heavy-duty wet/dry vacuum used for water mitigation — pulling standing water out of basements after burst pipes, fire suppression runoff, or flooded structures. Salvage and customer-service tool — the faster water leaves the structure, the less secondary damage.

🧩Parts
  • Tank / canister: Holds water — empty before it stalls the motor.
  • Motor head / lid: Contains the motor and float shutoff.
  • Hose, wands, attachments.
  • Float ball / shutoff: Prevents water from entering the motor.
  • Power cord.
🏷️Alternate names

"Shop vac," "wet/dry vac," "water vac."

🛢️
Rookie Mistake — Vacuuming HazmatWet vac is for water. NOT fuel, oil, sewage, or unknown chemicals. Smell and look first.
Portable Lights
AKA: Hand lights, work lights, portable scene lights, "the portables"
+
📖What it is & what it does

Smaller portable lights — handheld or compact stand-mount lights. Used for individual task lighting (overhaul work in a single room, illuminating a specific tool area, helping read information at night). Less coverage than the big scene light; faster to deploy.

🏷️Alternate names

"Portable lights," "hand lights," "task lights," "work lights."

🔦
Charge State MattersIf they're rechargeable, verify they take a charge and hold it. Portable lights that die after ten minutes are useless when you needed two hours.
Tool Box
AKA: Tools, hand tools, mechanical kit, "the toolbox"
+
📖What it is & what it does

A general-purpose toolbox containing pliers, screwdrivers, hammer, channel locks, vise grips, tape measure, utility knife, and the everyday mechanical tools that don't have a dedicated home elsewhere. The Squad and the Tower both turn into mobile workshops more often than people realize — a Phillips screwdriver solves problems the spreaders can't.

🧩Parts (typical contents)
  • Pliers (needle-nose, lineman's, slip-joint).
  • Channel locks.
  • Vise grips.
  • Screwdrivers (Phillips, slotted).
  • Tape measure.
  • Utility knife.
  • Hammer.
🏷️Alternate names

"Toolbox," "general tools," "hand tools."

🧹
Rookie Mistake — Tools Don't Walk Home With YouStandard pliers and screwdrivers walk off easily. They stay on the rig. Take ten extra seconds at end-of-call to return each tool to the box. The next crew is counting on you.
Submersible Pump
AKA: Dayton pump, trash pump, submersible, "the water pump"
+
📖What it is & what it does

An electric submersible pump for dewatering — pulling standing water out of flooded basements, sumps, window wells, and low-lying structures. Runs off the rig's generator or inverter. Drop it in the water, run the discharge hose out a window or floor drain, and it moves a lot of water fast without a crew member having to run a wet vac repeatedly. Used on burst-pipe calls, spring flooding, and post-suppression water mitigation.

🧩Parts
  • Pump body: Sealed motor + impeller, designed to run fully submerged.
  • Discharge port + hose: Where the pumped water exits — needs a hose run to a drain or outside.
  • Float switch (some models): Shuts off automatically when water level drops below the intake.
  • Power cord: Plugs into generator or inverter.
  • Carry handle.
🏷️Alternate names

"Submersible pump," "sump pump," "Dayton pump" (brand), "water pump," "dewatering pump."

⚡
Rookie Mistake — Running in Contaminated WaterSubmersible pumps are rated for clean or lightly contaminated water. Sewage, fuel-contaminated water, or water with large debris will damage the impeller and potentially spray the hazmat outward. If the water smells like fuel, sewage, or unknown chemicals, stop and reassess before deploying the pump.
💧
Don't Run DryRunning the pump without water burns the motor seal quickly. If the water level drops and the float switch doesn't cut it off, shut it down manually. Check periodically on long pumping operations.
🧯

Officer's Side Front Compartment — Extinguishers & Hoist

Hose Hoist · Silver Bullet · Pump Can · CO2 · ABC
Hose Hoist
AKA: Hoist rope, hose rope, hauling rope, "the hoist"
+
📖What it is & what it does

A rope and bag used for hoisting hose lines (and other equipment) up to upper floors or to the aerial bucket. The rope is dropped/lowered from the upper position; the crew at ground level ties on the hose end with a hoisting knot, then the upper crew pulls the line up. Standard truck-company technique for taking a working line up the side of a building when the ladder/stairwell isn't the right path.

🧩Parts
  • Rope: Strong enough to support a charged hose line.
  • Bag: So the rope deploys clean without tangles.
  • Often paired with a specific hoist knot (clove hitch + half hitch is common).
🏷️Alternate names

"Hoist rope," "hose rope," "hauling rope," "tagline" (related).

⚖️
Rookie Mistake — Hoisting With a Sloppy KnotA bad knot drops a charged hose line on whoever is below. The hoist knot must be tied right and verified. If you don't know the knot cold, ASK before you hoist. Charged lines weigh hundreds of pounds; failure is catastrophic.
Silver Bullet — Pressurized Water Extinguisher
AKA: Silver bullet, water can, pressurized water, "the can"
+
📖What it is & what it does

A 2½-gallon pressurized water extinguisher in a shiny stainless-steel canister. The "Silver Bullet" nickname comes from the polished finish. Class A only — used for small incipient fires of ordinary combustibles (wood, paper, cloth, garbage). Carry it ahead of the hose line on small/contained fires, into small structures where stretching a line is overkill, or use it during overhaul to hit small spots.

🧩Parts
  • Stainless cylinder body.
  • Pressure gauge: Green zone good, red zone service.
  • Pull pin + tamper seal: Pin pulls; seal must be intact pre-shift.
  • Discharge lever / trigger handle.
  • Discharge hose & nozzle.
  • Carry handle.
  • Refill cap.
🏷️Alternate names

"Silver bullet," "water can," "pressurized water extinguisher," "2½ gallon," "the can," "PWE."

⚡
Rookie Mistake — Using Water on a Class C FireThe Silver Bullet is water — Class A ONLY. Water on energized electrical equipment is a conduction path to YOU. Water on a Class B (flammable liquid) spreads the fuel. If the fire is anything but ordinary combustibles, switch to CO2 or ABC.
Pump Can
AKA: Pump tank, garden sprayer, water pump, "the pump can"
+
📖What it is & what it does

A manual hand-pump water sprayer — like a heavy-duty garden sprayer. Operator pumps the handle to pressurize the can, then sprays water through a wand. Lower capacity than the Silver Bullet but mechanically simpler — won't leak pressure if the gauge fails. Used for small grass/brush fires, mop-up after extinguishment, and wetting down overhaul areas.

🧩Parts
  • Tank (smaller than Silver Bullet, typically 1–2 gal).
  • Pump handle on top: Pump to pressurize.
  • Wand / spray nozzle.
  • Trigger or thumb-valve.
  • Shoulder strap.
🏷️Alternate names

"Pump tank," "Indian pump" (older term, refers to similar shoulder-pack design), "back pump," "pump can."

💪
Rookie Mistake — Trying to Pressurize While SprayingSome pump cans require you to pump first, then spray. Trying to do both at once produces a weak intermittent stream and tires you out. Pump fully, spray fully, repeat.
CO2 Extinguisher
AKA: CO2 can, CO2 extinguisher, "the CO2"
+
📖What it is & what it does

A carbon-dioxide extinguisher — pressurized liquid CO2 in a heavy steel cylinder. Discharges as a cold cloud/snow that smothers the fire by displacing oxygen. Class B and Class C — flammable liquids and ENERGIZED electrical. Big advantage: no residue. Leaves no chemical mess on electrical equipment. Big disadvantage: short range (3–8 feet) and the cold can frostbite skin.

🧩Parts
  • Heavy steel cylinder (CO2 is stored at high pressure).
  • Pull pin + tamper seal.
  • Discharge horn (the flared funnel at the end): Directs the CO2 cloud. GET COLD — frost forms instantly.
  • Squeeze handle / trigger.
  • Carry handle.
  • No pressure gauge on most CO2 units — they're WEIGHED instead. Pre-shift: check the weight against the date-of-fill stamp.
🏷️Alternate names

"CO2," "CO2 can," "snow can," "BC extinguisher" (Class rating)."

🧊
Rookie Mistake — Bare Hand on the HornThe discharge horn gets COLD — instant frostbite cold. Hold the carry handle, never the horn. Probies who grab the horn for "better aim" leave skin behind.
⚖️
Weigh Don't ReadCO2 extinguishers don't have a gauge. They're verified by weight — full vs. tare weight stamped on the cylinder. Weigh during annual service. A leaking CO2 can looks fine but has no agent.
ABC Extinguisher
AKA: ABC, dry chem, multi-purpose, "the ABC"
+
📖What it is & what it does

An ABC dry chemical extinguisher — monoammonium phosphate powder propelled by nitrogen. Rated for Class A (ordinary combustibles), B (flammable liquids), and C (electrical). Most versatile of the portable extinguishers — covers nearly any common fire type. Big disadvantage: leaves a sticky corrosive residue that ruins electrical equipment and is hard to clean.

🧩Parts
  • Cylinder body (typically red, painted steel).
  • Pressure gauge: Green zone good.
  • Pull pin + tamper seal.
  • Discharge handle.
  • Discharge hose + nozzle.
  • Carry handle.
  • Class label (A, B, C ratings + capacity).
🏷️Alternate names

"ABC," "dry chem," "DC," "multi-purpose extinguisher," "Purple-K" (different chemistry — that's K-powder, BC only)."

🅿️
P.A.S.S. TechniquePull pin · Aim at the base of the fire · Squeeze the handle · Sweep side to side. Aim at the BASE — flames don't ignite, the FUEL ignites. If you're spraying flames instead of fuel, you're wasting agent.
🧹
Residue CleanupABC dry chem ruins electronics, leaves a corrosive film on metal, and is messy. If you have a choice on a Class C fire with valuable electronics, use CO2 instead.
🚐

Inside Cab Compartment

Caution Tape · Batteries · Water · AED · Sterile/PPE Box · Spare Mask · TIC
Caution Tape
AKA: Yellow tape, scene tape, fire-line tape, "the tape"
+
📖What it is & what it does

Standard plastic warning tape — yellow with "CAUTION" or red with "FIRE LINE — DO NOT CROSS." Used for scene perimeter control, keeping the public off the operating area, marking hazards (downed wires, unstable structures), and segmenting hot/warm/cold zones at hazmat or technical-rescue scenes.

🏷️Alternate names

"Yellow tape," "caution tape," "scene tape," "fire-line tape," "bunting" (older)."

🚧
Rookie Mistake — Putting It Up Too LateCrowds gather fast. By the time you decide to set a perimeter, civilians are already inside the line. Set the tape EARLY and FAR OUT. Easier to shrink a perimeter than to push the public back.
Spare Batteries
AKA: Spares, backup batteries, "the spares"
+
📖What it is & what it does

Reserve batteries for radios, flashlights, the gas detector, headlamps, and other portable electronics. Stocked in the cab so a crew member doesn't have to leave their post to find power when their handheld dies.

🏷️Alternate names

"Spares," "extras," "backup batteries."

🔋
Rookie Mistake — Old Spares Sitting at ZeroA spare that's been on the shelf six months has self-discharged. Pre-shift: verify spares are charged. A dead spare is a useless spare.
Water Bottles
AKA: Water, hydration, "the bottles"
+
📖What it is & what it does

Sealed bottled water for crew hydration. On long calls, especially summer fire operations, dehydration is a real and disabling threat. Cardiac events on the fireground are the leading cause of LODD (Line of Duty Death) for firefighters — heat stress is a major contributor. Drink water. Often. Don't be a hero about it.

🏷️Alternate names

"Water," "hydration," "bottles."

💧
Rookie Mistake — Refusing WaterProbies who think they need to "tough it out" without water are the probies who collapse in rehab. Drink BEFORE you're thirsty, during work cycles, and AT rehab. Hydration is a tactical advantage, not a weakness.
AED — Automated External Defibrillator
AKA: AED, defib, shock box, "the AED"
+
📖What it is & what it does

An automated external defibrillator. Apply the pads to the patient's chest, the AED analyzes the rhythm, advises shock if V-fib or pulseless V-tach, and delivers the shock when you press the button. EVERY cardiac arrest gets the AED until ALS arrives. Survival drops 7–10% for every minute of delay between collapse and shock — SPEED matters.

🧩Parts
  • Main unit.
  • Defibrillation pads (adult & pediatric): Verify in-date.
  • Battery: Sealed with expiration date.
  • Status indicator (green ready / red service): Verified at every rig check.
  • Speaker: Voice prompts.
  • Pediatric switch (some units): Reduces energy for kids under 8 / 25 kg.
🏷️Alternate names

"AED," "defib," "shock box," "Zoll," "LIFEPAK," "Philips" (brands)."

⏱️
Rookie Mistake — HesitatingThe moment cardiac arrest is confirmed, AED comes out, pads go on. Don't wait for the medic. Don't worry about looking foolish if the device says "no shock advised." EVERY MINUTE without defibrillation in a shockable rhythm costs the patient 7–10% chance of survival. MOVE.
💧
Dry the Chest FirstWet chest = electrical path across the surface instead of through the heart, AND it can shock bystanders. Towel the patient dry — sweat, water, blood, vomit. Hair too thick? Razor with the AED. Bare and DRY.
Clear Plastic Box — Sterile Gloves, N95, Eye Pro, Gowns, Bio Bags
AKA: PPE box, sterile box, BSI box, EMS PPE
+
📖What it is & what it does

A clear plastic bin holding BSI (Body Substance Isolation) and respiratory-PPE supplies for EMS calls and any incident with body-fluid exposure risk. Built so contents are visible without opening — saves time when you need to grab gloves and a mask before stepping out.

🧩Parts (contents)
  • Extra sterile (or non-sterile exam) nitrile gloves: Multiple sizes.
  • N95 particulate masks: Sized small/medium/large.
  • Eye protection: Wraparound safety glasses or goggles.
  • Disposable gowns: For full-coverage isolation.
  • Bio bags: Red bio-waste bags for contaminated material disposal.
🏷️Alternate names

"PPE box," "BSI box," "EMS box," "sterile box," "iso box."

🦠
