Rookie Mistake — Skipping PPE Because the Call "Looks Routine"You don't know what infections the patient has. Hepatitis B, HIV, TB, COVID — none of them announce themselves at the door. Gloves on EVERY patient contact. Mask on respiratory complaints. Don't gamble with the next 30 years of your career.
🧔
N95 Requires Clean-Shaven SkinBeard stubble breaks the seal. Just like your SCBA. Both straps, pinched nose clip, inhale-test.
Extra SCBA Mask — Size M
AKA: Spare facepiece, M mask, swap mask, "the spare M"
+
📖What it is & what it does

A spare SCBA facepiece, size Medium. Used for swap-out if a primary mask is damaged, contaminated, or fails seal-check; OR if a crew member needs a Medium and didn't get one assigned. Glen Ellyn standard SCBA platform is MSA G1 — the spare must match.

🧩Parts (see SCBA Study Guide for detail)
  • Facepiece body (rubber/silicone).
  • Lens (polycarbonate).
  • Inhalation valve.
  • Exhalation valve.
  • Head harness with five-point adjustment.
  • Regulator connection port.
🏷️Alternate names

"Spare mask," "spare facepiece," "M mask," "MSA G1 mask."

📏
Rookie Mistake — Forcing a Bad FitIf you're a size Large or Small and the only spare is Medium, your seal will fail and you'll be sucking smoke. Mask size is fitted to YOU. Spare Medium is for someone who is Medium. If you're sized differently, your individual mask stays with you.
TIC — Thermal Imaging Camera (Officer's Seat)
AKA: TIC, thermal camera, infrared camera, "the thermal"
+
📖What it is & what it does

A handheld thermal imaging camera that detects heat signatures and displays them on a screen — hot objects appear bright, cool objects appear dark. Used by the officer or search crew to find victims through smoke, locate the seat of the fire, identify hot spots during overhaul, and navigate in zero-visibility conditions. Stored in the officer's seat so the company officer has it in hand the moment they step off the rig.

🧩Parts
  • Sensor array (microbolometer): Detects infrared radiation — heat, not visible light.
  • Display screen: Shows the thermal image in real time.
  • Housing / handle: Pistol-grip or binocular-style, rated for fireground temps.
  • Battery (rechargeable): Verify charge pre-shift — kept in charger between calls.
  • Wrist strap / lanyard.
🏷️Alternate names

"TIC," "thermal imaging camera," "thermal camera," "infrared camera," "FLIR" (brand name used generically), "the thermal."

🔥
Rookie Mistake — Trusting the TIC as an All-ClearA TIC shows surface temperatures — it does NOT see through walls with perfect accuracy, and it can miss smoldering fires behind insulation or in void spaces where temps are equalized. Use the TIC as ONE tool in overhaul, not the only tool. Pull ceilings. Open walls. A thermal "clear" followed by a rekindle hours later is a common and preventable failure.
🌡️
Rookie Mistake — Battery Not ChargedA TIC with a dead battery is a useless brick the moment you need it most. Verify charge at every rig check. Keep it on the charger between runs. If it's not on the charger, someone took it off — ask why.
🪜

Top of Tower

NY Hook · Double-Hook Roof Ladder
New York Hook (Top of Tower)
AKA: NY hook, top-mounted hook, "the topside hook"
+
📖What it is & what it does

An NY hook mounted on top of the tower — accessible from the rear hose bed and the bucket. Placed up top so a firefighter doesn't have to descend to the side compartment when they need a hook in the bucket or on the bedladder. Same construction as the rear-compartment NY hooks (REAR-12) but positioned for fast access from aloft.

🏷️Alternate names

"NY hook," "topside hook," "ridge hook" (informal)."

⚓
Rookie Mistake — Hook Not Secured for TravelA loose hook on top of the tower can shift, fall, or strike crew during transit. Verify it's clipped/strapped in BEFORE the rig moves. Tools falling off moving fire apparatus are a recurring hazard.
Roof Ladder with Hooks on Both Ends
AKA: Double-hook roof ladder, two-hook ladder, "the double-hook"
+
📖What it is & what it does

A roof ladder with retractable HOOKS on BOTH ends. Most roof ladders have hooks only at the tip; this one is built so it can be used in either orientation OR locked into specialized positions like a bridge across a gap, or extended from the bucket onto a roof surface to provide a stable working platform. Particularly useful for tower work where the bucket is positioned next to a roof and the firefighter steps from bucket onto the ladder onto the roof.

🧩Parts
  • Two rails + rungs.
  • Retractable hooks at BOTH ends: Either end can grip a ridge.
  • Butt spurs at both ends or center-mount (varies).
🏷️Alternate names

"Double-hook roof ladder," "two-hook ladder," "bridging ladder" (when used to bridge gaps)."

🪝
Rookie Mistake — Hooks Not Set on the Working EndBoth ends have hooks — you have to deliberately set the hooks on whichever end is anchoring. Probies have flipped this ladder and forgotten to engage the working-end hooks because they assumed it was set. CHECK both ends every time before climbing or transferring weight.
🚑

Coffin Compartment

Stokes Basket
Stokes Basket
AKA: Stokes, rescue basket, basket litter, "the Stokes"
+
📖What it is & what it does

A rigid basket-style patient litter — wire-cage or rotomolded plastic. Used for moving patients over rough terrain, through tight spaces, up/down rope rescue, off rooftops, out of basements, AND — critically for the Tower — for lowering patients FROM the bucket to the ground via the aerial. The Stokes locks into the bucket so a patient can be packaged, lifted, and brought down without a separate rope rescue rig.

🧩Parts
  • Basket / shell: Wire-cage or plastic rotomold.
  • Rails / runners: Reinforced frame the rescuers grip.
  • Tie-down straps / spider: Multi-point harness over patient.
  • Bridle / lift attachment points: Rated for rope rigging.
  • Foot plate: Solid end so the patient doesn't slide out.
🏷️Alternate names

"Stokes," "Stokes basket," "rescue basket," "basket litter," "Junkin basket."

🪦
Rookie Mistake — Loose Patient StrapsA patient not strapped firmly will slide when the Stokes tilts during lifting or rope work. People have died falling out of Stokes baskets. Cross-strap pattern, snug, foot stop. If patient is unconscious, check twice.
🪣

Bucket Contents

Pick Axe · Master Stream Nozzle · Halligan
Pick Axe (Bucket)
AKA: Bucket axe, aloft pickhead, "the bucket pick"
+
📖What it is & what it does

A pickhead axe carried IN the bucket, ready to use from aloft. Used to chop through roof decking, breach upper-floor windows, pry sheathing, and any task requiring an axe at height. Lives in the bucket so the operator doesn't have to lower the bucket and grab one from the ground compartment.

🏷️Alternate names

"Bucket axe," "aloft axe," "PH axe (bucket)." Same parts as OSM-03."

⬇️
Rookie Mistake — Dropping Tools From the BucketA pick axe falling 80 feet hits the ground with lethal force. EVERY tool in the bucket is secured — clip, strap, or held with two hands. Probies who set tools down loosely on the floor of the bucket eventually knock one over the edge. Look down before you swing.
Master Stream Nozzle
AKA: Master stream, bucket nozzle, deluge nozzle, "the master stream"
+
📖What it is & what it does

The high-volume nozzle attached to the bucket's plumbed waterway. Pumped water comes UP the tower's internal waterway to the bucket; the master stream nozzle is what's on the outlet. Flows are typically 500–1,000+ GPM depending on the system. Used for elevated stream attack on upper floors, ventilation cooling, defensive operations from above, and flooding a large open area faster than ground monitors can. The aerial nozzle is what makes Tower 62 a TOWER and not just a really tall ladder.

🧩Parts
  • Inlet coupling: Connects to the bucket's internal waterway outlet.
  • Smoothbore tip or fog head: Stacked tips (1¼, 1⅜, 1½, 1¾, 2 inch) for smoothbore; rotating barrel for fog.
  • Pattern adjustment (fog version): Straight stream to wide fog.
  • Pivot ball / swivel: Aim the stream from inside the bucket.
  • Operator handle / aim lever.
  • Shutoff valve in the bucket waterway: The bucket operator can shut it off without involving the engineer.
🏷️Alternate names

"Master stream," "bucket nozzle," "elevated stream," "deluge nozzle," "Stang nozzle" (brand)."

💨
Rookie Mistake — Opening to Full Flow Suddenly500+ GPM of water hitting a wide-open nozzle at full pressure produces enormous nozzle reaction. The bucket is moving. The operator needs to brace, the engineer needs to coordinate the ramp-up of pressure, and the aim needs to be SET before you open the bail. Slow, deliberate, controlled. Don't snap open at full pump pressure.
🏠
Coordinate With Interior CrewsPushing 1,000 GPM through a window at interior crews will steam-burn them and push fire onto them. Master streams are EXTERIOR / DEFENSIVE operations, OR coordinated with confirmed interior evacuation. Engine company OUT before tower goes IN.
Halligan (Bucket)
AKA: Bucket Halligan, aloft Halligan, "the bucket bar"
+
📖What it is & what it does

A Halligan bar carried IN the bucket. Used for breaching windows, prying open upper-floor entry points, removing screens or storm windows from aloft, and any forcible-entry work that needs to happen at height without descending. See OSM-02 for full Halligan anatomy and use.

🏷️Alternate names

"Bucket Halligan," "aloft Halligan," "the bucket bar."

⬇️
Same Rule — Don't Drop ItA Halligan over the side of the bucket falling 80 feet kills whoever's underneath. Secure it, hold it with both hands during use, look down before any motion.
🧰

Bucket Compartment

1¾ Hoses · 5 ft Jumper · Fog Nozzle · Ladder Brackets · Air Hoses
2× 50 ft Lengths of 1¾" Hose
AKA: Bucket attack lines, aloft hose, "the bucket hoses"
+
📖What it is & what it does

Two 50-foot sections of 1¾" attack hose, stored in or near the bucket. When the operator needs to stretch a smaller attack line FROM the bucket — into an upper-floor window, off the side for short reach — these are pre-positioned. Lighter, more maneuverable than running a fresh line off the rig and up. Two sections = up to 100 ft of effective reach.

🧩Parts
  • 50 ft of 1¾" double-jacket hose × 2.
  • NH-thread couplings.
  • Bagged or coiled for fast stretch from the bucket.
🏷️Alternate names

"Aloft hose," "bucket attack lines," "the 50s."

🪜
Rookie Mistake — Stretching Without SecuringHose stretched from a bucket can pull on the bucket as it gets weight or kinks. Anchor the hose to the bucket frame before stretching out. Don't let the hose swing the bucket.
5 ft 1¾" Hose Jumper
AKA: 5-foot section, jumper, "the short 1¾"
+
📖What it is & what it does

A 5-foot jumper section of 1¾" hose. Bridges connections between the bucket waterway outlet and an attack hose, or between two hoses where a short flexible link is needed. Saves you from having to swap a full 50-ft section in for a small geometry problem.

🏷️Alternate names

"Jumper," "5-footer," "short section."

🧠
Right Tool for Tight ConnectionsShort jumpers solve geometry problems faster than reconfiguring whole stretches. Carry the awareness that it exists.
Fog Nozzle (Bucket)
AKA: Bucket nozzle, aloft fog, "the bucket fog"
+
📖What it is & what it does

A standard fog nozzle stored in the bucket for use on the 1¾ attack lines stretched from up top. Lets the operator put precise patterns into upper-floor windows or sweep cooling fog over an exposure. See DSFM-10 for full fog nozzle anatomy.

🏷️Alternate names

"Bucket nozzle," "aloft nozzle," "the fog."

🌀
Indoor Wide Fog ReminderWide fog INSIDE a burning structure pushes fire on interior crews. Tower attack with fog patterns into windows must be coordinated. STRAIGHT STREAM for direct attack; fog only for cooling exposures and ventilation.
Brackets to Attach Ladder to Bucket
AKA: Ladder brackets, bucket-to-ladder mounts, ladder hangers, "the ladder brackets"
+
📖What it is & what it does

Hardware brackets that mount a ladder (typically a roof ladder, like TOP-02) to the side of the bucket. This lets the bucket operator carry a ladder up to a roof, deploy it from the bucket, and use it as an extension of the platform. Critical for rescues and roof operations where the bucket can't get directly to the working point but a short ladder bridges the gap.

🧩Parts
  • Mounting brackets: Bolted or quick-release attachment to bucket frame.
  • Cradles / hooks: Hold the ladder rails in place.
  • Locking pins or straps: Secure the ladder against shifting during bucket movement.
🏷️Alternate names

"Ladder brackets," "bucket brackets," "ladder mounts," "ladder hangers."

⬇️
Rookie Mistake — Ladder Falls From BucketA ladder dropping from the bucket on the way up takes out anybody underneath. Mounting brackets must be FULLY ENGAGED and locking pins/straps verified before the bucket moves. Visual confirmation, two-person check on heavy ladders.
Air Hoses — Direct Connection to Tower Air Supply
AKA: SAR lines, supplied-air hoses, air-line hoses, "the bucket air"
+
📖What it is & what it does

Air hoses that connect directly from the tower's onboard breathing-air supply to a firefighter's airpack — effectively a Supplied-Air Respirator (SAR) configuration. Lets a firefighter work in a smoke or contaminated atmosphere from the bucket WITHOUT depleting their SCBA cylinder, because air is being supplied from the rig. Particularly useful for long-duration master-stream operations from the bucket where the firefighter would otherwise burn through bottles fast.

🧩Parts
  • Air supply hose: Low-pressure breathing-air rated, color-coded.
  • Quick-disconnect fittings: Connect at the tower air panel and at the user's SCBA.
  • Tower-mounted air outlet panel: Where the hose plugs in on the rig.
  • Reducer / pressure regulator: Steps cascade pressure down to breathing-air working pressure.
🏷️Alternate names

"SAR line," "supplied-air line," "air hose," "bucket air," "airline" (industrial term)."

🫁
Rookie Mistake — Air Hose Snags Without Backup BottleIf the supplied-air hose gets cut, kinks, or the rig's supply fails, the firefighter has NO air. SAR systems used in IDLH atmospheres REQUIRE an SCBA escape cylinder on the user. The bucket air is a comfort-of-operation system, not a sole source of breathing air. Wear your SCBA, breathe the rig's air, but have your bottle ready if the supply line fails.
📏
Maximum Hose LengthNIOSH limits SAR hose length (typically 300 ft). Read the system documentation. Going too far from the rig with the supplied-air hose creates pressure drop and possible breathing problems.
⚙️

Pivot Compartment

Chainsaw · K-12 Rotary Saw
Chainsaw
AKA: Chain saw, gasoline saw, "the chainsaw"
+
📖What it is & what it does

A gasoline-powered saw with a continuous chain of cutting teeth running around a guide bar. Used primarily for structural ventilation — cutting holes in roofs — and forcible entry through wood. Can also cut debris during rescue operations. The pivot compartment version is dedicated for aerial operations, allowing the crew in the bucket to bring it up or access it during elevated roof work.

🧩Parts
  • Engine (2-stroke gasoline): Provides power to drive the chain.
  • Guide bar: The flat metal bar the chain rides around.
  • Cutting chain: Hardened steel links with cutting teeth.
  • Chain brake: Safety mechanism — stops the chain instantly if kickback occurs.
  • Throttle trigger + trigger lockout: Prevents accidental throttle.
  • Bar nose / tip: The end of the guide bar — the kickback danger zone.
  • Fuel + bar oil reservoirs: Gas mix for engine; bar oil lubricates chain.
  • Starter cord / pull start.
🏷️Alternate names

"Chain saw," "gasoline saw," "wood saw," "roof saw," "vent saw," "the chainsaw."

⚠️
Rookie Mistake — KickbackThe most dangerous thing about a chainsaw is the bar tip. If the tip contacts material unexpectedly, the saw can kick back violently — toward the operator's face and neck. Keep the tip clear. Use the chain brake. Never cut with the tip zone. Proper cutting technique is learned in person with supervision, not from a study guide alone.
⛽
Fuel Mix — Not Straight GasA 2-stroke chainsaw engine requires a gas/oil MIX — straight gasoline will seize and destroy the engine within minutes. Confirm the correct mix ratio before refueling. Fuel is stored in the DS Rear-Middle compartment.
K-12 Rotary Saw
AKA: K12, partner saw, rescue saw, rotary saw, "the K-12," "the partner"
+
📖What it is & what it does

A gasoline-powered rotary (circular) saw designed for fire and rescue operations. Cuts metal, concrete, masonry, and hardened steel — the jobs a chainsaw cannot do. Used for cutting vehicle roofs, padlocks, roll-up doors, rebar, and reinforced concrete. Blades are application-specific: composite (abrasive) blades for metal and masonry; diamond blades for concrete. Note: a second K-12 is in the DS Rear-Middle compartment; this one is positioned in the pivot for aerial access.

🧩Parts
  • 2-stroke gasoline engine.
  • Circular cutting blade (12-inch diameter): Composite abrasive or diamond depending on application.
  • Blade guard: Covers the non-cutting arc of the blade.
  • Handle (front + rear): Two-hand operation for control.
  • Throttle trigger + lockout.
  • Blade wrench: For changing blades.
  • Fuel reservoir (2-stroke mix).
🏷️Alternate names

"K12," "K-12," "Partner saw" (brand name), "rescue saw," "rotary saw," "chop saw" (different tool — don't confuse), "disc cutter."

💥
Rookie Mistake — Wrong Blade for the MaterialRunning a composite abrasive blade on hardened steel (padlocks, bolts) destroys the blade fast and throws fragments. Running a diamond blade on wood can shatter the blade. Match the blade to the material. The K-12 in this compartment should have the correct blade for its assigned role — confirm blade type before use.
👁️
Sparks + Fuel = ProblemThe K-12 throws sparks aggressively when cutting metal. At a fuel leak or around compressed gas cylinders, that's a serious ignition hazard. Survey the area before cutting. Have a charged line nearby when cutting near fuel sources.

🚒 Snorkel 61 — Compartment Study Guide

Snorkel 61 is an aerial snorkel with a 75-foot reach, a 2,000 GPM pump, and a 1,000 GPM waterway — but no water tank. That last part matters: this rig needs a continuous water supply from a hydrant or another engine. It also runs a 10kW onboard generator and carries 8 floodlights and 6 spotlights, making it a serious lighting and elevated water platform.

Listen up, probie. No tank means no margin. If the water supply drops, the master stream stops. Know the pump operations, know how to support the engineer, and know every compartment cold so you're not the reason the crew is standing still on a working fire.

📅 Study guide synced from Google Doc: July 30, 2026

🚒

Snorkel 61 Overview

Apparatus specs · Key capabilities
OV-01
Apparatus Specifications aka: Spec sheet, rig specs
+
📖 What It Is
  • 75ft Aerial reach
  • 2,000 GPM pump
  • 1,000 GPM waterway
  • NO TANK — requires continuous water supply
  • 10kW onboard generator
  • 8 Floodlights
  • 6 Spotlights
❓ Why It Matters To You

No tank = no buffer. Every other rig on this fleet has a water supply to work from while you're getting the hydrant line established. Snorkel 61 does not. The pump stops the moment water supply is interrupted. Support the engineer. Get that line established fast.

The 10kW generator and 14 lights (8 flood, 6 spot) make this rig a major scene lighting asset — know how to deploy them.

🚨
Rookie Mistake — Forgetting You're Riding a Bucket, Not a TankProbies who cut their teeth on E60/E61 walk onto this rig and treat it like an engine with a tank. It isn't. If you arrive on scene and haven't established a water supply, you have a very large, very expensive piece of equipment that can do nothing. This is not a mistake you make twice.
🚿

Crosslay Hoses

Pre-connected attack lines
CL-01
1¾" Crosslay — 200 ft, Fog Nozzle (×2) aka: Crosslays, preconnects, attack lines, minute-man load
+
📖 What It Is

Two crosslay bays, each loaded with 200 feet of 1¾" attack hose pre-connected to a fog nozzle, running perpendicular to the rig so either side of the street can pull from either bay.

❓ Why It's Needed

Your primary interior attack lines on this rig — pull and go. 1¾" flows roughly 150–180 GPM, enough for most structure fires with good mobility.

🔧 How To Use
  1. Know which side each bay opens from and how the hose is loaded before you commit — pull it wrong and you create a kink before you reach the door.
  2. Pull only what you need to reach the door, then have your partner feed line.
  3. Confirm the hydrant is established before you charge — see the danger callout below.
🚨
Rookie Mistake — Pulling Before Water's ComingThese lines go dead the instant water supply drops, and this rig has zero tank behind them to buy you time. Probies used to engines with a tank will pull and advance on habit. On this rig, confirm the hydrant is charged before you commit to the door.
🚰

DS Pumping Area

Driver's Side · Pump panel · Shore power
DSP-01
20 Amp Shore Power & 250' Cord (Both Sides) aka: Shore power, station power connection
+
📖 What It Is

A 20-amp shore power connection that lets the rig plug into station power, plus 250 feet of heavy-duty cord available on both sides of the rig — not just one.

❓ Why It's Needed

Keeps batteries charged and onboard systems ready without idling the engine in quarters. The cord also lets you run tools or lights from external power on scene when the generator isn't the right choice.

🔧 How To Use

Confirm the rig is plugged in and drawing power every time it's parked in quarters. When laying the 250' cord on scene, remember it's available from both sides — don't assume you're limited to a single side's reach.

💡
Pump Panel Is the Engineer's DomainThe pump panel controls water flow and pressure for the entire rig. If you haven't been walked through pump operations by your engineer, make that happen. Every firefighter should understand the basics even if they're not running the panel.
⚡

DS Generator Compartment

Driver's Side · 10kW onboard generator
DSG-01
10kW Onboard Generator aka: Gen, onboard generator, power plant
+
📖 What It Is

A 10-kilowatt onboard generator, mounted in its own driver's-side compartment, that powers the rig's 8 floodlights, 6 spotlights, and any electric tools plugged in on scene.

❓ Why It's Needed

10kW is substantial output. It makes Snorkel 61 a capable scene lighting platform — at a nighttime structure fire or a large incident, this rig can light up the scene significantly.

🔧 How To Use

Know how to start it, what it powers, and how to connect external loads. Verify fuel level and test-start it during rig check — every shift, not just when you remember.

⚠️
Rookie Mistake — Skipping the Test-StartA generator that won't start at 2am on scene is a failure you could've caught at 0900. Probies skip this check because "it started fine last shift." Test it every shift. No exceptions.
🔧

DS Engineers Compartment

Driver's Side · High-rise packs · Adapters · Hydrant tools
DS3-01
High-Rise Pack — 100' × 2½" w/ Smooth Bore Nozzle aka: 2½" high-rise pack, smooth bore standpipe pack
+
📖 What It Is

A pre-assembled 100-foot length of 2½" hose fitted with a smooth bore nozzle, packaged for standpipe operations in multi-story buildings.

❓ Why It's Needed

The engine can't stretch hose up 20 floors. You connect to the building's standpipe on the floor below the fire and advance up with a pack sized for heavier flow than a handline alone.

🔧 How To Use

Carry it shoulder-loaded up the stairwell — it's heavy once you factor in a charged line above you. Connect to the standpipe outlet, bleed air, and advance with a partner. Smooth bore means no pattern adjustment — aim matters.

✅
Rookie TipKnow which pack is which before you're climbing stairs in full gear. Grabbing the wrong pack because you didn't check the tag costs you a trip back down and up — time you don't have on a working fire.
DS3-02
High-Rise Pack — 150' × 1¾" w/ Gated Wye & 150/75 GPM Fog Nozzle aka: 1¾" high-rise pack, gated-wye standpipe pack
+
📖 What It Is

A pre-assembled 150-foot length of 1¾" hose built around a gated wye, feeding a 150/75 GPM fog nozzle — the lighter, more maneuverable of the two high-rise packs.

❓ Why It's Needed

Same standpipe job as the 2½" pack, but sized for a smaller crew or tighter interior spaces. The gated wye means you can shut down one leg without killing water to the whole line.

🔧 How To Use

Deploy the same way as the 2½" pack — connect below the fire floor, advance up. Because the wye is gated now, you can isolate a leg for a hoseline failure or a second team without losing the whole pack's water.

💡
Know Both Packs ColdTwo different high-rise packs means two different capabilities. Know how each is packed and how to carry them — these are heavy loads fully charged, and standpipe ops are not the place to be learning your gear on the fly.
DS3-03
High-Rise Tool Bag aka: HR bag, standpipe tool bag
+
📋 Contents

A dedicated bag of standpipe hardware carried alongside the two high-rise packs — the fittings you need to actually make the connection and control pressure at the outlet.

❓ Why It's Needed

Standpipe outlets vary — stiff valves, odd threads, unknown pressure. The bag carries what you need to adapt and control the connection instead of guessing.

✅
Rookie TipGrab the bag with the pack — don't leave it behind because "we probably won't need it." Standpipe valves you've never touched before are exactly when you need every fitting in this bag.
DS3-04
Gated Wye (2½" to 1½") & Siamese Adapter (2½" Female to 5" Storz) aka: Gated wye, wye valve, siamese
+
📖 What It Is

Gated wye: splits one 2½" source into two 1½" gated outlets. Siamese adapter: combines two 2½" female lines into a single 5" Storz outlet — the opposite job of a wye.

❓ Why It's Needed

The wye lets you split water to two lines from one supply. The siamese lets you combine two supply lines into one big feed — useful for boosting flow to the pump or a master stream from two sources.

✅
Rookie TipDon't confuse these two — a wye splits, a siamese combines. Grabbing the wrong one wastes critical seconds while you're standing at the panel figuring out why your connection doesn't make sense.
DS3-05
Fog Nozzles — General & 1½" Adjustable (60–200 GPM) aka: Combination nozzle, adjustable nozzle, fog tip
+
📖 What It Is

A general-purpose fog nozzle plus a 1½" nozzle adjustable from 60 to 200 GPM. This adjustable unit replaced the old fixed 300 GPM tip.

❓ Why It's Needed

Spare nozzles for lines that need a fog pattern beyond what's already preconnected — and the adjustable one lets you dial in flow for the line you're actually running instead of being locked to one fixed rate.

⚠️
Rookie Mistake — Treating It Like the Old Fixed NozzleThis one's not a fixed-flow tip anymore. If you grab it out of habit and don't check the adjustment ring, you could be flowing far less — or far more — than you think. Dial it in before you commit to the line.
DS3-06
1000 GPM Fog Nozzle (Basket Turret) — CURRENTLY MISSING aka: Basket turret nozzle, master stream nozzle
+
📖 What It Is

A high-flow master stream nozzle dedicated to the basket turret — the master stream device mounted in the aerial bucket, not a handline nozzle. Flows up to 1,000 GPM.

🚨
Confirm This Before You Need ItThe doc flags this one as currently missing from the compartment. Don't assume it's sitting where it's supposed to be. Check this compartment at every rig check, and if it's not there, report it up the chain before this rig goes on a run where you need a master stream off the basket. Finding out mid-fire that your turret has no nozzle is not a lesson you get a second chance to learn.
DS3-07
Steamer-to-Storz Adapter & Elbow aka: Steamer adapter, storz elbow
+
📖 What It Is

Converts a hydrant's 4½" steamer port (NST thread) to a Storz connection, plus an elbow version for awkward hydrant angles.

❓ Why It's Needed

Storz and NST are two different coupling systems. This adapter bridges them so your 5" LDH can connect straight to the hydrant steamer port. The elbow saves you from fighting a stiff hose bend right at the hydrant.

✅
Rookie TipSeat the Storz locking lug fully before the line is charged. A half-connected Storz under pressure will blow off — verify it every time, don't just eyeball it.
DS3-08
Thread Adapters — M-M, F-F, CFD & Garden Hose aka: Double male, double female, sexless adapters
+
📖 What It Is

A set of thread adapters covering male-to-male, female-to-female, CFD, and garden hose threads.

❓ Why It's Needed

Not every fitting you encounter matches. These let you connect mismatched threads — mutual aid rigs, hydrants outside your district, or odd building connections.

DS3-09
Hydrant Bag aka: Hydrant kit, hydrant pack
+
📖 What It Is

The grab-and-go bag for establishing water supply — carried to the hydrant while the rig lays out 5" LDH behind you.

💡
No Tank Means This Bag Matters More HereOn a tank engine, a slow hydrant hookup is an inconvenience. On this rig, it's the difference between flowing water and standing there useless. Know this bag cold.
DS3-10
Spanner Wrenches aka: Spanner wrench, coupling wrench
+
📖 What It Is

A flat, bar-shaped wrench with hooks/jaws for tightening or loosening hose couplings.

❓ Why It's Needed

Couplings tighten under water pressure and you can't break them by hand after a line has been flowed. The spanner gives you leverage without destroying the gasket or threads.

✅
Rookie TipBleed the line before you try to uncouple it. A charged hose under even residual pressure will resist — and when it finally pops free, water and the fitting will fly. Bleed first, then spanner.
DS3-11
Hose Rope aka: Utility hoisting rope, hose hoist rope
+
📖 What It Is

A dedicated length of rope used for hoisting hose or securing it against a windowsill or edge — not the same item as the utility rope bags carried on the officer's side.

❓ Why It's Needed

Dragging charged hose over a sill or up a building damages it and creates drop hazards. Hose rope lets you haul it up cleanly and tie it off.

DS3-12
50' of 5" Donut Roll aka: Donut roll, LDH donut, supply hose roll
+
📖 What It Is

A 50-foot section of 5" LDH packed in a donut roll — a compact, self-contained coil you can carry and deploy without dragging the whole hose bed.

❓ Why It's Needed

Short supply gaps, finishing a lay, or extending a connection a short distance without breaking down the main hose bed load.

DS3-13
2 Spare Air Bottles aka: SCBA cylinders, spare bottles
+
📖 What It Is

Two spare SCBA cylinders stored in the engineer's compartment.

❓ Why It's Needed

Air management on scene — a firefighter running low doesn't have to walk back to the rig empty-handed.

⚠️
Full Means FullCheck pressure on both bottles every shift. A half-empty spare is a liability, not an asset — someone's going to grab it assuming it's full.
DS3-14
Oil Dry aka: Kitty litter, absorbent, floor dry, Speedy Dry
+
📖 What It Is

Granular absorbent material for containing and soaking up fluid spills — fuel, oil, hydraulic fluid.

❓ Why It's Needed

Vehicle fires, leaks on scene, and station floor spills all need containment before they spread or become a slip hazard.

DS3-15
Engineer's Odds & Ends — Card, Dry Silicone Spray, Duct Tape & Folding Chair aka: Engineer's misc kit
+
📋 Contents

Engineer's Card: Quick-reference pump/apparatus data card for the driver operator. Dry Silicone Spray: Lubricates coupling threads and gaskets without attracting grit. Duct Tape: The universal fix-it — sealing, marking, temporary repairs. Folding Chair: Yes, a folding chair. Small comforts matter on long details — just don't let it wander off to another compartment.

🪓

DS Over The Wheel Compartment

Driver's Side · Irons · Forcible entry
DS4-01
Halligan Bar aka: The Hooligan, bar, Pro-bar, Halligan tool
+
📖 What It Is

A forged steel bar with an adze, a fork, and a pick — the single most versatile forcible entry tool on the rig.

❓ Why It's Needed

Pairs with the flathead axe to make "the irons" — your primary forcible entry team. Prying, gapping, striking, and locking-mechanism defeat all run through this tool.

🔧 How To Use

One firefighter drives the adze into the door gap, the other strikes it home with the flathead axe. Work as a pair — the axe does the driving, not brute strength on the bar alone.

🚨
Know Your Irons ColdForcible entry under fire conditions with poor visibility, bad air, and a ticking clock is not the time to figure out how this tool works. If you can't do it fast in daylight, you can't do it when it counts. Practice.
DS4-02
Flathead Axe aka: Fire axe, striking tool, flat-head
+
📖 What It Is

A flat-poll axe used as the striking half of the irons, driving the Halligan's adze into a door gap.

❓ Why It's Needed

You need controlled, repeated striking force to set the Halligan without deforming the tool or wasting your energy on wild swings.

✅
Rookie MistakeSwinging wide, uncontrolled strikes tires you out fast and misses the target half the time. Short, controlled strikes at the Halligan's striking surface — not wherever it happens to land.
DS4-03
Pick Axe aka: Pick head axe
+
📖 What It Is

An axe with a pointed pick instead of a flat poll on one side, blade on the other.

❓ Why It's Needed

The pick punctures and penetrates roofing, plaster, and thin materials during ventilation and overhaul in ways a flathead can't.

DS4-04
Sledge Hammer aka: Maul, sledge, striking tool
+
📖 What It Is

A heavy, double-faced striking tool for breaching walls, breaking through masonry, and heavy demolition work.

❓ Why It's Needed

When the irons aren't enough — reinforced doors, block walls, or creating an emergency breach — the sledge brings raw force the Halligan/axe combo can't.

⚠️
Mind Your Swing RadiusThis is a heavy, long-handled tool. Know what and who is around you before you wind up — in a tight compartment or hallway, a full swing can hurt your own crew.
DS4-05
K-Tool aka: Lock puller, key tool
+
📖 What It Is

A small wedge-shaped tool driven behind a lock cylinder to pull the cylinder itself out of the door.

❓ Why It's Needed

Pulls lock cylinders out of commercial doors — faster and cleaner than forcing the whole door when it applies.

🔧 How To Use

Set the K-Tool behind the rim of the cylinder, drive it with the flathead axe until it bites, then pull. Once the cylinder's out, reach in with a straight tool to actuate the mechanism.

DS4-06
Closet Pike Pole aka: Short pike, closet hook, rubbish hook
+
📖 What It Is

A short-handle pike pole for tight spaces — closets, small rooms — where you can't swing a full-length pole.

❓ Why It's Needed

Overhaul and ceiling/wall opening in confined spaces where the full-size pike poles on the rear of the rig simply won't fit or swing.

🔩

DS Behind The Wheel Compartment

Driver's Side · Power saws · Fuel
DS5-01
Rotary Saw (K12) — Metal Blade aka: K12, rotary saw, cut-off saw
+
📖 What It Is

A gas-powered rotary saw fitted with a metal-cutting blade.

❓ Why It's Needed

Steel doors, security gates, and vehicle extrication work that a chainsaw or hand tool can't touch.

🔧 How To Use

Start it clear of the fuel can and any fuel spill. Let the saw come up to speed before contacting the material. Keep the blade guard oriented so sparks and debris throw away from your body and crew.

⚠️
Rookie Mistake — Grabbing the Wrong SawThis compartment no longer stocks spare blades. These two saws carry the only blades you've got on this rig. Confirm you have the metal blade before you commit to a steel door — burning up the wrong blade on the wrong material wastes your only spare.
DS5-02
Rotary Saw (K12) — Composite Blade aka: K12, rotary saw, masonry saw
+
📖 What It Is

A second K12 rotary saw fitted with a composite (masonry) blade.

❓ Why It's Needed

Concrete, masonry, and hard composite materials that would destroy a metal-cutting blade in seconds.

✅
Rookie TipTwo K12s with different blades means you can switch materials without a blade change on scene — but only if you know which saw is which before you're standing in front of the cut. Check the blade before you grab, every time.
DS5-03
Chainsaw aka: Chain saw, roof saw
+
📖 What It Is

A gas-powered chainsaw carried alongside the K12s for wood-cutting operations.

❓ Why It's Needed

Roof ventilation cuts, wood-frame structural work, and any cutting job on wood that a rotary saw isn't suited for.

⚠️
Chain Tension & SharpnessA dull or loose chain is a hazard, not just an inconvenience — it binds, kicks back, and takes twice as long to cut. Check it every shift, not just when it feels wrong mid-cut.
DS5-04
Saw Tool Box & Fuel aka: Saw kit, fuel can
+
📋 Contents

A tool box for saw maintenance plus dedicated fuel for both the chainsaw and the K12s.

🚨
Fuel Check — Every Single ShiftBoth saws need correct fuel mix. Cross-contaminating fuel — gas-only versus oil mix — will destroy an engine. Check fuel level and confirm correct fuel before leaving the station.
🛡️

DS Second to Last Compartment

Driver's Side · Tarp · Blades · Eye protection
DS6-01
Plastic Tarp aka: Poly tarp, salvage cover
+
📖 What It Is

A heavy plastic salvage tarp for covering contents or blocking water damage.

❓ Why It's Needed

Poly folds up wet and goes right back in the compartment — unlike the canvas tarps carried on the officer's side, which need to dry first.

DS6-02
Spare Saw Blade aka: Replacement blade
+
📖 What It Is

A single replacement saw blade — the only spare carried anywhere on this rig.

❓ Why It's Needed

A blade fails or burns up mid-job, and this is what stands between you and being down a saw for the rest of the incident.

✅
Rookie TipKnow what size and type fits which saw before you're doing a blade swap on scene. Practice the change with gloves on — you won't be doing it bare-handed at 2am.
DS6-03
Eye Protection Kit (Black Box) aka: Safety glasses box, PPE box
+
📖 What It Is

A black storage box holding safety glasses and/or goggles for saw operations.

❓ Why It's Needed

Required PPE any time a saw is running near you. Full stop.

⚠️
No Eye Pro, No Saw WorkMetal shavings, wood chips, and masonry dust at close range will cost you an eye. There's no version of "I'll be quick" that makes skipping this box acceptable.
🧯

DS Rear Compartment

Driver's Side · Extinguishers · Climbing belt · Basket equipment
DS7-01
Climbing Belts For Basket (×4: 1 Medium, 2 Large, 1 XL) aka: Basket belt, aerial climbing belt
+
📖 What It Is

Four belts worn when operating in or from the aerial basket — sized 1 Medium, 2 Large, and 1 Extra Large so there's a fit for whoever's riding the bucket.

❓ Why It's Needed

Fall protection any time you're in the bucket at height. Having four sizes on hand means nobody skips clipping in because the one belt on the rig doesn't fit them.

🚨
Inspect It Every ShiftLook for wear, fraying, and damaged hardware before you ever step into that basket. This is a life-safety item at height — don't skip this step, ever.
DS7-02
Breather Lines for Basket aka: Basket air lines, remote air supply lines
+
📖 What It Is

Air supply lines that connect to the basket, allowing personnel in the bucket to breathe from the rig's air supply during extended operations.

❓ Why It's Needed

Extended basket operations at a working fire can outlast a single SCBA cylinder. These lines let crew stay up without cycling bottles.

💡
Know the Connection Before You're Up ThereFiguring out how to connect these for the first time while you're already in the basket wastes air and time. Learn it on the ground.
DS7-03
ABC Fire Extinguisher aka: Dry chem, multi-purpose extinguisher
+
📖 What It Is

A dry chemical extinguisher rated for ordinary combustibles, flammable liquids, and electrical fires.

❓ Why It's Needed

The most versatile extinguisher on the rig, but messy and corrosive — use it deliberately, not by default.

🚨
Wrong Extinguisher = CatastropheThis compartment carries four different extinguisher types. Know all four cold — grabbing the wrong one under pressure is not a mistake you get to walk back. See CO2 and Silver Bullet entries below for what NOT to use ABC on.
DS7-04
Pump Can Extinguisher aka: Pump can, water can, indian pump
+
📖 What It Is

A hand-pumped, pressurized water extinguisher.

❓ Why It's Needed

Class A fires only — wood, paper, ordinary combustibles. Good for small outdoor fires, hot spots, and mop-up where you don't want to break out a hoseline.

⚠️
Never on Electrical or Flammable Liquid FiresWater conducts electricity and spreads burning liquid. This can is for Class A material only — nothing else.
DS7-05
Silver Bullet — Pressurized Water Extinguisher aka: Water can, stored-pressure water extinguisher
+
📖 What It Is

A stored-pressure water extinguisher, similar function to the pump can but a different platform.

❓ Why It's Needed

Same Class A role as the pump can — quick knockdown on wood and paper fires without pulling a line.

⚠️
Do NOT Use on Electrical or Flammable Liquid FiresSame rule as the pump can. Water is the wrong answer for anything energized or liquid-fuel based.
DS7-06
CO2 Extinguisher aka: Carbon dioxide extinguisher, CO2 can
+
📖 What It Is

A CO2 extinguisher that displaces oxygen and leaves no residue.

❓ Why It's Needed

Your go-to for energized electrical equipment and sensitive gear where a mess or corrosion would cause more damage than the fire itself.

💡
Doesn't Work Well Outdoors or in WindThe gas dissipates before it can smother anything in open air. Save it for indoor, contained equipment fires.
🪜

DS Ladders

Driver's Side · Ground ladders
DS8-01
28' Extension Ladders (×2, DS Rack) aka: Ground ladders, extension ladder
+
📖 What It Is

Two 28-foot extension ladders racked on the driver's side.

❓ Why It's Needed

Your primary reach ladders — good to second-floor and some third-floor windows. Two means you can ladder two openings simultaneously.

⚠️
Ladder Placement Matters75-degree working angle. Tip even with or one rung above the sill. Footing secured. No exceptions — a ladder set wrong has killed firefighters.
DS8-02
16' Roof Ladders (×2, DS Rack) aka: Roof ladder, hook ladder
+
📖 What It Is

Two 16-foot roof ladders with fold-out hooks that lock onto a ridge line, racked here on the driver's side. This count does NOT include the third 16' roof ladder mounted on the aerial boom itself (see TOP-05) — that one lives in its own spot and isn't part of this pair.

❓ Why It's Needed

Used on pitched roofs to give firefighters a stable work platform during ventilation or search.

🚨
This Rig Carries Five 16' Roof Ladders, Not TwoIt's easy to undercount these. Two live right here in the DS rack, a third rides on the aerial boom itself (TOP-05), and two more are stowed topside (TOP-06). Know all three locations before you go looking for "the roof ladder" under pressure — assuming there's only one or two will leave you short.
🏗️

Back of Snorkel — Left (Driver) Side

Rear exterior · Pry bars · Pike poles · Attic ladder
RRL-01
5' Pry Bar aka: Pry bar, gorilla bar
+
📖 What It Is

A 5-foot pry bar stowed at the rear driver's side.

❓ Why It's Needed

For moving heavy debris, opening access panels, and bracing operations — more leverage than a Halligan in certain situations.

💡
Only One on This SideThe rig went down to a single 5' bar here — don't assume there's a spare on this side.
RRL-02
Pike Poles — 5' & 12' (Driver's Side Rear, ×3) aka: Pike pole, plaster hook, ceiling hook
+
📖 What It Is

One 5' pike pole and two 12' pike poles stowed on this side.

❓ Why It's Needed

Pulling ceilings and opening walls from a safe distance. The 12-footers give you reach without getting directly under the drop zone; the 5' works tight interior spaces where a 12-footer can't swing.

⚠️
Stand Clear of the DropWhatever length you're using, don't stand directly under what you're pulling. Ceiling debris, insulation, and worse comes down fast and without warning.
RRL-03
8' New York Hook (Driver's Side) aka: NY hook, drywall hook, plaster hook
+
📖 What It Is

A large angled hook for pulling plaster ceilings and heavy lathe. This rig carries one on each side now — this one lives on the driver's side.

❓ Why It's Needed

The curved head gives mechanical advantage and keeps hands clear of the drop zone when you're pulling overhead — more purchase than a standard pike on heavy lathe.

RRL-04
Attic Ladder — 10' aka: Folding ladder, interior ladder
+
📖 What It Is

A compact folding ladder for attic access through small hatches.

❓ Why It's Needed

Lighter than an extension ladder and fits through tight attic access points a full-size ladder can't.

RRL-05
Scoop Shovels (×2) aka: Snow shovel, scoop
+
📖 What It Is

Two scoop shovels stowed at the rear.

❓ Why It's Needed

Debris clearing, overhaul, and — depending on season — digging out around the rig or outriggers.

🏗️

Back of Snorkel — Right (Officer) Side

Rear exterior · 5" hose bed · Pike poles · NY hook
RRR-01
400' of 5" LDH Hose Bed aka: Large diameter hose, LDH, five-inch, supply line
+
📖 What It Is

400 feet of 5" LDH loaded at the rear of the rig — this rig's primary water supply capability, since there's no tank to fall back on.

❓ Why It's Needed

400 feet gives you real distance from the hydrant to the rig. Five-inch is heavy and stiff — know how to lay it without kinking it.

⚠️
5" Hose — Handle It RightA kinked 5-inch line cuts your water supply, and on this rig that means the pump stops entirely. Practice the lay before you need to do it at a working fire.
RRR-02
Pike Poles — 6' & 8' (Officer's Side Rear) aka: Pike pole, ceiling hook, overhaul hook
+
📖 What It Is

An 8' pike pole and a 6' pike pole, both stowed on this side.

❓ Why It's Needed

The 8-footer gives you reach; the 6-footer works tighter interior spaces. Know which one you grabbed before you commit to a pull.

RRR-03
8' New York Hook (Officer's Side) aka: NY hook, drywall hook, plaster hook
+
📖 What It Is

Large angled hook designed for pulling plaster ceilings and heavy lathe, stowed on the officer's side. This rig is down to one on this side now — the other lives on the driver's side (see RRL-03).

❓ Why It's Needed

The curved head gives mechanical advantage and keeps hands clear of the drop zone when pulling overhead.

💨

Officers Side Rear

Officer's Side · Smoke Ejector · Electric Adapter
OSR-01
Smoke Ejector & Electric Adapter (OS Rear) aka: Fan, blower, PPV fan, smoke ejector
+
📖 What It Is

An electric fan used for positive pressure ventilation (PPV) or smoke removal, paired with the adapter that powers it off the rig's generator. This is one of two ejectors on the rig — the second lives OS Behind Wheel (see OSB-02).

❓ Why It's Needed

PPV pushes fresh air through a doorway, forcing smoke out of designated openings — critical for search and overhaul visibility.

🔧 How To Use

Connect the electric adapter to a live generator outlet before you need the fan running. Position it in the doorway at the correct angle and distance — too close and you lose the cone of air, too far and you lose pressure.

🪢

Officers Side Second to Rear

Officer's Side · Utility rope
OS2-01
Utility Rope — 3 Bags of 150' aka: Utility rope, rigging rope, general-purpose rope — NOT rescue rated
+
📖 What It Is

Three bags, each containing 150 feet of general-purpose utility rope.

❓ Why It's Needed

Rated for tethering, rigging, hoisting equipment, and securing loads — the day-to-day rope work that isn't life-safety related.

🔧 How To Use

Inspect each bag every shift for cuts, abrasion, and contamination before it's trusted with any load.

🚨
Utility Rope Is Not Rescue RopeThis was mislabeled as life-safety rope in older references — it isn't. Don't you dare tie in a person, raise a firefighter, or use this for any load-bearing-on-a-human operation. Snorkel 61 does not carry a dedicated life-safety rope in this compartment. If a job needs a rescue-rated line, it has to come from a rig or bag actually rated for it. Assuming any rope on the truck is rescue rope has gotten people killed.
💡

Officers Side Behind Wheel

Officer's Side · Electrical cord · Smoke Ejector · Air Bottles
OSB-01
135' Electrical Cord aka: Extension cord
+
📖 What It Is

A heavy-gauge extension cord for running tools and fans off the rig's generator.

❓ Why It's Needed

Lets you power equipment away from the rig without dragging a compartment's worth of cable.

💡
Know Your Amperage LimitsHeavy-gauge doesn't mean unlimited. Know what you're loading it with before you daisy-chain multiple tools off one cord.
OSB-02
Smoke Ejector (OS Behind Wheel) aka: Fan, blower, PPV fan
+
📖 What It Is

A second electric smoke ejector — this rig carries two total, one here and one at OS Rear (see OSR-01).

❓ Why It's Needed

Two fans lets you run PPV and smoke removal simultaneously at different openings, or keep one in reserve.

OSB-03
Spare Air Bottles (×3, OS Behind Wheel) aka: SCBA cylinders, spare bottles
+
📖 What It Is

Three spare SCBA cylinders in this compartment — separate from the two carried in the DS Engineers Compartment (see DS3-13).

❓ Why It's Needed

More air management redundancy for extended operations — five spare bottles total on this rig across two locations.

⚠️
Full Means FullCheck pressure on all three every shift, same as the DS spares. A half-empty bottle grabbed in a rush is worse than no bottle at all.
OSB-04
Duct Tape (OS Behind Wheel) aka: Universal fix-it tape
+
📖 What It Is

A second roll of duct tape, stocked here in addition to the roll in the DS Engineers Compartment.

❓ Why It's Needed

Sealing, marking, and temporary fixes — handy to have on both sides of the rig instead of hunting across the apparatus for one roll.

✂️

Officers Side Over Wheel

Officer's Side · Boltcutters · Irons · RASP Rope
OSW-01
Bolt Cutters — Medium & Large aka: Bolt cutters, chain cutters
+
📖 What It Is

Two sizes of bolt cutter on the top shelf of this compartment.

❓ Why It's Needed

Cutting padlocks, chains, and fencing without waiting for a saw.

🔧 How To Use

Match bolt cutter size to the lock. Medium for light padlocks and chain links, large for heavy-duty chains and reinforced padlocks. Hardened steel locks will destroy standard bolt cutters — if the medium won't cut, go large; if large won't cut, go to the K12.

OSW-02
Second Set of Irons — Halligan, Flathead Axe, Pick Axe & Sledge Hammer (Officer's Side) aka: OS irons — see DS4-01 through DS4-04 for full detail on each tool
+
📖 What It Is

A complete duplicate set of irons — Halligan, flathead axe, pick axe, and sledge hammer — stored on the officer's side, identical in function to the set on the driver's side (DS4-01 through DS4-04).

💡
Two Sets of Irons Is DeliberateDriver's side and officer's side both carry irons so two crews can tool up simultaneously without crossing each other on the way to their tools. Know which set is on which side so you go to the right place without thinking.
OSW-03
Silver Pick Axe aka: Spare pick axe
+
📖 What It Is

A second pick axe on this shelf, distinguished from the standard pick axe by its silver finish — the doc doesn't spell out why it's finished differently, so ask your engineer or officer about this rig's specific reasoning. Treat it as a fully functional pick axe either way.

❓ Why It's Needed

A spare pick axe on this side means officer-side crews aren't left without one if the standard pick axe is already in use elsewhere.

OSW-04
Roof Shovel aka: Ventilation shovel
+
📖 What It Is

A flat-bladed tool for clearing debris off a roof or scraping through roof coverings during ventilation.

❓ Why It's Needed

Not the same job as the pike poles — this one's for pushing and clearing, not pulling. Roof work needs a tool built for that motion.

OSW-05
Closet Pike Pole (Officer's Side) aka: Short pike — see DS4-06 for full entry
+
📖 What It Is

A duplicate closet pike pole carried on this side, same tool and purpose as the one on the driver's side over-the-wheel compartment (see DS4-06).

OSW-06
RASP Rope — 200' Bag aka: Rapid Assisted Search Procedure rope, RASP bag
+
📖 What It Is

A 200-foot RASP (Rapid Assisted Search Procedure) rope bag system.

❓ Why It's Needed

Used for elevated rescue, controlled descent, and personnel safety during aerial operations around the snorkel.

🚨
Train on This Before You're at HeightIf you haven't been trained on the RASP system, that training needs to happen before you're working around the snorkel at height. This is not equipment to improvise with. One more thing — some older training materials and crews still call this "Rapid Ascent and Safety Profile." That's not the correct expansion; the doc's been corrected to Rapid Assisted Search Procedure. Don't let the mismatch throw you if you hear the old version on scene.
OSW-07
Pipe Wrench aka: Stillson wrench, pipe grip
+
📖 What It Is

A newer addition to this shelf — a grip tool for turning pipe, fittings, and stuck fasteners.

❓ Why It's Needed

Gives you purchase on pipe, fittings, and stuck fasteners that a spanner or channel-lock can't grab — useful around plumbing shutoffs and some forcible-entry situations involving pipe or conduit.

🔦

Officers Side In Front of Tire

Officer's Side · Lights · Cones · Traction materials
OSF-01
Plug-in Lights (×3) aka: Scene lights, portable lights
+
📖 What It Is

Three portable lights that run off the rig's generator.

❓ Why It's Needed

Scene lighting for work areas beyond what the rig's fixed floodlights reach.

💡
Position Them RightKnow where the outlets are and how to position lights to illuminate the work area without blinding the crew or oncoming traffic.
OSF-02
Traffic Cones (9) aka: Road cones, pylons
+
📖 What It Is

Nine traffic cones for scene protection.

❓ Why It's Needed

Traffic control and hazard marking around the rig and hose lays on roadways.

OSF-03
Road Salt & Road Sand aka: Traction material
+
📖 What It Is

Salt and sand for traction in icy conditions.

❓ Why It's Needed

Under outrigger pads, around the perimeter, or for crew footing. Slippery ground around a 70,000 lb rig with outriggers deployed is a serious hazard.

OSF-04
Hose Hoist aka: Hoist rig — replaced the old hose roller, not the same tool
+
📖 What It Is

A rope-and-webbing rig used to haul charged hose, tools, or equipment vertically up to the aerial basket or an upper floor rather than making someone carry it up a ladder.

❓ Why It's Needed

Saves a crew member from climbing with a load, and gets equipment up faster than a person could carry it.

⚠️
This Replaced the Hose Roller — Don't Go Looking for ItThe hose roller that used to live in this compartment is gone. A roller just protected hose dragged over a windowsill; a hoist hauls loads up vertically. Different job — know which tool you actually need before you grab one.
🧱

Officers Side Front Compartment

Officer's Side Front · Tarps
OSC-01
2 Canvas Tarps aka: Salvage tarps
+
📖 What It Is

Heavy-duty canvas salvage tarps. Used to cover contents from water damage during overhaul, cover roof holes after ventilation cuts, or establish a debris drop zone beneath ceiling pulls. Know where these are so you're not digging for them when the crew is ready to overhaul.

⚠️
Canvas Isn't Poly — Dry It Before It Goes BackThese are canvas now, not poly. Poly you can fold up wet and toss back in the compartment. Canvas mildews and rots if it goes back damp — get it dried out before it's returned to the rig, or you'll find a ruined tarp next time someone needs it.
🚗

Cab Compartment

Inside the cab · Detection · Safety · Master stream
CAB-01
RIT Pack aka: Rapid Intervention Team pack, PASS pack
+
📖 What It Is

A full SCBA pre-assembled for a crew member who has to go in after a downed firefighter.

❓ Why It's Needed

This is a life-safety item. When a mayday comes in, seconds matter for the firefighter down.

🚨
Know It Before You Need ItThe RIT Pack exists for one reason: to bring air to a firefighter who is down or trapped inside. You will not have time to figure out how it works when that call comes. Know the pack, know the deployment, know it now.
CAB-02
Master Stream Control Unit aka: Waterway controller, aerial waterway panel
+
📖 What It Is

Controls the snorkel's aerial waterway and master stream nozzle from the cab.

❓ Why It's Needed

Lets the crew direct and adjust the master stream from the basket turret without someone standing exposed at the panel.

💡
Understand the BasicsUnderstand what this unit does before you're operating near it on scene — this ties directly to the missing basket turret nozzle flagged in DS3-06. No nozzle, no stream, no matter how well you run this panel.
CAB-03
4-Gas Detector aka: Multi-gas monitor, 4-gas meter
+
📖 What It Is

An atmospheric monitor for O2, CO, combustible gas, and H2S.

❓ Why It's Needed

Confined space entries, gas leak calls, and any environment where you can't visually tell if the air is breathable.

⚠️
Bump Test It Before Every ResponseA detector you haven't verified is a detector you can't trust. Pre-check it — don't find out it's dead when you're already standing in a bad atmosphere.
CAB-04
Gas Trac aka: Gas Track Monitor — distinct from the 4-Gas Detector
+
📖 What It Is

A separate atmospheric monitoring unit carried alongside the 4-Gas Detector — don't assume they're the same device.

❓ Why It's Needed

Additional or specialized gas monitoring coverage beyond the standard 4-gas readings.

CAB-05
Hot Stick aka: Voltage detector, non-contact voltage tester
+
📖 What It Is

A non-contact voltage tester used to check whether a wire, panel, or piece of equipment is energized before you touch it.

❓ Why It's Needed

Downed wires, damaged electrical panels, and vehicle accidents involving power lines all require verification before anyone gets close.

🚨
Never Assume It's DeadTest it, don't guess it. A downed line that looks dead can still be energized. This tool exists because "looks safe" has killed people.
CAB-06
Sawzall aka: Reciprocating saw, recip saw, demo saw
+
📖 What It Is

An electric reciprocating saw carried in the cab.

❓ Why It's Needed

Fast, controlled cutting for extrication, forcible entry, and demolition tasks that don't call for a gas saw.

CAB-07
Safety Vest aka: High-visibility vest, ANSI vest
+
📖 What It Is

A high-visibility vest kept in the cab.

❓ Why It's Needed

Roadway operations require it — a rig, a working scene, and moving traffic is a bad combination without visibility.

CAB-08
Box Lights aka: Portable hand lights
+
📖 What It Is

Portable hand lights kept in the cab for quick access.

❓ Why It's Needed

Immediate lighting for search, size-up, or any low-light task before you've deployed the rig's fixed lighting.

CAB-09
Caution Tape aka: Scene tape, barrier tape
+
📖 What It Is

Barrier tape for marking scene boundaries and hazards.

❓ Why It's Needed

Keeps bystanders and non-essential personnel out of a hazard area or active work zone.

CAB-10
Fire Wipes aka: Decon wipes
+
📖 What It Is

Decontamination wipes carried in the cab.

❓ Why It's Needed

On-scene decon of skin and gear after exposure to soot and fireground contaminants — cancer prevention isn't optional, it starts on scene.

CAB-11
Spare Masks — 2 MSA Masks & Surgical Face Mask aka: Spare SCBA facepieces
+
📋 Contents

2 MSA Masks: Spare SCBA facepieces for this rig's MSA air pack system — for a crew member whose mask fails or a mutual-aid firefighter without one. Surgical Face Mask: Infection control, unrelated to SCBA — for patient contact or scene conditions requiring basic respiratory protection.

🧺

On Top or In The Basket

Roof-stored & basket-stored equipment
TOP-01
100' of 1¾" Hose (Topside) aka: Topside hose
+
📖 What It Is

100 feet of 1¾" hose stowed on top of the rig, separate from the crosslays and the boxed 50' length (see TOP-06).

❓ Why It's Needed

Extra attack line capacity accessible from the top of the rig or basket operations.

TOP-02
Pick Axe (Topside) aka: Pick head axe — see DS4-03 for full entry
+
📖 What It Is

An additional pick axe stowed on top of the rig — same tool and use as the one in the DS Over-the-Wheel compartment (see DS4-03).

TOP-03
6' Pike Pole (Topside) aka: Pike pole, plaster hook
+
📖 What It Is

A 6-foot pike pole stowed topside.

❓ Why It's Needed

Available for pulling and overhaul work directly from a rooftop or basket position without climbing back down for a pole.

TOP-04
28' Extension Ladders (×2, Topside) aka: Ground ladders — separate stock from the DS ladder rack (DS8-01)
+
📖 What It Is

Two more 28' extension ladders stowed on top of the rig, in addition to the two on the DS ladder rack (DS8-01) — this rig carries four total across two locations.

⚠️
Don't Assume "The Ladders" Means Only the RackThere's more ladder capacity on this rig than what's on the DS ladder rack alone. Know both locations cold before you go looking under pressure.
TOP-05
16' Roof Ladder (Boom-Mounted) aka: Aerial ladder — see DS8-02 for the DS rack pair
+
📖 What It Is

A single 16' roof ladder with hooks on both ends, mounted directly on the aerial boom — this is the third ladder referenced in DS8-02's callout, not part of the DS rack pair or the topside pair (TOP-06).

💡
Same Ladder, Different AngleThis is the ladder DS8-02 tells you not to count in that rack's total. One physical ladder, one location — it just gets referenced from both entries so you're not caught looking for it in the wrong place.
TOP-06
16' Roof Ladders (×2, Topside) aka: Roof ladder, hook ladder — separate from DS8-02 and the boom-mounted ladder (TOP-05)
+
📖 What It Is

Two 16' roof ladders stored topside, separate from the two racked on the driver's side (DS8-02) and the single one mounted on the boom (TOP-05). That's five 16' roof ladders total on this rig across three locations — confirm all five are present at rig check.

TOP-07
In-Box — 50' of 1¾" Hose w/ Fog Nozzle aka: Boxed quick-deploy hose
+
📖 What It Is

A separate, boxed-off 50-foot length of 1¾" hose with its own fog nozzle, distinct from the 100' length stowed topside (TOP-01).

💡
Keep It Separate in Your HeadThis is a quick-deploy length for the basket, not extra length to tie into the 100'. Don't confuse the two when you're grabbing hose under pressure.
⚠️
Topside Access = Ladder Belt, Every TimeAnything stored on top of this rig means someone's climbing up there to get it. Ladder belt, three points of contact, spotter if you've got one free. A fall off the top of an apparatus on a wet ramp is exactly the kind of injury that ends careers.

🚑 Squad 61 — Compartment Study Guide

Squad 61 is your heavy rescue rig. It carries the cutters, spreaders, rams, air bags, cascade, water rescue gear, and the technical tools you'll grab when a regular engine response isn't enough. Every compartment on this truck exists because somebody, somewhere, needed exactly what's inside it — and they didn't have time to wait. Walk it. Know it. Don't guess.

Listen up, probie. The Squad doesn't get called for grass fires. When we roll, somebody is trapped, pinned, drowning, electrocuted, or already dead and we're trying to keep more people from joining them. Every minute you spend hunting for a tool is a minute somebody isn't breathing. Learn this rig cold.

💡

Engineers Compartment

Pics
Light Tower · Fire Investigation · Wet Vac · Particulate Mask
Light Tower Controller
AKA: Light tower remote, scene light controller, tower panel, "the joystick"
+
📖What it is & what it does

This is the hand-held control unit for the roof-mounted scene light tower. The tower turns night into noon at an MVA, a structural overhaul, an extrication, or any scene where you need real area lighting. The controller raises, lowers, rotates, and aims the tower from the ground so you're not climbing on the rig in the dark with traffic at your back.

🧩Parts
  • Up/Down toggle: Raises and lowers the mast.
  • Rotate switch: Spins the head left/right.
  • Tilt control: Aims the lamp heads up or down.
  • Power/lamp switches: Individual head on/off so you can throw light only where it's needed.
  • Coiled cord/tether: Plugs into the receptacle in the compartment.
🏷️Alternate names

"Light tower remote," "tower stick," "the wand," "scene light controller." On older rigs the tower may have been a hand-cranked telescoping pole — same job, different decade.

⚠️
Rookie Mistake — Driving Off With The Mast UpThis has happened on real jobs and ripped towers clean off rigs, snapped wires, smashed traffic lights, and ended careers. Before the wheels move, the tower is DOWN and STOWED. Verify visually. Walk to the rear and look up. Every single time.
⚡
Watch for Overhead HazardsPower lines, tree limbs, parking deck ceilings, station bay doors. The tower goes up 15–20 feet. Look UP before you raise it. Energized power line contact will kill you and anyone touching the rig.
Fire Investigation Box
AKA: Fire investigation kit, cause-and-origin kit, arson kit, "the evidence box"
+
📖What it is & what it does

A self-contained box of evidence-collection and documentation tools the Fire Investigator uses to determine cause and origin after the fire is out. It supports the overhaul phase when you're sifting through char looking for the point of origin, accelerant patterns, and the story of what burned and in what order.

🧩Parts (typical contents)
  • Evidence cans/jars: Clean metal containers for accelerant samples — must be uncontaminated.
  • Evidence bags & tags: Chain of custody documentation.
  • Camera/measuring tools: Tape, scale, gloves, markers.
  • Probes & trowels: Hand tools for digging through debris carefully.
  • PPE — nitrile gloves, mask: You handle char with bare hands and you'll regret it.
🏷️Alternate names

"Cause-and-origin kit," "C&O box," "arson kit," "investigator's box."

⚖️
Rookie Mistake — Touching, Moving, or Pitching EvidenceOnce you suspect this fire might be intentional, the scene is a crime scene. Probies have ruined real prosecutions by kicking a gas can out of the way to make room or hosing down a burn pattern that would have been the evidence. Don't touch anything in the investigation box unless the investigator hands it to you, and stop disturbing the fire scene the second cause becomes questionable.
📋
Chain of CustodyIf you collect a sample, you sign it, you bag it, you hand it to the next person and they sign for it. Break that chain and the evidence is worthless in court.
Dust / Particulate Face Mask
AKA: N95, dust mask, particulate respirator, "the paper mask"
+
📖What it is & what it does

A disposable filtering facepiece respirator — typically N95 rated — for protection against airborne particulates during overhaul, post-fire cleanup, dusty extrications (drywall, concrete, fiberglass), and certain medical incidents involving airborne pathogens. It is NOT a substitute for SCBA. It filters particles. It does not provide oxygen and does not stop CO, HCN, or other toxic gases.

🧩Parts
  • Filter media body: The cup or fold-flat fabric.
  • Nose clip: Bendable metal strip — mold it tight to your nose bridge.
  • Elastic straps: One above the ears, one below — both, every time.
  • Seal edge: The soft inner edge that must contact clean-shaven skin to seal.
🏷️Alternate names

"N95," "particulate respirator," "filtering facepiece," "dust mask," "paper mask" (informal — and inaccurate, because the media is non-woven polypropylene).

☠️
Rookie Mistake — Wearing a Dust Mask in SmokeI've seen probies pull a dust mask out and head into overhaul thinking they're protected. They are not. Carcinogenic combustion byproducts laugh at an N95. Lung cancer is the leading occupational killer of firefighters. If there is ANY smoke, soot, or combustion atmosphere, you wear SCBA — not a dust mask. Period.
🧔
Seal Requires Clean-Shaven SkinBeard stubble breaks the seal. Same rule as your SCBA facepiece. Both straps. Pinched nose clip. Test the seal with a sharp inhale — it should pull in against your face.
Wet Vac
AKA: Shop vac, wet-dry vac, wet vacuum, "the vac"
+
📖What it is & what it does

An industrial wet/dry vacuum used for sucking up standing water, spilled liquids, and debris at scenes. On Squad you'll use it at vehicle extrication scenes with water intrusion, fire cleanup, and hazmat spill mitigation. Faster and more controlled than a mop — and it gets into spots a mop can't reach.

🧩Parts
  • Tank/drum: The collection vessel. Check the fill level — it gets heavy fast.
  • Motor/suction head: The power unit that mounts on top of the tank.
  • Hose: Flexible suction hose — check for cracks or blockages before use.
  • Nozzles/attachments: Floor nozzle, crevice tool — stored with or inside the unit.
  • Filter: Must be correct type for wet use. Some foam sleeve filters, some run filter-free for liquids.
  • On/off switch: Simple toggle on the motor head.
🏷️Alternate names

"Shop vac," "wet-dry vac," "wet vacuum." On scenes you'll just hear "grab the vac."

⚠️
Rookie Mistake — Wrong Filter for Wet UseMost wet/dry vacs ship with a paper or pleated filter meant for dry use only. Run it wet with that filter installed and you'll destroy the filter and possibly burn out the motor. For wet use, remove the paper filter and use a foam sleeve or run filter-free per manufacturer spec. Check before you power on.
💧
Watch the Tank LevelThe tank fills faster than you think. When the float shuts off suction, empty it before continuing. A full tank of water is heavy — and dump it somewhere appropriate, not into a storm drain at a hazmat scene.
🪝

Driver's Side Traverse — Bottom Shelf

Pics
Winch · Steering Wheel Cutter
Winch with Remote
AKA: Portable winch, come-along (mechanical version), pull tool, "the winch"
+
📖What it is & what it does

A powered winch — typically electric, with a fairlead and cable or synthetic rope — used to pull, drag, stabilize, or extract a heavy load along a line of force. This unit is rated for a 10,000 lb max load with 80 feet of cable. We use it for vehicle stabilization (anchoring a teetering car), moving a wreck a few feet so we can reach a patient, or dragging debris. The hand remote keeps you out of the snap-back zone.

🧩Parts
  • Drum: The spool the cable winds onto.
  • Cable/synthetic rope: The pulling line. Synthetic is lighter and safer when it parts — steel cable can decapitate.
  • Hook with safety latch: The business end. Inspect the latch every time.
  • Fairlead: Roller or aluminum hawse guide that protects the rope and the drum.
  • Motor & gearbox: Powers the drum.
  • Wired/wireless remote: Pendant for IN/OUT, lets you stand clear.
  • Clutch/freespool lever: Disengages the drum so you can pull rope out by hand.
  • Power leads: Connect to the rig battery or 12V source.
🏷️Alternate names

"Winch," "puller," "electric winch," "Warn winch" (brand). A manual cable puller is a "come-along" or "ratcheting puller" — different tool, same idea, no battery.

☠️
Rookie Mistake — Standing In Line With the CableIf a winch cable parts under load, it snaps back like a steel whip with energy that will kill a grown adult. NEVER stand in line with a loaded winch line. Stand 90° offset. Lay a heavy jacket, salvage cover, or winch damper over the cable to absorb whip energy. Use the remote at the end of its lead — that's why it exists.
🧤
Always Wear Gloves Handling CableSteel cable develops broken strands called "meathooks" that go straight through skin and into the bone. Leather gloves, every time. And never let the cable run through your hand under power.
⚓
Anchor ProperlyThe winch is only as strong as your anchor. Bumper hitches, tow rings, and rated D-rings — not random bodywork. If you anchor to sheet metal, you'll pull the panel off the car and the winch with it.
🪝
Handle the Cable by the Strap, Operate Under TensionFeed and handle the cable using the strap on the hook — not bare-handed on the wire itself, which frays and bites. Once you're pulling, keep the line under rope tension the whole time; a loose, slack cable that suddenly comes tight can snap-load and jump off the fairlead or the anchor point.
📡
Know the Remote May Be DownThere's a wireless remote for this winch, but it has a history of not working. Check it on rig check — don't discover it's dead when you're trying to keep clear of the line on a live pull. If it's not responding, use the corded remote and brief the crew before you load the line.
Steering Wheel Cutter
AKA: Wheel chopper, steering wheel saw, column cutter, "the wheel cutter"
+
📖What it is & what it does

A purpose-built cutter for severing a steering wheel rim and/or steering column components during an extrication when the wheel is pinning a driver's chest or trapping their legs. This is a manual, hand-powered tool — no battery, no hydraulics — so it's faster to grab and more controlled than reaching for the spreaders or the recip saw inside a tight cab.

🧩Parts
  • Cutting blades / jaws: Hardened steel cutting edges sized for steering wheel rim diameter.
  • Handles: Long levers for mechanical advantage (manual units) or trigger (powered units).
  • Pivot/fulcrum bolt: The hinge — keep it serviced, never side-load it.
  • Spring return (some models): Reopens the jaws between cuts.
🏷️Alternate names

"Steering wheel cutter," "wheel cutter," "rim cutter," "wheel chopper." Some older departments call it a "column tool" but a column tool is technically a different beast for cutting the column itself.

💥
Rookie Mistake — Cutting Near an Undeployed AirbagIf the airbag in that steering wheel hasn't fired, you are about to. Disconnect battery first. Cover the airbag module. Stay out of the deployment path (typically 18–20 inches from a driver bag, 24+ from a side curtain). A live airbag firing into your face while you're working an extrication will break it.
🧑‍🤝‍🧑
Protect the PatientHard protection (a board, salvage cover, or a rescuer's hands shielded with a blanket) between the cutter and the patient. Metal fragments fly. Patients are already injured — don't add lacerations to that list.
🪚

DS Compartment 3 (Over Wheel) — Top Shelf

Pics
Circular Saw · K12 Saw · Chainsaw · Chain Oil · Extra Chains
Circular Saw
AKA: Skilsaw, worm-drive saw, sidewinder, "the circ saw"
+
📖What it is & what it does

A standard 7-1/4" handheld circular saw for cutting dimensional lumber, plywood, sheet goods, and softer building materials. Used in cribbing prep, on-scene wood cutting, fabricating shoring, opening floor decks during overhaul, and any time you need a clean straight cut in wood.

🧩Parts
  • Blade & arbor: Match blade to material — wood blade for wood, period.
  • Blade guard (retractable): Springs back when the cut starts; covers the blade at rest. Never tie or wire it open.
  • Base/shoe: The flat plate that rides the workpiece.
  • Depth adjustment: Set depth to just below the material.
  • Bevel adjustment: Tilts the shoe for angled cuts.
  • Trigger & safety: Two-stage trigger prevents accidental start.
  • Power source: Corded or battery — know which.
🏷️Alternate names

"Skilsaw" (brand-as-generic), "circular saw," "circ saw," "sidewinder" (motor on the side), "worm-drive" (motor in line — different power profile).

🩸
Rookie Mistake — Wiring the Guard Open or Reaching Under the CutThe retractable lower guard is a safety device, not a nuisance. Probies have wired it back to "make the saw cut faster." That saw bit a man's thumb off in three seconds. Let the guard work. And never reach UNDER the workpiece while the saw is running — that's where kickback throws your hand into the blade.
🦺
Eyes and EarsSafety glasses non-negotiable. Hearing protection if you'll be cutting more than a few seconds. Splinters in the eye are a career-ender.
K12 Saw
AKA: K-saw, cut-off saw, rescue saw, partner saw, Stihl saw, "the K12"
+
📖What it is & what it does

A high-RPM gas-powered abrasive cut-off saw — historically the Partner/Husqvarna K12 — used for cutting steel, masonry, concrete, rebar, and roof decks. This is the workhorse for forcible entry on commercial roll-up doors, for cutting locks and bars, and for ventilation cuts in metal-decked roofs. It runs a 12–14" abrasive or diamond blade at violent speed.

🧩Parts
  • Blade: Abrasive composite for metal/masonry, OR diamond for concrete. The wrong blade for the material is dangerous AND ineffective.
  • Blade guard (rotating): Set to deflect sparks/debris AWAY from you and the patient.
  • Two-cycle gas engine: Requires a fuel/oil mix. Plain gas will seize it.
  • Pull starter, choke, throttle lock: Standard small-engine controls.
  • Air filter: Gets choked with concrete dust fast — check it.
  • Front and rear handles, belly guard: Two-hand operation, always.
🏷️Alternate names

"K-saw," "K12" (model name, used as the generic), "cut-off saw," "rescue saw," "Stihl saw" (different brand, same job), "Partner saw" (the original maker), "quickie saw."

🔥
Rookie Mistake — Cutting Without Flammable-Atmosphere CheckThis saw throws a shower of red-hot sparks 20 feet. Cutting near a leaking gas main, in a fuel-soaked structure, or on a fuel tank has killed firefighters. Before you pull the trigger, somebody needs eyes on the spark path AND a charged hose line in position. Always.
💀
Wrong Blade = Blade FailurePutting a masonry blade on metal, or vice versa, can shatter the disc at 5000 RPM and send shrapnel into your femoral artery. Verify the blade matches the material before you start. Diamond blades have a "max RPM" stamp — respect it.
⛽
Two-Stroke Fuel Mix OnlyThis is a two-stroke engine. It runs on premixed gas/oil at the manufacturer's ratio (commonly 50:1). Putting pump gas in it with no oil will destroy the engine on the first start. Fuel is stored separately and labeled — don't guess.
Chainsaw
AKA: Vent saw, ventilation saw, "the chainsaw," Stihl
+
📖What it is & what it does

A gas-powered chainsaw — typically with a carbide-tipped chain for fire service — used for vertical ventilation cuts on wood-decked roofs, cutting through downed trees blocking access, and storm/wind/tornado response. The carbide chain handles nails, roofing tar, and the occasional staple without dulling instantly the way a standard woodcutting chain does.

🧩Parts
  • Bar: The flat metal guide the chain rides on.
  • Chain: Carbide-tipped for fire service work — verify tooth direction when re-installing.
  • Sprocket: Drives the chain.
  • Bar oil reservoir: Lubricates the chain. Empty = burned bar.
  • Two-stroke engine: Same fuel rules as the K12.
  • Chain brake: Forward bar that stops the chain instantly during kickback. Test it before EVERY use.
  • Throttle, choke, primer bulb: Starting controls.
  • Tip guard (some fire service saws): Wraps the very nose of the bar to suppress kickback when you plunge-cut a roof.
🏷️Alternate names

"Vent saw," "ventilation saw," "roof saw," "Stihl" (brand-as-generic for many crews), "chainsaw."

↩️
Rookie Mistake — Underestimating KickbackKickback is when the tip of the bar contacts something and the saw flips back violently toward your face and neck. This kills firefighters. Cut with the body of the bar, never the tip. Plunge-cut technique is taught for a reason — don't freestyle it on a working roof.
🏠
Don't Cut Yourself Off the RoofOn a vent cut, position yourself so your retreat path is always uphill of the cut and OPPOSITE side from where the hole will be. Probies have cut around themselves and dropped into the fire below. Plan the cut, plan the exit, then start the saw.
🛢️
Check Bar Oil AND FuelTwo separate reservoirs. Running dry on bar oil cooks the chain and bar in under a minute. Top both, every time.
Chain Oil
AKA: Bar oil, bar & chain oil, saw oil, "the bar oil"
+
📖What it is & what it does

Tacky, high-cling lubricating oil formulated specifically for chainsaw bars and chains. Auto-fed from the saw's oiler onto the chain as it runs. Reduces friction, dissipates heat, and dramatically extends bar and chain life.

🧩Parts (related)
