Inside The Cab Behind Passenger Seat

❤️‍🩹 Medic 62 — Compartment Study Guide

Medic 62 is our ALS transport unit — the rig that gets a sick or hurt patient from the worst moment of their life to the hospital in one piece. It carries the immobilization gear, the airway equipment, the IV supplies and cardiac meds, and the box itself is set up so every drawer and cabinet has a job. This isn't an engine you're pulling hose off of. This is where you keep somebody alive for the next fifteen to twenty minutes.

Listen up, probie. Every other rig in this fleet exists to make the fire go out or the person get free. This one exists so the person keeps breathing. You do not get to "kind of" know where the airway bag is or "kind of" remember which drawer has the tourniquets. When you're elbow-deep in a code in the back of this box, your hands need to already know where everything lives — because your eyes are going to be on the patient, not the cabinets.

🚪

Driver's Side Front Compartment

Stair Chair · Oxygen Tank
Stair Chair
AKA: Evac chair, carry chair, "the chair"
+
📖What it is & what it does

A folding, wheeled chair built to move a seated, conscious patient down (or up) stairwells and through narrow hallways where the full cot won't fit. It straps the patient in upright and lets two rescuers carry or track-walk them down a stairwell in control, instead of trying to muscle a flat stretcher through a space it was never designed for.

🧩Parts
  • Fold-out frame: Collapses flat for storage in the compartment, opens to a rigid seated chair.
  • Patient straps: Chest and lap straps — both go on, every patient, every time.
  • Rear tread wheels / stair-track (some models): Lets the chair roll down stair nosings in a controlled descent instead of being carried dead-weight the whole way.
  • Handles (front and rear): One rescuer at the head, one at the foot — communicate every step.
⚠️
Rookie Mistake — Skipping the Straps "Because It's Just One Flight"A patient who slumps, seizes, or simply loses balance mid-stairwell with no straps on goes down the stairs, not you. Strap every patient, every trip, no exceptions — even the guy who swears he can "just hold on."
🗣️
Communicate Every StepThe rescuer at the bottom calls the count. On tread models, know how your chair's mechanism works before you're on the stairs with a 200-lb patient — not while you're on them.
Oxygen Tank (DS Front)
AKA: O2 bottle, O2 cylinder, "the D tank" / "the jump bottle"
+
📖What it is & what it does

A portable compressed-oxygen cylinder for supplemental O2 delivery outside the fixed onboard system — the tank you grab when you're carrying gear to the patient before the cot ever gets there. Feeds nasal cannulas, non-rebreather masks, and BVMs.

🧩Parts
  • Cylinder body: Pressurized steel or aluminum tank — check the gauge before every shift.
  • Regulator: Steps tank pressure down to a usable flow rate.
  • Flow meter: Dial to set liters-per-minute delivery.
  • Pin-index or CGA valve: Ensures only an oxygen-rated regulator can be attached — don't force a mismatched fitting.
🔥
Rookie Mistake — Oil, Grease, or Petroleum Products Near the ValveOxygen under pressure plus a petroleum product is a flash-fire hazard. Never lubricate a fitting with anything but oxygen-safe lubricant, and keep greasy hands off the valve and regulator threads.
📉
Check Your Pressure Before You Leave the StationA tank reading below 500 psi doesn't leave the bay unswapped. Running out of O2 mid-transport on a patient who needs it is a completely preventable failure — check it every shift.
🎒

Middle Cabinet

Hydrant Bag · Kevlar Vests
Hydrant Bag
AKA: Hydrant kit, hydrant wrench bag
+
📖What it is & what it does

A bag of hydrant tools carried on the medic unit for the rare-but-real scenario where the ambulance is first on scene at a working fire, a vehicle fire near a hydrant, or is asked to secure a water supply before an engine arrives. It's not the primary job of this rig, but the tools are there because "not our job" doesn't hold up when nobody else is on scene yet.

🧩Parts
  • Hydrant wrench: Operates the hydrant valve stem and nozzle caps.
  • Spanner wrench: Tightens/loosens hose couplings.
  • Hydrant bag itself: Keeps the tools together and grab-and-go.
🏷️Alternate names

"Hydrant kit," "hydrant tools," "the hydrant bag."

💡
Know Why It's HereDon't assume every tool on this rig is EMS-only. This bag is a reminder that Medic 62 is still a fire department vehicle first — you may be asked to assist an engine crew before you ever touch a patient.
Kevlar Vests
AKA: Ballistic vests, body armor, "the vests"
+
📖What it is & what it does

Ballistic protective vests for crew use on calls with a known or suspected violence component — active threat staging, domestic disturbances with weapons involved, or any scene where law enforcement has requested EMS stage until the scene is secure. These are for YOUR protection, not the patient's.

🚨
Rookie Mistake — Not Staging on Violent CallsA Kevlar vest does not make you bulletproof to poor decision-making. If dispatch flags a scene as unsafe, you stage at a safe distance until law enforcement clears it — vest or no vest. The vest is your backup plan, not your reason to go in early.
🦺
Know Where They Are, Know How to Put One On FastYou don't want to be fumbling with straps while a scene is going sideways. Know the compartment, know the fit, practice the donning motion until it's automatic.
🧥

Driver's Side Rear Cabinet — Turnout Gear

Turnout Coat · Turnout Pants · Turnout Boots · Helmet
Turnout Gear (Coat, Pants, Boots, Helmet)
AKA: Bunker gear, structural PPE, "turnouts"
+
📖What it is & what it does

A full set of structural firefighting PPE kept on the medic unit so the crew isn't caught without protective gear if Medic 62 gets flagged to assist at a fire scene, an extrication, or any hazard environment. EMS providers don't wear this on routine medical calls — it's here for the calls that turn into something bigger.

🧩Parts
  • Turnout coat: Multi-layer thermal and moisture barrier for upper body.
  • Turnout pants: Same construction, lower body — worn with suspenders.
  • Turnout boots: Steel or composite toe/shank, puncture and thermal resistant.
  • Helmet: Impact and thermal protection with face shield/goggles.
📏
Rookie Mistake — Not Checking Fit Before You Need ItThe worst time to find out your spare turnouts don't fit is when you're being told to suit up at a working fire. Try this gear on during your first week. Know it fits. Know where it is.
🩼

Officer's Side Rear Compartment — Immobilization Gear

Backboards · Scoop Stretcher · Head Beds · C-Collar Bag · Spider Straps · KED · Short Boards
Backboards
AKA: Long spine board, LSB, "the board"
+
📖What it is & what it does

A rigid full-body board used for extrication and moving a patient with a suspected spinal injury as a single rigid unit, and for carrying a patient across uneven terrain where the cot can't roll. Works together with the head bed, spider straps, and C-collar to fully immobilize the spine during movement.

🧩Parts
  • Rigid board body: Plastic composite — X-ray permeable, won't flex under load.
  • Hand holes: Cutouts along the edge for carrying and cross-strapping.
  • Runners (bottom): Raised rails on the underside that let the board slide on the ground during log-rolls.
🦴
Rookie Mistake — Rushing the Log-RollA sloppy, uncoordinated log-roll onto the board can move an unstable spine exactly the way you're trying to prevent. One person calls the count, everyone moves together, the head stays in-line the entire time. This is not a race.
Scoop Stretcher
AKA: Orthopedic stretcher, clamshell stretcher, "the scoop"
+
📖What it is & what it does

A split-frame stretcher that separates into two halves and slides under the patient from each side, then locks together underneath them — no log-roll required. Ideal for patients you don't want to roll (suspected pelvic or hip fracture) or tight spaces where a log-roll isn't practical.

🧩Parts
  • Two split halves: Adjustable length, latch together at head and foot.
  • Latching mechanisms: Must click fully — a half-latched scoop can separate under load.
  • Carry handles.
⚠️
Rookie Mistake — Not Confirming Both LatchesIf either latch isn't fully seated, the scoop can pop open mid-lift and drop the patient. Check both ends. Visually and physically. Every time, before you lift.
Head Beds
AKA: Head immobilizer, head blocks, CID (cervical immobilization device)
+
📖What it is & what it does

Foam or adjustable side blocks that strap to the backboard and lock the patient's head from side-to-side rotation — the final piece of full spinal immobilization, applied after the collar and straps are in place, never before.

🧩Parts
  • Base plate: Straps or Velcro-mounts to the board under the patient's head.
  • Side blocks: Foam wedges that pin the head from both sides.
  • Forehead/chin straps: Cross the block assembly to lock it down.
🔢
Sequence MattersC-collar first, torso strapped to the board second, head bed last. Immobilize the head before the torso is secured and you can still torque the neck if the body shifts.
C-Collar Bag
AKA: Cervical collars, C-collars, neck collars
+
📖What it is & what it does

A bag holding an assortment of rigid cervical collars in multiple sizes (and often an adjustable one-size collar). Restricts flexion/extension of the neck for patients with a suspected cervical spine injury, applied before any major patient movement.

🧩Parts
  • Rigid collar shell: Chin support and trach cutout in front, occipital support in back.
  • Sizing options: Sized by neck-to-shoulder measurement — know how to size one on a patient fast.
  • Velcro closure strap.
📏
Rookie Mistake — Grabbing Whatever Collar Is on TopA collar that's too big won't restrict motion. Too small and it can compress the airway or push the chin up, hyperextending the neck. Size it properly — this takes seconds and matters.
Spider Straps
AKA: Spider harness, backboard straps
+
📖What it is & what it does

A multi-point strap harness that fans out across the patient's torso and legs to secure them to the backboard — replaces the old buckle-strap setup with a faster, more even multi-point restraint pattern.

🧩Parts
  • Central attachment point: Anchors to the board.
  • Multiple strap legs: Cross the chest, hips, and legs in a spider-web pattern.
  • Quick-release buckles.
💡
Practice the PatternSpider straps are fast once you know the routing — and slow and tangled if you don't. Practice on a dummy board, not for the first time on a real patient.
KED (Kendrick Extrication Device)
AKA: KED, vest-type extrication device, short spine board (vest style)
+
📖What it is & what it does

A rigid vest-style device that wraps around a seated patient's torso and head, used to extricate a patient from a vehicle when they're seated and stable enough that immediate removal isn't required — it immobilizes the spine while they're still sitting, so you can then rotate and lower them onto a long board.

🧩Parts
  • Rigid panel body: Wraps the torso, wood or plastic slats sewn into fabric.
  • Torso straps (3): Chest, mid, and lower — secure around the torso.
  • Leg straps (2): Under each thigh, crossed.
  • Head flaps & straps: Fold around the head after the torso is secured.
⏱️
Know When NOT to Use ItThe KED is for a stable patient in a stable vehicle. If the scene is unsafe, the vehicle is unstable, or the patient is critical, you do a rapid extrication straight onto a long board instead — the KED takes time you may not have.
Short Boards (for Splinting Limbs)
AKA: Limb splint boards, arm/leg boards
+
📖What it is & what it does

Short rigid boards used to splint an injured arm or leg — providing a firm surface to secure the limb against with cravats or straps, immobilizing the joint above and below a suspected fracture.

🩹
Splint the Joint Above and BelowA fracture splint that only crosses the injury site itself doesn't stop rotational movement. Immobilize the joint above and the joint below every time.
🫀

Officer's Side Front Cabinet

LUCAS Mechanical CPR Device
LUCAS (Mechanical CPR Device)
AKA: "The Lucas," mechanical compression device, auto-CPR, "the piston"
+
📖What it is & what it does

A battery-powered mechanical chest compression device that delivers continuous, consistent compressions at guideline depth and rate — hands-free, tireless, and immune to rescuer fatigue. On a working code, it frees up a set of hands for airway, IV access, and medication while compressions never lose quality or stop for crew changeover.

🧩Parts
  • Back plate: Slides under the patient's torso.
  • Piston/compression arm: The powered arm that delivers the compression.
  • Suction cup pad: Contacts the sternum — sizes/positions to the patient's chest.
  • Upper frame/straps: Locks the piston arm over the chest, secures to the back plate.
  • Battery pack: Rechargeable — verify charge status before every shift.
  • Control panel: Start/stop, mode selection (continuous vs. 30:2).
🏷️Alternate names

"The Lucas" (brand name used generically, like Kleenex), "mechanical CPR," "auto-compressor," "the piston."

☠️
Rookie Mistake — Fighting the Device or Placing It Wrong Under PressureThe Lucas has to be positioned correctly — centered, seated flush against the chest — or it will deliver compressions that are ineffective or that cause additional injury. Placing it correctly under the pressure of an active code takes practice. Drill this on a manikin until it's muscle memory, not your first time doing it live.
🔋
Dead Battery = No DeviceThis tool is worthless with a dead battery mid-code. Verify charge at the start of every shift, and know where the spare/backup battery lives.
🚑
Access to the LUCAS Isn't Limited to This CabinetThe device is also reachable from inside the patient compartment for rapid deployment during transport — know both access points cold.
🩹

Trauma & Wound Care Cabinet

Trauma Dressings · Tourniquets · Splints/Slings · Ice/Heat Packs · Saline · Bulb Syringe
Trauma Dressings (Bulk Gauze, ACE Wraps)
AKA: Bulk dressings, trauma pads, kerlix, ACE bandages
+
📖What it is & what it does

Bulk sterile gauze and elastic wraps for direct wound packing, bleeding control, and securing dressings in place. The workhorse supply for any bleeding-control call — from a minor laceration to major hemorrhage control before a tourniquet goes on, or in addition to one.

🩸
Restock Immediately After Every CallA bleeding-control call that uses your bulk gauze and nobody restocks it means the next crew opens this drawer to nothing on the next hemorrhage call. Restock before you clear the hospital, not "when you get back to quarters."
Tourniquets
AKA: TQ, CAT (Combat Application Tourniquet), windlass tourniquet
+
📖What it is & what it does

A windlass-style tourniquet for controlling life-threatening extremity hemorrhage that direct pressure alone can't stop. Applied high and tight above the wound, tightened until bleeding stops and a distal pulse is absent — not just "until it feels tight."

🧩Parts
  • Strap/band: Wraps around the limb.
  • Windlass rod: Twists to tighten the band.
  • Windlass clip: Locks the rod in place once tightened.
  • Time strip: Write the application time — every tourniquet, every time.
⏱️
Rookie Mistake — Forgetting to Write the TimeHospital staff need to know exactly how long a tourniquet has been on. Write it on the strip the moment you apply it — in the field, under stress, you will not remember later. This isn't optional documentation, it changes patient care downstream.
💪
Tight Enough Means Bleeding StopsA "loose enough to still see bleeding" tourniquet is worse than no tourniquet — it can restrict venous return while still letting arterial bleeding continue. Tighten until it stops completely.
Arm Splints & Slings
AKA: SAM splints, triangular bandages, cravats
+
📖What it is & what it does

Malleable splints and fabric slings for stabilizing suspected fractures and dislocations, and for supporting an injured arm in a position of comfort during transport.

Ice / Warm Packs
AKA: Instant cold packs, chemical heat packs
+
📖What it is & what it does

Single-use chemical activation packs — cold packs for soft tissue injuries, swelling, and heat-related illness cooling; warm packs for hypothermic patients and comfort. Squeeze/flex to activate — no refrigeration or heating required.

🧊
Never Direct Skin ContactBoth cold and hot chemical packs can cause tissue damage — frostbite-like injury from cold packs, burns from hot packs — with prolonged direct skin contact. Always wrap in a towel or dressing layer first.
Saline
AKA: Normal saline, NS, irrigation saline
+
📖What it is & what it does

Sterile saline solution used for wound irrigation, eye flushing, and moistening dressings. Kept separate from the IV fluid stock — this is the topical/irrigation supply, not the IV bag inventory.

Bulb Syringe
AKA: Ear syringe, suction bulb, neonatal aspirator
+
📖What it is & what it does

A simple squeeze-bulb suction device most commonly used for clearing a newborn's mouth and nose immediately after delivery — a core piece of OB kit support. Also useful for basic wound or oral irrigation.

👶
Mouth Before NoseOn a newborn, suction the mouth first, then the nose — clearing the nose first can trigger a reflex gasp that aspirates whatever's still in the mouth.
🫁

Airway & Respiratory Cabinet — Left Front

CPAP · NRB · Capnography · Airway Adjuncts · BVM · ET Tubes · I-Gel · Nebulizer · Nasal Cannula · Cric Kit
CPAP (Continuous Positive Airway Pressure)
AKA: CPAP, "the CPAP mask"
+
📖What it is & what it does

A non-invasive ventilation device that delivers continuous positive pressure through a sealed mask — used for patients in respiratory distress from pulmonary edema, CHF, or severe asthma/COPD flares who are still breathing on their own but struggling. It keeps alveoli open and can prevent the need for intubation if applied early.

🧩Parts
  • Mask with seal: Must seal fully around the face — leaks defeat the pressure.
  • Generator/flow valve: Creates the positive pressure using oxygen flow.
  • Headgear straps: Secures the mask without the patient having to hold it.
  • Pressure relief valve.
😨
Patients Fight the Mask — Coach Them Through ItCPAP feels claustrophobic. A patient who's already air-hungry and scared will often pull at the mask. Stay with them, talk them through it, don't just strap it on and walk away.
NRB (Non-Rebreather Mask)
AKA: NRB, non-rebreather
+
📖What it is & what it does

A high-concentration oxygen delivery mask with a reservoir bag and one-way valves that prevent exhaled air from mixing back into the supply — delivers the highest FiO2 you can get without positive pressure ventilation.

🎈
Prime the Bag FirstAn NRB applied to the patient's face before the reservoir bag is inflated with oxygen doesn't deliver high-concentration O2 — it just makes them rebreathe their own air. Fill the bag, then apply.
Capnography
AKA: EtCO2 monitor, waveform capnography, "cap-no"
+
📖What it is & what it does

Measures exhaled carbon dioxide and displays a real-time waveform — the gold standard for confirming and continuously monitoring correct ET tube or supraglottic airway placement, and a critical trend indicator during CPR and for any patient in respiratory distress.

🫁
Rookie Mistake — Confirming a Tube Once and Never Checking AgainA tube can migrate. Capnography isn't a one-time check at intubation — it's continuous confirmation for the entire time that airway is in place. A lost waveform means you reassess the airway immediately, every time.
Nasopharyngeal / Oropharyngeal Airways
AKA: NPA, OPA, nasal trumpet, oral airway
+
📖What it is & what it does

Basic airway adjuncts that hold the tongue off the back of the throat in an unconscious patient. OPA for a patient with no gag reflex; NPA tolerated by patients who still have one. Simple, fast, foundational airway management before anything more advanced.

🤮
Rookie Mistake — OPA on a Patient With a Gag ReflexPlacing an OPA in a patient who still gags can trigger vomiting and aspiration. Check for a gag reflex first. If they still have one, use the NPA instead.
BVM (Bag Valve Mask)
AKA: Ambu bag, bag mask, "the bag"
+
📖What it is & what it does

A self-inflating bag with a one-way valve and mask (or adapter for an advanced airway) used to manually ventilate a patient who isn't breathing adequately on their own. One of the most fundamental — and most frequently misused — tools in EMS.

🧩Parts
  • Self-inflating bag: Squeeze to ventilate.
  • One-way valve: Prevents exhaled air from returning to the bag.
  • Mask: Seals over nose and mouth — or connects directly to an advanced airway.
  • O2 reservoir bag/tubing: Boosts delivered FiO2 close to 100% when connected to oxygen.
💨
Rookie Mistake — Bagging Too Fast, Too HardOver-ventilation is one of the most common and most dangerous errors on scene. It causes gastric insufflation (air in the stomach, raising vomiting/aspiration risk) and can drop cardiac output during a code by increasing intrathoracic pressure. Squeeze only enough to see visible chest rise, at the correct rate — not as fast and hard as you can.
🤲
Mask Seal Is EverythingA one-handed E-C grip that leaks air is doing almost nothing. If you're not seeing chest rise, fix your seal before you assume the airway is the problem — two-person BVM technique (one sealing, one squeezing) is often better and should not be seen as a last resort.
ET Tubes (Endotracheal Tubes)
AKA: ET tube, endo tube, "the tube"
+
📖What it is & what it does

A flexible tube inserted through the vocal cords into the trachea to secure a definitive airway — used for patients who can't protect their own airway or need prolonged advanced ventilatory support. Carried in multiple sizes for different patient ages and builds.

🫁
Confirm Placement Every Time — Then Confirm It AgainEsophageal intubation is a preventable, patient-killing error. Confirm with direct visualization, bilateral breath sounds, absence of epigastric sounds, and waveform capnography — then reconfirm after every patient move. A tube that was good five minutes ago can dislodge.
I-Gel Airways
AKA: I-Gel, supraglottic airway, SGA
+
📖What it is & what it does

A blind-insertion supraglottic airway with a gel cuff that seats over the laryngeal opening without the need for direct visualization or a laryngoscope — faster to place than an ET tube, commonly used during codes when rapid airway control matters more than the most definitive option.

⚡
Fast Doesn't Mean CarelessThe I-Gel is quick to insert, but sizing still matters and confirmation is still required — capnography and chest rise, same as any other airway.
Nebulizer
AKA: Neb, neb treatment, updraft
+
📖What it is & what it does

Converts liquid respiratory medication into a fine mist the patient inhales through a mouthpiece or mask — used for bronchospasm from asthma, COPD, and reactive airway events. Runs off compressed oxygen or a compressor.

Nasal Cannula
AKA: NC, "the cannula"
+
📖What it is & what it does

Low-flow supplemental oxygen delivery through two soft prongs at the nostrils — for patients who need modest oxygen support and can tolerate/prefer something less intrusive than a mask.

Cricothyrotomy Kit
AKA: Cric kit, surgical airway kit, "the cric"
+
📖What it is & what it does

A last-resort surgical airway kit for the true "can't intubate, can't ventilate" emergency — a definitive airway placed directly through the cricothyroid membrane when every other airway option has failed. This is the tool nobody wants to need and everybody needs to know is there.

🚨
Know This Kit Exists and Where It Lives — That's Your Job as a ProbieThis is an advanced procedure performed under your department's protocols by credentialed providers. Your responsibility right now is knowing exactly where this kit is and having it in hand instantly if it's called for — hesitation in a can't-ventilate emergency costs the patient the outcome.
💉

IV & Medication Cabinet — Right Door

Clear Cabinet · Top Drawer · Bottom Drawer
Clear Cabinet — IV Fluid Warmer, Portable Suction, Masks & Gloves
AKA: "The clear cabinet"
+
📖What it is & what it does

The see-through cabinet on the right door groups three quick-grab items: an IV fluid warmer (prevents cold fluids from dropping an already-compromised patient's core temperature further), a portable suction unit (clears the airway of blood, vomit, or secretions fast), and masks/gloves for immediate BSI.

🩸
Suction Before Anything Else on an Airway Full of FluidYou cannot bag or intubate through vomit or blood. Suction first, every time, before any other airway intervention on a soiled airway.
Top Drawer — Syringes, IVs, Band-Aids, IV Tubing
AKA: "The top drawer"
+
📖What it is & what it does

Day-to-day IV starting supplies — syringes, IV catheters, adhesive dressings, and tubing. This is the drawer you're in for the overwhelming majority of your IV starts and basic wound care on every call.

🧤
Sharps Discipline Starts HereEvery needle that comes out of this drawer goes straight into the sharps container after use — not set down on a seat, not recapped by hand. A needlestick from a sloppy habit can end your career before it starts.
Bottom Drawer — IV Fluids, Cardiac Meds, Med Boxes
AKA: "The bottom drawer," med drawer
+
📖What it is & what it does

IV fluid bags, additional IV tubing, and locked med boxes containing ALS medications — including magnesium sulfate (Mag) and dopamine, both high-alert cardiac/critical care medications. This drawer is why Medic 62 is an ALS transport unit and not just a truck with a cot in it.

🏷️Note

Dosing, indications, and administration of everything in the med boxes is governed by your department's protocols and medical director — that's ALS provider territory, not something to freelance from a study guide. As a probie, your job is knowing this drawer exists, knowing it's locked/secured, and knowing to hand it to the paramedic the second it's needed — not administering from it yourself.

🔒
Rookie Mistake — Treating the Med Drawer CasuallyHigh-alert medications get respect. Verify seals are intact at shift check, know immediately if something looks tampered with or missing, and never let this drawer sit open and unattended in a public area.
📦

Right Bench Storage

Triage Bag · Vacuum Splints · Extra Splints · Blankets
Triage Bag
AKA: MCI bag, triage kit
+
📖What it is & what it does

A bag of triage tags and supplies for rapidly sorting patients by acuity during a multi-casualty incident (MCI) — colored tags (typically red/yellow/green/black) that travel with each patient and tell every provider downstream how urgent that patient is at a glance.

🏷️
Know Your Triage System Before You Need ItSTART, SALT, whatever your department runs — learn the algorithm now. An MCI is not the time to be reading the instructions on the inside of the bag.
Vacuum Splints
AKA: Vac splints, vacuum immobilizer
+
📖What it is & what it does

Bead-filled splints that conform to a limb's exact shape, then rigidify when air is pumped out with a hand pump — molds around angulated fractures better than a rigid board splint without needing to straighten the limb first.

Extra Splints
AKA: Spare splint stock
+
📖What it is & what it does

Backup splinting supplies kept here so a multi-patient extremity injury call — or a busy shift with multiple splinting calls back to back — doesn't leave you short.

Blankets
AKA: Patient blankets, warming blankets
+
📖What it is & what it does

Standard patient blankets for warmth, dignity, and basic hypothermia prevention. Stored here and also above — check both locations when you're restocking.

🌡️
Don't Underestimate a BlanketTrauma patients and medical patients alike lose heat fast, and hypothermia worsens coagulopathy in a bleeding patient. A blanket is basic, not optional.
👶

Left Bench — Under Seat Storage

ACR (Child Restraint) · Psych Restraints · OB Pack
ACR (Ambulance Child Restraint)
AKA: Pedi restraint system, child safety seat (ambulance-rated)
+
📖What it is & what it does

An ambulance-rated child restraint system, weight-coded to fit different pediatric sizes, for safely transporting a child who does not need to be secured to the cot itself. Regular car seats are not rated for ambulance mounting — this equipment is purpose-built.

👶
Rookie Mistake — Improvising With a Parent's Car SeatA standard vehicle car seat is not crash-tested or rated for ambulance mounting hardware. Use the department's ACR, sized correctly to the child's weight — every time, no exceptions, no matter how much a parent insists on using their own seat.
Restraints (Psych)
AKA: Soft restraints, psychiatric restraints
+
📖What it is & what it does

Soft physical restraints used, per protocol and with proper documentation, to protect a combative or altered patient — and the crew — from injury during transport when de-escalation and chemical restraint (if applicable, by ALS provider) aren't sufficient alone.

⚖️
Restraints Are a Last Resort, Not a First MovePhysical restraint use has legal, medical, and safety implications — positional asphyxia is a real risk if a patient is restrained improperly, especially face-down. Follow your protocol exactly, document thoroughly, and never restrain a patient prone.
OB Pack (Obstetrical)
AKA: OB kit, delivery kit, precip kit
+
📖What it is & what it does

A self-contained sterile kit for assisting an out-of-hospital delivery — sterile drape, clamps, cord scissors/scalpel, bulb syringe, receiving blanket, and a bag for the placenta. When a baby is coming and there's no time to wait, this kit has everything for a clean, controlled delivery.

👶
Know This Kit Cold — There's No Time to Read Instructions Mid-DeliveryAn imminent delivery does not wait for you to figure out which clamp goes where. Open this kit, know every item in it, and know the sequence before your first real OB call — not during it.
☣️

Infectious Waste Station

Infectious Waste Bin · Sharps Container
Infectious Waste Bin
AKA: Biohazard bin, red bag bin
+
📖What it is & what it does

OSHA-regulated container, lined with a red biohazard bag, for disposal of blood- and body-fluid-contaminated materials — used gloves, dressings, and anything that contacted bodily fluids.

Sharps Container
AKA: Sharps box, needle box
+
📖What it is & what it does

A puncture-resistant, one-way-drop container for used needles, lancets, and any sharp medical waste — mounted where it's reachable from wherever you're starting an IV, not buried somewhere you have to walk to.

💉
Rookie Mistake — Recapping a Needle by HandMost accidental needlesticks happen during recapping. Never recap by hand. The needle goes straight from the patient's arm into the sharps container — no detour, no exceptions, no "I'll just set it down for a second."
📏
Don't Overfill ItA sharps container filled past its fill line becomes a stick hazard itself when something is forced in on top. Swap it out before it's full, not after.
🛏️

Ambulance Cot / Stretcher

Power Cot Operation · Loading & Unloading
Ambulance Cot (Power-Load Stretcher)
AKA: The cot, power cot, gurney, stretcher
+
📖What it is & what it does

The powered, self-loading stretcher that is the centerpiece of the patient compartment — it carries every patient you transport. Its own onboard oxygen and monitor pad storage, powered leg-raise system, and self-loading mechanism make it fast to deploy and load, but only if you know the exact sequence. Get it wrong and you can drop a patient or damage a very expensive piece of equipment.

🧩Parts
  • Head-of-cot storage: Portable oxygen tank and airway equipment staged under the head end.
  • Side bags: Monitor and defib pads stored in bags on the sides.
  • Red-marked controls: Anything marked red on the cot relates to raising, lowering, or locking the legs — the bar under the head of the cot can be shortened to fit into elevators but must be fully extended before the cot goes back into the ambulance.
  • Legs and locking mechanism: Power-actuated, extend and retract as the cot loads/unloads.
  • Release controls: Small buttons that release the cot for movement — covered in the procedure below.
🔧Unloading Procedure
  • Open the rear doors.
  • Make sure the rear of the ambulance has dumped (lowered) — if it hasn't, close the doors and reopen them.
  • Push in the release.
  • Pull the stretcher out until you get a solid green light.
  • Push the Plus (+) button to "add legs."
  • Hold the Plus (+) button until the release arm underneath swings free.
  • Release the cot by pushing the small red button above the Plus/Minus buttons (manual release also works).
🔧Reloading Procedure
  • Push the stretcher into the receiving track until you get a green light.
  • Push the Minus (-) button until the legs fully retract and you get a solid green light.
  • Push the stretcher in until it locks.
  • If the stretcher won't move, pull it out slightly, then push in until it locks.
  • Confirm it is locked before you walk away from it.
⚠️
Rookie Mistake — Skipping the "Confirm It's Locked" StepA cot that "feels" locked but isn't will let go under load — during transport, on a ramp, or the moment weight shifts wrong. Confirm the lock every single time, visually and physically, before you move away or the rig moves.
🛗
The Head Bar Must Be Fully Extended to ReloadYou can shorten the bar under the head of the cot to squeeze it into a tight elevator — but it has to be returned to fully extended before the cot goes back into the ambulance, or it won't seat and lock correctly.
💡
Drill This Until It's AutomaticThe sequence above sounds simple written out. Under time pressure, with a critical patient and a nervous new partner, muscle memory is what keeps it clean. Practice loading and unloading empty before you ever do it with a patient on board.
🎒

Patient Compartment — General Access Items

Breathing Bag · LUCAS Access Point
Breathing Bag
AKA: Spare BVM, secondary bag
+
📖What it is & what it does

A spare bag-valve device staged inside the patient compartment itself, separate from the airway cabinet stock — so if you're already in the box working a patient, you don't have to leave the compartment to grab one.

LUCAS Access Point (From the Box)
AKA: Interior Lucas access
+
📖What it is & what it does

The LUCAS device is stored in the officer's side front exterior cabinet, but it's also reachable from inside the patient compartment — so a crew member already in the box during a code doesn't have to exit and re-enter the rig to retrieve it.

💡
Know Both Access PointsWhichever way you learn the rig first, go back and confirm the other access point too. In a code, whoever's closest grabs it — that could be either side.
🗺️

Inside The Cab

Maps · Fuel Keys
Maps
AKA: Hard-copy maps, paper maps, map book
+
📖What it is & what it does

Backup paper maps of the response area kept in the cab. The MDT and phone GPS are your primary navigation, but both are electronics — and electronics fail, lose signal, or lock up at the worst possible time. The map is what you fall back on when that happens.

⚠️
Know How to Read It Before You Need ItDon't wait for a dead MDT on an unfamiliar street at 0300 to find out you don't know how the map book is organized. Look it over on a slow shift so you're not learning the index under pressure.
Fuel Keys
AKA: Fuel cards, gas keys, fuel fob
+
📖What it is & what it does

The key or fob that unlocks the department's fuel pump so you can fill the rig. Kept in the cab so whoever's on the fuel run doesn't have to track one down.

⛽
Rookie Mistake — Not Confirming It's There at Shift CheckA rig that runs low on fuel mid-shift because the key walked off — or nobody checked for it — is a rig that's out of service when a call drops. Verify it's in the cab every shift, same as any other piece of equipment.
🚗

Behind Passenger Seat

Extra Oxygen Tanks · ABC Extinguisher · Pediatric Bag
Extra Portable Oxygen Tanks
AKA: Spare O2, backup bottles
+
📖What it is & what it does

Backup portable oxygen cylinders kept in the cab so a long transport or a call that goes longer than expected doesn't leave the crew scrambling when the primary tank runs low.

ABC Dry Chem Extinguisher
AKA: ABC extinguisher, dry chem, fire extinguisher
+
📖What it is & what it does

A multi-purpose dry chemical extinguisher rated for ordinary combustibles, flammable liquids, and electrical fires (Class A, B, C) — required equipment on the rig itself and useful at vehicle incidents before an engine arrives.

📅
Check the Gauge at Shift CheckAn extinguisher with a discharged or low-pressure gauge is dead weight. Verify it's in the green every shift — same as every other rig.
Pediatric Bag
AKA: Pedi bag, kid bag, Broselow bag
+
📖What it is & what it does

A dedicated bag of pediatric-sized airway adjuncts, BVMs, C-collars, and BP cuffs so you're not trying to make adult-sized equipment work on a small child under pressure. Often organized by length/weight (Broselow-style) so sizing is fast under stress.

👶
Rookie Mistake — Grabbing Adult Gear on a Pediatric Call Because It's CloserAdult-sized airway and BP equipment doesn't just work "close enough" on a kid — it can actively harm them. Go to the pediatric bag. Every pediatric call, no exceptions, even when adrenaline says grab whatever's nearest.
🫁 SCBA — Equipment Study Guide
MSA G1 Self-Contained Breathing Apparatus · Treat it like a vehicle. It carries you when nothing else can.

MSA G1 Platform

SCBA Study Guide

Cylinder · Harness · Regulator · Facepiece · HUD · ICM · Power Module · Alarms · Buddy Breather · RIT Pack

Listen up. This is your lifeline. Not your radio, not your hood, not your boots — this. The day comes you're crawling through black smoke and the only thing standing between you and a lungful of cyanide is the rig on your back. So we're going to go through it piece by piece, and you're going to know it cold. Not "kind of." Cold.

What we're covering

  1. The Cylinder (Bottle / Tank)
  2. The Harness & Carrier Assembly
  3. The Second-Stage Regulator
  4. The Facepiece (Mask)
  5. The HUD (Heads-Up Display)
  6. The Control Module (ICM)
  7. The Power Module
  8. PASS & Bell Alarms
  9. The Buddy Breather (EBSS)
  10. The RIT Pack
Source Note This guide is built from the SCBA notes you handed me, dated December 2025, on the MSA G1. Manufacturer specs change. Department SOPs change. If your instructor or your department's SOP says something different than what's on this page, theirs wins. Every time.

📄 Click here for more visual aids

1. The Cylinder

What it is & what it does

This is your air supply. The whole reason you can walk into a place that would kill an unprotected person in two breaths. It's an aluminum core wrapped in carbon fiber and epoxy resin — light, strong, and full of breathing air at pressures that will absolutely hurt you if you treat it like a gym bag.

You charge it to about 4,800 psi while it's filling because the air heats up under compression. Once it cools, it settles to your service pressure of 4,500 psi. That's your starting point. Everything from there is countdown.

Key Numbers — Memorize These Service pressure: 4,500 psi (filled to ~4,800 hot)  |  High-pressure release valve: blows at 5,600 psi  |  Burst disc: 7,000 psi  |  Bells deploy at 1,500 psi (~1,575 spec) — that's your ⅓ point  |  Hydrostatic test: every 5 years

Parts of the cylinder assembly

  • Aluminum tank, carbon fiber wrap, epoxy resin shell — Aluminum is the pressure vessel. Carbon fiber is the muscle that holds the pressure in. Epoxy is the skin. If you ever see bare aluminum showing through the carbon fiber, the bottle is done. Out of service. MSA can repair carbon fiber, but they can't repair an aluminum vessel that's been compromised. You don't repair it on the apparatus floor. You don't tape it. You red-tag it.
  • Cylinder valve coupling nut (a.k.a. "the nut," "hand-tight nut") — How you couple the bottle to the harness. Hand-tight is the rule. You don't put a wrench on it. The dovetail in the harness mates with this and the nut snugs it home.
  • Dovetail connection — The mechanical fit that holds the bottle to the back plate. The nut is the lock; the dovetail is the rail it slides into.
  • Air valve (on/off) (a.k.a. "the bottle valve," "main valve," "knob") — The hand wheel you crank to turn the bottle on. Turn it ALL the way open, then back it off a quarter turn. (More on why in a minute.)
  • Pressure gauge (cylinder) — The little face on the bottle itself. Direct read of bottle pressure. This is the gauge you read before you don the rig.
  • High-pressure hose (off the cylinder) — Carries 4,500 psi air to the splitter, which feeds both the second-stage regulator and the ICM/PASS. Rated for 4,500 psi.
  • High-pressure release valve — Safety valve. Blows at 5,600 psi to relieve overpressure before things get exciting.
  • Burst disc — Last-ditch safety. A sacrificial disc that ruptures at 7,000 psi to vent the bottle catastrophically rather than letting the bottle itself fail catastrophically. If a burst disc goes, you'll know — it sounds like a small bomb.
  • URC — Universal RIT Connector (a.k.a. "UAC," "RIC connector," "fill port") — The fitting a RIT team uses to dump air into your bottle from outside. Universal — meaning a Scott RIT pack can refill an MSA bottle through it. That's the whole point.
Rookie Mistakes — Cylinder
  • Carrying the bottle by the valve. The valve is not a handle. You bang the valve on a tailboard, you've just earned yourself a bottle that's possibly out of service and an officer who is not happy. Carry by the body of the bottle or by the harness handles.
  • Cracking the valve open and closing it. Old habit from old SCBAs. On the G1, you open it fully, then back it off a quarter turn. Cracking it open chokes your air supply when you suck hard, and that's exactly when you don't want to be choked.
  • Ignoring the hydro date. Five years. Not "around five." Read the stamp. An expired bottle is not a usable bottle, and rolling out with one is on you.
  • Dropping a bottle and putting it back in service. Carbon fiber damage isn't always visible. If a bottle takes a serious hit, it gets inspected, period. People have been killed by composite cylinders that failed under pressure after impact damage. This is not the corner you cut.
  • Confusing the burst disc and the relief valve. Relief valve resets. Burst disc does not — once it's blown, the bottle is empty and the disc gets replaced.
↑ Back to top

2. The Harness & Carrier Assembly

What it is & what it does

The harness is what gets the bottle on your back and keeps it there when you're crawling, falling, getting dragged, or being hauled out a window by your partner. It's not just straps. The back plate is essentially the chassis of the whole SCBA — it houses the power module, the battery, and the pressure reducer that drops 4,500 psi down to about 110 psi for the regulator to work with.

Parts of the harness

  • Back plate (a.k.a. "frame," "chassis") — Houses the power module, battery module, and pressure reducer. This is the brain and the spine of the SCBA.
  • Cylinder band (a.k.a. "bottle strap," "retention strap") — Holds the bottle to the back plate. Combined with the dovetail and coupling nut.
  • Shoulder pads — Padding on the shoulder straps. Don't overlook these — a worn-out pad means you're going to feel that bottle on your collarbone for the rest of the shift.
  • Adjustable pull straps — The straps you grab and yank to tighten the rig down on your shoulders. Pull DOWN and OUT, not back.
  • Lumbar pad — Adjustable to 3 positions. This is what transfers the weight of the bottle from your shoulders to your hips. Get the right setting for your torso. A wrong lumbar setting will wreck your back over a 24-hour shift.
  • Waist belt (a.k.a. "hip belt") — Connects to the lumbar pad. The belt is what actually carries the load. Snug it tight before you tighten the shoulder straps.
  • Waist belt buckle — Big plastic buckle. It also contains the tool to open the battery holder. That's not a gimmick — it's there because the tool is always with the rig and never lost in a drawer.
  • Top handle — The handle on the top of the harness. Rated to 1,000 lbs. This is your drag handle for a downed-firefighter rescue.
  • Side handles — Rated to 500 lbs each. For lifting and dragging.
  • Regulator keeper (a.k.a. "reg holster," "park") — The clip on the harness that holds the second-stage regulator when it's not on your facepiece. Use it. A regulator banging around on the deck gets damaged.
  • Chest strap — Across your chest, between the shoulder straps. Keeps the harness from spreading off your shoulders.
A Word on Load Order Belt first, then shoulders, then chest. If you tighten shoulders first, the bottle hangs off your traps and your hips do nothing. Do it right and the bottle rides on your hips like a backpack should.
Rookie Mistakes — Harness
  • Loose straps. A sloppy harness shifts when you move, throws your balance, and bangs equipment. Worse — in a Mayday, your partner needs to grab a handle and drag you, and that handle better be where it should be.
  • Not knowing the handle ratings. The top handle is the rescue handle. 1,000 lbs. The side handles are 500 lbs each. If you're hauling a 250-lb firefighter through a window, you grab the top.
  • Forgetting the buckle has a tool in it. Comes up on practical exams. Comes up when you need to swap a battery. Don't be the probie who's hunting around the apparatus floor for a screwdriver.
  • Hanging the regulator off the hose instead of the keeper. The hose isn't a strap. It's a pressurized line. Treat it that way.
↑ Back to top

3. The Second-Stage Regulator

What it is & what it does

This is the small black device that connects to your facepiece. It takes the ~110 psi coming from the pressure reducer on the back plate and brings it down to 1.5 mm of water column above atmospheric pressure — which is barely above ambient (atmospheric is 14.7 psi at sea level). That tiny positive pressure is what keeps smoke and contaminants from leaking into your mask if your seal isn't perfect.

It hooks to the facepiece with a push-to-connect (PTC) fitting. You shove it on, you hear it click, you're breathing.

Parts of the regulator

  • Main valve — The valve that opens and gives you air. Turns on automatically the first time you take a deep inhalation. You don't push a button. You don't flip a switch. You breathe, and it opens.
  • Shut-off tabs — The two tabs on opposing sides of the regulator body. Squeeze them at the same time and you do two things: you shut off the main valve, AND you release the regulator from the facepiece. One motion.
  • By-pass valve (a.k.a. "purge valve," "red knob," "the red one") — The red one. Red means red. When you turn it, it dumps a continuous flow of higher-pressure air directly into your facepiece. This is your backup if the main valve fails. It's an emergency air supply, not a "my mask is fogging" toy. It will eat your bottle fast.
  • Microphone — Located in the bottom of the regulator. Picks up your voice and feeds it to the speaker module so people can actually understand you under air.
  • Push-to-connect (PTC) fitting — The connector that mates the regulator to the facepiece. Fixed position, locks in. You'll feel and hear the click.
Why Positive Pressure Matters The whole game is keeping air pressure inside your mask higher than the air outside. If your seal breaks for a half-second — a strap shifts, you turn your head wrong against your hood — air rushes out of your mask, not in. Smoke does not get to your face. That is the entire engineering miracle of a positive-pressure SCBA. Don't ever defeat it.
Rookie Mistakes — Regulator
  • Hitting the bypass to clear fog. The bypass blasts air at full bottle pressure. You will burn through air at a frightening rate. Use the bypass only for an actual main-valve failure or to clear water/contaminant from the mask in an emergency.
  • Yanking the regulator off without squeezing both tabs. You'll either fight it, damage the PTC, or get a face full of pressurized air. Two tabs, opposing sides, squeeze together.
  • Not parking the regulator in the keeper. A regulator dragging on the floor takes a beating, picks up debris, and on the next call you're trying to mate a dirty PTC to your mask. Park it.
  • Not knowing your bypass works until you need it. Test it during your morning check, not in a hallway full of smoke.
↑ Back to top

4. The Facepiece

What it is & what it does

The mask. The single most important piece of PPE on your body in an IDLH atmosphere. If the mask doesn't seal, the bottle on your back is just dead weight. Doesn't matter how much air you have. If it leaks, you're breathing the same poison as everyone else in the building.

The lens is a single-piece polycarbonate with a scratch- and heat-resistant coating, rated for a 500-degree environment and giving you a wide field of view.

Parts of the facepiece

  • Facepiece lens (a.k.a. "the lens," "the visor") — Single-piece polycarbonate. Wide field of view. 500°F rating. Inspect it every shift for scratches, cracks, heat distortion. A scratched lens reduces visibility, period — and a heat-damaged lens can fail without warning.
  • Face seal / skirt (a.k.a. "the skirt," "the seal") — Soft rubber or silicone. This is what forms the airtight seal against your skin. Skin contact only. Hood, mask straps, eyeglass arms, beard stubble — anything that crosses the seal breaks it.
  • Head harness / head straps (a.k.a. "spider," "spider straps," "five-point harness") — Five-point harness in rubber or fabric. You go bottom straps first (the lower two), then temple straps, then top. Tighten symmetrically. Crooked harness = crooked mask = leaks.
  • Speaking diaphragm / voice amplifier port — The disc that lets your voice transmit out. On the G1, this also interfaces with the EVA (Electronic Voice Amplifier).
  • Nose cup (inner mask) — The small mask inside the mask. Reduces the dead air space, directs your exhalation through the exhalation valve, and dramatically reduces lens fogging by keeping warm wet breath off the lens. Don't pop it out trying to "clean" the mask.
  • Inhalation valves — One-way valves that let air flow in from the regulator and maintain that positive pressure inside the mask.
  • Exhalation valve — One-way valve that lets your exhaled air out and prevents backflow. If this gets gummed up or stuck, you'll feel it — you can't push your breath out and CO₂ builds up fast.
  • Regulator receiver / connection port (a.k.a. "reg port") — Where the second-stage regulator clicks in. Has the locking mechanism that secures the PTC.
  • HUD (Heads-Up Display) — LED indicators inside the mask that show air supply, alarms, and system status without you having to look at the gauge. (Full breakdown in the next section.)
  • Facepiece seal retainer / frame — The rigid structure that holds the lens to the skirt and keeps the whole assembly from collapsing or distorting.
Rookie Mistakes — Facepiece
  • Bad seal because of facial hair. Stubble breaks the seal. Period. NFPA and OSHA are clear on this. There's a reason your department has a shaving policy and it's not aesthetics — it's that stubble lets contaminated air in and you breathe it. Firefighters have died because of facial hair under SCBAs. Keep your face clean where the seal sits.
  • Hood hair, eyeglass arms, mask straps under the seal. The skirt seals to skin, not to fabric, hair, or plastic. Sweep your hood back, get hair out of the way, use the mask-mounted eyeglass kit.
  • Tightening top straps first. Pulls the mask up and away from your chin, opens the bottom seal. Bottom straps first. Always.
  • Skipping the seal check. Inhale sharp with the regulator off — the mask should suck to your face and stay there. If it leaks, find out now, not at the front door of a working fire.
  • Storing the mask loose in a turnout coat or compartment. Lens scratches. Skirt deformation. Find your designated mask bag and use it.
↑ Back to top

5. The HUD (Heads-Up Display)

What it is & what it does

Inside your mask, you'll see colored LEDs across your field of view. Left side, right side, with a gold diaphragm in the center. That's your HUD. It tells you what's going on with your air and your alarms without you having to fish your gauge out of your shoulder strap.

HUD Layout — Memorize It Left side = alarms.   Right side = air supply.   Center (gold) = the diaphragm.

Pushing the green button on the control module activates the HUD. So you don't have to wait for a low-air alarm to see your status — you can flash it on demand.

Rookie Mistakes — HUD
  • Treating the HUD as your only gauge. It's a quick reference. Your analog gauge on the shoulder strap is your truth. Cross-check.
  • Ignoring the alarm side. If the left side is lighting up, something is telling you something. Don't dismiss it because the right side still says you have air.
  • Forgetting which side is which under stress. Drill it now. In smoke, in the dark, sweating, with adrenaline up — you should not be trying to remember if red on the left means low air or low battery.
↑ Back to top

6. The Control Module (ICM)

What it is & what it does

The ICM — Integrated Control Module — is the little device with a screen and buttons that lives on your left shoulder strap. It is the interface between you and the SCBA, and it doubles as your PASS (Personal Alert Safety System). It's fed by a high-pressure hose, so it always knows what your bottle pressure actually is.

Parts of the ICM

  • Analog gauge (a.k.a. "needle gauge," "the dial") — Mechanical needle showing bottle pressure. Full bottle pressure is fed to it so the read is accurate.
  • LCD (digital display) — Shows you cylinder pressure, battery status, time remaining, and active alarms. Time-remaining is calculated based on your current breathing rate, not just a static estimate.
  • Red ALARM button (a.k.a. "panic button," "manual PASS") — Manually activates the PASS alarm. If you're pinned, lost, or down and need to scream for help with 100 dB of piezo, you mash this button. It is your distress signal.
  • Reset / Green buttons (a.k.a. "the green buttons") — Located on BOTH sides of the control module. Used to silence and reset the integrated PASS. Also turns the control module off after the air pressure has been bled out. Two-button press is intentional — it prevents accidental shut-off.
  • Bleeder / bypass valve (a.k.a. "bleed valve") — The little valve you crack open to bleed pressure out of the system after you've shut the bottle off. You watch the digital display drop and then double-click the green buttons to shut the ICM down.
Shutdown Sequence — Don't Botch This 1. Close the bottle valve.   2. Open the bleeder to vent the high-pressure system.   3. Once pressure is gone, double-click the green buttons to shut off the ICM/PASS.

If you skip step 2, you've trapped 4,500 psi in the hoses and seals — bad for the equipment. If you skip step 3, the PASS is going to start screaming on the apparatus floor in a few minutes when motion stops.
Rookie Mistakes — ICM
  • Setting the PASS off in quarters and panicking. If your PASS goes full alarm in the firehouse, don't slap it. Find the green buttons, press both, and reset. Slapping won't work — the full alarm requires a manual reset.
  • Forgetting the green buttons are on BOTH sides. You can reach across with one hand. You don't need two.
  • Not bleeding pressure before shutdown. The system holds pressure. You need to vent it through the bleeder, not just close the bottle and walk away.
  • Ignoring the digital time-remaining number. It's a real number based on how hard you're sucking air. If it drops fast, it's because you're drinking air fast. Slow your breathing.
↑ Back to top

7. The Power Module

What it is & what it does

The power module is the brain's power supply. It's mounted on the back plate. It powers the control module, the regulator electronics, and the speaker module. It's also the part of the SCBA that emits the actual audible PASS alarm through dual piezo speakers — 100 dB at 3 meters. Loud enough that a search team will hear you through a wall.

Parts & features

  • Rechargeable lithium-ion batteries — Take about 6 hours to recharge. When the battery is replaced, the system runs an automatic system check on power-up. Beeps every 10 seconds when batteries need replacement or recharge — that's your "feed me" warning. Don't ignore it.
  • Dual piezo speakers / Piezo Emitters (a.k.a. "PASS speakers," "screamers") — Produce the audible PASS tone. 100 dB at 3 meters. There's one on each side of the back plate.
  • Buddy lights (4) (a.k.a. "PASS alarm lights," "indicator lights") — Four LEDs visible from outside the SCBA. They tell teammates your status from a distance — bottle pressure quartile, alarm condition. They turn YOU into a status indicator.
  • UAC LED light — An LED that illuminates the UAC (URC) connection during a low-air alarm. So when a RIT team is reaching for your fill port in zero visibility, there is literally a light pointing at the connection. That's not luck — that's design.
  • Battery housing — Opened with the tool built into the waist belt buckle. Battery slides out, fresh one in, system runs its self-check.
Rookie Mistakes — Power Module
  • Ignoring the 10-second battery beep. Means your battery is dying. Means in a few minutes you may lose your control module, your HUD, your PASS audible. Swap the battery. Don't ride a low battery into a working call.
  • Not putting a freshly charged battery on after use. The next person on that rig might be you, or might be someone else. Either way, the SCBA goes back in the bracket fully ready.
  • Not knowing the buddy lights mean something to your team. When you walk into the room and your captain glances at your back, those four LEDs are telling him your air status from across the room. Know what color means what for your department.
  • Assuming the UAC light is a flashlight. It's specifically the low-air-alarm UAC indicator. If it's lit, you're in low-air alarm. That is not a small thing.
↑ Back to top

8. PASS & Bell Alarms

What they are & what they do

You have two independent alarm systems on this rig. One is electronic. One is mechanical. The redundancy is on purpose — if the electronics fail, the mechanical one still tells the world you're in trouble.

PASS — Personal Alert Safety System

Motion-activated electronic alarm. If you stop moving for a set period, the SCBA assumes you might be down. It progresses through 4 levels:

StageWhat happens
Level 1Pre-alarm starts at 15–20 seconds of no motion. Soft chirp. Move and it resets.
Level 2 & 3Escalating alerts as time passes without motion.
Level 4 (Full Alarm)Triggers after 30 seconds of no motion. Cannot be reset by movement. Requires manual reset by clicking the green buttons.

You can also manually trigger the PASS at any moment by pushing the red ALARM button on the ICM. That's your panic button. If you're trapped, lost, pinned, hurt — you make this thing scream.

Bells

The mechanical low-air alarm. Powered by air remaining in the tank itself — no electronics, no battery. As air depletes, the bell rings slower. It's old-school, it's mechanical, and it works when nothing else does.

Bell Activation Bells deploy at 1,500 psi (1,575 spec) — that's your ⅓ point. Adding air stops the bells. They are a "you should already be heading out" signal, not an "uh-oh" signal.
Rookie Mistakes — Alarms
  • Treating the bells as a "now I should think about leaving" alert. The bells are LATE. By the time the bells ring, you should already be on your way out. The rule on the job is "out of the building before the bells." Plan your air. Watch your gauge.
  • Letting your PASS go to full alarm by accident. You stop to take notes, hold a hose line, do the size-up — and your PASS goes off. Now everyone on the fire ground thinks you're down. Move occasionally. Or hit the green buttons to reset proactively.
  • Not knowing the manual PASS. The red button is your last call for help. If you can press one button before you go down, that's the one.
  • Forgetting full alarm requires manual reset. Once you cross 30 seconds, shaking the rig won't fix it. Green buttons, both sides. Period.
  • Not knowing the difference between bells and PASS in the dark. Bells are mechanical, slow, ringing. PASS is electronic, piercing, escalating. They mean different things. Know them by ear.
↑ Back to top

9. Buddy Breather (EBSS)

What it is & what it does

The Buddy Breather is an Emergency Breathing Support System. It lets you share air with a partner whose air is gone, whose mask failed, or who is otherwise in trouble. There's a male end and a female end on the system. You connect, and the air flows from the higher-pressure bottle to the lower-pressure one — but it equalizes the demand, it does not fill the empty bottle.

Key facts about the Buddy Breather

  • Male and female ends — Mate together to connect two SCBAs.
  • Proprietary connection — MSA to MSA only. Same maker. Same model family. You cannot Buddy Breather an MSA to a Scott. That's what the URC is for.
  • Daisy-chainable — You can connect more than two firefighters in a chain if needed.
  • Air pulls from the higher-pressure tank — Both firefighters then breathe from that supply. The lower bottle does NOT get topped up.
  • 110 psi at the connection — That's why it can't fill a tank. The pressure at the buddy line is regulator-pressure, not bottle-pressure.
  • 3-foot (39-inch) hose — Once both ends are deployed and connected, you have 6+ feet of working distance between you and your partner. Enough to move together but not enough to be sloppy.
Rookie Mistakes — Buddy Breather
  • Thinking the Buddy Breather "fills" your partner's tank. It doesn't. It shares a single supply between two breathers. Both of you are now drinking from one bottle. Plan your egress accordingly — you have less time, not more.
  • Trying to use it across brands. Proprietary. MSA-to-MSA. If your downed firefighter is on a different brand, the Buddy Breather isn't your tool — coordinated egress and the URC for RIT refill is.
  • Deploying it without a clear plan to exit. You're now tethered to your partner by a 3-foot hose. Trip hazards, snag points, separation under stress. Communicate. Move together. Get out.
  • Not practicing the connection. First time you fumble for the male end shouldn't be in zero visibility with someone gasping next to you.
↑ Back to top

10. The RIT Pack

What it is & what it does

The RIT Pack is a dedicated air supply that the Rapid Intervention Team brings to a downed firefighter. Unlike the Buddy Breather, the RIT pack uses the Universal RIT Connector (URC) — meaning it works regardless of brand. MSA pack, Scott bottle, no problem. That's the whole reason it exists.

Key facts about the RIT Pack

  • Universal connection (URC/UAC) — Works across manufacturers. Cross-brand compatible by design.
  • Tops up an air tank — Unlike the Buddy Breather, this one actually transfers air into the downed firefighter's bottle.
  • Tank pressure: 6,000 psi — Higher than your service pressure of 4,500 psi. That's deliberate — the higher source pressure lets it actually push air across into a partially full bottle.
  • Partial fill, not full — At 6,000 psi, the RIT pack will only partially fill a bottle. The goal is to give the downed firefighter enough air to get out, not to bring them back to a full bottle.
  • Spare facepiece (size medium) — Stored in the RIT pack for use only if the downed firefighter's facepiece is cracked or damaged. Not a comfort swap. Not because they don't like theirs. Damaged-only.
Rookie Mistakes — RIT Pack
  • Confusing RIT pack with Buddy Breather. Buddy Breather shares your air. RIT pack delivers fresh air from a dedicated supply. Different tools. Different jobs.
  • Swapping facepieces unnecessarily. The medium in the RIT pack is for damaged facepieces only. If the downed firefighter's mask is intact, you keep them in their own seal. Their mask is fitted to their face — yours might not be.
  • Not checking the RIT bottle pressure on shift check. It's at 6,000 psi when ready. If it's not, your RIT capability is degraded. Don't assume the off-going crew checked it. Verify yourself.
  • Forgetting that the UAC light on the SCBA points right at the connection. When you're the RIT and you're locating a downed firefighter's fill port in smoke, that LED is your friend.
↑ Back to top

Final Word

Probie, here's the truth. Anyone can list parts. Anyone can pass a written test. What separates the firefighter who comes home from the one who doesn't, sometimes, is whether the SCBA is muscle memory.

You should be able to don this rig in the dark. You should know, without looking, which strap is which. You should hear a bell vs a PASS and know which is which without thinking. You should feel a low battery beep and reach for the buckle tool without breaking stride. You should know your bypass works because you tested it this morning, not because you read about it in a book.

Your bottle is not unlimited. Your air is not unlimited. The fire does not care that you're tired or that your gauge is hard to read or that you forgot to check your hydro date. Your SCBA is the difference between making it home and being a name on a wall. Treat it like that. Every shift. Every call. Every time you pick it up.

And when you're a senior guy someday and a probie hands you a study guide like this — you stop, you read it, and you take the time to teach the next one the way someone took the time to teach you.

— Stay sharp. Stay alive.
